articles.title: Technology, bumping grades among school board candidate priorities
articles.description: Technology, bumping grades among school board candidate priorities Jackson Hole News&Guide
articles.description_html: Technology, bumping grades among school board candidate priorities  Jackson Hole News&Guide
articles.article_title: Technology, bumping grades among school board candidate priorities
articles.heading: Jackson Hole, WY News
authors: Alex Viveros / Town and Health Reporter
articles.summary: Candidates were united behind supporting the school, though they questioned technology’s role in preparing children for the future.
articles.content:
Though four candidates vying for three spots on the Teton County School District Board of Trustees spoke to individual priorities during a voter forum on Thursday, they all were united in supporting Jackson Hole’s public schools at large.
“I’m here because I just can’t give up walking into the schools and smelling that school kid smell,” Reade Dornan, an 86-year-old retired education professor, said. “There’s just something nostalgic about that.”
Technology usage, improving academic proficiency and the overall benefits of a public education were top of mind for the school board hopefuls, including three incumbents and one newcomer. The school board panel took up about an hour of the League of Women Voters forum at the Teton County Library, before gears switched to the hospital board and Teton Conservation District board.
Ongoing questions about the role of technology in schools was an important topic for school board candidates on Thursday, as technology and artificial intelligence has become an increasingly crucial component of many adult jobs.
“We have to prepare kids for the future,” Dornan said. “And what the heck is that? We’re not sure yet where AI will lead us.”
Screens are especially important for Ashley Sinclair, a parent of two children in the district and the lone newcomer in the school board race. This summer, Sinclair raised concerns about students’ screen time, presenting a petition to the board that called for stricter technology regulations.
Sinclair’s petition led the board to take a deeper look at technology use, current board member Keith Gingery said, ultimately leading it to realize that students’ screen time may, indeed, be greater than school principals may have been aware of. For example, one teacher might assign only 10 minutes of screen time for worksheets, but they may not know that other teachers down the hall also may be assigning 10 more minutes of screen time.
“When you started adding all those up, [students] were spending a considerable amount of time on the iPads,” Gingery, who has served on the board for 12 years and is the county’s chief deputy attorney, said. “Way more than anybody realized.”
The responsibility now has been placed on principals to curtail screen use at schools, Gingery said. At Jackson Hole Middle School, students are no longer sent home with iPads. Sinclair appreciated the attention the board gave to the issue.
“The engagement and focus from the administration was wonderful,” Sinclair said Thursday. “That being said, we can definitely still do better.”
Teachers have told Sinclair that their students aren’t allowed to use screens for more than 40 minutes a day. She questioned whether that limit, even, was too much and said the school district should continue to explore what level of screen usage was best for children.
Like Sinclair, Stephan Abrams — a school board incumbent and the part owner of The Liquor Store of Jackson Hole — did not have an answer for what level of screen usage would be ideal for children in schools. He pointed out that the state’s standardized test is taken on iPads, and that students needed to be prepared for that and how technology would be used in their next steps of life.
“Technology’s here,” Abrams said on Thursday. “It’s not going away.”
Sinclair said she was not anti-technology, but rather “pro-purpose” of using it.
“While it’s very important we prepare our kids for the world ahead of them, which includes technology, I think that we can be more intentional with the time we’re using with them,” Sinclair said. “I don’t think they need 40 minutes a day in order to be able to do standardized testing.”
Candidates also weighed grades and test scores.
Teton County School District had a 96.9% graduation rate in 2025, placing it 14% higher than the state’s average. Still, Sinclair said the school could further fine-tune its math proficiency for sixth graders.
Gingery said the board’s three-member education committee, which he formed a few years ago, already was focusing on improving the math curriculum at Jackson Hole Middle School. Scores fall off between eighth and ninth grades, he said, as well as between fifth and sixth grades.
“We’ve made substantial changes at our middle school, and I think you’ll be very happy, Ashley, to see the scores,” Gingery said to Sinclair during the forum. “It’s those transition years which are really difficult years, and that’s where we need to spend more focus.”
Public education often has a broader role than private education, candidates said. Dornan pointed out that public schools are responsible for feeding kids who come to school hungry, as well as teaching a large portion of students whose first language is not English. Gingery praised the school’s special education curriculum, which he credited with helping higher-needs children and teens develop the life skills they need after exiting school at 20.
“We’ve just seen some really wonderful children go on to lead very wonderful, independent lives,” Gingery said.
Following closing statements from school board contenders, candidates for the St. John’s Health Board of Trustees seeking reelection and one candidate for the Teton Conservation District Board of Supervisors were given a brief time to shine. Taxes took the limelight.
St. John’s Health is asking Teton County voters to double its property tax share, from three mills to six. Candidates seeking reelection to the board explained to the audience members why.
The hospital has been facing budget challenges, leading to an $11.7 million deficit in the most recent fiscal year. As the hospital considers other challenges — including older Jackson residents switching over to Medicare, which reimburses St. John’s at lower rates than commercial insurers — it hopes that increasing its property tax dollars will help the hospital stay independent.
“I think it would be irresponsible for us not to ask the citizens to increase their support,” Dr. Pam Cutler, the board’s chair, said. “One of the things that makes this community great, and there are many, is the fact that we do have this amazing hospital that gives great quality care.”
All three incumbents on the health board are up for reelection. Cutler, Katharine Conover-Keller and Dr. Brent Blue will keep their seats if no write-in campaign is successful.
The Conservation District is asking voters to re-approve its existing one mill. The mill levy allows the conservation district to fund its staff, which works toward securing Teton County’s water quality, performing wildfire risk assessments and other conservation work.
David Adams, Cate Watsabaugh and Bob Lucas will have to defend one of their Conservation District board seats from newcomer Lee Bauknight.
“The mill levy is essential,” Watsabaugh, the only candidate present at Thursday’s forum, said. “It’s just the entire existence of the Conservation District. Without it, there would be pretty significant changes to the program and staffing.”

articles.title: America wants to wean itself off Chinese technology. Will the pain pay off?
articles.description: America wants to wean itself off Chinese technology. Will the pain pay off? CNN
articles.description_html: America wants to wean itself off Chinese technology. Will the pain pay off?  CNN
articles.article_title: America wants to wean itself off Chinese technology. Will the pain pay off? | CNN Business
articles.heading: America wants to wean itself off Chinese technology. Will the pain pay off?
articles.summary: Seven years after founding a robotics startup in San Francisco, Rajat Bhageria is confronting a daunting new task: building robots without any help from China.
articles.content:
Seven years after founding a robotics startup in San Francisco, Rajat Bhageria is confronting a daunting new task: building robots without any help from China.
Like most US-based robotics firms, Chef Robotics has come to rely heavily on Chinese components to make the robot arms it sells to food manufacturers to automate the assembly of ready-made meals. China’s ability to churn out cheap parts at incomparable volumes has made it an integral source of competitive tech products around the world.
But as China has begun to dominate advanced industries from electric vehicles to automated factories, an increasingly protectionist US under President Donald Trump has ratcheted up restrictions on domestic use of Chinese technology, including drones, mobile robots and other critical electronics.
“For a while of course, it was like, ‘Hey, let’s find the best components, and let’s find them at the cheapest price,’” Bhageria said.
Now investors and customers have begun asking him a different question: “Why are you still using foreign-made parts?”
The intensifying rivalry between the US and China has deepened concerns about the national security risks that come with over-dependence on Chinese systems and supply chains.
In banning foreign-made technologies, US officials cite the need to protect sensitive consumer and government data, while incentivizing domestic manufacturing. But experts warn the curbs may be having an unintended effect: hindering American companies’ ability to keep up with their Chinese rivals.
Decades of outsourcing have left American manufacturers ill-equipped to meet demand, leading to higher costs and longer wait times for companies, universities and consumers that require both cutting-edge and everyday electronics.
“A lot of our digital lives are built on the infrastructure of foreign-made components and goods assembled abroad, and that’s not going to change anytime soon,” said Ben Armstrong, executive director of MIT’s Industrial Performance Center, who researches manufacturing competitiveness and automation.
“We just don’t know how to make them in the US. So, there will be a learning curve, and during that learning curve process, the price will be high,” he said.
Bhageria hopes that by starting his search for alternative suppliers now, his company can mitigate potential economic pain down the line.
He has that luxury, because the components in his robotic arms are not yet affected by the bans. But he’s worried the list will grow. “You can imagine what’s the next shoe to drop, right? Like, the next thing might be fixed robot arms.”
Robots made in America
The company’s final assembly is done in the US, Bhageria said. However, the machine utensil components attached to the end of its robot arms are all currently made in China.
Bhageria initially wanted to shift that production last year, as Trump escalated tariffs on Chinese imports. He quickly discovered it would be prohibitively expensive to make the plastic grabbers in the US, and that many suppliers outside China didn’t have the capability to fill his order.
“It’s actually been a much harder process than we had initially hoped,” he said. “We will even talk to some really good machine shops in the US and they’re like, ‘We can’t do this.’”
Those challenges underscore how important Chinese industrial advancement has become to US companies. But the US administration remains insistent on discouraging use of Chinese technology, and the range of prohibited products continues to expand.
In July, the Federal Communications Commission added power inverters and new advanced robotics – like the humanoids that can run, jump, dance and fight – to its list of restricted foreign-made technology. The US has also forbidden cars using Chinese software and enacted a 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles. Similar tariffs on drones took effect last month, following a ban on new models in December.
The ever-growing list has left even American corporate giants like Ford struggling to keep up. The blue-chip automaker drew criticism from the Trump administration earlier this month for improper links to Chinese technology, namely its use of Chinese electric car batteries made by CATL.
Ford rejected claims that it was ceding US manufacturing to Chinese entities.
Michael Murray, chief executive of Kopin Corporation which makes optical components for drones used by the US military, said it has taken the company more than two years to relocate manufacturing for some of its micro display screens from China to the US.
He estimates that making those components in the US costs as much as 25% more, though the expenses of moving the supply chain have been offset by funding from the Department of Defense.
“We don’t have the volumes to get the costs down as much as the rest of the market, so there is a price squeeze there that we have to accommodate for,” he said.
As regulation has become more stringent on the sourcing of sensitive technologies, more companies are looking for US-made parts, Murray said. Still, China can produce more micro displays in one week than the US can produce in a year, he added.
Falling behind
Gavin Kenneally, whose company makes industrial and military robot dogs, is working to find a new source of rare earth metals, of which China has nearly a global monopoly.
Ghost Robotics has already moved its motor production from China to South Korea, and currently procures its neodymium magnets from a European company. But the raw material comes from China, which means it will be subject to a government ban starting in January.
“It’s an extremely difficult supply chain problem to solve in the short term,” said Kenneally, who added that such policies are often telegraphed in advance to give companies time to adjust. “In the long term, I think these bans have had the stimulative effect that the government had designed them to have.”
As US suppliers work to catch up, analysts and executives said limited access to China’s extensive supply chain could hinder American progress in both cutting-edge industries like AI and robotics, and traditional manufacturing.

Seven years after founding a robotics startup in San Francisco, Rajat Bhageria is confronting a daunting new task: building robots without any help from China.

Like most US-based robotics firms, Chef Robotics has come to rely heavily on Chinese components to make the robot arms it sells to food manufacturers to automate the assembly of ready-made meals. China’s ability to churn out cheap parts at incomparable volumes has made it an integral source of competitive tech products around the world.

But as China has begun to dominate advanced industries from electric vehicles to automated factories, an increasingly protectionist US under President Donald Trump has ratcheted up restrictions on domestic use of Chinese technology, including drones, mobile robots and other critical electronics.

“For a while of course, it was like, ‘Hey, let’s find the best components, and let’s find them at the cheapest price,’” Bhageria said.

Now investors and customers have begun asking him a different question: “Why are you still using foreign-made parts?”

The intensifying rivalry between the US and China has deepened concerns about the national security risks that come with over-dependence on Chinese systems and supply chains.

In banning foreign-made technologies, US officials cite the need to protect sensitive consumer and government data, while incentivizing domestic manufacturing. But experts warn the curbs may be having an unintended effect: hindering American companies’ ability to keep up with their Chinese rivals.

Decades of outsourcing have left American manufacturers ill-equipped to meet demand, leading to higher costs and longer wait times for companies, universities and consumers that require both cutting-edge and everyday electronics.

“A lot of our digital lives are built on the infrastructure of foreign-made components and goods assembled abroad, and that’s not going to change anytime soon,” said Ben Armstrong, executive director of MIT’s Industrial Performance Center, who researches manufacturing competitiveness and automation.

“We just don’t know how to make them in the US. So, there will be a learning curve, and during that learning curve process, the price will be high,” he said.

Bhageria hopes that by starting his search for alternative suppliers now, his company can mitigate potential economic pain down the line.

He has that luxury, because the components in his robotic arms are not yet affected by the bans. But he’s worried the list will grow. “You can imagine what’s the next shoe to drop, right? Like, the next thing might be fixed robot arms.”

Robots made in America

The company’s final assembly is done in the US, Bhageria said. However, the machine utensil components attached to the end of its robot arms are all currently made in China.

Bhageria initially wanted to shift that production last year, as Trump escalated tariffs on Chinese imports. He quickly discovered it would be prohibitively expensive to make the plastic grabbers in the US, and that many suppliers outside China didn’t have the capability to fill his order.

“It’s actually been a much harder process than we had initially hoped,” he said. “We will even talk to some really good machine shops in the US and they’re like, ‘We can’t do this.’”

Those challenges underscore how important Chinese industrial advancement has become to US companies. But the US administration remains insistent on discouraging use of Chinese technology, and the range of prohibited products continues to expand.

In July, the Federal Communications Commission added power inverters and new advanced robotics – like the humanoids that can run, jump, dance and fight – to its list of restricted foreign-made technology. The US has also forbidden cars using Chinese software and enacted a 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles. Similar tariffs on drones took effect last month, following a ban on new models in December.

The ever-growing list has left even American corporate giants like Ford struggling to keep up. The blue-chip automaker drew criticism from the Trump administration earlier this month for improper links to Chinese technology, namely its use of Chinese electric car batteries made by CATL.

Ford rejected claims that it was ceding US manufacturing to Chinese entities.

Michael Murray, chief executive of Kopin Corporation which makes optical components for drones used by the US military, said it has taken the company more than two years to relocate manufacturing for some of its micro display screens from China to the US.

“We don’t have the volumes to get the costs down as much as the rest of the market, so there is a price squeeze there that we have to accommodate for,” he said.

As regulation has become more stringent on the sourcing of sensitive technologies, more companies are looking for US-made parts, Murray said. Still, China can produce more micro displays in one week than the US can produce in a year, he added.

Falling behind

Gavin Kenneally, whose company makes industrial and military robot dogs, is working to find a new source of rare earth metals, of which China has nearly a global monopoly.

Ghost Robotics has already moved its motor production from China to South Korea, and currently procures its neodymium magnets from a European company. But the raw material comes from China, which means it will be subject to a government ban starting in January.

articles.title: Industrial real estate firm Meritex acquires 121 Technology Park in Allen, plans 2027 expansion
articles.description: Industrial real estate firm Meritex acquires 121 Technology Park in Allen, plans 2027 expansion Community Impact Newspaper
articles.description_html: Industrial real estate firm Meritex acquires 121 Technology Park in Allen, plans 2027 expansion  Community Impact Newspaper
articles.article_title: Meritex acquires 121 Technology Park in Allen
articles.heading: Industrial real estate firm Meritex acquires 121 Technology Park in Allen, plans 2027 expansion
articles.summary: Minneapolis-based industrial real estate firm Meritex acquired the 58-acre 121 Technology Park in Allen and plans a second phase of development in 2027.
articles.content:
121 Technology Park, a 58-acre industrial park in Allen, has a new owner that is looking ahead to the development’s next phase of growth.
Minneapolis-based industrial real estate firm Meritex announced the acquisition of the Class A industrial park Oct. 1. 121 Technology Park is slated to see another phase of development kick off in 2027, per a company news release.
The specifics
The industrial park, which was developed by Stillwater Capital, currently includes four buildings that span a total of about 371,000 square feet. The spaces accommodate a variety of light industrial uses including high-tech manufacturing, assembly, distribution and logistics.
The existing buildings are about 55% leased, the release states. Current tenants include Amphenol Fiber Systems International, Acis, Comba, Globe Life and Xtera. Leasing efforts are underway to fill remaining spaces, per the release, and are being led by Josh Barnes and Blake Troiani of commercial real estate company Holt Lunsford Commercial.
“121 Technology Park’s location, quality, and growth potential make it an excellent fit for our portfolio,” Meritex Regional Director Ben Lieser said in the release. “We look forward to supporting the existing and future tenants through a local, hands-on approach and delivering the responsive and professional customer service that Meritex is known for.”
A second phase of development on the property is slated to begin in early 2027 and will add three more buildings. Once built out, the industrial park will include about 740,000 square feet of space across seven buildings, according to the release.
The context
The industrial park is located along the SH 121 corridor between Allen and McKinney, an area that is slated to see ongoing investment and development of commercial and residential projects as well as entertainment and hospitality uses. The area is the focus of 121 North, a joint initiative of the Allen Economic Development Corp. and the McKinney Economic Development Corp. that launched in May to highlight growth, development and major projects along the SH 121 corridor.
“121 Technology Park plays an important role in the continued evolution of the [SH] 121 corridor and in Allen’s ability to attract innovative employers and quality jobs,” AEDC President and CEO Dan Bowman said in the release. “The flexibility of this industrial park for advanced manufacturing, technology and industrial users complements the tremendous mix of office, residential, retail and entertainment investment taking shape around it.”
Other major projects along the corridor include The Farm in Allen, Sloan Corners and Kalahari on the Allen side, as well as Cannon Beach, 121 Commerce Park and the VENU Sunset Amphitheater on the McKinney side.
“121 Technology Park is a great fit for our investment strategy and our continued growth in North Texas,” Meritex Director of Acquisitions Drew Evans said in the release. “We look for high-quality, multi-tenant industrial properties in dynamic markets with strong long-term fundamentals. … Allen’s growth, skilled workforce and extraordinary momentum along the 121 corridor made this a compelling investment for Meritex.”
With the property acquisition and planned second phase of development, the company’s Dallas-Fort Worth portfolio grows to 1.6 million square feet, the release states.

articles.description: California man Greg Lui arrested by feds for allegedly smuggling $300 million in AI tech to China ABC7 Los Angeles
articles.description_html: California man Greg Lui arrested by feds for allegedly smuggling $300 million in AI tech to China  ABC7 Los Angeles
articles.article_title: San Gabriel Valley CEO accused of smuggling $300 million in AI tech to China
articles.heading: San Gabriel Valley CEO accused of smuggling $300 million in AI tech to China
articles.summary: A San Gabriel Valley CEO is facing federal charges after prosecutors accused him of smuggling American AI technology to China.
articles.content:
Saturday, October 3, 2026 2:03AM
LOS ANGELES (KABC) -- A San Gabriel Valley tech CEO is facing federal charges after prosecutors accused him of smuggling sensitive American artificial intelligence technology to China.
Federal prosecutors allege that 38-year-old San Gabriel resident Greg Lui, also known as Yiu Kong Lui, worked with co-conspirators between 2023 and 2024 to funnel more than $300 million worth of AI technology to China through his company, Earthmade Computer Inc., a City of Industry-based technology company.
Lui is accused of falsifying paperwork and redirecting deliveries through third-party countries while knowing that the final destination was China.
Lui was charged in a three-count indictment with conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act and Export Administration Regulations, outbound smuggling and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
If convicted, Lui faces up to 30 years in prison.
City News Service contributed to this report.

articles.title: Walton family breaks ground on Bentonville Institute of Technology
articles.description: Walton family breaks ground on Bentonville Institute of Technology Talk Business & Politics
articles.description_html: Walton family breaks ground on Bentonville Institute of Technology  Talk Business & Politics
articles.article_title: Walton family breaks ground on Bentonville Institute of Technology - Talk Business & Politics
articles.heading: Walton family breaks ground on Bentonville Institute of Technology
articles.summary: Members of the Walton family were among more than 200 attendees at a groundbreaking ceremony Friday (Oct. 2) for the approximately 444,000-square-foot Bentonville Institute of Technology at the former Walmart Home...
articles.content:
Walton family breaks ground on Bentonville Institute of Technology
Members of the Walton family were among more than 200 attendees at a groundbreaking ceremony Friday (Oct. 2) for the approximately 444,000-square-foot Bentonville Institute of Technology at the former Walmart Home Office site in Bentonville.
An investment amount for the work at Southwest Eighth Street and South Walton Boulevard was not disclosed.
The first undergraduate class of about 300 students is expected to start in August 2029. Tuition is expected to be fully covered in the institute’s initial years of operation. The institute’s name was also unveiled at the Friday ceremony. It was previously known as STEM University.
Tom Walton, Steuart Walton, and Alice Walton, through the Alice L. Walton Foundation, are supporting the creation of the institute focused on science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Tom Walton and his brother Steuart Walton are the grandsons of Walmart founders Helen and Sam Walton and the sons of Jim Walton, chairman of Arvest Bank Group. Alice Walton is the only daughter of Helen and Sam Walton.
In May 2025, Tom Walton and Steuart Walton announced plans to establish a university at the former home office site, along with the mixed-use development. In February, Dr. David Mazyck was named the inaugural president. In June, Copenhagen, Denmark-based BIG-Bjarke Ingels Group was selected to plan and design the campus.
At the Friday ceremony, Mazyck said that Tom Walton and Steuart Walton’s idea is taking physical form. The idea was to build a new model of higher education: “One designed for the realities of today’s economy and the challenges of tomorrow.”
Mazyck said the institute’s location is meaningful because it will be built where Sam Walton had his office, “a place associated with extraordinary culture, of entrepreneurship, experimentation and building something that had not existed before.” The institute’s purpose starts with a gap in STEM education, Mazyck said.
“Universities can produce technically capable graduates,” he said. “Technical capability alone is no longer enough. The people who create meaningful impact must also know how to identify the right problems, understand human needs, work across disciplines, exercise judgment, communicate complex ideas, understand how value is created and turn ideas into solutions that actually work in the world.”
Those abilities are often developed years after graduation through experience, business school, entrepreneurship, or trial and error, he said.
“We have an unusual opportunity because we are starting with a blank canvas,” Mazyck said. “We don’t have to retrofit artificial intelligence, entrepreneurship, storytelling, human-centered design, business thinking and learning by building into an academic structure designed for another era. We can design them together from the beginning. And AI makes that opportunity even more important.”
As knowledge and powerful technical capabilities become more accessible, he said, “what will distinguish people is not simply what they know but what they can do with that and how they know.”
“We exist to dramatically shorten the distance between learning and impact,” Mazyck said. “We want students to learn by building, to connect knowledge with action and to graduate, not waiting years for the opportunity to make a difference, but prepare to begin making one.”
According to a news release, the master plan integrates the institute with Bentonville’s parks and public spaces, connecting the campus to downtown.
On Friday, Tom Walton said one reason the university is being built here is its proximity to downtown Bentonville and the opportunities students will have to experience it. The university will sit on 64 acres and that the campus is downtown Bentonville “and all the downtown has to offer.”
“We hope to build a new neighborhood here over time, not immediately, but over time, you’ll see industry with office buildings,” he said. “You will see a variety of housing, a new hotel and even…another square for the town of Bentonville.”
He said “our ambition is that, as Bentonville rises, the university will rise too and accelerate that rise. So that’s why we think it’s important for Bentonville to be in the name. The institute is relatively straightforward. It’s seriousness. It’s academic rigor. It is focused…
“Technology is really the language that the university will use. So when you think about systems, capabilities and tools, those are the areas that our students will go out and lead with. So you’ll have mobility, energy, healthcare, automation and robotics. Those are the systems, powered by AI, learning, live learning and design thinking that will help our students be leaders in this world.”
Steuart Walton said the new Walmart Home Office, which has positively impacted the company, allowed the university to locate at the former home office site.
“This site is important,” he said. “It’s important to Bentonville. It’s important to our family. It’s important to the new university and maintaining the heritage, understanding and borrowing aspects of culture of the region, implementing it into the way that we educate, I think will put the university in a really key position and power it to success going forward.”
He noted that architecture matters, and “Alice has led that charge in our family more obviously and clearly than anybody else. And the folks at Bjarke Ingels have done a masterful job in helping us imagine what this can be.”
BIG-Bjarke Ingels Group is designing the campus in collaboration with Arkansas-based Polk Stanley Wilcox Architects, the architect of record. Columbus, Kan.-based Crossland Construction is the general contractor. Houston-based Walter P Moore and Lenexa, Kan.-based Henderson Engineers are the engineering consultants. Fort Lauderdale, Fla.-based EDSA leads landscape architecture and planning.
The release shows the institute’s first phase will include about 444,000 square feet of academic, residential, and innovation space across three buildings: the academic building, student residences and a makerspace.
“We want spaces that encourage students, faculty and employers to work across boundaries, bring different perspectives together and solve problems that actually exist in the world,” Mazyck said. “I think that the makerspace is one of the clearest physical expressions of our educational philosophy. At the Bentonville Institute of Technology, we want students to learn by building, and ideas should not have to wait until a senior capstone project to become real. From the beginning, students should be designing, prototyping, testing, failing, learning, rebuilding and improving. The makerspace will be approximately 130,000 square feet and is envisioned as a flexible innovation hub at the center of the experience.”
The institute is expected to grow to a capacity of 1,500 undergraduate students and 500 working professionals. He said working professionals can learn specific topics, such as an entrepreneurial mindset, and earn a certificate.
Mazyck expects to reach the institute’s 1,500-student capacity in its fourth year. The second phase of construction is expected to start in late 2030 or 2031. This phase will include an additional residence hall.
“The next phases of what we’re building are mainly focused on the curriculum for the bachelor’s degree,” he said. “We have the opportunity to think about those skills that graduates will need in this AI economy and then work backward. To think in terms of the sets of courses on how they build together to achieve the desired graduate capabilities. Unlike traditional learning, where a student would take one particular semester—maybe they would take history, calculus and a communications class. We are looking to embed these learning experiences so that while they’re concurrently learning technology and problem solving, they’re also learning the entrepreneurial mindset. They’re learning business principles. They’re learning communication skills.”
He said a physics class might also include instruction in business principles and communication skills. For example, students might present what they’ve learned to the class instead of completing a written exam.
He said the institute is focusing on a single degree, a bachelor of science. The degree name has yet to be determined but will likely be finalized next year.
Mazyck said in a Thursday panel discussion that the institute will offer a three-year degree experience. Mazyck said Friday that prospective students can apply starting in 2028. He expects at least half of the initial class to come from Arkansas or a neighboring state. The first class is expected to graduate in 2032.
“We want to attract the brightest students from the region, and thinking ahead, that students tend to pursue careers within that same geography of where they were educated,” he said.
He said the institute will also recruit students from across the country who have “that natural curiosity and an interest in learning through building prototypes, building teamwork, looking at how they can incorporate AI into systems to create new devices or solutions.” The institute is hiring faculty and staff and is expected to have 75 faculty and staff when it opens. Its first faculty member started last Monday, and the second one starts this Monday, he said.
The institute is also collaborating with K-12 schools on its curriculum. This spring, Bentonville High School students will take some of the first courses that the new institute will offer. The first will be chemistry class Molecules to Markets, followed by a four-week module on agentic AI building.
Bentonville Schools Superintendent Debbie Jones said its teachers and leaders have worked “hand-in-hand” with the institute’s staff “to build a university-level curriculum that they will teach in the schools next semester in Bentonville Schools. Together, our teams have dreamed big, creating rare and transformative STEM opportunities for both high school and college-level students. The university will supply our community with engineers and entrepreneurs and industry leaders, but even more importantly, it gives our brightest students a meaningful reason and opportunity to give back to the very community that raised them.”

“We have an unusual opportunity because we are starting with a blank canvas,” Mazyck said. “We don’t have to retrofit artificial intelligence, entrepreneurship, storytelling, human-centered design, business thinking and learning by building into an academic structure designed for another era. We can design them together from the beginning. And AI makes that opportunity even more important.”

As knowledge and powerful technical capabilities become more accessible, he said, “what will distinguish people is not simply what they know but what they can do with that and how they know.”

“We exist to dramatically shorten the distance between learning and impact,” Mazyck said. “We want students to learn by building, to connect knowledge with action and to graduate, not waiting years for the opportunity to make a difference, but prepare to begin making one.”

According to a news release, the master plan integrates the institute with Bentonville’s parks and public spaces, connecting the campus to downtown.

On Friday, Tom Walton said one reason the university is being built here is its proximity to downtown Bentonville and the opportunities students will have to experience it. The university will sit on 64 acres and that the campus is downtown Bentonville “and all the downtown has to offer.”

“We hope to build a new neighborhood here over time, not immediately, but over time, you’ll see industry with office buildings,” he said. “You will see a variety of housing, a new hotel and even…another square for the town of Bentonville.”

He said “our ambition is that, as Bentonville rises, the university will rise too and accelerate that rise. So that’s why we think it’s important for Bentonville to be in the name. The institute is relatively straightforward. It’s seriousness. It’s academic rigor. It is focused…

“Technology is really the language that the university will use. So when you think about systems, capabilities and tools, those are the areas that our students will go out and lead with. So you’ll have mobility, energy, healthcare, automation and robotics. Those are the systems, powered by AI, learning, live learning and design thinking that will help our students be leaders in this world.”

Steuart Walton said the new Walmart Home Office, which has positively impacted the company, allowed the university to locate at the former home office site.

“This site is important,” he said. “It’s important to Bentonville. It’s important to our family. It’s important to the new university and maintaining the heritage, understanding and borrowing aspects of culture of the region, implementing it into the way that we educate, I think will put the university in a really key position and power it to success going forward.”

He noted that architecture matters, and “Alice has led that charge in our family more obviously and clearly than anybody else. And the folks at Bjarke Ingels have done a masterful job in helping us imagine what this can be.”

BIG-Bjarke Ingels Group is designing the campus in collaboration with Arkansas-based Polk Stanley Wilcox Architects, the architect of record. Columbus, Kan.-based Crossland Construction is the general contractor. Houston-based Walter P Moore and Lenexa, Kan.-based Henderson Engineers are the engineering consultants. Fort Lauderdale, Fla.-based EDSA leads landscape architecture and planning.

The release shows the institute’s first phase will include about 444,000 square feet of academic, residential, and innovation space across three buildings: the academic building, student residences and a makerspace.

“We want spaces that encourage students, faculty and employers to work across boundaries, bring different perspectives together and solve problems that actually exist in the world,” Mazyck said. “I think that the makerspace is one of the clearest physical expressions of our educational philosophy. At the Bentonville Institute of Technology, we want students to learn by building, and ideas should not have to wait until a senior capstone project to become real. From the beginning, students should be designing, prototyping, testing, failing, learning, rebuilding and improving. The makerspace will be approximately 130,000 square feet and is envisioned as a flexible innovation hub at the center of the experience.”

The institute is expected to grow to a capacity of 1,500 undergraduate students and 500 working professionals. He said working professionals can learn specific topics, such as an entrepreneurial mindset, and earn a certificate.

Mazyck expects to reach the institute’s 1,500-student capacity in its fourth year. The second phase of construction is expected to start in late 2030 or 2031. This phase will include an additional residence hall.

“The next phases of what we’re building are mainly focused on the curriculum for the bachelor’s degree,” he said. “We have the opportunity to think about those skills that graduates will need in this AI economy and then work backward. To think in terms of the sets of courses on how they build together to achieve the desired graduate capabilities. Unlike traditional learning, where a student would take one particular semester—maybe they would take history, calculus and a communications class. We are looking to embed these learning experiences so that while they’re concurrently learning technology and problem solving, they’re also learning the entrepreneurial mindset. They’re learning business principles. They’re learning communication skills.”

He said a physics class might also include instruction in business principles and communication skills. For example, students might present what they’ve learned to the class instead of completing a written exam.
He said the institute is focusing on a single degree, a bachelor of science. The degree name has yet to be determined but will likely be finalized next year.

Mazyck said in a Thursday panel discussion that the institute will offer a three-year degree experience. Mazyck said Friday that prospective students can apply starting in 2028. He expects at least half of the initial class to come from Arkansas or a neighboring state. The first class is expected to graduate in 2032.

“We want to attract the brightest students from the region, and thinking ahead, that students tend to pursue careers within that same geography of where they were educated,” he said.

He said the institute will also recruit students from across the country who have “that natural curiosity and an interest in learning through building prototypes, building teamwork, looking at how they can incorporate AI into systems to create new devices or solutions.” The institute is hiring faculty and staff and is expected to have 75 faculty and staff when it opens. Its first faculty member started last Monday, and the second one starts this Monday, he said.

The institute is also collaborating with K-12 schools on its curriculum. This spring, Bentonville High School students will take some of the first courses that the new institute will offer. The first will be chemistry class Molecules to Markets, followed by a four-week module on agentic AI building.

Bentonville Schools Superintendent Debbie Jones said its teachers and leaders have worked “hand-in-hand” with the institute’s staff “to build a university-level curriculum that they will teach in the schools next semester in Bentonville Schools. Together, our teams have dreamed big, creating rare and transformative STEM opportunities for both high school and college-level students. The university will supply our community with engineers and entrepreneurs and industry leaders, but even more importantly, it gives our brightest students a meaningful reason and opportunity to give back to the very community that raised them.”

articles.title: El Paso family renews push to find missing relative with new technology
articles.description: El Paso family renews push to find missing relative with new technology KFOX
articles.description_html: El Paso family renews push to find missing relative with new technology  KFOX
articles.article_title: El Paso family renews push to find missing relative with new technology
articles.heading: El Paso family renews push to find missing relative with new technology
articles.summary: A sister born after Joseph’s kidnapping in his early 70s near the Rio Grande shares how the case shaped her family for decades. A new age-progression image and a push for DNA and genealogy could finally bring answers.
articles.content:
El Paso family renews push to find missing relative with new technology
EL PASO, Texas (KFOX14/CBS4) — After a child organization released a digital image showing what a missing El Paso toddler from 1970 might look like 50 years later, KFOX14/CBS4 spoke with the family of the missing kid as they hope that technology could bring closure.
On Sept. 9, 1974, 20-month-old Joseph Hurtado was last seen playing outside his grandmother's home at the 800 block of Elmwood Court in El Paso's Upper Valley. According to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC), Joseph's mother was washing the family car in the driveway when she noticed Joseph was gone. At first, she believed Joseph had just gone back inside the home, but the family later realized he was missing and called the authorities.
On Monday, NCMEC released an image where forensic artists imagined what Joseph would look like now, 50 years later.
KFOX14/CBS4 reached out to the family and spoke with Marie Hurtado George, Joseph's youngest sister, who shared more about what she knows of the day Joseph went missing and how DNA technology could bring her family some needed closure.
RELATED: New age-progression image released in 52-year-old El Paso missing child case
“It’s been very heartbreaking,” Marie said, talking about growing up knowing her brother had been kidnapped. “Just growing up my whole entire life. It’s being a huge impact on our family.”
Marie said she was born after Joseph disappeared and that what she knows comes from what her family has shared and what has circulated publicly.
Recounting the disappearance, as she has pieced it together from what she was told, Marie said it all started with "miscommunication" on who had the baby, as her mother was outside washing the car and her father was inside.
Marie said that by the time both parents realized neither of them had Joseph, the family believed he may have wandered next door to look at fish in a nearby pond-- but he wasn't there.
Next, the family searched the back area of the home-- which is up against the Rio Grande-- before calling authorities when they could not find him.
Marie said seeing an age-progression image of what Joseph might look like today was difficult.
“That one hit hard,” Marie said, crediting the NCMEC with working “really hard” with her and her brother to get the image right.
Marie said that even after five decades, the family's commitment to finding Joseph has never stopped.
Marie understands that if Joseph is still alive, he could have another family and may not know his story, so she emphasized the importance of genetic genealogy and DNA testing.
“This is why I stress DNA,” Marie said. “If you think you just want to know about your family history, take that DNA test. I think that is the biggest tool that we have out there that could actually help us help millions of other people that are searching for their children.”
Marie said DNA and genealogy can also help families find answers even if a missing loved one is deceased, providing a path to closure.

articles.title: Longboat Key tests AI technology to track foot traffic
articles.description: Longboat Key tests AI technology to track foot traffic ABC7 WWSB
articles.description_html: Longboat Key tests AI technology to track foot traffic  ABC7 WWSB
articles.article_title: Longboat Key tests AI technology to track foot traffic
articles.heading: Longboat Key tests AI technology to track foot traffic
articles.summary: Town officials say the data could help businesses with staffing, inventory and promotions during slower months
articles.content:
Longboat Key tests AI technology to track foot traffic
LONGBOAT KEY, Fla. (WWSB) - The Town of Longboat Key is testing new technology that tracks foot traffic around the island, with officials saying the data could help local businesses plan for the off-season.
According to the Town of Longboat Key, Placer.ai estimates visits to real places from mobile devices. The anonymous signals are mapped to an area the town defines, such as a beach, park, town facility, shopping plaza or a single business, then scaled to provide data patterns. The town says the technology does not identify a person, follow a specific phone or produce a precise headcount, and that figures are estimates generally treated as reliable for trends, comparisons and time-of-day patterns.
A typical report shows visits, unique visitors, how long people stay, and when they come, by hour, day and season, according to the town. The data separates audiences, including people whose home location is on the island, seasonal or part-time residents, employees, day visitors from nearby cities, and tourists from farther away. Trade-area maps show where visitors live or work, allowing officials to tie a beach, event or business to Longboat Key residents versus visitors from Sarasota, Bradenton or out-of-market areas.
The town says reports are aggregated only, and that sensitive places such as schools, places of worship and health facilities are blocked. Officials said the technology cannot be used to track a resident.
Town manager says data will be shared with businesses
Longboat Key Town Manager George Landry said the data will eventually be shared with local businesses to help shape their strategies, especially during the off-season.
“Small businesses contribute a large portion to the quality of life here on Longboat and we want to make sure that we are giving them all the information that we can to help them be as successful as they can so they can stay here and stay serving people,” Landry said.
Business reaction
Harry’s on Longboat Key has been in business for 47 years. General Manager Hal Christensen said the difference between peak and off-season is significant.
“Night and day... the difference is we are busy for 12-16 weeks out of the year and the rest of the time it is either slow or really slow,” Christensen said.
Christensen said the restaurant closes on slower months.
“We just came off a closure. We were closed for the month of September because that is normally the slowest month of the year,” Christensen said.
Christensen said he supports the idea of gathering more data.
“Where they are coming to and why they are coming to those places. I think any information is good information,” Christensen said.
Some visitors have concerns
Not everyone supports the use of the technology. Tayvin Galanakis, visiting Longboat Key from Iowa, said he is not comfortable with the tracking.
“For AI to track our foot traffic when we are on vacation and all that I mean I don’t feel like that’s a good thing,” Galanakis said.
What’s next
Landry said the town is working with businesses to determine what information would be useful to them.
“So we can see if the software provides those reports,” Landry said.
The technology is starting on a small scale. Over the next six months, a few locations will begin gathering data as a trial before Placer.ai is rolled out across Longboat Key, according to the town manager.

articles.content:
The Big Story
How did the beltway take Trump’s AI accord?
In a deep dive, The Hill’s Julia Shapero and Mallory Wilson examine how Trump’s “self-policing” AI accord is landing in Washington as concerns mount over the tech’s safety.
© Alex Brandon, Associated Press
While Trump says industry officials can self-police, critics argue AI needs more oversight to keep development from getting out of hand — even as some described the accord as a step in the right direction.
One expert told us the administration’s concerns may be “sincere,” but the pledge is not a “solution” to preventing the potential risks of AI development.
Several of the biggest players in the industry signed the one-page document Tuesday, which included four “layers of controls and audits.”
It declares that AI companies should implement “robust” internal controls over models, empower an internal crew to crosscheck controls and mediate any issues, partner with external auditors to evaluate their controls and designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee reports from the operating teams.
Some lawmakers, including members of his own party, expressed skepticism over the accord.
Sen. Josh Halwey (R-Mo.) called it a “good step” but stopped short of saying lawmakers can take AI executives at their world.
Subscribe to The Hill’s Insider to read more on where Washington figures landed on the “morally binding” agreement.
Welcome to The Hill’s Technology newsletter, we’re Julia Shapero and Miranda Nazzaro — tracking the latest moves from Capitol Hill to Silicon Valley.

The bill, titled the Ban Flock Act, would both prohibit federal agencies from ALPR usages and pause federal grant funding to state and local governments with ALPR contracts. It would also allow Americans to sue the federal government …
NASA’s dexterous humanoid robots built to assist humans on the moon
(NewsNation) — At NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, the 16-member Dexterous Robotics Team, is working on new machines to join crews on future lunar missions. These robots, however, are not just built for repetitive tasks. Their objective is to act as a hands-on support team for the crew while on the moon. “It’s really about the human elements — either working in environments designed for humans or working alongside humans. …
Amazon investing $1B in data center communities
Amazon plans to invest $1 billion in communities where it builds data centers over the next five years, the company announced Friday. The e-commerce and cloud computing giant will put the funds toward free community college and workforce training for residents, as well as energy efficiency upgrades. “We understand why there is apprehension in some communities where data centers are being built,” Amazon Web Services …

Crypto Corner
SEC’s ‘crypto mom’ says adieu
© Andrew Harnik, AP
Hester Peirce, who became known as “crypto mom” at the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), is bidding the agency adieu.
The SEC commissioner, who departs Friday after eight years in the role, was a key advocate for the industry during a period that saw Washington’s views on digital assets shift wildly.
“Serving this great nation at the Securities and Exchange Commission has been the honor of my professional lifetime,” she wrote in her resignation letter, which she shared to social media last week.
“The United States is exceptional because its unifying thread is a commitment to liberty,” Peirce continued. “A nation that elevates freedom of thought, expression, and action unlocks the great potential of its people to meet one another’s needs.”
“That ethos runs through the American securities markets, where innovates meet retail and institutional investors so that together they can build a vibrant economy.”
Her departure leaves the SEC with just two commissioners, Chair Paul Atkins and Mark Uyeda. Both are Republican appointees.
The agency typically has a five-member bipartisan commission but has dwindled down over the past two years.
Notably, the SEC issued a final rule Wednesday updating its quorum requirements. The new rule declares that one commissioner can constitute quorum if they are the only member who can participate.

articles.title: Bryan Johnson: Adapting to technology and modernizing campuses
articles.description: Bryan Johnson: Adapting to technology and modernizing campuses Mountain View Voice
articles.description_html: Bryan Johnson: Adapting to technology and modernizing campuses  Mountain View Voice
articles.article_title: Bryan Johnson: Adapting to technology and modernizing campuses
articles.heading: Bryan Johnson: Adapting to technology and modernizing campuses
articles.summary: Bryan Johnson is one of four candidates vying for three seats on the Los Altos School District Board of Trustees in this November's General Election. His top priorities include updating technology best practices, modernizing school facilities and improving support for underserved students.
articles.content:
| Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... |
Bryan Johnson
Incumbent | bryanjohnsonforlasd.com
Top priorities
- Updating best practices for learning with emerging technologies and AI
- Modernizing existing school facilities and building a new campus
- Adding and improving support systems for underserved students inside and outside the classroom
Public service
- Los Altos School District Board of Trustees (2016-present)
Community involvement
- Santa Rita Elementary School PTA
- 2014 Measure N bond campaign committee
With a decade on the dais already under his belt, Bryan Johnson is running for another four years on the Los Altos school board, hoping to continue advocating for facility modernization and the construction of a new school campus in Mountain View.
“I do want to see that the rest of the way through to completion, now that we finally have shovels in the ground and are moving earth and are creating this beautiful new facility,” Johnson said.
Johnson is one of four candidates running for three seats on the Los Altos School District Board of Trustees, which governs seven elementary and two middle schools throughout Los Altos, Los Altos Hills and Mountain View. His children, who are now in college, attended Santa Rita Elementary and Egan Junior High schools.
Even though his children have aged out of the district, Johnson said he’s eager to help LASD move forward on large projects — namely the construction of the San Antonio campus in Mountain View, also called the “10th school site.” Demolition on the 11.7-acre plot of land, which was formerly a strip mall, began earlier this year.
Johnson’s long tenure and subsequent involvement in many of the district’s major projects is part of why he was inspired to run again. He was first elected to the board in a 2016 special election, and then won reelection in 2018 and 2022. Before joining the school board, Johnson was an active member of the Santa Rita Elementary School PTA.
“I think it is valuable to have someone in the room who was there and has the context,” Johnson told the Voice.
One of Johnson’s stated priorities is helping underserved students achieve success — “the kind of thing where your work is never done,” he said, noting that the way the district goes about supporting students continually fluctuates. Children have increasingly complex obstacles to contend with, Johnson said, and he hopes to help continue to find ways to support students inside and outside the classroom.
This school year, the district hired a Family Engagement Facilitator to connect underserved students’ families with local resources, whether they need food, housing or other forms of assistance.
“There are resources in the area, but often families that are overwhelmed like that don’t know who to ask or where to look,” Johnson said. “Having somebody from the district who can go out, understand those needs and make the connection … can make a huge difference in unlocking that child’s abilities.”
Similarly, Johnson wants to work with teachers and administrators to iron out the district’s best practices around artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies. Education technology has evolved quickly over the past decade, Johnson said, and the district needs to be mindful of how it’s deployed in classrooms.
A perennial topic of local controversy has been the relationship between the school district and Bullis Charter School. Since the charter school’s founding more than two decades ago, interactions between the two entities have been tumultuous, sometimes involving legal battles over campus space allocations.
Most recently, the district and charter school have been at odds over the district’s intent to move Bullis to the 10th site. Johnson described the plan as a “path to a long term solution” — even though charter school administrators have been strongly against it.
Despite the opposition, Johnson said he’s optimistic about Bullis using the San Antonio campus. He’s also focused on modernizing all of the district’s campuses, most of which haven’t seen an overhaul in decades. Similarly, the charter school is currently housed in portable classrooms at Egan Junior High and Blach Intermediate schools.
“Those facilities are not intended to last that long,” Johnson said. “We were always going to need to eventually find permanent facilities for the charter school.”
The Voice has published an individual profile of each Los Altos School District Board of Trustees candidate. To view those articles, and the rest of our election coverage, head over to our 2026 Election Center.

articles.title: Governor Gianforte, Montana Chamber of Commerce to Host Technology Summit in Bozeman
articles.description: Governor Gianforte, Montana Chamber of Commerce to Host Technology Summit in Bozeman State of Montana Newsroom (.gov)
articles.description_html: Governor Gianforte, Montana Chamber of Commerce to Host Technology Summit in Bozeman  State of Montana Newsroom (.gov)
articles.article_title: Governor Gianforte, Montana Chamber of Commerce to Host Technology Summit in Bozeman
articles.heading: Governor Gianforte, Montana Chamber of Commerce to Host Technology Summit in Bozeman
articles.summary: HELENA, Mont. – Governor Greg Gianforte and the Montana Chamber of Commerce are scheduled to host the 3rd Annual Big Sky, Bright Future Economic Summit on Thursday, October 15th, in Bozeman. This year’s summit will focus on technology innovation in Montana.
articles.content:
Governor Gianforte, Montana Chamber of Commerce to Host Technology Summit in Bozeman
HELENA, Mont. – Governor Greg Gianforte and the Montana Chamber of Commerce are scheduled to host the 3rd Annual Big Sky, Bright Future Economic Summit on Thursday, October 15th, in Bozeman. This year’s summit will focus on technology innovation in Montana.
“Montana’s technology sector is helping drive our state’s economic future,” Gov. Gianforte said. “From advancing precision agriculture and strengthening national security to opportunities in artificial intelligence and photonics, Montana’s innovators are creating good-paying jobs. I look forward to joining the Montana Chamber of Commerce in bringing leaders together to build on our momentum to ensure the Treasure State remains a great place to start a business.”
The summit will facilitate collaboration and impactful conversations about Montana’s role in the technology industry from national security, artificial intelligence in traditional industries such as precision agriculture, photonics, data centers, and online safety. Panelists include top executives and policymakers focused on innovative solutions and the forces shaping Montana’s economy. Speakers include Congressman Troy Downing, Montana State University President Brock Tessman, Montana State Senator Daniel Zolnikov, R-Billings, and representatives of the governor’s cabinet.
“The tech sector is the fastest growing business sector in Montana representing 5% of our GDP” said Todd O’Hair, President and CEO of the Montana Chamber of Commerce. “As entrepreneurs starting Right Now Technologies, Governor Greg Gianforte and First Lady Susan Gianforte were some of the original sparks that led to the rapid growth we see today. The Montana Chamber of Commerce is excited to join the Governor and First Lady as co-hosts for a conference that explores Montana’s national role in Artificial Intelligence, national security, data security and other technology related issues.”
The 3rd Annual Big Sky, Bright Future Summit agenda may be viewed here. Registration is still open, and those interested in attending may RSVP here.
###

articles.content:
Superintendent plans to address AI, technology use
Superintendent Amy Hartley-Matteson wants to tackle early literacy and limit technology use.
Her hefty improvement plan for the 2026-27 school year, presented to the School Committee at its Oct. 2 meeting, has a range of goals for improving student performance on assessments.
Hartley-Matteson said she is committed to equity. She wants to identify which students the district’s current practices aren’t working well for and figure out what needs to change to make learning more equitable.
She wants to tackle early literacy through creating a new program for teaching reading and writing, which was discussed at a previous School Committee meeting.
“If there are particular practices that impact student learning, we lean into those practices,” said Hartley-Matteson.
She also plans to create guidelines for artificial intelligence, technology and cell phone usage. This will include conducting a technology use study and creating a team to recommend guidelines by grade level.
District leaders and principals will meet three times over the school year to reflect on progress. School-based teams will similarly reflect on school-wide goals.
School Committee member Joyce Bacchiocchi said she is looking forward to the technology use study. She questioned if increased screen time is what students need for better learning.
“”You’ve been here for three months, and in those three months, you’ve put together this plan that is more relevant to students and our district than our previous plan,” Bacchiocchi said.

articles.article_title: Emerging in Tech Summit Connects Wisconsin Communities to Technology’s Future
articles.heading: Emerging in Tech Summit Connects Wisconsin Communities to Technology’s Future
articles.summary: The Emerging in Tech (EIT) Summit brings together the people, ideas, and technologies shaping Wisconsin’s future.
articles.content:
Source: http://vecteezy.com/
Emerging in Tech Summit Connects Wisconsin Communities to Technology’s Future
The Emerging in Tech (EIT) Summit brings together the people, ideas, and technologies shaping Wisconsin’s future. Taking place Oct. 13, 2026, from 1–5 p.m. at Kenosha Innovation Neighborhood, the summit centers on one idea: Connected Through Innovation.
Nadiyah Johnson, founder of Jet Constellations, created Wisconsin Tech Month to make the state’s tech ecosystem more accessible and visible, connecting people across technology, entrepreneurship, education, and community.
“Emerging in Tech Summit is part of Wisconsin Tech Month. It's one of our flagship events, and our overall vision is to extend our reach outside of the city of Milwaukee and to start creating bridges with some of our neighboring tech hubs,” Johnson said. “I’m really excited to be working with Kenosha Innovation Neighborhood and City Cream Cyber.”
The goal for the summit is to inform and educate communities about available resources, how the technology industry is evolving, and how emerging technologies can be incorporated into daily life and the workforce.
One of the workshops Johnson is especially excited about is the Virtual Reality workshop, which will explore how emerging technology can create greater equity. Speakers will highlight how virtual reality is being used to help justice-involved individuals build skills while incarcerated, preparing them for successful reentry and employment opportunities from day one.
Johnson said a lack of awareness can be a barrier to preventing people from pursuing careers in tech.
“When I was just starting out, I didn’t know what sort of opportunities technology could afford me.
I had to go to a conference in Texas to get hired at GE, which was right in my backyard,” Johnson said. “There’s more exposure to what opportunities are right here in the state and also a mentality shift. People think you have to be a genius or a super nerd or really good at math to thrive in technology, and that’s just not the case.”
Technology is part of virtually every industry, offering numerous career opportunities that can provide family-sustaining wages.

articles.title: ‘Just like my big brothers’: boy with cerebral palsy passes GCSEs with eye-tracking technology
articles.description: ‘Just like my big brothers’: boy with cerebral palsy passes GCSEs with eye-tracking technology The Guardian
articles.description_html: ‘Just like my big brothers’: boy with cerebral palsy passes GCSEs with eye-tracking technology  The Guardian
articles.article_title: ‘Just like my big brothers’: boy with cerebral palsy passes GCSEs with eye-tracking technology
articles.heading: ‘Just like my big brothers’: boy with cerebral palsy passes GCSEs with eye-tracking technology
articles.summary: Patrick McCabe’s herculean feat shows limits and possibilities of special educational needs and disabilities system
articles.content:
Patrick McCabe is instantly recognisable in the early autumn sunshine, his wheelchair surrounded by fellow pupils at Fallibroome Academy in Macclesfield, Cheshire as they move from lesson to lesson, chatting, laughing and joking around.
His extraordinary GCSE success this summer has become the stuff of legend. The 16-year-old has cerebral palsy and it took four months for him to complete his exams using eye-tracking technology. Now Patrick has started his A-levels – French, business and media studies – and fresh challenges lie ahead.
In person, Patrick is impish, thoughtful, articulate, witty, intelligent and honest. Using his augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) device, he tells the Guardian school has been a good experience overall. Born in Switzerland, his family moved back to England when he was six. Since then, he has gone to local mainstream schools, where he wanted to learn like everyone else.
“The best thing has been that, just like my big brothers, I’ve been able to learn and develop skills and gain knowledge of the world around me,” he said. “Even if some days I didn’t always want to go [to school], I think the opportunity to learn has helped me to grow and develop an independent mind.”
It has not been easy. “The most difficult things have been building meaningful relationships, and communication barriers do exist,” said Patrick. “People are not always familiar with Eyegaze technology and are not always willing or able to give it a chance in terms of friendships.”
In many ways, Patrick epitomises the Labour government’s ambitions for students with special educational needs and disabilities (Send). Forthcoming reforms are built on an inclusive approach, keeping children and young people in local – rather than special – schools with all the necessary expertise and support on hand.
But Patrick’s story also illustrates the scale of change required if education and assessment in England are to be truly inclusive. His experience shows that exams are far from accessible to all, his family and school say vital expertise is not always available and – crucially – funding is never enough.
“All we wanted was for Patrick to have the opportunity to demonstrate his knowledge and be given something resembling a level playing field compared to other students,” said the headteacher, Ross Martland. The school and Patrick’s mother, Jo, battled with the exam boards to try to ensure he was given a fair chance.
In the end, it doesn’t sound very fair at all. While his peers spent the first part of the year revising, Patrick’s exams got under way on 2 February and went on every morning until 5 June. It required a herculean effort from him, which left him exhausted, frustrated and sometimes ill.
A 30-mark question that might form just one element of an exam could take up to six hours. Patrick was supported throughout by CandLE, an organisation that helps students using AAC technology to access education across the UK. That he passed all seven GCSEs and achieved the grades he needed to continue into sixth form is testament to his determination.
“Revising for my GCSEs was very exhausting because it took extra time and effort to revise in the first place,” said Patrick. “I felt I had to work harder to express what I know, even when I understand the subject. This was tiring, both physically and mentally. I needed extra breaks to rest, but I still wanted to do my best to show what I had learned.”
Martland is fully supportive of the government’s Send ambitions. “I think the plans are right. Morally and values-wise, it’s absolutely right.” The issue is funding, he said, adding: “I’m concerned it will add significant pressures to schools if it’s not resourced properly.”
Throughout his time at Fallibroome, Patrick has worked with a devoted team of teaching assistants who support him not only with his learning in class but also his personal care. “We are incredibly proud of Patrick and all of our Send students,” said Rachel Crew, one of the teaching assistants working with him.
Patrick says the transition to sixth form is going well. He’s shed the bottle green uniform in favour of a smart blue suit and he says the school is doing everything it can to support him.
He says his mum has been “amazing” and he thinks students with physical disabilities who use eye-tracking technology should be assessed in a more appropriate way, so they don’t face additional barriers. But it is not only exams that worry him. “My concerns remain around friendships, if I’m honest,” he says.
So what’s Patrick planning next? After A-levels, he wants to study media at university. “I find it interesting and I’d like to go into the industry.” His mum tentatively suggests nearby Salford. Patrick’s looking at Bournemouth, 200 miles away. Is he daunted? No chance. “I feel excited about the experience.”

articles.title: Ground broken on STEM-focused university dubbed Bentonville Institute of Technology
articles.description: Ground broken on STEM-focused university dubbed Bentonville Institute of Technology Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
articles.description_html: Ground broken on STEM-focused university dubbed Bentonville Institute of Technology  Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
articles.article_title: Ground broken on STEM-focused university dubbed Bentonville Institute of Technology | Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
articles.heading: Ground broken on STEM-focused university dubbed Bentonville Institute of Technology
articles.summary: BENTONVILLE -- Ground was broken Friday for a STEM-focused university at the site of the former Walmart Home Office.
articles.content:
BENTONVILLE -- Ground was broken Friday for a STEM-focused university at the site of the former Walmart Home Office.
School officials also announced the institution's official name: the Bentonville Institute of Technology.
"Bentonville Institute of Technology captures the essence of who we are: a technology-focused university rooted in one of the nation's most innovative communities," David Mazyck, the institute's president and founder, said in a news release about the groundbreaking and naming. "The name reflects our belief that the next generation of technological advances can emerge from the heartland of America through an institution rooted in education, collaboration and innovation."
STEM stands for science, technology, engineering and math.
In 2025, Steuart and Tom Walton announced a vision to reimagine STEM education through the founding of a new university in their hometown of Bentonville, the release states. Multiple members of the Walton family are supporting this vision, including Alice Walton through the Alice L. Walton Foundation.
"Bentonville has a long history of turning bold ideas into real change," Tom Walton said in the release. "Bentonville Institute of Technology is a chance to create a new model of education, one built for the world students are entering, with deep industry engagement from day one."
Institute leaders envision the campus as a gateway for companies, entrepreneurs and innovators to engage directly with students, helping create talent pipelines, incubate new ideas and drive long-term economic growth, the release states.
Mazyck, who spent nearly two decades in higher education at Penn State University and the University of Florida before coming to Bentonville, said during a panel discussion Thursday that the opportunity to turn technical ideas into real-world applications is familiar.
"It was (at Penn State and Florida) where I started several manufacturing companies, and that was because I wanted to create high-paying jobs in these technical fields," Mazyck said. "But what I really enjoyed and what was amazing to see (was ideas) go from napkins to manufacturing."
Bentonville Institute of Technology expects to welcome its first undergraduate class of approximately 300 students in August 2029 and eventually grow to approximately 1,500 undergraduate students and 500 working professionals.
During the institute's initial years of operation, tuition is expected to be fully covered, according to the release.
Earlier this year, the institute announced the selection of BIG-Bjarke Ingels Group, an architecture and urban design firm led by Bjarke Ingels, to plan and design the campus. The master plan integrates the institute with Bentonville's network of parks and public spaces, creating a campus that connects downtown with surrounding green spaces, according to the release.
The campus's first phase will include approximately 444,000 square feet of academic, residential and innovation space, anchored by three primary facilities: an academic building, student residences and a makerspace. Together, these spaces are designed to support the institute's mission of preparing students to thrive in an era shaped by AI and rapid technological change, the release states.
The institute will be part of the mixed-use development planned for the former Walmart Home Office site, where Sam Walton had his final office.
"Our grandfather's curiosity drove everything he did," Steuart Walton said in the release. "He walked his own stores and his competitors' with a notepad and came back to this site with ideas that changed an industry. It's fitting that this ground will now be home to students who share that curiosity and have a drive to build."
Those involved in the design and construction of Bentonville Institute of Technology include:
Polk Stanley Wilcox Architects, architect of record.
Crossland Construction, general contractor.
Walter P Moore and Henderson Engineers, engineering consultants.
EDSA, leading landscape architecture and planning.
