articles.title: 'Sometimes it's more expensive than having humans': Ecolab gets real about AI's limits in the physical world
articles.description: 'Sometimes it's more expensive than having humans': Ecolab gets real about AI's limits in the physical world fortune.com
articles.description_html: 'Sometimes it's more expensive than having humans': Ecolab gets real about AI's limits in the physical world  fortune.com
articles.article_title: 'Sometimes it's more expensive than having humans': Ecolab gets real about AI's limits in the physical world | Fortune
articles.heading: Trending now
articles.summary: Honeywell CTO Suresh Venkatarayalu said customers “really demand 99.9999%” accuracy, while frontier models “could be at 85%.”
articles.content:
Putting the latest AI models into buildings, factories and kitchens is much harder than putting them into a chatbot. That was the message from executives at Honeywell and Ecolab, though they were fairly positive about AI overall.
Honeywell Technologies Chief Technology Officer Suresh Venkatarayalu said at Fortune’s AIQ Summit at the New York Stock Exchange on Thursday that the problem is accuracy. The industrial giant’s customers “really demand 99.9999%,” he said, while frontier models “could be at 85%.”
Ecolab Chief AI Officer AJ Wijesinghe described a different limit: cost. When the company put “the best model that’s out there” on high-volume work, “the tokenomics go off the roof,” he said. “Sometimes it’s more expensive than having humans.”
The water-management company then optimized its models and cut token costs by about 70% to 80%, he said. Ecolab uses both frontier and open-source models, including Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s. “Sometimes you don’t have to have the fastest car,” he said.
Neither executive described a fully autonomous future. Venkatarayalu said the move is toward “a semi-autonomous world” where operators build trust in the systems, and that “autonomy is also not about removing people.” Wijesinghe described a “human in the lead” model, saying agent technology “is not matured enough” to run at scale on its own.
Slower than software
Physical equipment can’t be updated like a phone. Venkatarayalu said over-the-air upgrades are coming to commercial buildings, but with an operator in the loop. Buildings and industrial sites are “mission critical and safety critical,” he said. A Tesla can be down for 1.5 hours for an update, but “you cannot afford to have a building shut down for one and a half hours.”
Moderator Emily Forlini, senior AI reporter at Fortune, noted the company recently announced work being done, not a partnership, with Nvidia at its investor day. Venkatarayalu said it’s fine-tuning open-source models partly because customers want sovereignty over their data and models. He said Honeywell Technologies hand-picks them and works with Nvidia’s Nemotron team, because an unsupported open-source model without guardrails would be “dangerous.”
Honeywell Technologies describes a “see, think, act, and learn” framework. It starts by cataloguing a building’s assets, including HVAC, fire control, and security and access control, and connecting them over the BACnet protocol. AI agents then learn how the systems relate and run them. Venkatarayalu also said the company is exploring how to teach AI about chemistry, such as catalyst formulation.
Ecolab uses sensors in dishwashers, pest traps and water systems to cut service visits and predict maintenance. Its executive said the company also manages water for chip production, power and cooling in AI infrastructure.
What separates results from stalls
An audience member from a systems integrator asked what separates AI work that creates value from work that stalls. Wijesinghe said individual AI adds little measurable value at the enterprise level, and vertical AI within a function adds some. The most value, he said, comes from “horizontal” AI that works backward from an outcome across functions such as sales, finance and supply chain.
AI “should not be just another technology,” he said, and should be tied to a company-wide transformation. Ecolab expects $325 million in annual run-rate savings by 2027, and he said “significant” amounts are already in hand. Data foundation, process readiness and cost discipline matter equally, he said: “If one is heavier than the other, then you don’t get the value.”
Venkatarayalu said where AI runs, at the edge, on a customer’s premises or in the cloud, depends on latency, data-transaction cost and sovereignty. Customers who got 7% energy savings from existing controls now ask whether AI can deliver 30% or 40% more, he said.
For this story, Fortune journalists used generative AI as a research tool. An editor verified the accuracy of the information before publishing. The report has been updated to clarify that while Honeywell Technologies said it works with NVIDIA, it is not in the form of an official partnership.

articles.title: Navy selects 3 companies to develop mine countermeasure technology
articles.description: Navy selects 3 companies to develop mine countermeasure technology Navy Times
articles.description_html: Navy selects 3 companies to develop mine countermeasure technology  Navy Times
articles.article_title: Navy selects 3 companies to develop mine countermeasure technology
articles.heading: Navy selects 3 companies to develop mine countermeasure technology
articles.summary: BeeX, BlackSea Technologies and Vatn Systems were selected as prize winners after successfully completing a mine countermeasures modernization challenge.
articles.content:
The Navy selected three defense companies as prize winners of a challenge to advance mine countermeasure technology capable of destroying mine threats from a safe distance.
The service’s Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Robotic and Autonomous Systems and Defense Innovation Unit selected BeeX, BlackSea Technologies and Vatn Systems after they successfully completed the Mine Countermeasure Modernization Prize Challenge, according to a recent release.
“Through the partnership with DIU, in less than four months we were able to quickly move from open call to on-water testing, to contracting options and initial operational planning,” George Saroch, DRPM RAS program manager for mine warfare, said in the announcement.
DIU launched the competition on May 29, offering $200,000 to companies selected to participate and up to $3 million to the winning company.
Out of 80 applicants, only 11 companies were chosen to compete.
The competition asked companies to tackle near-surface mine neutralization, bottom mine detection and bottom mine neutralization.
Those that were awarded the prize proved that their technology was capable of locating, identifying and destroying underwater mine threats, the Navy said.
The Navy has faced mine warfare during the Iran war, with Iran placing sea mines along the Strait of Hormuz.
The suite of options the service has to address the threat, however, remains limited.

articles.article_title: Documenting the tech worker movement
articles.heading: Documenting the tech worker movement
articles.summary: MIT PhD student JS Tan co-wrote with Clarissa Redwine the book "Against Tech Oligarchy," on the rise and fall of the tech worker labor movement of the past decade. The book chronicles how tech workers organized themselves, effective strategies they used, and effects the movement and tech development had on Silicon Valley labor politics.
articles.content:
Despite the “dot-com crash” in 2000, the tech industry remained an attractive career destination for many who believed technology represented the future. The digital age — defined by global connectivity and computers — had firmly taken hold, and over time, the tech industry emerged as a dominant force in the labor market. High-paying jobs for engineers, designers, and professionals across a wide range of fields became increasingly common.
MIT PhD student JS Tan SM ’22 was among those who, upon graduating from Brown University and Rhode Island School of Design in 2015, joined the tech industry.
“A lot of us had this idea that technology, and in particular the technologies related to the internet, had the potential for bringing about a more progressive version of the world,” Tan says.
Google echoed this ethos to its employees with its once-famous motto, “don’t be evil,” as their informal corporate philosophy and code of conduct guideline. They’ve since dropped the tagline.
But in time, particularly with the start of the first Trump administration, some tech industry employees found themselves questioning if their employers were really intent on supporting policies to support a more democratic world. According to Tan, their willingness to publicly oppose their employers’ actions — at first successfully — is currently experiencing an anti-worker backlash.
Now, Tan and his former tech industry colleague Clarissa Redwine have published a book on the rise and fall of the tech worker labor movement. “Against Tech Oligarchy: Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry” (Haymarket Books, 2026) chronicles how tech workers organized themselves, the effective strategies they used, and the effect the movement had on Silicon Valley labor politics over the past decade.
Documenting a movement from within
In 2017, Tan was working for Microsoft and Redwine for Kickstarter, when President Donald Trump signed an executive order suspending entry into the United States for nationals from seven predominantly Muslim countries for 90 days, and suspending Syrian refugees from entering the country indefinitely.
“As a whole, I think the tech sector really pushed back against this,” says Tan. “[OpenAI co-founder] Sam Altman participated in protests of this ban at the airport. In fact, the day before he joined these protests, he wrote in his blog that the tech industry needed to take a stand against the Trump administration, and particularly its immigration policies.”
Altman’s Jan. 28, 2017, blog post read, in part, “Tech companies go to extraordinary lengths to recruit and retain employees; those employees have a lot of leverage. If employees push companies to do something, I believe they’ll have to. At a minimum, companies should take a public stance. But talking is only somewhat effective, and employees should push their companies to figure out what actions they can take.”
Tan says Altman’s words inspired tech workers across the industry to publicly voice their opposition and “push for the values they believed in.” For the next several years, workers staged walkouts and protested their employers’ contracts with U.S. military and immigration enforcement agencies, as well as workplace policies they considered sexist.
“That was a time in which a lot of tech workers felt that their companies were walking back the values that they had initially promised,” says Tan.
Their objections initially met with some success. In 2018, following protests by Google employees, the company decided not to renew its contract for Project Maven, a Pentagon initiative using artificial intelligence to analyze drone surveillance footage. Nearly 4,000 employees signed an open letter to their CEO stating, “Google should not be in the business of war.”
Fast forward eight years. Earlier this year, more than 600 employees signed an open letter urging Google’s CEO to reject classified AI work with the Pentagon, citing concerns about potential uses including lethal autonomous weapons and domestic surveillance.
“The way Google responded to them this time was to say, basically, ‘Too bad, we’re committed to working with the Pentagon,’” says Tan. “So, there is this kind of shift as to how Google is positioning itself politically, as well as to their employees.”
What happened to the tech industry employee leverage?
Tan’s book outlines several events that he argues have negatively impacted their formerly strong influence. First, following interest rate hikes in 2022, the tech industry lost hundreds of billions in market valuation and set out to cut costs, the most significant of them being the expensive salaries of their employees. In other words, the labor market soured on tech workers, giving employers opportunity to wrest back control, Tan suggests.
Second, he points to the drastic effect of agentic AI coding systems on the nature of their work, arguing that these tools have deskilled workers and made everyone much more worried about job security.
“Tech workers had to face these shocks on their own. With a union or some ability to coordinate across workers and bargain as a group, they might’ve had more power to actually push back,” says Tan.
Documenting the past to support the future
Tan enrolled at MIT in 2020, earning a master’s degree at the MIT Media Lab. He is currently a doctoral student in the Department of Urban Studies and Planning with a focus on the political economy of the tech sector.
At various points in their careers, Tan and his co-author had been involved with organizing in the tech sector. Redwine was a prominent organizer in the union drive at Kickstarter. She was fired from the company in 2019; Redwine said her dismissal was retaliation for her organizing activity, while Kickstarter denied that claim. One reason Tan and Redwine wrote this book is because they saw that the bandwidth for labor organizing among tech workers had hit a new low.
“Tech workers want to have a say over the way their technologies are designed,” says Tan. “They want to be able to push for the right guardrails around technologies that they’re building. We wanted to use this book as an opportunity to analyze why it was that, within eight years, the tech worker movement had sort of fallen into this state of paralysis.”
They began writing the book in 2024, reliving the highs and lows of the past decade. This is Tan’s first book. He says writing it was an “exhilarating experience” and one that he profoundly enjoyed.
“It’s why, in part, I’m drawn to academia. To a large extent, I believe in the power of research and of writing. To have the opportunity to do this about a subject that I care deeply about has been an amazing experience.”
A book launch and discussion about “Against Tech Oligarchy,” co-hosted by the Department of Urban Studies and Planning, will take place on Oct. 26.

articles.title: Pentagon partners with CIA’s In-Q-Tel for ‘technology scouting’
articles.description: Pentagon partners with CIA’s In-Q-Tel for ‘technology scouting’ Breaking Defense
articles.description_html: Pentagon partners with CIA’s In-Q-Tel for ‘technology scouting’  Breaking Defense
articles.article_title: Pentagon partners with CIA’s In-Q-Tel for ‘technology scouting’ - Breaking Defense
articles.heading: Pentagon partners with CIA’s In-Q-Tel for ‘technology scouting’
articles.summary: The CIA-funded investment firm, which has helped finance startups from Anduril to Palantir, is now formally coordinating with the Pentagon’s Critical Technologies office.
articles.content:
WASHINGTON — After years of informal cooperation, today the Pentagon’s research and engineering arm announced a formal agreement with the CIA-backed investment firm, In-Q-Tel (IQT), to aid in systematic “technology scouting” for military use.
“Over the next 12 months, our benchmark for success is simple and unambiguous: moving validated commercial prototypes out of the lab and into active operational field evaluations with our combatant commands,” said Michael Dodd, Assistant Secretary for Critical Technologies, in the Pentagon release. Dodd’s organization leads the Pentagon’s side of the partnership, which will focus on the six Critical Technology Areas set by Pentagon CTO Emil Michael 11 months ago: artificial intelligence, biomanufacturing, directed energy (lasers, microwaves, et al), hypersonics, quantum and information technologies, and “contested logistics.”
Although IQT is an investment organization — technically a 501(c)3 non-profit founded by but independent of the CIA — money isn’t the main contribution it’s bringing to this partnership. Indeed, over the last five years of financial filings (2021-2025), IQT current total assets have hovered around $1 billion, less than 1 percent of what the Pentagon spends on Research, Development, Test, & Evaluation (RDTE) in a single year.
But IQT’s early investments often have an outsize impact, helping jumpstart firms as prominent as Anduril and Palantir. Those investments are not only a cash infusion but a vote of confidence that encourages other investors to follow, with IQT boasting that each dollar it invests leads to $40 from other sources.
IQT’s primary mission has been fostering companies to serve the tech needs of the Intelligence Community, with the military as a secondary emphasis. But the new partnership has IQT performing “technology scouting and technical due diligence” for the Defense Department and serving as a feeder into Pentagon development and production pipelines.
“The integration leverages In-Q-Tel’s proven venture capital methodology to vet early-stage commercial solutions that align directly with the Department’s urgent mission requirements,” the announcement says. “By combining CT’s strategic transition pathways with IQT’s deep-tech scouting infrastructure, the partnership aims to significantly de-risk the integration of commercial hardware and software for national security applications, signaling to the commercial tech sector that the Department of War is open for business.”
Said Dodd: “Technological superiority will not be determined by who invents a capability first, but by who delivers it to the warfighter fastest. The Department is fundamentally shifting its posture: we are moving from acting solely as a long-cycle technology developer to operating as an agile, credible, and rapid customer for America’s most innovative non-traditional performers.”
In-Q-Tel was founded in 1999 on the urging of then-CIA director George Tenet. Its name is a reference to the fictional Q who supplies James Bond with high-tech gadgets.

articles.title: Boston class teaching senior citizens how to use technology
articles.description: Boston class teaching senior citizens how to use technology NBC Boston
articles.description_html: Boston class teaching senior citizens how to use technology  NBC Boston
articles.article_title: Boston class teaching senior citizens how to use technology
articles.heading: Boston class teaching senior citizens how to use technology
articles.summary: The computer class is held at Central Boston Elder Services in Roxbury, a nonprofit organization that helps seniors live independently.
articles.content:
Senior citizens in Boston are going high tech -- taking a special class to learn about how to use computers, smart phones, social media and how to protect themselves against scammers.
"I’ve learned how to send emails, I've learned how to Facebook. I’ve learned how to do so many things," said Barbara Stephens.
Stream NBC10 Boston news for free, 24/7, wherever you are.
The class in Roxbury keeps Stephens current on the latest technology, and it helps her communicate with her 8-year-old grandson, too.
"When I get into a problem, I say, 'baby come and help Nana do the computer.' He says, 'Ah Nana, all you gotta do is hit that button right there Nana," she said.
Nina Ruffs teaches the computer class at Central Boston Elder Services in Roxbury. The nonprofit organization helps seniors live independently, and this class is one of the most popular things offered.
"It makes them feel included in the technological world," Ruff said. "There are no stupid questions in this class...Not only is it a good time but they get to ask the questions about technology that they wouldn’t be asking if they were at home."
Not only does the class teach the seniors about how to communicate but it also helps them avoid becoming a victim.
Local
In-depth news coverage of the Greater Boston and New England area.
"I didn’t want to be phished. I didn’t want to be scammed," Dominque Jean said. "I’m protecting myself. And here is teaching you how to protect yourself."
Anyone who wants to sign up for the class can contact Central Boston Elder Services.

articles.summary: Evolv Technologies Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ: EVLV), a leading security technology company pioneering AI-based solutions designed to create safer experiences, today announced that Major League Soccer team, St. Louis CITY SC, has entered a multi-year renewal agreement for Evolv Express®, the company’s people-screening solution. Express has been in use at Energizer
articles.content:
Evolv Technologies Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ: EVLV), a leading security technology company pioneering AI-based solutions designed to create safer experiences, today announced that Major League Soccer team, St. Louis CITY SC, has entered a multi-year renewal agreement for Evolv Express®, the company’s people-screening solution. Express has been in use at Energizer Park, the team’s 22,423-seat home stadium, since its opening in 2023. Nearly two million people have been screened to date using Evolv Express at CITY SC matches and community events.
The renewal, which maintains Evolv’s status as CITY SC’s “Official Fan Screening Partner,” has updated the Express fleet to all Gen2 hardware, which went live in April. Evolv Express uses advanced sensor technology and AI to detect concealed threats and identify the person and location of the potential threat, while allowing people to move through checkpoints at their natural walking pace. The system is designed to screen visitors effectively while helping minimize congestion and disruption to traffic flow at entry points. The new Gen2 hardware adds enhanced mobility, improved camera resolution, and other features to the equipment fleet. Gen2 has progressively been rolling out across North American sports facilities as existing Evolv customers renew, and new teams and venues join Evolv’s roster.
“Since our inaugural season, our partnership with Evolv has helped enhance our fan experience while not compromising safety,” said Matt Sebek, Chief Experience Officer, St. Louis CITY SC. “It’s our goal to make Energizer Park one of the most innovative and efficient stadiums in MLS. Extending our relationship with Evolv and updating our Express units to the latest hardware helps us continue to deliver an efficient arrival experience for our fans and staff from the moment they enter the stadium.”
“CITY SC is another in a growing list of teams and venues that have elected to renew and extend their Express subscription agreement far ahead of the end of the initial term,” said John Baier, Evolv Vice President of Sports & Entertainment. “We’re grateful for the vote of confidence that these renewals illustrate, and appreciate the opportunity to deliver our latest product and enhanced fan arrival experience to hundreds of thousands of St. Louis soccer fans each season.”
The CITY SC renewal is further evidence of Evolv’s strong and stable position in American professional soccer. With other recent additions in MLS, Evolv serves 15 professional soccer teams, a 50% market share. These soccer teams join many other professional sports teams and venues around the world on the Evolv sports and entertainment customer list.

articles.title: Ben Affleck rejects 'propaganda' opposing AI, insists emerging technology will help filmmakers
articles.description: Ben Affleck rejects 'propaganda' opposing AI, insists emerging technology will help filmmakers Fox News

articles.article_title: Ben Affleck rejects 'propaganda' opposing AI, insists emerging technology will help filmmakers
articles.heading: Ben Affleck rejects 'propaganda' opposing AI, insists emerging technology will help filmmakers
articles.summary: Ben Affleck slammed AI "propaganda" while speaking at Bloomberg Screentime 2026, saying he used the technology for "lots of things" for his new film.
articles.content:
LOS ANGELES — Ben Affleck is fed up with what he calls "propaganda" against artificial intelligence as he has become one of Hollywood's most vocal proponents of the emerging technology.
Affleck made headlines in July when it was announced that Netflix paid him a whopping $587 million for his AI startup InterPositive, a venture virtually no one in the industry knew he had been working on.
Appearing Wednesday at the Bloomberg Screentime summit, Affleck was asked about the "cynical take" critics had over the deal, which claimed Netflix bought his company so it can do "despicable things" with AI with a reputable filmmaker attached to "provide cover."
"Well, that's a very cynical view indeed," Affleck reacted to the question.

articles.article_title: Florida State University prepares to host two-day "Google Days" AI and Tech Event
articles.heading: Florida State University prepares to host two-day “Google Days” AI and Tech Event
articles.summary: Florida State University Information Technology Services welcomes Google specialists to campus on Wednesday, Oct. 7 and Thursday, Oct. 8, for "Google
articles.content:
Key Points
- Google specialists will visit campus Oct. 7–8 to introduce emerging artificial intelligence tools to the university community.
- Interactive training sessions will demonstrate how modern technological resources can enhance academic productivity and instructional design.
Florida State University Information Technology Services welcomes Google specialists to campus on Wednesday, Oct. 7 and Thursday, Oct. 8, for “Google Days,” a two-day event featuring hands-on technology demonstrations, emerging AI tools and professional development workshops.
The campuswide event is part of Google for Education and gives students, faculty and staff direct access to the latest advances in Google Workspace, Google Gemini and Gemini Notebook.
Event Schedule and Highlights
Google Tent on the Student Union Green
Oct. 7 and 8 | 10 a.m. – 5 p.m.
Curious about how AI can help you work smarter, study better and create more? Stop by the Google Tent for a hands-on look at Gemini for Google Workspace and Gemini Notebook. You’ll see live demos, explore new ways to enhance your coursework and productivity, chat with Google experts and discover tools designed to support your success at FSU.
Plus, grab some free swag while you’re there!
Gemini Back to School Faculty Training at the Innovation Hub
Oct. 7 | 9 a.m. – 2:45 p.m.
Led by specialists from the Google AI Educator Series, these 45-minute interactive workshops focus on using AI to support teaching, simplify course administration and boost research productivity.
Oct. 7 | 9 – 9:45 a.m. | Faculty Innovator Chat
Kick off Google Day with FSU’s Faculty Innovator Coffee Chat! Join faculty and staff from across campus for an exciting presentation on Google Gemini in Higher Education — then stick around the Innovation Hub for mini-trainings, live Q&A and swag giveaways. The Faculty Innovator Coffee Chats are a recurring conversation series sponsored by the Office of the Provost held every Wednesday morning.
Oct. 7 | 10 – 10:45 a.m. | Teaching & Learning: Create Process-Based Assessments
Explore using Gemini as a creative partner rather than as a shortcut for final deliverables. This session demonstrates how to build process-focused instructional frameworks and design evaluation rubrics that preserve authentic student voice and critical thinking.
Oct. 7 | 11 – 11:45 a.m. | Accelerate Research: Planning the Inquiry
Learn to design course activities using Deep Research — an agentic Gemini feature. Discover how to guide students in automating comprehensive literature searches and synthesizing complex, cited research reviews.
Oct. 7 | 1 – 1:45 p.m. | Teaching & Learning: Create Process-Based Assessments (Repeat Session)
An afternoon offering of the morning session on leveraging Gemini for framework generation, rubric creation and process-oriented student evaluation.
Oct. 7 | 2 – 2:45 p.m. | Accelerate Research: Planning the Inquiry (Repeat Session)
An afternoon offering of the morning session on incorporating Gemini’s Deep Research tool into academic research workflows and course design.
Workshop Attendee Requirements & Certification
BYOD Requirement: Workshop participants must bring a fully charged laptop or tablet for hands-on exercises.
Earn Official Credentials: Attendees can earn official digital badges through the Google AI Educator Series portal by enrolling before their session.
Pre-registration is required for workshop attendance and digital badge tracking. Faculty, staff and students can reserve their preferred sessions directly through the Google Days Event Registration Portal.

articles.title: Is Technology Redefining Sovereignty?
articles.description: Is Technology Redefining Sovereignty? The National Interest
articles.description_html: Is Technology Redefining Sovereignty?  The National Interest
articles.article_title: Is Technology Redefining Sovereignty?
articles.heading: Is Technology Redefining Sovereignty?
articles.summary: History shows that states eventually subordinate or incorporate strategic and highly profitable entities.
articles.content:
Is Technology Redefining Sovereignty?
History shows that states eventually subordinate or incorporate strategic and highly profitable entities.
Nvidia is not a country. It has no territory, citizens, army, flag, or seat at the United Nations. It is a US technology company best known for designing the advanced computer chips that power the artificial intelligence revolution. Yet in the first three months of 2026 alone, Nvidia generated roughly $60 billion in profit. If sustained, that totals around $240 billion a year. Iraq, a country with one of the world’s largest oil reserves, maintains a $100 billion annual budget. And Nvidia is only one of a handful of American technology giants whose profits are approaching the scale of national budgets and economies. Taken together, Nvidia, SpaceX, Microsoft, Apple, Google, Amazon, and Meta are on track to generate hundreds of billions of dollars in annual profits, approaching $1 trillion.
So what does it mean when corporations can generate more revenues and profits in a year than the governments of entire countries? Nvidia has enormous financial resources without sovereignty. Iraq, as a case in point, has sovereignty without anything approaching Nvidia’s financial or technological resources.
In Iraq, sovereignty has always been a primordial political question. Foreign intervention, occupation, and the struggle for control over territory and political institutions have made the question central to the country’s modern history. The digital age adds another layer, forcing Iraq and other states to reconsider what sovereignty means when new forms of power lie beyond the state’s direct control.
For centuries, power rested on controlling territory, commanding populations, and raising armies. After the 1648 Treaty of Westphalia, the modern nation-state became the dominant political unit because it could mobilize resources on a scale individuals and private companies could not match. This model is arguably eroding as states come to rely on corporations to exercise power.
The largest technology companies operate infrastructure spanning continents, control communications platforms used by billions, and possess pools of capital that rival the resources of states. They also control technologies on which modern economies and militaries depend. But technological dependence does not necessarily mean a loss of sovereignty. Hasan S. Alkhatib, who served as advisor to the prime minister of Iraq for digital transformation and Telecommunications from 2023 to 2026, argued in an interview with the authors that no modern country can realistically be technologically self-sufficient. He says the more useful concept is digital sovereignty. That is, “the ability of the state to retain control, choice and resilience over the digital systems on which its government, economy and national security depend.”
The digital domain includes data, communications, computing infrastructure, digital identity, cybersecurity, and artificial intelligence.
In Iraq, this new infrastructure is already impacting geopolitics. Alongside its oil pipelines, Iraqi telecom company IQ Group has built the Silk Route Transit, a terrestrial fiber-optic cable network carrying data out of the Gulf toward Europe, a 21st-century version of the telegraph lines that once linked the British Empire. Major US hyperscalers have purchased capacity on the route, providing a crucial alternative to vulnerable submarine cables. Iraq’s old strategic geography was built around moving goods. The movement of data is redrawing its geography.
But, Alkhatib cautions, “geography alone does not create digital sovereignty.” Fiber-optic cables may cross Iraqi territory, but their strategic value to Iraq depends on who owns and operates the infrastructure, where the data is processed, who controls the network, which legal jurisdiction governs it, and whether Iraq develops domestic technical capabilities around that infrastructure. “Done correctly,” he argues, “Iraq’s emergence as a data corridor could therefore strengthen rather than weaken its sovereignty.”
The Silk Route Transit is an almost perfect metaphor for the transition underway. An infrastructure corridor built through a sovereign state can simultaneously serve the needs of corporations whose reach extends far beyond that state. In other words, the state operates through the corporation, while the corporation increasingly operates beyond the state.
“Iraq does not need to manufacture its own AI processors, satellites or cloud platforms to remain sovereign, any more than it must manufacture every aircraft or power turbine it operates,” says Alkhatib, emphasizing the importance of Iraq retaining effective control over how these technologies operate within the country.
What makes today’s technology giants different from traditional multinationals is that their decisions can reverberate through national economies, information ecosystems, elections, telecommunications networks and global supply chains. Their technologies are embedded in military and national security systems. Governments may still have the legal power to regulate them, but regulation is more complicated when the state itself depends on the companies it seeks to control.
A government can impose rules on a cloud provider, for example, but what happens when that same cloud infrastructure supports its public services, intelligence systems or military operations? The same dilemma applies to AI chips, satellite networks and digital communications. The relationship becomes one of asymmetrical dependence.
A historical parallel appears in the East India Company. As historian William Dalrymple has argued, it began as a commercial enterprise. Eventually, it acquired an army, controlled territory in India, administered populations, collected taxes, negotiated with rulers, and exercised powers that resembled sovereignty. Today’s technology companies are not chartered colonial powers, but some are accumulating capabilities once associated almost exclusively with states. SpaceX, for instance, has no army, but its Starlink network is indispensable to modern warfare and communications, particularly in Ukraine, while its launch capabilities give it extraordinary access to space. Its Starships might be what the East India Company’s ships were to maritime trade.
Add artificial intelligence, Grok, satellite communications, and other social media technologies, like X (formerly Twitter), which could affect US electoral outcomes, all controlled by the same entrepreneur. The concentration of power becomes substantial, akin to a character from a James Bond film. Elon Musk is not a modern East India Company governor-general, and SpaceX is not a state. But technology is allowing private corporations to acquire capabilities that can give them influence over governments, militaries and societies on a scale that would have been unimaginable for a private company a generation ago.
“This undoubtedly gives these companies significant influence,” says Alkhatib. “However, influence should not automatically be interpreted as sovereignty. The decisive issue is whether a state has alternatives.”
Iraq brings the argument back down to earth. Much of the media discourse about Iraq still revolves around Iran-backed militias and American strategic interests, eclipsing developments in which Iraqi companies are helping build the infrastructure that is positioning Iraq within the global digital economy. Nvidia’s profits dwarf Iraq’s national budget, and it must defend its sovereignty in a digital environment whose infrastructure and technologies are beyond the state’s control.
Cybercrime is already threatening Iraqi commerce, critical infrastructure, and political institutions, while weaknesses in digital systems leave essential sectors exposed. Iraq has responded by treating cybersecurity as a national security issue and strengthening its institutional capacity to confront it.
This creates the central paradox. Iraq is sovereign, but sovereignty does not mean technological autonomy. A state can control its borders and still be vulnerable to attacks on the networks that keep its electricity, communications, health systems, and economy functioning. It can possess the legal authority to regulate technology while depending on technologies developed and controlled elsewhere. In the digital age, sovereignty depends not only on the ability to command, but on the ability to secure the infrastructure through which that command is exercised.
For Alkhatib, the practical dividing line is replaceability. “If Iraq can procure technology from multiple suppliers, move workloads between platforms, maintain strategic data within its jurisdiction, regulate providers effectively, develop national technical expertise and preserve alternative communications routes,” he argues, “then the relationship remains largely one of economic and technological interdependence.” But if a critical government function becomes dependent upon a single proprietary platform that Iraq cannot operate, audit, replace or continue without the provider’s cooperation, “then dependence begins to translate into political power.”
This does not mean the nation-state is in its death throes. States still ultimately possess the legal authority to regulate or dismantle companies. The United States can break up a corporation, seize its assets, restrict its exports, or impose sanctions. But here’s the paradox. Governments increasingly need the very companies they are supposed to regulate. They rely on private firms for cloud computing, advanced chips, satellite communications, artificial intelligence, and other critical infrastructure.
Iraq should therefore not respond by isolating itself from global technology. As Alkhatib puts it, that would slow its development considerably. Instead, he advocates what he calls “strategic technological interdependence”—aggressively adopting the world’s best technologies while deliberately retaining national control over critical data, architecture, regulation, cybersecurity, and strategic decision-making.
The old measure of state power was the ability to command resources. The emerging problem is that a state can possess sovereignty while lacking control over the infrastructure through which it exercises that sovereignty. The nation-state has not disappeared. It has become dependent.
So is Nvidia more powerful than Iraq? Of course not. But that is the wrong question. The more important question is whether Iraq, or any other sovereign state, can exercise all the powers of a modern state without depending on technologies and infrastructures controlled elsewhere—the ultimate sovereignty dilemma. Nvidia does not need to become a country to change what state power means.
The East India Company once showed what happens when a corporation becomes powerful enough to behave like a state. It becomes part of the state. The British government assumed the company’s political control in India in 1858 after the rebellion of the previous year, and the company itself dissolved in 1874. Within the looming international order, states are likely to remain powerful, but may have to share the stage with corporations that control the infrastructure through which power is exercised. Technology is redefining sovereignty, but it is not eliminating it.
About the Authors: Tanya Goudsouzian and Ibrahim al-Marashi
Tanya Goudsouzian is a Canadian journalist who has covered Afghanistan and the Middle East for over two decades. She has held senior editorial roles at major international media outlets, including serving as opinion editor at Al Jazeera English. Her work has also appeared in The National Interest, Responsible Statecraft, War on the Rocks, The New Arab, and Engelsberg Ideas.
Ibrahim al-Marashi is an associate professor of Middle East history at California State University, on the board of the International Security and Conflict Resolution (ISCOR) program at San Diego State University, and a visiting faculty member at The American College of the Mediterranean and the Department of International Relations at Central European University. His publications include Iraq’s Armed Forces: An Analytical History (2008), The Modern History of Iraq (2017), and A Concise History of the Middle East (2024).

Instead, he advocates what he calls “strategic technological interdependence”—aggressively adopting the world’s best technologies while deliberately retaining national control over critical data, architecture, regulation, cybersecurity, and strategic decision-making.

The old measure of state power was the ability to command resources. The emerging problem is that a state can possess sovereignty while lacking control over the infrastructure through which it exercises that sovereignty. The nation-state has not disappeared. It has become dependent.

So is Nvidia more powerful than Iraq? Of course not. But that is the wrong question. The more important question is whether Iraq, or any other sovereign state, can exercise all the powers of a modern state without depending on technologies and infrastructures controlled elsewhere—the ultimate sovereignty dilemma. Nvidia does not need to become a country to change what state power means.

The East India Company once showed what happens when a corporation becomes powerful enough to behave like a state. It becomes part of the state. The British government assumed the company’s political control in India in 1858 after the rebellion of the previous year, and the company itself dissolved in 1874. Within the looming international order, states are likely to remain powerful, but may have to share the stage with corporations that control the infrastructure through which power is exercised. Technology is redefining sovereignty, but it is not eliminating it.

About the Authors: Tanya Goudsouzian and Ibrahim al-Marashi

Tanya Goudsouzian is a Canadian journalist who has covered Afghanistan and the Middle East for over two decades. She has held senior editorial roles at major international media outlets, including serving as opinion editor at Al Jazeera English. Her work has also appeared in The National Interest, Responsible Statecraft, War on the Rocks, The New Arab, and Engelsberg Ideas.

Ibrahim al-Marashi is an associate professor of Middle East history at California State University, on the board of the International Security and Conflict Resolution (ISCOR) program at San Diego State University, and a visiting faculty member at The American College of the Mediterranean and the Department of International Relations at Central European University. His publications include Iraq’s Armed Forces: An Analytical History (2008), The Modern History of Iraq (2017), and A Concise History of the Middle East (2024).

articles.summary: The company combines artificial intelligence with human review to help users organize information and assemble documentation.
articles.content:
How VetClaims.ai Uses Technology to Support Veterans With Claims Preparation
Applying for veterans’ disability benefits can involve gathering records, organizing supporting information, and completing detailed forms. VetClaims.ai offers a technology-assisted service intended to help veterans prepare their claims before submitting them to the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA).
The VA administers benefits and services for millions of veterans, their families, caregivers, and survivors. Veterans seeking disability compensation may prepare a claim independently or obtain help from accredited representatives, including Veterans Service Organization representatives, attorneys, and claims agents. VetClaims.ai positions its service as an additional claims-preparation option rather than a replacement for the VA or an accredited representative.
The company combines artificial intelligence with human review to help users organize information and assemble documentation. Its stated role relates specifically to preparing materials for submission; it does not provide medical care or determine whether a veteran qualifies for benefits. Decisions regarding eligibility and compensation remain with the VA.
A Technology-Assisted Preparation Process
VetClaims.ai says its platform was developed to make the administrative preparation process more manageable. Veterans provide information relevant to their claims, after which the company’s technology helps organize the material for review. According to the company, every prepared claim is also reviewed by a person before it is made ready for the veteran to file.
This model is intended to help users identify relevant information and present it in an organized format. It does not guarantee that a claim will be approved, shorten the VA’s official processing time, or influence the benefits decision. The time required and outcome can vary according to the individual claim, the available evidence and the VA’s review process.
VetClaims.ai charges a flat fee for its preparation service rather than a commission based on a veteran’s eventual benefits award. Prospective customers should review the company’s service terms carefully so that they understand its scope, fees and limitations before proceeding.
Developing an Additional Claims-Support Option
Veterans have several possible sources of claims assistance. Alongside self-filing, they may seek support from VA-accredited attorneys, claims agents, and Veterans Service Organization representatives. VetClaims.ai operates within this broader landscape by offering administrative and technology-assisted preparation.
The company reports that it has worked with more than 55,000 veterans. It also states that claims prepared through its service take approximately 14 days from intake to a ready-to-file stage and average 1.8 claim cycles. These are company-reported operational figures and should not be interpreted as guarantees of individual processing times, approval or benefit amounts.
VetClaims.ai also reports creating more than 400 employment opportunities for veterans. The involvement of veterans in its workforce may provide the company with insight into some of the practical questions and concerns users encounter while preparing claims.
Understanding the Service’s Scope
The distinction between claims preparation and representation is an important one. VetClaims.ai states that it helps customers organize and prepare claims but does not represent them before the VA. The company describes its service as AI-assisted preparation with human review, offered for a flat fee.
Veterans who want formal representation or advice about their individual legal rights can consult the VA’s accreditation resources to locate a recognized attorney, claims agent or Veterans Service Organization representative. Clearly communicating these different roles allows users to decide which form of assistance best suits their circumstances.
VetClaims.ai cannot determine an applicant’s eligibility, approve a claim or control the VA’s review timeline. Its service is limited to the stage preceding submission, with the veteran retaining responsibility for filing the materials and communicating with the VA unless the veteran separately appoints an accredited representative.
Supporting a Detailed Administrative Process
Digital tools are increasingly being used to help people organize documents and complete administrative procedures. Within the veterans’ benefits field, VetClaims.ai applies this approach to claims preparation while maintaining human review as part of its process.
For veterans considering the platform, its potential value lies in administrative organization rather than any promised outcome. The service may offer another way to prepare information for filing, while the VA remains responsible for reviewing claims and making benefits decisions. By defining its role carefully and presenting its reported results with appropriate context, VetClaims.ai can explain its offering without overstating what claims-preparation technology can accomplish.

articles.summary: A new Chamber report finds AI use is leading to small business job growth.
articles.content:
A new Chamber report finds AI use is leading to small business job growth.

2026 Empowering Small Business Report

- Download

Published

October 02, 2026

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce Technology Engagement Center (C_TEC) report Empowering Small Business: The Impact of Technology on U.S. Small Business examines the pivotal role that diverse technology platforms play in helping small businesses operate and compete.

This 5th edition, introduced in 2026, continues our nationwide analysis of U.S. small businesses, exploring the various types and applications of technology used by small businesses, how these factors have changed over time, and the effects of these trends on enterprises and the economy at large.

Key Findings

- AI is a job growth engine for small businesses: 47% say AI is creating jobs today, while 6% say it is enabling headcount reductions.

- U.S. small businesses run on technology: Nearly 100% of small businesses report using at least 1 technology platform at work.

- High-rate technology adoption is accelerating: 41% now use 6+ platforms, up 9 points from 2025 and nearly 3 times the 2022 level.

- 2/3 of small businesses now use AI. (66%), up 8 points from 2025 and nearly 3 times the share using it in 2023 (23%).

- Small businesses using AI outpace non-AI enabled businesses and are at least 7 points more likely to report sales, profit, and workforce growth.

- 95% of small businesses using AI are working to upskill employees, including 47% providing on-the-job training.

- 84% plan to increase their use of technology over the next 2–3 years, including businesses at every current adoption level.

- AI has become operationally important: 78% of users say limiting access would slow growth, and 75% say it would hurt their bottom line.

- Six in ten small businesses worry about increased litigation and compliance costs from a patchwork of state privacy and AI laws.

- Technology intensity continues to correlate with stronger business performance: Businesses using 2+ platforms are roughly 10 points more likely than low-tech businesses to report growth in sales, profits, and employment.

- Inflation continues to be the top small business challenge, cited by 32% and up 9 points from 2025.

articles.description: Oak View Group Names Cisco as Official Technology Partner for Infrastructure Management Across OVG's Venue Network sportsvideo.org

articles.heading: Oak View Group Names Cisco as Official Technology Partner for Infrastructure Management Across OVG's Venue Network
articles.summary: Oak View Group (OVG) has announced Cisco as an Official Technology Partner. Through the partnership, OVG will look to standardize its technological infrastructure on Cisco’s industry-leading solutions across its expansive...
articles.content:
Oak View Group (OVG) has announced Cisco as an Official Technology Partner. Through the partnership, OVG will look to standardize its technological infrastructure on Cisco’s industry-leading solutions across its expansive venue network, building an AI-ready, scalable foundation capable of growing with their business.
“A seamless, exceptional guest experience across our ecosystem of operations is at the forefront of every decision we make at OVG Venues,” says Katee LaPoff, Chief Technology Officer, OVG. “Our strategic technology partnership with Cisco enables greater consistency, reliability, and a leading-edge experience for the teams, talent, and guests across our venues. We’re excited to continue expanding our partnership with Cisco and harness the power of technology to unlock new possibilities for live events.”
Through the agreement, Cisco will also become an Official Partner of five prominent OVG venues – Climate Pledge Arena (Seattle), UBS Arena (New York), Moody Center (Austin,TX), Acrisure Arena (Palm Desert, CA) and CFG Bank Arena (Baltimore).
“Managing a vast, global network of premier venues requires a partner who understands both the scale and the complexity of modern live entertainment,” says Anne Ristau, Cisco’s Head of Global Sponsorships. “We are proud to work alongside OVG to deliver a consistent, high-performance technology backbone across their entire portfolio. This collaboration allows OVG to focus on what they do best—creating unforgettable moments—while we offer a highly secure, reliable, and builtto-scale infrastructure.”
Climate Pledge Arena, UBS Arena, and CFG Bank Arena each currently deploy a wide range of Cisco solutions across enterprise networking, data center, security, collaboration and more, while Moody Center and Acrisure Arena will be outfitted with updated Cisco technology throughout the course of the partnership.
“If you look at the world-class brands we do business with across our OVG enterprise—AMEX, UBS, Oracle, Verizon, KraftHeinz, Lyft, and others, Cisco is a natural fit,” says Dan Griffis, President, Global Partnerships, Oak View Group. “Cisco, like OVG, is aspirational, innovative and trusted. We are excited to build marketing programs together that transcend sports and entertainment.”
Oak View Group joins an esteemed list of marquee sports and entertainment organizations, teams, events and venues around the world that rely on Cisco technology and expertise, including McLaren Mastercard Formula 1 Team, Real Madrid F.C., United States Golf Association (USGA), Live Nation Entertainment, Madison Square Garden and many more.

When the Artemis astronauts step onto the lunar surface, they will have spent considerable time and effort installing themselves in their bulky, heavy spacesuits. They will lumber onto the surface having limited mobility and time, struggling to accomplish their assigned tasks. Their activities will kick up clinging, razor-sharp lunar dust that they will invariably carry back into their capsule on their suits. WISeSat.Space Ordinary Shares to Begin Trading on Nasdaq on October 2

Listing Marks a New Chapter in the Company's Mission to Bring Cybersecurity to Space and Deliver Trusted Satellite Connectivity

WISeSat.Space to Celebrate Milestone with Nasdaq Opening Bell Ceremony on October 9

GENEVA, Switzerland, October 2, 2026 -- WISeSat.Space Holdings Corp. (Nasdaq: SAIQ) ("WISeSat.Space"), a space technology company focused on PQC secure satellite communications and Internet of Things connectivity, announced on October 1, 2026 that it completed on that date its previously announced business combination ("Business Combination") with Columbus Acquisition Corp ("CAC"), a publicly traded special purpose acquisition company. The Business Combination was approved by CAC's shareholders at an extraordinary general meeting held on September 30, 2026. Effective today, October 2, 2026, WISeSat.Space's ordinary shares will begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "SAIQ".

To celebrate this achievement, Carlos Moreira, Founder, Chairman and CEO of WISeSat.Space and its parent company, WISeQey Corp ("WISeQey"), is scheduled to ring the Nasdaq Opening Bell ceremony on Friday, October 9, 2026, at Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City's Times Square.

The Nasdaq listing supports the Company's ambition to expand its space infrastructure while leveraging WISeQey's expertise in cybersecurity, digital identity and secure semiconductors. WISeSat.Space's mission is to extend trusted connectivity beyond terrestrial networks, enabling connected devices to communicate securely through satellite infrastructure.

"Nasdaq listing represents an extraordinary milestone for WISeSat.Space and for everyone who has contributed to this journey," said Mr. Moreira. "I want to thank our employees, management team, technology partners, advisors, investors and all those whose dedication has made this achievement possible. Their commitment has helped turn our vision of bringing cybersecurity to space into a growing business."

Mr. Moreira continued: "As more devices and essential services rely on satellite connectivity, trust and PQC security must be built into the infrastructure from the outset. Our ambition is to combine satellite communications with digital identity, secure chips and post-quantum technologies to help protect data from the connected device to the space network. This listing opens a new chapter in advancing that mission."

Bringing Cybersecurity to Space WISeSat.Space has deployed satellites into orbit since 2024 and is developing satellite connectivity designed to support secure communications for connected devices, including applications in remote monitoring, logistics, defense, and infrastructure management.

Working within the WISeKey technology ecosystem, including collaboration with it sister company SEALSQ Corp (Nasdaq: LAES), the Company aims to integrate hardware-based security, device authentication and post-quantum protection into its satellite communications architecture. These capabilities are intended to help address both today's cybersecurity threats and the evolving risks associated with future quantum computing.

Nasdaq Opening Bell Ceremony The celebration is currently scheduled to take place on Friday, October 9, 2026, with the Nasdaq Opening Bell at 9:30 a.m. Eastern Time / 3:30 p.m. Swiss time. The ceremony will recognize the teams and partners behind WISeSat.Space's development and its mission to build trusted connectivity for an increasingly connected world.

Advisors Maxim Group LLC served as WISeSat.Space's financial advisor. Ellenoff Grossman & Schole LLP represented WISeSat.Space as legal counsel and Harney Westwood & Riegels (BVI) LP represented WISeSat.Space as British Virgin Islands legal counsel. Loeb & Loeb LLP represented CAC as legal counsel and Ogier represented CAC as Cayman legal counsel. The Equity Group, Inc., served as WISeSat's strategic communications advisor.

About WISeSat.Space WISeSat.Space Holdings Corp. is a space technology company focused on secure satellite communications for Internet of Things applications. Its approach combines satellite infrastructure with cybersecurity and digital identity technologies to support trusted communications between connected devices and ground-based systems.

Listing Marks a New Chapter in the Company's Mission to Bring Cybersecurity to Space and Deliver Trusted Satellite Connectivity

WISeSat.Space to Celebrate Milestone with Nasdaq Opening Bell Ceremony on October 9

GENEVA, Switzerland, October 2, 2026 -- WISeSat.Space Holdings Corp. (Nasdaq: SAIQ) ("WISeSat.Space"), a space technology company focused on PQC secure satellite communications and Internet of Things connectivity, announced on October 1, 2026 that it completed on that date its previously announced business combination ("Business Combination") with Columbus Acquisition Corp ("CAC"), a publicly traded special purpose acquisition company. The Business Combination was approved by CAC's shareholders at an extraordinary general meeting held on September 30, 2026. Effective today, October 2, 2026, WISeSat.Space's ordinary shares will begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "SAIQ".

To celebrate this achievement, Carlos Moreira, Founder, Chairman and CEO of WISeSat.Space and its parent company, WISeQey Corp ("WISeQey"), is scheduled to ring the Nasdaq Opening Bell ceremony on Friday, October 9, 2026, at Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City's Times Square.

The Nasdaq listing supports the Company's ambition to expand its space infrastructure while leveraging WISeQey's expertise in cybersecurity, digital identity and secure semiconductors. WISeSat.Space's mission is to extend trusted connectivity beyond terrestrial networks, enabling connected devices to communicate securely through satellite infrastructure.

"Nasdaq listing represents an extraordinary milestone for WISeSat.Space and for everyone who has contributed to this journey," said Mr. Moreira. "I want to thank our employees, management team, technology partners, advisors, investors and all those whose dedication has made this achievement possible. Their commitment has helped turn our vision of bringing cybersecurity to space into a growing business."

Mr. Moreira continued: "As more devices and essential services rely on satellite connectivity, trust and PQC security must be built into the infrastructure from the outset. Our ambition is to combine satellite communications with digital identity, secure chips and post-quantum technologies to help protect data from the connected device to the space network. articles.heading: Aurora town hall with area police leaders focuses on camera technology and fentanyl laws
articles.summary: "Law enforcement has become kind of a catch-all for every system that has failed, whether that's homelessness or mental health, ... and that's not working" — Todd Chamberlain
articles.content:
AURORA | Aurora and regional law enforcement officials at a town hall discussion backed surveillance technology, tough fentanyl penalties and the need for more resources to support community mental health and reduce recidivism.
Arapahoe County Sheriff Tyler Brown, Douglas County Sheriff Darren Weekly and Aurora Police Chief Todd Chamberlain spoke at the Sept. 30 town hall meeting held by the Arapahoe County chapter of Colorado Citizenry. The newly formed group plans to offer political and civic engagement events, which the group says are non-partisan, although organizers promoted some conservative political candidates before the panel discussion began at the Angry Clover pub in Aurora.
Both Brown, a Democrat, and Weekly, a Republican, are up for reelection this November. Chamberlain’s position is unelected, and he was appointed by the Aurora city manager.
The conversation was moderated by Colorado Springs and Denver Gazette political columnist Jimmy Sengenberger. The event covered a variety of topics, including police recruitment, dropping crime rates and recently proposed and passed legislation, though a large portion of the discussion focused on police technology and responding to mental health issues and drug crimes.
All three police leaders agreed on the importance of technology, like automated license plate readers, which they said are a crucial tool for solving crimes. Chamberlain highlighted the recent assistance of traffic cameras in identifying a suspect in a fatal hit-and-run. He said the cameras help police be more precise and timely.
“If we get a car that’s involved in a hit-and-run, and it’s a black Chevy truck, we’re going to be out stopping every Chevy truck,” Chamberlain said. “Instead, we can get an ALPR hit on that car and (search for) damage on the right front corner panels or by part of the license plate. Then an officer can do the human component of following up.”
Brown called the tech a “silver bullet” for addressing crimes such as car theft and noted how it bolsters police capacity. In Arapahoe County, Brown said 46 ALPR cameras cover roughly 4,600 yards of roadway.
“It would take me about 200 deputies to collect all those photos that the ALPR cameras do on any given day but instead I can do it for $60,000 and 46 cameras,” Brown said. “We’re able to recover stolen vehicles. We’re able to get information on people as they set up to distribute illegal narcotics. We’re able to find at-risk individuals who go missing.”
The men acknowledged privacy and misuse concerns, but said guardrails can be put in place to minimize those issues, while still allowing police to utilize the crime-solving tech.
“I hope it doesn’t turn into throwing the baby out with bathwater,” Chamberlain said. “We can’t go back. This technology is so incredibly important and so imperative in what it allows us to do, especially in times of staffing issues. This is a force multiplier.”
Chamberlain said the tools can give “a voice to the voiceless,” pointing to an incident where a car was stolen in Denver with a baby in the back. Aurora police found the car within two hours, abandoned in an alley, thanks to cameras, which Chamberlain said saved the baby’s life.
Another hot topic the group discussed is the rise of fentanyl use and Proposition 132, a ballot measure which seeks to implement mandatory minimum sentences for possession and distribution of any amount of fentanyl.
Weekly highlighted his support of the measure, saying it’s needed to impose real penalties and give enforcement “teeth.” He said jails often provide resources for substance abuse.
“Sometimes an addict is safer on the inside than they are on the outside. And, again, I think there needs to be consequences for those decisions,” Weekly said. “Yes, they’re a user and they need help but guess what? That stint in jail might be the catalyst they need to get clean.”
Brown agreed, saying he advocates for a system that prosecutes people for possessing or distributing fentanyl, but also allows people who successfully complete treatment to have their records expunged.
“If you’re a user and you’re trying to get yourself better, we have compassionate accountability. We can do that through our system,” Brown said. “But drug dealers? No thank you, I don’t have time for them. We have to hold them accountable to the fullest extent.”
Chamberlain said accountability for drug crimes has been “watered down,” pointing to advocacy for safe consumption sites and free Narcan.
“I think that as long as we continue to make it where users can have it and it can be done in a secure location and a place that makes everybody feel good, I think this problem will never go away,” Chamberlain said.
The law enforcement officials’ support for Proposition 132 is in contrast with the opinions of several district attorneys who came out against the measure, including Arapahoe County DA Amy Padden. The Aurora City Council also formally opposed Proposition 132.
Research, while limited, has shown that safe consumption sites can lower infection and overdose rates and increase access to treatment, though it’s less clear if the sites reduce drug use.
When it comes to the intersection of public safety and mental health, Brown, Chamberlain and Weekly said law enforcement has come a long way in how to handle crises and working with professionals, but they also cautioned against relying on police and jails to be the main solution when other social safety nets fail.
The group praised their teams dedicated to responding to mental health calls, which include police officers and mental health clinicians, while advocating for more investments in mental health institutions.
“Law enforcement has become kind of a catch-all for every system that has failed, whether that’s homelessness or mental health, … and that’s not working,” Chamberlain said, noting three recent officer-involved shootings in Aurora have included someone experiencing a mental health crisis.
Brown said he feels that sheriffs run many of the state’s mental health facilities because jails often provide healthcare services. He estimated that of 800 people detained at the county jail, 65% will report a mental health issue or substance use disorder.
“That’s where people fall,” he said. “The state forensic hospital is not equipped to handle the amount of people we have right now.”
The discussion ended with Brown, Chamberlain and Weekly encouraging the audience to share what they learned with other community members and thanking the group for supporting police.
