articles.article_title: ACSD1 candidates weigh funding, technology and student well-being
articles.heading: ACSD1 candidates weigh funding, technology and student well-being
articles.summary: Five candidates for the Albany County School District 1 Board of Trustees discussed fiscal situations, technology, public trust and student well-being during a recent forum co-sponsored by the League of
articles.content:
Five candidates for the Albany County School District 1 Board of Trustees discussed fiscal situations, technology, public trust and student well-being during a recent forum co-sponsored by the League of Women Voters of Laramie and Albany County Public Library.
Moderator Carrie Bennett and League co-President Matthew Link delivered brief statements before Bennett questioned candidates Beth Bear, Abe Lentner, Jessica Taylor, J. James Learned and Sarah Roberts. At-large candidate Carrie Murthy could not attend but submitted a recorded introduction.
Families and parents
When asked about what families may not understand when the board makes difficult decisions, all candidates answered similarly.
Lentner said parents are usually their children’s best advocates, but they may not have all the information needed to decide for the whole district. He said trustees must bring the right people together, share information and listen closely, adding, “If I can’t stand behind them, I shouldn’t be making them.”
Taylor agreed that parents know their children well, however, she added that the district must serve every student, including those without support at home or parents who will not speak up for them. She also said the board must listen to the people who will be directly affected by a decision and explain limits created by the Wyoming Legislature.
Learned said parents are right to speak with passion and expect the board to listen. However, most decisions are not simple choices, and helping one group of students may require the district to reduce something for another group. He said the district should talk with the public before bills reach the governor’s desk, not after the decisions have already been made.
Roberts said parents can get stuck in “a little bit of an echo chamber” with people who share their views and that a choice that is best for one child may not be best for another. She said many board decisions are also forced by state rules.
Bear said community involvement is important because residents bring new ideas and show that they care. However, funding laws and other legal rules are hard to understand, adding that the district should explain those limits more clearly and involve the public before major decisions are made.
Online technology
Questions addressing screen time, privacy, online safety and artificial intelligence (AI) also arose during the conversation.
Taylor said the district should be careful and use research before increasing technology in classrooms. Technology can help students, but it can also reduce creativity and face-to-face contact. She added that students must learn how to think carefully about information created by AI.
Learned said increased screen time has hurt students’ attention spans. He is especially concerned when AI replaces a student’s own thinking or writing. Still, he said students must learn how to use it. “It can either warm you or it can burn you,” he said.
Roberts said technology cannot simply be removed because it is part of daily life and that schools should teach safety, responsibility and honesty. Students also need to understand that material placed online may stay there forever, but at the same time, schools should make room for conversations, creativity and pencil-and-paper work.
Bear said the district has already created a group of parents, teachers and technology staff to study AI and other technology and said the district has screen-time limits and policies for technology use. She encouraged families to review the policies and provide feedback.
Lentner said technology has changed quickly, but human relationships remain most important. He said teachers understand how students use technology in the classroom, so the board should listen to educators and give them the tools to teach responsible use.
Funding
The query of how candidates would respond to changes in state funding, possible property-tax cuts and rules limiting how certain education funds can be spent had varying responses.
Learned said he would first consult the district’s business manager and attorney. He rejected the idea that the board can solve every problem by making small cuts.
“You cannot trim your way into prosperity, ever,” he said. The board must understand what money is available and what legal limits control its use.
Roberts said the district will need creative solutions and more freedom to move money where it is needed and also said voters need better information about how elections affect education funding. In the short term, the district may need to use reserve money.
Bear said the district has already combined schools, removed buildings and made many cuts. Reserves helped protect programs and activities, but declining enrollment remains a major problem. She said the district should fight for full state funding and ask lawmakers to remove funding “silos” that limit local choices.
Lentner said the budget should be based on clear goals, not only numbers on a spreadsheet. The district should fight for programs the community values, including special education and activities. It must also protect students and families who do not have a strong public voice.
Taylor said she would depend on the district’s financial experts because finance is not her main area of experience. Her first priority would be protecting teachers and staff. She said the district should seek local control and cut expenses before cutting strong educators.
Bonus round
During a bonus round, Roberts and Bear passed on the opportunity to answer. Lentner used his time to say that his son has received strong special education support, though his family has also faced difficult meetings and uneven service. He wants every school to provide strong support for vulnerable students.
Taylor said teacher and staff burnout is a serious concern. She praised staff members who know students and families personally and said the district must keep them from leaving.
Learned agreed that the district must protect everyone who works with students. He included teachers, paraprofessionals and custodians because each one affects a student’s school experience.
School choice
Several different responses were voiced when candidates were asked what the district should do when families choose either private, religious, home or charter schools.
Roberts said that families must choose what is best for their children. Public schools can compete by supporting teachers and showing families the programs they offer, including Nordic skiing, gifted education and language courses.
Bear also supported family choice and said the district should promote its career and technical education courses, electives, college-credit classes, sports and activities. She also wants the district to contact families before their children reach preschool age.
Lentner said strong programs matter, but schools must also create a sense of community and board members can help families feel connected to their schools and to one another.
Taylor said public schools give children the chance to learn with classmates from many backgrounds, but warned that moving students with strong family support into certain schools may increase unfair differences between schools. She said the district should invest in every school.
Learned said public schools have trained teachers who understand their subjects, student behavior and teaching methods. He said those professionals are the strongest advantage public schools have.
Student safety and support
Questions concerning drugs, concussions, students dropping out and other threats to student safety were also asked to the candidates during the forum.
Bear answered that every student and staff member should feel included. Clubs, sports and activities can give students a reason to attend school and adults who check on them. She also discussed school climate surveys, mental-health programs, suicide awareness and school resource officers who build relationships with students.
Lentner said one of the best protections for a child is a trusted adult outside the family and he went on to detail coaches, teachers and activity leaders who can become mentors, notice problems and help students seek support.
Taylor focused on concussions and communication with parents saying that schools should quickly report possible injuries and follow concussion rules. She also supported counselors and social workers who build close relationships with students. In addition, she wants schools to teach practical skills, such as handling taxes.
Learned said drugs and mental health are major issues that schools must prepare to address. Schools may need more specialized counselors. He said educators must understand the whole child and “form relationships before we implement rigor.”
Roberts said her mentoring program shows how relationships keep students involved, explaining that an older student can check on a younger student’s grades, encourage attendance and help that student stay away from drugs. She added that students are more likely to attend when they know someone is looking out for them.
Conflicts of interest
Bennett also asked how candidates would keep family ties and personal interests from affecting decisions.
Lentner said conflicts must be reported and managed and detailed that he has already discussed creating a plan to keep his advocacy for his son separate from his legal duty to the district.
Taylor answered that trustees should report conflicts, listen to other views and seek out people who may not speak at meetings. She specifically said the board must remember Rock River and the rest of Albany County instead of focusing only on Laramie.
Learned said his wife is an assistant principal at Laramie High School and he wouldn’t vote on matters involving her pay or benefits, although he believes he could still take part in some discussions. He said trustees have a legal duty to put the district first.
Roberts said disclosure is the first step and trustees must also be honest about whether they can make a fair decision. Sometimes disclosure is enough, but sometimes a trustee must step away from the vote.
Bear said the board reviews conflicts as part of its code of conduct. She said personal ties made school closures painful for her, but she based her decision on the question of “what is best for all students?”
Most important issues
When questions concerning what are the district’s key issues, Taylor answered that the biggest problem is keeping good teachers and staff. Better pay matters, but employees also need support and freedom to make choices in their classrooms.
Learned said schools need stronger partnerships among teachers, parents, other professionals and students, and that working together can help schools provide useful learning experiences even when time and money are limited.
Roberts said teachers are trapped between state demands and family expectations. They face changing lessons, long hours and strict rules. It was also made clear that this kind of pressure can lead to burnout and weaker relationships with families.
Bear listed school funding as the biggest problem saying that funding silos make it hard to pay employees, maintain buildings and support activities. She also said state lawmakers have taken too much control away from local school boards.
Lentner agreed that funding is the most immediate threat. He added that a loss of public trust has led to lower support for schools and more state rules. He said leaders must explain why public education is worth supporting.

Lentner said the budget should be based on clear goals, not only numbers on a spreadsheet. The district should fight for programs the community values, including special education and activities. It must also protect students and families who do not have a strong public voice.

Taylor said she would depend on the district’s financial experts because finance is not her main area of experience. Her first priority would be protecting teachers and staff. She said the district should seek local control and cut expenses before cutting strong educators.

Students and parents lock up their bikes while others take family photos near the main entrance of Slade Elementary School as it opens its doors during the morning of Aug. 24, 2023, to celebrate the first day of school for the academic year in Albany County School District 1. The newly-built school opened in August 2022 in Laramie.

Bonus round

During a bonus round, Roberts and Bear passed on the opportunity to answer. Lentner used his time to say that his son has received strong special education support, though his family has also faced difficult meetings and uneven service. He wants every school to provide strong support for vulnerable students.

Taylor said teacher and staff burnout is a serious concern. She praised staff members who know students and families personally and said the district must keep them from leaving.

Learned agreed that the district must protect everyone who works with students. He included teachers, paraprofessionals and custodians because each one affects a student’s school experience.

School choice

Several different responses were voiced when candidates were asked what the district should do when families choose either private, religious, home or charter schools.

Roberts said that families must choose what is best for their children. Public schools can compete by supporting teachers and showing families the programs they offer, including Nordic skiing, gifted education and language courses.

Bear also supported family choice and said the district should promote its career and technical education courses, electives, college-credit classes, sports and activities. She also wants the district to contact families before their children reach preschool age.

Lentner said strong programs matter, but schools must also create a sense of community and board members can help families feel connected to their schools and to one another.

Taylor said public schools give children the chance to learn with classmates from many backgrounds, but warned that moving students with strong family support into certain schools may increase unfair differences between schools. She said the district should invest in every school.

Learned said public schools have trained teachers who understand their subjects, student behavior and teaching methods. He said those professionals are the strongest advantage public schools have.

Student safety and support

Questions concerning drugs, concussions, students dropping out and other threats to student safety were also asked to the candidates during the forum.

Bear answered that every student and staff member should feel included. Clubs, sports and activities can give students a reason to attend school and adults who check on them. She also discussed school climate surveys, mental-health programs, suicide awareness and school resource officers who build relationships with students.

Lentner said one of the best protections for a child is a trusted adult outside the family and he went on to detail coaches, teachers and activity leaders who can become mentors, notice problems and help students seek support.

Taylor focused on concussions and communication with parents saying that schools should quickly report possible injuries and follow concussion rules. She also supported counselors and social workers who build close relationships with students. In addition, she wants schools to teach practical skills, such as handling taxes.

Learned said drugs and mental health are major issues that schools must prepare to address. Schools may need more specialized counselors. He said educators must understand the whole child and “form relationships before we implement rigor.”

Roberts said her mentoring program shows how relationships keep students involved, explaining that an older student can check on a younger student’s grades, encourage attendance and help that student stay away from drugs. She added that students are more likely to attend when they know someone is looking out for them.

Conflicts of interest

Bennett also asked how candidates would keep family ties and personal interests from affecting decisions.

Lentner said conflicts must be reported and managed and detailed that he has already discussed creating a plan to keep his advocacy for his son separate from his legal duty to the district.

Taylor answered that trustees should report conflicts, listen to other views and seek out people who may not speak at meetings. She specifically said the board must remember Rock River and the rest of Albany County instead of focusing only on Laramie.

Learned said his wife is an assistant principal at Laramie High School and he wouldn’t vote on matters involving her pay or benefits, although he believes he could still take part in some discussions. He said trustees have a legal duty to put the district first.

Roberts said disclosure is the first step and trustees must also be honest about whether they can make a fair decision. Sometimes disclosure is enough, but sometimes a trustee must step away from the vote.

Bear said the board reviews conflicts as part of its code of conduct. She said personal ties made school closures painful for her, but she based her decision on the question of “what is best for all students?”

Most important issues

When questions concerning what are the district’s key issues, Taylor answered that the biggest problem is keeping good teachers and staff. Better pay matters, but employees also need support and freedom to make choices in their classrooms.

Learned said schools need stronger partnerships among teachers, parents, other professionals and students, and that working together can help schools provide useful learning experiences even when time and money are limited.

Roberts said teachers are trapped between state demands and family expectations. They face changing lessons, long hours and strict rules. It was also made clear that this kind of pressure can lead to burnout and weaker relationships with families.

Bear listed school funding as the biggest problem saying that funding silos make it hard to pay employees, maintain buildings and support activities. She also said state lawmakers have taken too much control away from local school boards.

Lentner agreed that funding is the most immediate threat. He added that a loss of public trust has led to lower support for schools and more state rules. He said leaders must explain why public education is worth supporting.

articles.article_title: Flock camera and data technology explained
articles.heading: How do these Flock cameras work anyway? Here’s a visual breakdown.
articles.summary: Flock cameras and other license plate readers are expanding rapidly across the United States and Massachusetts. This is how Flock technology works.
articles.content:
By John Hancock , Scooty Nickerson , and Yogev Toby , Globe Staff

Published Oct. 1, 2026

Across Massachusetts, small black cameras are photographing passing cars, capturing such details as the license plate, the color, and the roof rack. Police can search those records in seconds, sometimes from the other side of the country.

These automatic license plate readers are often referred to simply as Flock cameras after Flock Safety, an Atlanta-based manufacturer. But Motorola, Axon, and other companies sell them too.

While license plate readers have been around for more than a decade, the widespread integration of AI and a searchable nationwide database have spurred adoption in recent years by law enforcement and even private companies including Home Depot and Lowe’s. Among the manufacturers, Flock’s cameras are the most widely used.

The number of readers grew from 17 at the beginning of 2025 to over 1,200 through Sept. 24, 2026, according to crowd-sourced reports gathered by the website Deflock.org .

Source: Deflock.org. Note: Data as of Sept. 24, 2026.

JOHN HANCOCK/GLOBE STAFF

Police say the camera networks help them find missing people or vehicles involved in crimes quickly. For instance, officials touted the technology as instrumental in locating the Brown University shooter last year. But advocacy groups including the ACLU say they are tools of mass surveillance that can track anyone – regardless of whether they committed a crime – without a warrant and little oversight.

More than 100 communities in Massachusetts have contracted with Flock, per a Globe tally . Thirty-eight communities have moved to limit their use since last fall, according to the ACLU .

But how do these things actually work? We took a closer look at Flock’s system.

Advertisement

Flock cameras usually sit on poles about 12 feet off the ground where they take photos of passing vehicles. When a vehicle passes by a camera, a motion sensor triggers it to take a collection of still photos. Infrared technology makes the photos legible day or night.

After the camera snaps the photos, AI-enabled software reads each image. It pulls the license plate number, then logs details about the vehicle, such as its make, color, and body type. It also records details about the vehicle that a witness might remember, including roof racks, bumper stickers, or visible signs of damage.

While license plate readers have been around for a while, the incorporation of AI has supercharged their capabilities, as vehicles can be tracked down using just descriptions without a license plate number.

All the collected data are uploaded to a cloud server. Each sighting is logged with a timestamp, a location, and a direction of travel. By default, Flock keeps the data for seven days. According to Flock, the client owns the data, not the company. Less than 1 percent of the images are used to train Flock’s AI algorithms.

The collected data are automatically cross-referenced with a “hot list,” which may include vehicles marked as stolen, associated with a wanted or missing person case, or suspected of being involved in a criminal activity. These lists are constantly updated by local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies. When a camera spots a match, police agencies automatically get an alert, said Eric Piza, a professor and director of crime analysis initiatives at Northeastern University.

Police officers with access to Flock’s software can also search the system for vehicles based on the license number or other recorded characteristics. Each query requires a search reason, such as “stolen vehicle” or “missing person." But options also include vague and nondescript reasons like “investigation.” A spokesperson for Flock said that they will also require specific case codes for all law enforcement searches by the end of the year.

In shooting and major crime investigations, the search feature can narrow down suspects quickly, Piza said, by helping pinpoint vehicles and license numbers in the vicinity.

The general public cannot search Flock’s database on their own. But police departments can choose to publish a transparency portal showing their policies and the number of vehicles detected on their local network. Some portals also include a redacted list of recent searches. Police in Franklin and Lowell are among those in Massachusetts with public portals, but most departments do not publish one.

Departments can choose to share data with other departments in neighboring municipalities, the state, and around the country, giving them unlimited access to logged data. Once access is granted, which is akin to accepting a follow request on social media, departments can search their full network of data.

From 2023 through this May, Salem’s Flock data appeared in more than 1.2 million searches from the Houston Police Department. Most likely, Houston officers weren't looking for anything in Salem specifically. A nationwide Flock search can check the data for every camera that has opted into the network, so a search for a Texas plate can also check a database in Massachusetts.

The search volume is part of what makes oversight hard. The technology is “generating oceans of data that are going to need to be searched and mined to make sure they are being used to investigate appropriately,” Piza said.

In July, Salem announced it was ending its Flock contract, citing data security concerns, joining the growing list of Massachusetts communities that have stopped or moved to limit using Flock cameras since last fall. But Salem isn't giving up on license plate readers. It plans to replace Flock with a system they say will offer greater local control of data.

articles.heading: Alabama Forestry Commission deploys satellite technology for wildfire response
articles.summary: Read about National Fire News: Alabama Forestry Commission deploys OroraTech incident from Fire & Safety Journal Americas featured on Daily Dispatch (DD).
articles.content:
- October 2, 2026

The Alabama Forestry Commission (AFC) is deploying satellite-based thermal intelligence from OroraTech USA to enhance monitoring of prescribed burns and support wildfire response efforts across Alabama.

The technology is designed to provide additional visibility into fire activity, helping forestry officials identify potential escapes from prescribed burns, assess incidents and determine where and when a response is needed.

“Adopting the latest technology helps us detect and respond to wildfires more efficiently while improving safety for our firefighters and the people of Alabama,” said Alabama State Forester Rick Oates.

“OroraTech gives us another tool to help protect lives, property, and Alabama’s forest resources.”

AFC Protection Division Director John Goff said the technology represents the latest development in a long evolution of wildfire detection.

Fire & Safety Journal Americas

articles.title: OpenAI fires workers for 'mishandling sensitive information'
articles.description: OpenAI fires workers for 'mishandling sensitive information' BBC
articles.description_html: OpenAI fires workers for 'mishandling sensitive information'  BBC
articles.article_title: OpenAI fires workers for 'mishandling sensitive information'
articles.heading: OpenAI fires workers for 'mishandling sensitive information'
articles.summary: The former employees were investigated for sharing data with an outside AI evaluation group.
articles.content:
OpenAI fires workers for 'mishandling sensitive information'
OpenAI has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling information, including work which involved an external organisation analysing AI models.
"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson told the BBC.
The ChatGPT-maker did not name the sacked workers, but at least two of them were involved in safety research at the firm.
The firings come as the debate over AI safety and the risks the technology may pose to humanity intensified in recent months.
"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," a spokesperson for OpenAI said.
Concerns over AI safety have made headlines after some researchers and industry executives called for more guardrails around the technology.
OpenAI has come under under intense scrutiny after its models went rogue and hacked several platforms, including Australian government websites.
In an incident in July, one of the firm's AI models accessed the internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face.
That incident led OpenAI to review the activities of its AI agents, which are designed to execute tasks autonomously based on simple instructions.
The firm said this week it has notified more than 100 organisations about incidents involving unauthoritised activity linked to its systems.
Being notified "does not mean that any private information was accessed" or that a system was compromised, it said.
In September, researcher Jacob Coxon, who left Anthropic, called for AI development to slow down so its potential risks could be properly assessed.
Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman have also called for measures to address concerns over AI.
On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses - including leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - to discuss AI.
After the gathering at the White House, Trump posted a document that he called a "morally binding" agreement that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.
Some technology experts criticised the pact, pointing out that it allowed AI companies to regulate themselves.
Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight of the technology.

articles.title: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason
articles.description: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason MIT Technology Review
articles.description_html: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason  MIT Technology Review
articles.article_title: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason
articles.heading: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason
articles.summary: Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.
articles.content:
Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason
Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.
On an afternoon in Seoul in March 2016, I watched a program I helped build put a stone on the fifth line of a Go board in what looked like a gift to its human opponent. Move 37 in game two of the five-game match looked so absurd that some commentators thought it was a programming glitch.
It wasn’t. AlphaGo won the game, ultimately triumphing 4-1 over Lee Sedol, one of the greatest professional Go players of all time. “I thought AlphaGo was based on probability calculation and that it was merely a machine,” Lee said afterwards. “But when I saw this move, I changed my mind. Surely, AlphaGo is creative.”
When Deep Blue defeated then reigning world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, it did so by looking six to eight moves ahead per player and evaluating 200 million chess positions per second, using rules hard-coded by humans. Go is a vastly more complex game. A stone’s worth depends on how distant groups and territory unfold over dozens of moves. Computing even a fraction of the possible outcomes would take a supercomputer billions of years. To win, AlphaGo had to sense who was ahead at a glance and even invent moves no human had thought to play.
That is why many accounts of AlphaGo’s match against Lee portray move 37 as a flash of pure machine intuition. But that is a misunderstanding. It was actually AlphaGo’s powers of reasoning that made this creative choice—and these are powers that today’s AI lacks. If we want future AI systems to produce trustworthy results and really novel insights in fields like science and medicine, we need to equip them with genuine reasoning capabilities of this kind.
AlphaGo is made up of two systems. The first, its policy network, was trained to guess what move a strong human would play. This “intuitive” part regarded move 37 as nothing special—a play that had a roughly one in 10,000 chance of being made by an expert human player. What made AlphaGo choose it was the program’s search machinery, which looked beyond immediate plausibility and weighed the future consequences of proposed moves. It explicitly constructed and searched a game tree with thousands of branches, each representing a different possible future.
A well-known theory in the behavioral sciences, popularized by Daniel Kahneman, distinguishes between two modes of human thought: System 1 is fast, gut-level, effortless; system 2, slow, step-by-step, and deliberative. AlphaGo offered a striking machine analogue of that split. Its networks supplied the hunches—this move looks promising, this position looks won—and its search supplied the deliberation, testing those hunches against the moves and countermoves that would follow. As in human cognition, neither half works alone. Intuition alone would never have opted for move 37, and brute-force search would have struggled to sieve through all the many possible moves.
This is strikingly different from the way today’s AI models work. A large language model picks the next token, over and over. That amounts to system 1 in action—fast, associative, and surprisingly good pattern completion across almost every subject people write about.
Not long after ChatGPT debuted, the field realized that language fluency alone falls short of true usefulness. The apparent solution was to make models that deliberate: Instead of answering immediately, they can now generate intermediate steps that decompose a problem, carry forward partial results, and influence subsequent reasoning—a process known as chain of thought.
The gains have proved real, above all in mathematics and coding. But unlike AlphaGo’s search, this does not introduce a genuinely separate reasoning mechanism: The intermediate reasoning is still produced by the same next-token prediction process, iterated for longer before the model commits to an answer.
Three shortcomings prevent what chatbots do from qualifying as reasoning (in a way that a scientist might recognize). First, these models typically maintain no explicit, persistent, and inspectable epistemic state. There is no open ledger that lays out the hypotheses a model is considering, the confidence it has in various explanations, the evidence it’s weighing, and the unresolved questions it’s holding onto—all things that should be systematically revised as new information arrives.
Second, they lack a clean separation between what the system knows and how it manipulates that knowledge. Knowledge and reasoning are inextricably interwoven in the weights of the neural network—there is no independent, explicitly represented set of beliefs. Third, while the chains of thought chatbots produce look like deliberation, research has demonstrated that the bots often concoct them after the fact, reaching an answer by one route but reporting another.
This is a problem because in the high-stakes applications we all care about, such as medicine, engineering, and scientific research, it matters not only what a system concludes but also how it arrives at its conclusion. When mistakes happen—for example, in medical diagnosis and treatment—we need to be able to pinpoint what went wrong: Was the system’s reasoning at fault, did it draw on invalid evidence, or did it make incorrect assumptions?
This is why I recently left my position at Google DeepMind. I believe we need a fresh approach to machine reasoning—one that draws on AlphaGo’s architecture. AlphaGo maintains a record of what it knows about a given position: the game tree. This data structure contains all the variations, the possible futures, that AlphaGo has considered, each move and position being annotated with judgments made by its neural networks. As its reasoning progresses, AlphaGo updates the game tree and eventually synthesizes the information in it to decide which move to make.
Similarly, for general reasoning a system should maintain an epistemic state that represents what the system holds as settled, what it doubts, what it has ruled out, which questions stay open. Reasoning can then be understood as a sequence of moves that change the epistemic state to advance knowledge and reduce uncertainty: deducing consequences, breaking problems into parts, and—crucially—deciding what question to ask, calculation to perform, or experiment to run next.
Of course, open-world reasoning is harder than playing a board game such as Go or chess. In the real world the current state of affairs is only partially known, the set of available actions is large and variable, and the consequences of actions are stochastic or unknown.
But recent advances in LLMs and other neural models now give us the capability to take on such general reasoning problems. For example, LLMs can suggest ways of tackling a problem on the basis of what is known and what resources are available. They can interact with tools via APIs or code and help assess whether a claim is supported by available evidence.
Most important, to keep the system honest, an independent part of the system must evaluate each move by how much it actually resolves uncertainty, updating beliefs only when the change is backed by evidence. Once these rules are enforced, the model can accumulate certified knowledge and improve its reasoning policy by learning from past reasoning experiences. You can think of such a system as the scientific method on steroids, with the purpose of producing knowledge that can withstand scrutiny.
I do not think we reach trustworthy machine intelligence by making system 1 bigger. Scale sharpens intuition, but it does not make intuition more deliberative. Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

On an afternoon in Seoul in March 2016, I watched a program I helped build put a stone on the fifth line of a Go board in what looked like a gift to its human opponent. Move 37 in game two of the five-game match looked so absurd that some commentators thought it was a programming glitch.

It wasn’t. AlphaGo won the game, ultimately triumphing 4-1 over Lee Sedol, one of the greatest professional Go players of all time. “I thought AlphaGo was based on probability calculation and that it was merely a machine,” Lee said afterwards. “But when I saw this move, I changed my mind. Surely, AlphaGo is creative.”

When Deep Blue defeated then reigning world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, it did so by looking six to eight moves ahead per player and evaluating 200 million chess positions per second, using rules hard-coded by humans. Go is a vastly more complex game. A stone’s worth depends on how distant groups and territory unfold over dozens of moves. Computing even a fraction of the possible outcomes would take a supercomputer billions of years. To win, AlphaGo had to sense who was ahead at a glance and even invent moves no human had thought to play.

That is why many accounts of AlphaGo’s match against Lee portray move 37 as a flash of pure machine intuition. But that is a misunderstanding. It was actually AlphaGo’s powers of reasoning that made this creative choice—and these are powers that today’s AI lacks. If we want future AI systems to produce trustworthy results and really novel insights in fields like science and medicine, we need to equip them with genuine reasoning capabilities of this kind.

AlphaGo is made up of two systems. The first, its policy network, was trained to guess what move a strong human would play. This “intuitive” part regarded move 37 as nothing special—a play that had a roughly one in 10,000 chance of being made by an expert human player. What made AlphaGo choose it was the program’s search machinery, which looked beyond immediate plausibility and weighed the future consequences of proposed moves. It explicitly constructed and searched a game tree with thousands of branches, each representing a different possible future.

A well-known theory in the behavioral sciences, popularized by Daniel Kahneman, distinguishes between two modes of human thought: System 1 is fast, gut-level, effortless; system 2, slow, step-by-step, and deliberative. AlphaGo offered a striking machine analogue of that split. Its networks supplied the hunches—this move looks promising, this position looks won—and its search supplied the deliberation, testing those hunches against the moves and countermoves that would follow. As in human cognition, neither half works alone. Intuition alone would never have opted for move 37, and brute-force search would have struggled to sieve through all the many possible moves.

This is strikingly different from the way today’s AI models work. A large language model picks the next token, over and over. That amounts to system 1 in action—fast, associative, and surprisingly good pattern completion across almost every subject people write about.

Not long after ChatGPT debuted, the field realized that language fluency alone falls short of true usefulness. The apparent solution was to make models that deliberate: Instead of answering immediately, they can now generate intermediate steps that decompose a problem, carry forward partial results, and influence subsequent reasoning—a process known as chain of thought.

The gains have proved real, above all in mathematics and coding. But unlike AlphaGo’s search, this does not introduce a genuinely separate reasoning mechanism: The intermediate reasoning is still produced by the same next-token prediction process, iterated for longer before the model commits to an answer.

Three shortcomings prevent what chatbots do from qualifying as reasoning (in a way that a scientist might recognize). First, these models typically maintain no explicit, persistent, and inspectable epistemic state. There is no open ledger that lays out the hypotheses a model is considering, the confidence it has in various explanations, the evidence it’s weighing, and the unresolved questions it’s holding onto—all things that should be systematically revised as new information arrives.

Second, they lack a clean separation between what the system knows and how it manipulates that knowledge. Knowledge and reasoning are inextricably interwoven in the weights of the neural network—there is no independent, explicitly represented set of beliefs. Third, while the chains of thought chatbots produce look like deliberation, research has demonstrated that the bots often concoct them after the fact, reaching an answer by one route but reporting another.

This is a problem because in the high-stakes applications we all care about, such as medicine, engineering, and scientific research, it matters not only what a system concludes but also how it arrives at its conclusion. When mistakes happen—for example, in medical diagnosis and treatment—we need to be able to pinpoint what went wrong: Was the system’s reasoning at fault, did it draw on invalid evidence, or did it make incorrect assumptions?

This is why I recently left my position at Google DeepMind. I believe we need a fresh approach to machine reasoning—one that draws on AlphaGo’s architecture. AlphaGo maintains a record of what it knows about a given position: the game tree. This data structure contains all the variations, the possible futures, that AlphaGo has considered, each move and position being annotated with judgments made by its neural networks. As its reasoning progresses, AlphaGo updates the game tree and eventually synthesizes the information in it to decide which move to make.

Similarly, for general reasoning a system should maintain an epistemic state that represents what the system holds as settled, what it doubts, what it has ruled out, which questions stay open. Reasoning can then be understood as a sequence of moves that change the epistemic state to advance knowledge and reduce uncertainty: deducing consequences, breaking problems into parts, and—crucially—deciding what question to ask, calculation to perform, or experiment to run next.

Of course, open-world reasoning is harder than playing a board game such as Go or chess. In the real world the current state of affairs is only partially known, the set of available actions is large and variable, and the consequences of actions are stochastic or unknown.

But recent advances in LLMs and other neural models now give us the capability to take on such general reasoning problems. For example, LLMs can suggest ways of tackling a problem on the basis of what is known and what resources are available. They can interact with tools via APIs or code and help assess whether a claim is supported by available evidence.

Most important, to keep the system honest, an independent part of the system must evaluate each move by how much it actually resolves uncertainty, updating beliefs only when the change is backed by evidence. Once these rules are enforced, the model can accumulate certified knowledge and improve its reasoning policy by learning from past reasoning experiences. You can think of such a system as the scientific method on steroids, with the purpose of producing knowledge that can withstand scrutiny.

I do not think we reach trustworthy machine intelligence by making system 1 bigger. Scale sharpens intuition, but it does not make intuition more deliberative. Move 37 mattered because a machine held a position, weighed the possible futures, and chose the move its artificial instincts would likely have rejected.

Society needs such creative moves in drug discovery, materials, climate, diagnosis—fields where the board looks nothing like a Go board and nobody hands us the rules. We will get such insights only from systems that reason—systems whose conclusions arise from an auditable sequence of evidence, inference, and belief revision rather than from a convincing story told after the fact.

articles.summary: The Stevens Law and Technology Journal (SJOLT) has recently released its second edition, marking another milestone for the publication founded by Nicholas Russo. articles.content:
The Stevens Law and Technology Journal (SJOLT) has recently released its second edition, marking another milestone for the publication founded by Nicholas Russo. Following his bachelor’s degree, Russo is completing a Master’s in Computer Science at Stevens and will soon attend Harvard Law School.
Russo observed a significant gap while conducting his own personal research: “While researching places to publish my own work on the intellectual foundations and history of computational law, I spent a lot of time studying the world of undergraduate law reviews,” Russo shared. “I realized that there did not seem to be a publication dedicated to undergraduate (and master’s student) scholarship at the intersection of law and technology.”
Russo noticed that sufficient work was being done through school-run journals devoted to both law and technology, but these are typically inaccessible to people with no formal legal education. His realization became the inspiration to create SJOLT in early 2025. According to SJOLT’s mission statement, the journal is “the first and only undergraduate-led academic publication dedicated to advancing scholarship at the intersection of law and technology.” There is a strong emphasis on the journal being centered on accessibility and collaboration. “My main goal for SJOLT has been to make scholarship in law and technology more accessible. I strongly believe that students do not need formal legal education to produce thoughtful, rigorous, and valuable work about legal questions,” Russo said. “To address that, I’ve developed a more collaborative editorial model in which editors can meet with prospective authors, help them brainstorm and refine ideas, and give them the confidence and structure needed to turn an initial interest into a serious piece of scholarship.”
Within the newest edition of SJOLT, there are articles exploring the topics of artificial intelligence governance, digital privacy, intellectual property, and more that explore the niches within the intersection of law and technology. Authors from a wide range of educational backgrounds and exposures are featured within the journal, and their incredibly original thinking is proudly published in this edition. Russo views SJOLT as a platform that not only benefits authors, but editors as well. “Authors gain an opportunity to publish substantive work, while editors gain experience evaluating scholarship, working closely with writers, and helping shape a scholarly publication,” he said. “Those experiences can become meaningful parts of students’ applications for jobs, internships, research positions, law school, and other graduate programs.”
With the second edition now published, SJOLT is still continuing to expand its reach and influence beyond Stevens. Russo’s idea is an inspiration that legal and technological scholarship inquiry can start before, or even without, law school.

articles.summary: Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin visited a Portland company Thursday morning that's focused on a new form of PFAS destruction technology
articles.content:
EPA official praises Maine company for new technology to destroy PFAS
PORTLAND (WGME) – Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin visited a Portland company Thursday morning that's focused on a new form of PFAS destruction technology.
The developers of Onterris, a global environmental solutions and services company, say it could help give smaller communities a cheaper way to remove PFAS from drinking water through regenerable ion exchange resin technology.
Zeldin says this technology could even expand beyond Maine and be deployed nationwide.
"There was concern about that local rural system that might be lower income,” Zeldin said. “They cannot afford to invest in the more expensive granular activated carbon solutions. And they're looking for far more cost-effective ways to be able to remediate PFAS."
"We can make these systems much more cost effective for these small towns, as well as the larger municipalities," Onterris Chief Innovation Officer Steve Woodard said.
Though, as Zeldin highlights new technology to help remove PFAS contamination, Maine Congresswoman Chellie Pingree says she wants the EPA to do more to prevent it.
She sent a letter to Zeldin Thursday, demanding answers from the agency about PFAS contaminated sewage sludge spread on farmland.
Pingree says more than 50 Maine farms have contamination linked to the sludge.

articles.summary: This study presents a policy-sensitive diffusion modeling framework, the HDV-DIFFUSE model, tailored to the EU’s VECTO truck classes.
articles.content:
Spatiotemporal analysis of electric truck charging demand in Europe
Report
HDV-DIFFUSE model: Technology diffusion modeling of e-trucks in the EU27+3
The EU’s policy landscape is set to accelerate the adoption of zero-emission trucks in the coming years, with battery electric trucks (BETs) leading the way due to their stronger economic performance compared with other alternative powertrains. Assessing the effectiveness of these policies in terms of the number of BETs put on European roads remains challenging, because the economic drivers impacting technology adoption vary by vehicle model, freight application, and Member State. Reliable estimates of BET uptake are key for ensuring that freight electrification aligns with charging infrastructure deployment and grid expansion, which often operate in different planning and investment timelines. Vehicle technology diffusion modeling—which is used to generate estimates of vehicle uptake—is an important tool for policymakers to evaluate policies targeting BET uptake and support coordinated development of the freight electrification ecosystem.
This study presents a policy-sensitive diffusion modeling framework, the HDV-DIFFUSE model, tailored to the EU’s VECTO truck classes. By using total cost of ownership (TCO) and linking policy-driven changes in trucking economics to technology adoption, the model projects BET uptake across the EU27+3 for all truck classes under various policy scenarios, including the Emission Trading System (ETS2) and the Eurovignette Directive. An overview of the model structure is shown in Figure ES1.
Key capabilities of the model include:
- Quantifying the impact of individual policies on BET cost-competitiveness and adoption at a highly granular level: By capturing vehicle, operational, and country-specific parameters, the model can assess how individual policy measures impact specific TCO components and BET adoption across segments, which in turn enables policymakers to develop tailored policies for specific applications, vehicle types, and countries.
- Determining the pace and timing of market diffusion: By capturing economic variables, such as charging prices or carbon pricing schemes, the model can estimate BET adoption trajectories over time, revealing periods of quick growth or stagnated diffusion. Understanding these dynamics is crucial to align BET diffusion with investment and planning on charging infrastructure and grid energization.
- Identifying how and why policy effectiveness varies across countries and truck classes: By accounting for differences in market conditions such as fuel and charging prices, as well as the operational profiles of the vehicles (e.g., regional or long-haul) and policy implementations, the model captures an array of policy-relevant differences among Member States, allowing policymakers to quantify policy impact across different EU countries. For instance, the same policy measures (full road toll exemptions and ETS2) result in a BET diffusion of 66% in Germany by 2030, compared with 16% in Poland

articles.heading: Amphitheater in MLK Park named to honor Daniel Prude. Park is still named MLK Park
articles.summary: City officials have renamed the amphitheater in Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Park in honor of Daniel Prude.
articles.content:
Amphitheater in MLK Park named to honor Daniel Prude. Park is still named MLK Park
[anvplayer video=”5136065″ station=”998131″]
ROCHESTER, N.Y. — The City of Rochester has named the amphitheater in Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Park in honor of Daniel Prude. The park’s name remains Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Park.
It’s been more than two years since Prude died after being restrained by Rochester police officers. The amphitheater name is now “Daniel Prude Square” to honor what would’ve been Prude’s 44th birthday.
MLK Park also has a mural of Prude, created after Prude’s death was made public in September of 2020.
Mayor Evans released this statement:
“The City of Rochester will never forget Daniel Prude. His death reverberated across and beyond our region, and we will memorialize him and ensure his name is remembered.”
Rochester City Council Member Stanley Martin released this statement:
“Today we are able to honor the memory of Daniel Prude and, in doing so, begin a restorative process centered around this community’s ability to assist those in crisis. Daniel Prude did not die in vain. His death has challenged this community to rethink how we provide support to those experiencing mental health crises, expanded conversations on community investments, sparked policy changes and greater accountability when it comes to those, who, like Mr. Prude, all too often fall through the cracks. And we still have much work to do. Today’s naming of Prude Square at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Park is another step forward in transforming our community.”
Prude died in March 2020. He was not breathing and had no pulse after he was restrained and handcuffed by officers. He died in the hospital seven days later.

articles.content:
Technology Used in the Fight Against Invasive Species Across the State
Posted on Oct 1, 2026 in Main
The Hawaiʻi Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity (DAB) is using state-of-the-art mapping technology to help residents across the state keep tabs on the fight against invasive species like little fire ants (LFA), coconut rhinoceros beetles (CRB) and coqui frogs.
Act 250 was signed into law by Governor Green in June of last year. It appropriated $26.6 million for DAB and 44 new positions and biosecurity efforts.
One of the first things put in place was a new online dashboard, allowing people to find information such as the locations of little fire ant infestations across the state. “This record level of funding reflects our commitment to safeguarding our environment and ensuring the sustainability of our agriculture industry for future generations while also ensuring the responsible use of state funds,” Governor Green said at the bill signing.
The technology and staffing generated major results in the fight against the little pests. For example, the total number of LFA samples collected in fiscal year 2025 was 43,522. That number grew to 76,583 in fiscal year 2026, an increase of nearly 57%.
There is also a section dedicated to avian influenza, with a map graphic showing the number of tests conducted in the four counties in fiscal year 2026.
The dashboard also has a page where people can find out what types of pesticides DAB uses in the fight against the big three, with an overview, pros and cons.
“The fight against invasive species can be manpower intensive. Documenting all that work and sharing it with the public is a top priority for DAB,” said Deputy Director Dean Matsukawa. The invasive species dashboard can be found at biosecurity.hawaii.gov/.

articles.title: Engineering professor patents technology designed to prevent wildfires
articles.description: Engineering professor patents technology designed to prevent wildfires Fresno State Today
articles.description_html: Engineering professor patents technology designed to prevent wildfires  Fresno State Today
articles.article_title: Engineering professor patents technology designed to prevent wildfires – Fresno State Today
articles.heading: Engineering professor patents technology designed to prevent wildfires
articles.summary: Engineering professor patents technology designed to prevent wildfires Fresno State Today
articles.content:
Dr. Kerry McBee spent nearly two decades investigating fires and failures involving electrical systems. Now, the Fresno State associate professor of electrical and computer engineering has patented a monitoring system to identify power-line hazards before they spark wildfires.

The U.S. Patent and Trademark Office issued a patent for McBee’s Overhead Fire Prevention System in July. The Real-Time Overhead Autonomous Monitoring System, or ROAM System, continuously monitors overhead electrical equipment and is designed to detect deteriorating power lines and other hazards weeks or even months before they could cause a fire or power outage.

“Right now, much of what a utility does is reactive,” McBee said. “This would be a proactive prevention system because it could prevent the fire from ever occurring.”

Before joining Fresno State, McBee spent 17 years in the electrical and fire industry. As a forensic engineer and certified fire and explosion investigator, he investigated more than 1,500 fires involving electrical systems and led major investigations across 10 states.

That experience led him to recognize a gap in how power lines are monitored.

“Utilities monitor the electrical attributes, but they don’t necessarily monitor the physical condition of the system,” McBee said. “That made me wonder whether we could build a system that identifies physical deficiencies before they lead to a failure.”

Before working in higher education, McBee served in the U.S. Marine Corps during Operation Desert Storm and later worked as an industrial maintenance technician. Still feeling like he was missing something, he enrolled at the Colorado School of Mines at age 27 to pursue an engineering degree.

After graduating, he studied power engineering at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, focusing on power system failures. He later worked as a forensic engineer before joining Xcel Energy, where he spent 12 years investigating failures and helping design one of the nation’s first modernized smart grids.

While working as an engineer, McBee also taught as an adjunct faculty at the Colorado School of Mines and discovered a newfound passion.

“After two years of teaching, I realized I enjoyed teaching engineering more than I enjoyed my daily engineering position,” McBee recalled. “So I went back to school part-time. In the daytime, I was an engineer. At night, I was doing research for my Ph.D. and once I finished, I was able to get a tenure-track position in the Lyles College of Engineering at Fresno State in 2016.”

Building on that foundation, McBee began developing the fire prevention technology in 2021 and applied for a patent in 2023 with support from Fresno State’s University Patent Board. The board reviews inventions developed by faculty, staff and students; evaluates their patent and commercial potential; and helps determine the rights and financial interests of the parties involved.

“The larger goal is to translate ideas and discoveries developed at Fresno State into practical technologies, products, and businesses that contribute to economic growth and benefit our community,” said Dr. Jason Bush, associate vice president for Research and Sponsored Programs at Fresno State. “The applied nature of Dr. McBee’s technology, its potential real-world impact and possible commercial interest made it an attractive invention for the university to support and advance.”

“The larger goal is to translate ideas and discoveries developed at Fresno State into practical technologies, products, and businesses that contribute to economic growth and benefit our community,” said Dr. Jason Bush, associate vice president for Research and Sponsored Programs at Fresno State. “The applied nature of Dr. McBee’s technology, its potential real-world impact and possible commercial interest made it an attractive invention for the university to support and advance.”

The California Energy Commission recognized the ROAM System’s real-world potential by awarding a $150,000 CalSEED grant to inRG Solutions, LLC, a company McBee founded to develop and commercialize the fire-prevention technology.

As part of his research, McBee created a database examining the causes, fatalities and property damage associated with 25 of California’s deadliest and most destructive wildfires. He used his findings to help design the system.

Primarily intended for remote areas where deteriorating power-line equipment can be difficult to inspect regularly, the technology could also help prevent unplanned power outages in urban areas.

“What really makes it different is that it monitors a number of physical characteristics,” McBee said.

An onboard neural network, a form of artificial intelligence, analyzes data collected by the system’s sensors to identify conditions that could lead to a wildfire.

McBee and his collaborators have tested the technology in controlled environments and are now developing a market-ready version. In the coming months, he plans to build an outdoor field laboratory with mock overhead power lines to further test and refine the prototype.

They also hope to establish pilot programs with utility companies such as Pacific Gas and Electric Co. and Southern California Edison.

“Our goal is to validate it from a market standpoint and prove how valuable it is to the industry,” McBee said. “It’s inexpensive to install, and it has the potential to save millions of dollars in property damage and ultimately save lives.”

Since filing the patent in 2023, McBee has continued developing the system with help from engineering students who have contributed research and ideas, including improvements to its communication capabilities. He intends to involve students in the technology’s next phase.

For McBee, the patent marks a significant milestone in a journey spanning more than two decades, both personally and professionally.

“It means quite a bit,” McBee said. “It feels like the culmination of years of investigating, studying and researching failures. It is very satisfying to see all of that experience come together in this system.”

- Melissa Tav

- October 1, 2026

- Electrical and Computer Engineering

articles.title: Intel vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.description: Intel vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? Yahoo Finance
articles.description_html: Intel vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?  Yahoo Finance
articles.article_title: Intel vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: One is a turnaround story burning cash; the other generated $34.4 billion in free cash flow last year. The valuation gap tells the rest.
articles.content:
- INTC -0.19%

- TSM +0.66%

The semiconductor landscape is shifting as national security and manufacturing prowess collide. Investors must choose between a recovering American giant, Intel (NASDAQ:INTC), and the world's premier foundry, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC) (NYSE:TSM).

Intel designs and manufactures its own chips while expanding its foundry business to build for others. TSMC focuses solely on manufacturing, serving the world's most advanced technology firms. Both companies are central to the global supply chain, yet they offer vastly different paths for investors looking for growth or turnaround potential.

The case for Intel

Intel designs and manufactures processors and software for cloud, enterprise, and edge customers. In early 2026, the company granted the U.S. government a 10% equity stake, which has since triggered shareholder litigation. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $52.9 billion, a decrease of approximately 0.5% from the previous year. The company reported a net loss of roughly $267.0 million, resulting in a net margin of negative 0.5%. This reflects the heavy capital investments required to transition toward its foundry-first strategy.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was nearly 0.4x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. The current ratio, measuring the ability to cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets, was close to 2.0x. Free cash flow was negative at roughly $4.9 billion, and stock-based compensation accounted for nearly 25.1% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation because SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing operates as a pure-play foundry, manufacturing chips designed by other companies for smartphones and artificial intelligence. While major customers are not explicitly disclosed in its latest filings, it serves nearly every major chip designer among semiconductor stocks . This business model allows it to benefit from industrywide growth without the risk of competing with its own clients.

In FY 2025, revenue reached close to $122.4 billion, a significant increase of approximately 32% over the previous year. The company delivered a net income of nearly $55.1 billion, resulting in a net margin of about 46.3%. These figures demonstrate the immense demand for its advanced manufacturing nodes.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.2x. The current ratio stood at close to 2.5x, indicating a strong position to cover near-term obligations. Free cash flow was robust at approximately $32.2 billion, representing the cash remaining after a company pays for its operations and capital investments.

Risk profile comparison

Intel faces significant litigation risk following its decision to grant a 10% equity stake to the U.S. government. Shareholders have filed lawsuits alleging the deal was intended to mitigate political pressure rather than serve investor interests. Additionally, Intel continues to be described as a beleaguered chipmaker, reflecting its ongoing struggle to regain technical leadership and improve market sentiment.

TSMC faces risks related to its concentration of manufacturing facilities, which are largely based in a single geographic region. While the company has not disclosed specific recent risks in its 10-K, global supply chain disruptions and regional geopolitical tensions remain primary concerns for the foundry. It also faces competitive pressure from Samsung and other rivals as they race to develop more efficient chip-making processes.

Valuation comparison

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing carries a lower Forward P/E based on future earnings estimates, while Intel has a lower P/S ratio using sales over the past twelve months.

Metric

78.6x

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?

When it comes to choosing between the two tech stocks, TSMC appears to be the safer and more profitable option.

Indeed, Intel has made a dramatic comeback amid the technical improvements enabled by its 18A technology and the prospect of becoming the leading fab in the U.S.

Nonetheless, despite improvements, Intel's financial struggles continue as it continues to run net losses. While revenue growth returned in the first half of 2026, the $52.9 billion generated in 2025 indicates its lackluster performance in the recent past.

In contrast, TSMC dominates production of the world's most advanced semiconductors, and the $122 billion in revenue it generated in 2025 affirms its dominance. Additionally, it is also a cash generation machine, amid its $32.2 billion in free cash flow for 2025.

Given that, it makes little sense to pay the valuation premium that has arisen from the massive gains in Intel stock. Since demand for advanced chips remains robust, TSMC will likely continue to stand out over the potentially promising but still struggling Intel.

Should you buy stock in Intel right now?

Before you buy stock in Intel, consider this:

Intel vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?

Will Healy, The Motley Fool
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 3:20 PM PDT
  • INTC
    -0.19%
  • TSM
    +0.66%

The semiconductor landscape is shifting as national security and manufacturing prowess collide. Investors must choose between a recovering American giant, Intel (NASDAQ:INTC), and the world's premier foundry, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSMC) (NYSE:TSM).

Intel designs and manufactures its own chips while expanding its foundry business to build for others. TSMC focuses solely on manufacturing, serving the world's most advanced technology firms. Both companies are central to the global supply chain, yet they offer vastly different paths for investors looking for growth or turnaround potential.

The case for Intel

Intel designs and manufactures processors and software for cloud, enterprise, and edge customers. In early 2026, the company granted the U.S. government a 10% equity stake, which has since triggered shareholder litigation. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $52.9 billion, a decrease of approximately 0.5% from the previous year. The company reported a net loss of roughly $267.0 million, resulting in a net margin of negative 0.5%. This reflects the heavy capital investments required to transition toward its foundry-first strategy.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was nearly 0.4x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. The current ratio, measuring the ability to cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets, was close to 2.0x. Free cash flow was negative at roughly $4.9 billion, and stock-based compensation accounted for nearly 25.1% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation because SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing operates as a pure-play foundry, manufacturing chips designed by other companies for smartphones and artificial intelligence. While major customers are not explicitly disclosed in its latest filings, it serves nearly every major chip designer among semiconductor stocks. This business model allows it to benefit from industrywide growth without the risk of competing with its own clients.

In FY 2025, revenue reached close to $122.4 billion, a significant increase of approximately 32% over the previous year. The company delivered a net income of nearly $55.1 billion, resulting in a net margin of about 46.3%. These figures demonstrate the immense demand for its advanced manufacturing nodes.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.2x. The current ratio stood at close to 2.5x, indicating a strong position to cover near-term obligations. Free cash flow was robust at approximately $32.2 billion, representing the cash remaining after a company pays for its operations and capital investments.

Risk profile comparison

Intel faces significant litigation risk following its decision to grant a 10% equity stake to the U.S. government. Shareholders have filed lawsuits alleging the deal was intended to mitigate political pressure rather than serve investor interests. Additionally, Intel continues to be described as a beleaguered chipmaker, reflecting its ongoing struggle to regain technical leadership and improve market sentiment.

TSMC faces risks related to its concentration of manufacturing facilities, which are largely based in a single geographic region. While the company has not disclosed specific recent risks in its 10-K, global supply chain disruptions and regional geopolitical tensions remain primary concerns for the foundry. It also faces competitive pressure from Samsung and other rivals as they race to develop more efficient chip-making processes.

Valuation comparison

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing carries a lower Forward P/E based on future earnings estimates, while Intel has a lower P/S ratio using sales over the past twelve months.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?

When it comes to choosing between the two tech stocks, TSMC appears to be the safer and more profitable option.

Indeed, Intel has made a dramatic comeback amid the technical improvements enabled by its 18A technology and the prospect of becoming the leading fab in the U.S.

Nonetheless, despite improvements, Intel's financial struggles continue as it continues to run net losses. While revenue growth returned in the first half of 2026, the $52.9 billion generated in 2025 indicates its lackluster performance in the recent past.

In contrast, TSMC dominates production of the world's most advanced semiconductors, and the $122 billion in revenue it generated in 2025 affirms its dominance. Additionally, it is also a cash generation machine, amid its $32.2 billion in free cash flow for 2025.

Given that, it makes little sense to pay the valuation premium that has arisen from the massive gains in Intel stock. Since demand for advanced chips remains robust, TSMC will likely continue to stand out over the potentially promising but still struggling Intel.
