articles.article_title: Bentek Names Kevin Smith Chief Technology Officer as Company Advances AI and GovRAMP Strategy
articles.heading: Bentek Names Kevin Smith Chief Technology Officer as Company Advances AI and GovRAMP Strategy
articles.summary: /PRNewswire/ -- Bentek®, the benefits administration platform purpose-built for the public sector, today announced the promotion of Kevin Smith to Chief...
articles.content:
Longtime technology leader will advance Bentek's product modernization, responsible AI strategy and GovRAMP Ready program
PALM BEACH GARDENS, Fla., Oct. 1, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Bentek®, the benefits administration platform purpose-built for the public sector, today announced the promotion of Kevin Smith to Chief Technology Officer and Security Officer. In this expanded executive role, Smith will lead Bentek's technology strategy as the company advances AI modernization, strengthens security and compliance, and continues developing technology for state, local and education organizations.
During his 11 years with Bentek, Smith has helped guide the company's technology evolution across software engineering, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, product modernization, AI governance and technology compliance.
"Kevin has been instrumental in ensuring that security and privacy remain foundational to how we build, operate and serve our clients," said Julie Fink, President of Bentek. "He understands our platform, our clients and our security responsibilities, and he is the right leader to help advance our next phase of innovation."
Advancing Security and GovRAMP Readiness
Bentek's security program includes SOC 2 compliance, an A+ HIPAA rating and participation in the GovRAMP program. Bentek is continuing to advance its GovRAMP Ready posture as part of its long-term commitment to protecting sensitive public-sector data and supporting evolving government procurement requirements.
Under Smith's leadership, security, privacy and compliance will continue to be integrated into cloud architecture, software delivery, AI governance and day-to-day operations.
"Public-sector organizations deserve technology that is innovative without compromising trust," said Smith. "Our responsibility is to modernize thoughtfully, protect the information entrusted to us and give our clients confidence in the systems that support their employees and retirees."
Building a Secure and Governed AI Foundation
Smith will also lead Bentek's next phase of AI-enabled development and operational modernization. The company is building a secure, governed AI foundation designed to reduce administrative work, improve support, enhance configuration tools and provide greater visibility across the customer lifecycle.
"Our focus is not on adopting AI simply because it is available," Fink added. "We are focused on using it where it can make a meaningful difference while protecting our clients and maintaining accountability. As we look ahead, technology innovation and security must advance together."
Kevin Smith's promotion reflects Bentek's continued investment in secure technology modernization and responsible AI adoption for the public sector.
About Bentek
Since 2006, Bentek has helped public sector organizations manage complex benefits programs for active employees, retirees, dependents and administrators. Its benefits administration technology is purpose-built for state, local and education organizations and is supported by a partnership-driven implementation and service model. Bentek maintains a 98% client retention rate and an NPS of 84. The company also holds an A+ HIPAA rating, is SOC 2 compliant and participates in the GovRAMP program.
For more information, visit Bentek's website.

"He understands our platform, our clients and our security responsibilities, and he is the right leader to help advance our next phase of innovation."

Advancing Security and GovRAMP Readiness

Bentek's security program includes SOC 2 compliance, an A+ HIPAA rating and participation in the GovRAMP program. Bentek is continuing to advance its GovRAMP Ready posture as part of its long-term commitment to protecting sensitive public-sector data and supporting evolving government procurement requirements.

Under Smith's leadership, security, privacy and compliance will continue to be integrated into cloud architecture, software delivery, AI governance and day-to-day operations.

"Public-sector organizations deserve technology that is innovative without compromising trust," said Smith. "Our responsibility is to modernize thoughtfully, protect the information entrusted to us and give our clients confidence in the systems that support their employees and retirees."

Building a Secure and Governed AI Foundation

Smith will also lead Bentek's next phase of AI-enabled development and operational modernization. The company is building a secure, governed AI foundation designed to reduce administrative work, improve support, enhance configuration tools and provide greater visibility across the customer lifecycle.

"Our focus is not on adopting AI simply because it is available," Fink added. "We are focused on using it where it can make a meaningful difference while protecting our clients and maintaining accountability. As we look ahead, technology innovation and security must advance together."

Kevin Smith's promotion reflects Bentek's continued investment in secure technology modernization and responsible AI adoption for the public sector.

About Bentek

Since 2006, Bentek has helped public sector organizations manage complex benefits programs for active employees, retirees, dependents and administrators. Its benefits administration technology is purpose-built for state, local and education organizations and is supported by a partnership-driven implementation and service model. Bentek maintains a 98% client retention rate and an NPS of 84. The company also holds an A+ HIPAA rating, is SOC 2 compliant and participates in the GovRAMP program.

articles.summary: As a Kluge Chair, Jackson is invited to conduct research using the collections at the Library of Congress and to interact with congressional members and staff.
articles.content:
News directly from Cornell's colleges and centers
Jackson selected for Kluge Chair in Technology and Society
By Patricia Waldron
The John W. Kluge Center at the Library of Congress has chosen Steven Jackson, vice provost for academic innovation and professor of information science and science and technology studies, as the fall 2026 Kluge Chair in Technology and Society.
Established in 2000, the Kluge Center brings in leading scholars from around the world to make use of the library's collections and to interact with congressional members and staff. Chairs are selected by nominators from around the world, and are free to conduct their own research among the vast collections of the nation's library. Past chair-holders include Vaclav Havel, Manuel Castells and Wiliam Julius Wilson.
The Chair in Technology and Society is one of five chairs outlined in the Kluge Center’s founding documents.
During his tenure, Jackson will work with the library’s extensive holdings on science, technology and industry to pursue two projects. The first, technology and the extension ideal, investigates the imaginations of science, technology and democracy central to the history and practice of continuing education and cooperative extension. The second, a land-based history of American computing, explores the role of land and landscape in the constitution of contemporary computing infrastructures.
"I am honored to serve as a Kluge Chair at the Library of Congress and I look forward to engaging with and learning from the LOC collections, chairs, fellows and staff to advance our understanding of American computing and educational history,” Jackson said.

articles.article_title: The Store Has Become a Technology Platform
articles.heading: The Store Has Become a Technology Platform
articles.summary: Yesterday's network strategy may be limiting tomorrow's growth.
articles.content:
The Store Has Become a Technology Platform
Yesterday's network strategy may be limiting tomorrow's growth.
Oct 01, 2026 | 3 min read
This article is brought to you by Mako Networks.
For years, convenience retailers evaluated networks the same way they evaluated utility infrastructure: Did it work? Was it reliable? Could it connect the store?
That approach made sense when the primary purpose of the network was supporting point-of-sale systems and payment terminals.
Today, however, the modern convenience store is becoming a highly connected technology environment. Self-checkout, digital signage, video analytics, foodservice monitoring, loyalty programs, security systems and emerging AI applications all depend on one common foundation: the network.
"Retailers don't have a connectivity problem. They have an infrastructure problem," said Jon Kelly, chief revenue officer at Mako Networks. "Many stores are trying to support next-generation technology on infrastructure that was designed for a different era."
As retailers introduce new applications, they often discover that the network itself has become the bottleneck to innovation. The challenge is no longer simply connecting devices. It's securely supporting thousands of devices, applications and data streams across hundreds or even thousands of locations.
According to Kelly, leading retailers are shifting away from viewing the network as a collection of hardware components and toward viewing it as a business platform.
"The network is no longer just plumbing," he said. "It's becoming the operating system of the modern store."
That shift is changing how retailers evaluate technology partners. Security, connectivity, application support and centralized management increasingly need to work together as part of a unified architecture.
Cybersecurity is a prime example. Retailers face growing threats from ransomware, credential theft and increasingly sophisticated attacks. Kelly says security can no longer be bolted onto the network through separate appliances and software products.
"Security has to be embedded into the foundation of the platform itself," he said.
Centralized management is becoming equally important. Rather than managing multiple vendors and disconnected systems, retailers are increasingly looking for a consistent technology foundation that can be deployed, monitored and updated across every location.
Last year, Mako Networks introduced the Mako 6700, a platform designed to provide the flexibility, security and performance required for the next generation of convenience retail technology.
"The retailers that move fastest over the next decade will be the ones that standardize on a platform capable of evolving with their business," Kelly said. "The real question isn't whether your stores are connected. It's whether your infrastructure is ready to support what's next."
This article is the first in a two-part series from Mako Networks. Look for part two, which explores how retailers can prepare for AI and emerging edge technologies.

articles.title: Defense-Proven Drone Technology Moves Into the Commercial Market

articles.article_title: Defense-Proven Drone Technology Moves Into the Commercial Market
articles.heading: Defense-Proven Drone Technology Moves Into the Commercial Market
articles.summary: Utopia Compression brings defense-proven commercial drone tech to BVLOS, counter-UAS, passive sensing, navigation, autonomous operations.
articles.content:
Utopia Compression brings AI-based passive sensing, navigation and autonomy solutions developed for defense applications to BVLOS, counter-UAS and other commercial drone operations
By DRONELIFE Features Editor Jim Magill
Utopia Compression, an advanced technology company with more than two decades of experience providing services to the defense sector, is looking to branch out by providing artificial intelligence-based software solutions to the fast-growing commercial UAV and advanced air mobility (AAM) industries.
In an interview, Priya Ganapathy, customer success lead at Utopia Compression, said the company’s technology, which has already been vetted by defense sector customers including the U.S. Air Force and the U.S. Navy, is easily transferable to meet the needs of the growing commercial drone market.
“What we primarily do is we actually use the cameras which are on board the UAVs or drones, and we provide advanced situational awareness to the drone operator for BVLOS operations, for counter-UAS, and for general ISR [intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance],” she said.
The Los Angeles-based company has also developed a system that allows a single operator to handle multiple drones flying in a swarm to complete a single mission. While such a capability has obvious benefits in battlefield applications, commercial drone operators are just beginning to realize the potential of such a technology.
Ganapathy said the Commercial UAV Expo, recently held in Las Vegas, was the first venue where Utopia Compression demonstrated the capabilities of its products for the commercial UAV market customers. Among the company’s areas of expertise showcased at the Expo was the technology used to provide advanced situational awareness solutions in both the aerial and maritime domains.
“This is essentially detecting the threats, from non-cooperator actors, and then tracking them and classifying them,” she said.
Because the company’s technology is primarily passive, it does not need any radar-like sensors, a critical feature in defense operations where the aim is to detect without being detected, said Lakshmi Rangaraju, senior research and development engineer, at the company.
“And especially with the decreasing drone size, it is difficult for radar-like active sensors to capture these objects and make sure they are being identified at a good distance, to ensure the right maneuver or to avoid the collision or to take the right action,” Rangaraju said.
Background in maritime detection technology
Although it has only recently begun to market its aerial technologies to the commercial sector, the company has licensed its maritime surveillance solutions to Teledyne FLIR for about a dozen years, said Joseph Yadegar, Utopia Compression’s founder and president.
“We have also done a number of experimental tests of some of our aerial capabilities, such as swarm and others, with other companies in the recent year or so,” he said. “Currently we are speaking with commercial counter-UAS vendors as well as public safety agencies who’re testing our software for BVLOS and counter-UAS operations.”
The company offers a broad portfolio of detection and navigation products designed to fill the needs of its defense customers, as well as those of the commercial UAV and AAM industries.
To solve one of the biggest challenges confronting the drone delivery industry – how to complete the last-mile of delivery in GPS-denied urban environments – the company has introduced Co-NAVIGATE, a software solution, that employs sensor fusion to help identify “smart landmarks” to allow a drone to navigate itself, without the need of GPS.
The company’s AETHER, detect-and-avoid system, combines the use of computer vision with autonomous-system technologies to help usher in the future of widespread BVLOS flight and AAM operations. Its CO AIR system is designed to orchestrate the complex series of multiple interactions between ground and aerial vehicles.
Calling on its background in producing systems designed for military uses, Utopia Compression designed SwarmSync to augment the capabilities of UAS swarms, a feature that the company hopes will make it useful across a wide spectrum of civilian applications.
Layered approach to technologic development
Ganapathy said the company’s technology has been developed to fit in with the layered approach to sensing, detection and navigation challenges favored by the U.S. military.
“Our approach really does replace radar and we are able to do these operations either at short or long distances, depending on how far the object or the drone we want to detect is,” she said.
She said she believes this approach to developing software solutions will stand the company in good stead, as it pivots its marketing strategy to appeal to commercial UAV and counter-UAV customers. “I would say the transition is straightforward,” she said. “Our systems are agnostic as to the sensor. We can either use our payload or we can use the payload of the customer.”
Company officials hope to focus their efforts in the commercial space on helping to enable the development of a universal BVLOS standard. The lack of such a standard has proven to be a major impediment to the commercial drone industry’s ability to scale up, Ganapathy said.
“That’s where we would play a major role, because the capabilities that we provide as part of the passive sensing layer would enable those capabilities so that the drones can make effective, timely decisions,” she said.
Read more:
- Robin Radar Triples Capacity With New Counter-UAS Radar Facility
- Counter-Drone Optics Maker Opens US Headquarters, Plans Detroit Factory
- Powerus Signs $22.3M Counter-UAS Deal With Private Middle East Oil Firm
Jim Magill is a Houston-based writer with almost a quarter-century of experience covering technical and economic developments in the oil and gas industry. After retiring in December 2019 as a senior editor with S&P Global Platts, Jim began writing about emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence, robots and drones, and the ways in which they’re contributing to our society. In addition to DroneLife, Jim is a contributor to Forbes.com and his work has appeared in the Houston Chronicle, U.S. News & World Report, and Unmanned Systems, a publication of the Association for Unmanned Vehicle Systems International

articles.title: Wawa names new information technology chief
articles.description: Wawa names new information technology chief C-Store Dive
articles.description_html: Wawa names new information technology chief  C-Store Dive
articles.article_title: Wawa names new information technology chief
articles.heading: Don't miss tomorrow's convenience stores industry news
articles.summary: Bill O’Donnell takes on the role after more than 25 years with the retailer working across fuel operations and project management.
articles.content:
Wawa has promoted company veteran Bill O’Donnell to chief information technology officer, a spokesperson from the convenience retailer confirmed to C-Store Dive.
O’Donnell, who has been with Wawa for more than 25 years, now oversees the company’s technology strategy and operations, cybersecurity, digital platforms, data and analytics, according to his LinkedIn bio.
“Bill O’Donnell has more than 25 years of experience with Wawa in various roles and departments, including his newest role as Chief Information Technology Officer,” Wawa’s spokesperson said in a statement.
Technology plays a key role at Wawa’s convenience stores, particularly within its made-to-order foodservice business, which can take orders through mobile ordering and touchscreen kiosks. Last year, the retailer launched a machine-learning-based forecasting and replenishment program designed to reduce food waste.
O’Donnell earlier served as Wawa’s senior director of retail fuels and business development, according to the company’s website, and his LinkedIn bio indicates he held other roles in fuels and project management. He also serves on the board of The Wawa Foundation, a nonprofit supporting the company’s charitable initiatives.
Wawa’s spokesperson did not respond by press time to questions about O’Donnell’s responsibilities or who he is succeeding in his new position.

articles.title: Walmart is using light-up digital shelf labels to help shoppers and employees find items
articles.description: Walmart is using light-up digital shelf labels to help shoppers and employees find items CNBC
articles.description_html: Walmart is using light-up digital shelf labels to help shoppers and employees find items  CNBC
articles.article_title: Walmart is using light-up digital shelf labels to help shoppers and employees find items
articles.heading: Walmart is using light-up digital shelf labels to help shoppers and employees find items
articles.summary: Walmart is rolling out a light-up shelf label feature connected to its app to help customers better find the items they're looking for.
articles.content:
Walmart is aiming to make it as easy as possible for its customers to find exactly what they want.
The retailer is leveraging three new tools tied to its digital shelf labels for both customers and store associates to better find products. It's the latest part of the company's push to modernize its technology and incorporate artificial intelligence into its business.
"We are people-led, tech-powered," said Greg Cathey, Walmart's senior vice president of digital transformation. "But the way we look at it is AI as a way to help associates do their job and free up time to allow them to invest in what they love to do most, which is spend more time with customers and their fellow associates."
The new feature for shoppers, called Shop to Light, allows customers to find specific products on the Walmart app, navigate to the correct aisle in the store and then flash the digital shelf label of the product to locate it. The retailer is now incorporating it widely following a pilot program.
That tool is also paired with Pick to Light and Stock to Light, which use the same capabilities to help store associates pick items for digital orders and stock products. All three features will be rolled out to stores companywide by the holiday season, Cathey said.
"This is a use case that customers have asked us for, associates have asked us for," Cathey said. "It gives them time back, and I think if you look at a lot of what we're trying to do, it's all around convenience and being able to help associates and customers free up that time to invest it where they want."
The rollout comes as convenience and speed — particularly in the delivery and pickup segments — have become critical pieces of Walmart's efforts to increase sales. While Walmart's business has grown steadily, and its e-commerce sales continue to soar, investor concerns about its comparable sales and revenue outlook weighed on its stock after its most recent earnings report in August.
Walmart stores carry roughly 120,000 items. Cathey said it's a priority for the company to provide that large range of products while making it easier for customers to locate precise items.

He said these new features will be especially important as the retailer heads into the busy holiday season, and the company views them as "a big win" for time savings.
Walmart began using digital shelf labels, as opposed to paper labels, to allow automatic and systemwide price changes to be rolled out at once. The company currently has more than 4,300 stores with digital shelf labels, and expects them to be installed across the chain by the end of the year, according to Walmart.

"We don't look at it as technology for technology's sake," Cathey said. "So we always have a human in the loop, and we're very focused on human judgment and their ability to make decisions."
A broader technology push
Walmart has been investing in its technology to modernize the business on both the consumer-facing side and in internal operations.
It's rolled out an AI agent to help customers with shopping, automated its supply chain, invested in radio frequency identification tags and set the stage for agentic commerce as it embraces AI. It's also spent billions on modernizing its store locations.

"We believe AI will improve nearly every part of our business by making shopping better, and our associates' work easier," he said.

"It's not one or the other anymore. It's both," he said. "We don't look at it as a store or an e-commerce fulfillment. They're actually one and the same."

articles.article_title: AI and the impending third technology talent drought
articles.heading: AI and the impending third technology talent drought
articles.summary: AI is reshaping tech hiring, creating a talent pipeline challenge as fewer students enter computing and leaders anticipate less demand for entry-level roles.
articles.content:
AI is reshaping tech hiring, creating a talent pipeline challenge as fewer students enter computing and leaders anticipate less demand for entry-level roles.
Every technology professional working today owes their career, in part, to someone who took a chance on them. The software engineers, cybersecurity analysts and infrastructure specialists on our teams didn’t arrive fully formed and ready to perform. Someone hired them, trained them and gave them room to grow. That’s worth remembering now, because the tech talent pipeline is shrinking, and history shows it can take more than a decade to recover from a decline like this.
The pipeline is at risk on two fronts: fewer students are choosing to study computer and information science, and hiring managers anticipate weaker near-term demand for these graduates. This isn’t unprecedented. The computing profession has weathered two major talent declines in its short history, and each took more than a decade to recover.
After 15 years of growth, computing enrollment reverses
According to the U.S. National Center for Education Statistics, the number of computer science and information science B.S. graduates has grown steadily since 2010. A tech degree once meant a well-paying job and a career with a future, driven largely by increased demand for technology. That momentum now appears to be reversing across several regions of the world.
Research from the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center indicates that enrollment in CS and IS degree programs at U.S. colleges and universities fell by more than 8% in 2025, even as overall undergraduate enrollment grew by 1%. The trend is not confined to the U.S. According to BCS, the Chartered Institute for IT, the UK saw a similar decline, with 18-year-old UK students entering computing degree programs down 9% in 2025. In Australia, the decline appears even steeper. ACS/Information Age reports that the Australasian Conference of Tertiary Admissions Centres’ (ACTAC) January 2026 report shows a 21% decline in enrollment for IT-related degrees heading into 2026.
Three countries, three distinct education systems, one common outcome. What makes this notable isn’t any single data point but the swift, dramatic downturn across all three countries. If this were confined to one market, it could be dismissed as a local correction; however, a similar pattern across the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia at roughly the same time suggests a structural shift in how the next generation views a tech career.
What 1,200 tech leaders expect: Lower demand for graduates
If the problem were only fewer graduates, but hiring demand were strong, the situation would probably correct itself. Talent scarcity would drive up wages and attract more students. However, the demand side appears to be contracting as well.
In the second quarter of 2026, I surveyed more than 1,200 senior technology leaders across 53 countries and what they expected their organization’s hiring demand to look like five years from now for entry-level roles filled by graduates with bachelor’s degrees in computer science or information science. Respondents held titles including CIO, CTO, VP of IT and Head of IT. More than 6,600 surveys were sent to technology leaders via LinkedIn, resulting in a 19% response rate.
The results were sobering: 45% anticipated lower demand, 28% expected demand to remain the same, while 27% anticipated it to increase. (You can download a summary of the survey at https://www.impactfultechnologyleader.com).
This result was not limited to a specific country or region. Those expecting hiring demand to be lower in five years were in the majority across almost every country, industry and company size.
The reason, cited across every group, was the same: artificial intelligence. Leaders expect AI to automate much of the entry-level technical work, including routine coding, service-desk tickets and administrative tasks. This is the work where new graduates have traditionally begun their careers. The logic is that existing teams, aided by AI, can do more without adding entry-level employees.
Regardless of their responses to the survey question, many of the leaders noted that reducing the number of junior roles in their organization was problematic. They recognized that it would erode the pipeline for future senior talent and that recovery from this gap would take years.
We’ve seen this movie before
This is not the first time CS and IS graduate numbers have fallen. In the mid-1980s, universities were overwhelmed by demand for computing degrees and couldn’t staff their programs adequately. When computer science programs could no longer accommodate surging student interest, universities capped enrollment and tightened admission standards. The effect was dramatic: bachelor’s degrees in computer and information sciences fell sharply beginning in 1987. It was not until 2001, fifteen years later, that graduation rates recovered to their earlier level.
The second decline came in the early 2000s, in what might be called a perfect storm. The winding down of Y2K remediation, the bursting of the dot-com bubble and a rising wave of IT offshoring converged to shake confidence in technology as a career. Mass layoffs swept through IT departments and dot-com firms, and enrollment in computing programs fell once again. The resulting drop in tech degrees awarded began around 2005, and it was not until 2016, eleven years later, that graduation rates recovered to the same level.
The chart below from the U.S. National Center for Education Statistics depicts these two significant declines in graduates with technology degrees.
Is AI the new perfect storm?
If you map today’s forces onto that history, the parallels are hard to miss. AI-driven automation is creating a demand shock, declining technology enrollments are creating a supply shock, and growing skepticism about the value of a technology degree is creating a confidence shock. This mirrors the erosion of faith in the career path after the dot-com bubble burst.
What took three separate crises to unfold in the early 2000s is converging today into a single, self-reinforcing cycle: fewer students entering the field, fewer opportunities perceived to be waiting for them, and growing doubts about whether a technology career is still worth pursuing.
But the parallel to those earlier declines carries a warning, not a reassurance, and the difference is in how each one ended. The recoveries of 2001 and 2016 happened because demand never left. In both prior declines, the supply of graduates fell while the underlying need for tech professionals rebounded. That gap between shrinking supply and steady demand is exactly what refilled the pipeline: scarcity pushed up wages, wages pulled students back and the market corrected itself, however slowly. What makes today different is that supply and demand are falling together. If leaders are correct that AI will replace entry-level work, this is not a demand dip waiting to rebound, it is a demand replacement, with no scarcity signal to trigger the correction that saved the field twice before.
The most dangerous feature of a talent pipeline is its lag. The decisions made, or not made, over the next few years will not trigger a crisis next quarter or even next year. Their consequences will surface a decade or more from now, when today’s would-be entry-level personnel should have become tomorrow’s architects, technical experts and leaders.
By then, the shortage will already be baked into the pipeline. And that is not speculation. It is the exact pattern the historical record has already shown us, twice.
What is a technology leader to do?
It would be easy to read my survey results and conclude that the market will sort itself out. Nearly half of the IT leaders I surveyed plan to hire fewer entry-level computing graduates over the next five years. Many dismiss this: education will adapt, five years is an eternity and better tools will make new graduates more capable than ever. They may be right. But hope is not a workforce strategy, and the leaders best positioned five years from now will be those who treat this as a problem to solve, not a trend to watch.
The uncomfortable truth is in one respondent’s warning: “We will have to find a way to invest in new grads, or we will not have a pipeline of middle and senior talent later.” If every organization cuts entry-level hiring because AI now handles the routine work, our profession will slowly stop developing the senior engineers it will desperately need a decade from now, because senior people are simply junior people who were given room to grow. No single leader can solve this problem, but every leader can refuse to be the one who lets it happen to their organization.
That starts with treating early-career hiring as a strategic investment, not the first line item to cut. Set aside several junior roles intentionally as an investment in your future leadership, rather than as just headcount to cut in the upcoming budget cycle.
It also means redefining what “entry-level” even means. Survey respondents were consistent: the bar is changing. They want applicants with a strong portfolio over a strong transcript, demonstrable AI fluency over rote coding, and, in the words of one, “people who can ask the right questions” now that AI supplies the answers. Rewrite your junior roles and interviews around critical thinking and judgment, and recognize that a new graduate’s value now lies in growth potential and the ability to direct AI-assisted work, not raw output.
Finally, the talent pipeline begins with encouraging high school students to seriously consider a career in technology, and guiding them will take all of us. If history holds, many will steer away from computing if they believe it has no future. Before committing to an investment as large as four years of tuition, parents will point their children toward fields with steady or rising demand.
Technology leaders and their teams can cut through the hype and help students understand what a career in technology looks like in the age of AI. Through classroom talks and on-site job shadowing, they can give students a real chance to discover the opportunities computing offers. Through mentoring and hands-on, real-world projects, they can support STEM programs at both the primary and secondary education levels.
With the aid of other technology professionals and leaders, I have developed a directory of organizations that promote and support careers in computing across the globe. The directory, which can be found at impactfultechnologyleader.com, includes:
- Programs for grade school, high school and university students
- Support for working professionals, whether already in tech or breaking into it
- Groups serving those transitioning from the military, returning to work or navigating any other path
Every one of us in this profession got here because someone decided we were worth the investment before we had proven it. That decision was never really about what a junior professional could contribute on day one. It was a bet on who they could become. AI may change what that first job looks like, but it doesn’t change a fundamental truth: to become a senior technology professional, you first had to be a junior one. The leaders who understand that over the next five years won’t necessarily be the ones who predicted AI correctly. They’ll be the ones who understood that some risks are worth hedging against even when you can’t be certain, and that a talent pipeline, once broken, takes a decade or more to rebuild.
The question isn’t whether the pipeline is at risk; it’s what you will do to make sure it doesn’t break.

articles.title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
articles.description: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names BBC
articles.description_html: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names  BBC
articles.article_title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
articles.heading: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
articles.summary: The president wants AI to be called super intelligence - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian domains.
articles.content:
Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
President Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry.
The president wants AI to be called super intelligence - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites.
Register.si spokesperson Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%.
She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months.
President Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September.
"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said.
"It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence."
Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk.
Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to only President Trump's comments.
She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded.
One possible explanation for the purchases is a practice where people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit.
For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later.
On Tuesday, President Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age".
He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and they should no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.
Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath President Trump's signature.

She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months.

President Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September.

"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said.

"It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence."

Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk.

Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to only President Trump's comments.

She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded.

One possible explanation for the purchases is a practice where people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit.

For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later.

On Tuesday, President Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age".

He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and they should no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI.

SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.

Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath President Trump's signature.

articles.summary: The Community College of Baltimore County is investing $28 million to expand its Transportation Technology Center in Catonsville.
articles.content:
Actions

CATONSVILLE, Md. — The Community College of Baltimore County is investing $28 million to expand its Transportation Technology Center in Catonsville.

The college broke ground on the expansion Wednesday, while also celebrating the completion of an $11.6 million renovation of the existing auto repair center.

The project will add nearly 22,000 square feet to the existing 17,000-square-foot center, with new classrooms, specialized labs and bays for electric and hydrogen vehicles.

CCBC President Sandra Kurtinitis said the goal is to make sure students are prepared for where the automotive industry is headed.

“Everything we try to do at CCBC, if we're going to be getting students ready for the outside, has to be cutting edge,” Kurtinitis said.

The college says its automotive program has been at peak enrollment for nearly a decade. Because of limited space, the program has had to turn down some training opportunities, manufacturer partnerships and equipment donations.

The expansion will give CCBC more room for automotive training, including work with electric vehicles and other emerging technology.

CCBC is also building a new $13 million welding and trades center at its Dundalk campus. The college broke ground on that project in April. It will offer hands-on training, including specialized training in underwater welding.

articles.title: Hegseth returns to Quantico to lay out technology and people initiatives

articles.article_title: Hegseth returns to Quantico to lay out technology and people initiatives
articles.heading: Hegseth returns to Quantico to lay out technology and people initiatives
articles.summary: Hegseth returns to Quantico to lay out technology and people initiatives The American Legion
articles.content:
DoD Secretary Pete Hegseth gathers 600 rank-and-file troops to announce six new initiatives, including drone command and religious affairs office, and highlight plans to cut 20% of nation’s generals and admirals.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth gathered 600 rank-and-file troops on Wednesday at Marine Corps Base Quantico to announce six initiatives that included the creation of an autonomous warfare command, a religious affairs office that will report directly to the secretary, and the addition of a new corps of cadets at five universities.
Hegseth also highlighted a plan to cut 20% of the nation’s generals and admirals.
“I’m proud to stand on this stage and report that the warrior ethos has been revived, our military is being rebuilt and American deterrence is back,” the secretary said about five minutes into the “State of the Force” address, which he intends to make an annual event.
Hegseth, a 46-year-old Army National Guard veteran and former Fox News host, gave a speech exactly one year ago to about 800 generals and admirals and their top enlisted advisers to lay out his vision for the U.S. military. Some of the policies the services have worked to implement include more physical fitness tests, tighter body fat restrictions and fewer shaving waivers across the force.
“Now, I think the generals heard the message. Those who responded positively, which is most of them, are leading newly focused and newly empowered and disciplined formations,” Hegseth said. “Those generals who did not, who clung to the woke department, or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion. Well, they no longer work here.”
Hegseth began Wednesday by praising the force, particularly the troops in attendance, and celebrating what he called the return to a warrior ethos. He also lashed out at media members and reiterated that the Pentagon is no longer the “woke department.”
“The complainers, the ideologues and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat. No more silly PowerPoint trainings or drag queen shows,” Hegseth said. “No more gender pronouns. No more identity months. Only the warrior ethos.”
About 20 minutes into the speech, he got to the new part of the message — six new strategic initiatives to reshape the force. Hegseth first announced a new command to oversee and coordinate drone development and deployment supporting overseas operations.
“Today at my direction, we are announcing the creation of Autonomous Warfare Command — or AutoWarCom — a four-star combatant command with service-like authorities built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities,” Hegseth said.
The establishment of the command by Oct. 1, 2027, will require the Pentagon to work with Congress to get the necessary legislation, according to the memo signed Wednesday.
“This command will possess directed manpower, budget, acquisition authorities and create dedicated military career pathways for officers and enlisted personnel,” Hegseth said in the memo.
The second initiative, Project Meridian, is an effort to leverage the nation’s premier private-sector innovators, business leaders and technologists to accelerate “the fielding of advanced systems for the next generation battlefield.”
Emil Michael, the under secretary of defense for research and engineering, will lead the project that will be co-directed by Elon Musk, businessman and former senior adviser to President Donald Trump; Palmer Luckey, co-founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries; and Newt Gingrich, former Speaker of the House.
“We should have the humility to recognize that the best forecasters of future conflict do not solely reside inside the Pentagon,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth expects Project Meridian’s findings to be completed and submitted in 120 days. The group’s first meeting would be held in a SCIF 200 yards from where the speech was held on base.
The third initiative involves a plan called FORTRESS America (Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability) that is intended to ensure that every major U.S. military installation generates its own independent power.
“If an adversary takes down the grid by cyberattack, by sabotage, or by any means, our bases stay lit,” Hegseth said. “Our aircraft keep flying. Our command centers never go dark.”
Michael Duffey, the under secretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, has been directed to stand up the program office within 30 days, according to the memo.
The fourth initiative, Next Great American Base, involves building a new base on American soil.
“We’re calling on every governor in the country and adjutant general … to step up to the plate and bring us their best sales pitch. If your state wants the honor … show us why and how you’re going to do it — cutting through the red tape, offering up the land and rolling out the red carpet for our military families,” the secretary said.
Hegseth said there will be no “backroom Washington deals,” just a “merit-based contest” to see which is the best state. The state-of-the-art installation would host elite troops across hundreds of thousands of acres, the Pentagon said in a news release.
Engineered to operate completely off the commercial grid, it would feature independent power generation, autonomous systems and advanced air defenses.
The America’s Corps of Cadets initiative partners with a new set of institutions — Louisiana State University, Liberty University, Tuskegee University, Mississippi State University and Hillsdale College — to create additional full-time Corps of Cadets programs.
The Pentagon chief visited the Texas A&M Corps of Cadets on Sept. 19, where he also worked out with cadets at Kyle Field.
“The patriotic and selfless service being taught at places like Texas A&M, VMI, the Citadel, Norwich, Virginia Tech, and the University of North Georgia,” Hegseth said. “We need more officers from academic institutions like our military academies and senior military colleges. And today, we’re going to make that happen.”
The sixth initiative, the Office of Religious Affairs, will report directly to Hegseth and future defense secretaries to come.
“Faith in something greater than us,” Hegseth told the audience. Less than 5% of the force identifies as non-religious, which means 95% of the force “recognizes an Almighty God,” he said. “This is not going to be a paper-pushing shop. It’s going to have real teeth,” the secretary added. “The experts, our chaplains, will finally have an advocate at the highest levels.”
Christianity has been an emphasis since Hegseth took over the Defense Department, including a monthly prayer and worship service that started in May 2025. Americans United for Separation of Church and State, which has sued the Pentagon for its monthly services, criticized the announcement.
“The Department of Defense owes it to the nation’s service members to defend religious freedom as promised in our Constitution — a freedom they risk their lives protecting for all of us,” Rachel Laser, organization president and CEO, said in a statement. “Hegseth’s latest announcement violates that promise by elevating Christianity to an even higher role in shaping U.S. military policy.”
Hegseth and the troops who traveled for the speech started the morning with physical training at the Pentagon. The secretary and troops wore “This is War” shirts, referencing the Pentagon’s secondary name, “Department of War.”
“We are in a war of attrition against the Pentagon bureaucracy every single day, and it is a war that we intend to win,” the secretary said during his close to one-hour speech.
As troops arrived at the Marine Corps History Center an hour before the speech, a 144-page “War Department field manual” was on tables to grab. The book included four of Hegseth’s speeches, including last year’s Quantico address.
Trump wrote a foreword that said, “I will not ask you to fight dumb wars.” The audience consisted of E6 noncommissioned officers and junior commissioned officers with the rank of O3.
“Now it could have been E5s or E7s or O2s or O4s, but I’ve got a sweet spot, a special thing, for E6s and O3s,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth also, as expected, announced a 20% cut to general and flag officers. “The media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, and long overdue, and frankly, the bare minimum,” the secretary said. The planned reductions must take place by Jan. 1, according to multiple reports.
- Security

articles.article_title: DHS Science and Technology Directorate Reorganizes Research Capabilities
articles.heading: DHS Science and Technology Directorate Reorganizes Research Capabilities
articles.summary: The Homeland Security Department revamps research, development, test and evaluation to improve alignment with mission needs.
articles.content:
DHS Science and Technology Directorate Reorganizes Research Capabilities
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Science and Technology (S&T) Directorate has reorganized its laboratories and centers of excellence to strengthen their alignment with mission needs.
The reorganization affected the Office of National Laboratories (ONL), which leverages a coordinated network of DHS and Department of Energy national laboratories to deliver technologies vital to the DHS and the national homeland security mission.
The office ensures the safe, secure, and compliant management and operations of S&T’s five in-house laboratories, which include seven sites located in five states:
Chemical Security Analysis Center – Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland
National Biodefense Analysis and Countermeasures Center – Fort Detrick, Maryland
National Urban Security Technology Laboratory – New York City (Manhattan), New York
Plum Island Animal Disease Center – Orient Point, New York
Transportation Security Laboratory – Atlantic City, New Jersey
TSL Detection Technology Center – Terrorist Explosive Device Analytical Center, Improvised Explosives Detection and Synthesis Center, Huntsville, Alabama
TSL Tyndall Reactive Materials Group, Tyndall Air Force Base, Panama City, Florida
While the office “has not necessarily gone away,” S&T has added some functions and capabilities, according to Jamie Wells, executive director of S&T’s laboratories and academic centers, who oversees the directorate’s intramural, enduring research, development, testing and evaluation (RDT&E). That includes the five laboratories, academic centers of excellence and academic internship programs. It also includes a couple of divisions focused on specific technology areas, one on biometrics identity and advanced computing, and the other on expeditionary and red team assessment.
“The Office of National Laboratories, prior to the reshaping that Science and Technology has done over the last year, was focused on managing those five laboratories within DHS S&T and also managing our relationship with the Department of Energy national labs. Those functions still absolutely exist within the laboratories and academic centers,” Wells reported during a SIGNAL Media interview. “We’ve essentially added on to what have traditionally been ONL capabilities to include those other functions.”
The reorganization also affected the Homeland Security Advanced Research Projects Agency (HSARPA). “We created the Homeland Security Advanced Research Projects Agency around a mission center concept. So, HSARPA is the portion of S&T that’s responsible for delivering research and development to our components in support of their operational needs, and we’ve organized that into three different mission centers that are aligned with the various missions within the department,” Wells explained.
Overall, the changes help the labs and academic centers to better support HSARPA projects, he indicated. “What this new construct enables us to do is have HSARPA focused on managing research and development programs that deliver capabilities to components, while the laboratories and academic centers maintain our enduring capabilities that assist in delivering discrete capabilities through HSARPA projects.”
As early as 2024, officials began pursuing more unified research and development investments. “We decided that the best way to unify our investment approach was aligned with DHS missions, and so we embarked upon doing a functional continuity analysis to figure out the various functions we conduct across the directorate, the underlying statutory and regulatory reasons behind those, and how we more efficiently organize ourselves to make sure that we’re delivering return on investment in terms of mission capabilities.”
The next year, President Donald Trump’s administration initiated “a number of staffing efficiencies” across the federal government,” Wells noted, which resulted in S&T losing about 30% of its staff. “That further gave us some opportunity to realize efficiencies in the way that we were organized. Once we lost a certain number of federal employees through natural attrition, through a variety of efficiency programs in the federal government, this reshaping allowed us to realize the mission alignment that we were originally focused on, while also taking into account our streamlined staffing model.”
The reorganization “has allowed us to take advantage of the staffing that we have and align that with mission delivery in a way that’s most efficient for the number of people and the budget that we have,” he added.
The directorate has gone through several rounds of reshaping the leadership team. “I would say at this point, we have formed the leadership team down through the supervisory level, and we’ve asked each of our laboratories and divisions to conduct a staffing analysis to look at what missions and functions they are charged with delivering or performing, and how their current staffing supports that and what changes might we need to make in order to ensure we have adequate staffing within each of the divisions and laboratories.”
That analysis was expected to be completed in August, he said. “That’s the analysis that we’re going through now to inform any further movement within our existing staffing or any additional hiring actions we might need to make,” he said in July.
Wells said officials may “beef up” S&T’s research and development abilities. “We are certainly still going through making sure that our laboratory and academic capabilities cover the waterfront of the mission space and identifying gaps where we need to perhaps beef up laboratory capabilities or add or modify academic centers of excellence. Sure, there’s a ton to go there, but I think we’ve already realized a lot of the internal budgetary and communication benefits of the reshaping.”
Asked for specifics on potential beefing up efforts, Wells deadpanned: “That’s obviously not a technical term.”
Then he added that the directorate will continue taking stock of laboratory infrastructure and potential new enduring needs within the mission centers. “That beefing up may mean that we have a particular laboratory that can do more or different things than they currently do that are going to be persistent needs, and perhaps we need to invest in that,” he said. “It may mean that we need to add new laboratory capability. That may not mean we’re building a brick-and-mortar lab, but it may mean we need some enduring testing and evaluation capability, and perhaps we can take advantage of an interagency capability that already exists that we need to establish a memorandum of agreement to access. It may mean that we need to go back to the board and say, ‘Hey, we really have an enduring need here. Let’s go see if we can budget for that and make the argument that it is a good investment for DHS.’”
Ultimately, the reshaping will allow S&T officials to make more intelligent, clear decisions about which mission spaces they invest in, and why, and how that aligns with department and administration priorities. Additionally, it may help the directorate to deliver solutions more rapidly. “We are increasingly looking to adopt private sector solutions first. If there is a space where industry has already invested in a capability, we don’t necessarily need to reinvest in research and development of that capability. We really need to be aware of it, identify it and help our components quickly adapt it or configure it for their use, which can be a much more efficient and cost-effective way of getting them the capabilities they need.”
We decided that the best way to unify our investment approach was aligned with DHS missions, and so we embarked upon doing a functional continuity analysis to figure out the various functions we conduct across the directorate, the underlying statutory and regulatory reasons behind those, and how we more efficiently organize ourselves to make sure that we’re delivering return on investment in terms of mission capabilities.
Also in the interview, the executive director highlighted the DHS’s and S&T’s support of the homeland security mission during the FIFA World Cup earlier this year. Countering unmanned aerial systems proved central to that mission. The National Urban Security Technology Laboratory assesses existing counter-UAS systems to help federal, state and locals decide where to invest and also played a critical role in surveying each of the World Cup sites to help federal, state and local leadership make smart decisions about how to integrate the various systems into a system of systems for counter-UAS solutions, according to Wells. “A specific task that they undertook was doing radio frequency surveys at each of the locations in order to make sure that you can deconflict all of the sensors and mitigation techniques for counter UAS.”
He foresees counter-UAS continuing to be a vital part of the DHS mission. “And so, counter-UAS has become a massive mission space for the department, and as a result, is also a major lift for S&T, both on the research and development side and on the testing and evaluation side. I would expect that to continue as we move forward, so that’s a space where we’re actively evaluating our enduring needs for RDT&E in counter UAS.”
Countering drones is important to homeland security, but the “yin and yang” is that the unmanned systems also enhance many homeland security missions. “The department is clearly looking for ways to leverage unmanned systems. We already do that along the border with aerial systems. We are going to increasingly look to do that on the ground, on the surface, and undersea capabilities,” Wells stated. “I think there’s tremendous opportunity there for the department across many of its mission spaces to take advantage of unmanned systems.”
He also highlighted digital identity and biometrics as a critical technology area for the department. S&T maintains the Biometric and Identity Technology Center at its Maryland Test Facility. “We actually just recently completed a remote identity validation test event there that helped industry come bring in their products and understand what capabilities they bring to the table and where they might be brittle to potential fraud. I anticipate digital identity and biometrics will continue to be a focus moving forward.”

DHS Science and Technology Directorate Reorganizes Research Capabilities

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Science and Technology (S&T) Directorate has reorganized its laboratories and centers of excellence to strengthen their alignment with mission needs.

The reorganization affected the Office of National Laboratories (ONL), which leverages a coordinated network of DHS and Department of Energy national laboratories to deliver technologies vital to the DHS and the national homeland security mission.

The office ensures the safe, secure, and compliant management and operations of S&T’s five in-house laboratories, which include seven sites located in five states:

Chemical Security Analysis Center – Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland

National Biodefense Analysis and Countermeasures Center – Fort Detrick, Maryland

National Urban Security Technology Laboratory – New York City (Manhattan), New York

Plum Island Animal Disease Center – Orient Point, New York

Transportation Security Laboratory – Atlantic City, New Jersey

TSL Detection Technology Center – Terrorist Explosive Device Analytical Center, Improvised Explosives Detection and Synthesis Center, Huntsville, Alabama

TSL Tyndall Reactive Materials Group, Tyndall Air Force Base, Panama City, Florida

While the office “has not necessarily gone away,” S&T has added some functions and capabilities, according to Jamie Wells, executive director of S&T’s laboratories and academic centers, who oversees the directorate’s intramural, enduring research, development, testing and evaluation (RDT&E). That includes the five laboratories, academic centers of excellence and academic internship programs. It also includes a couple of divisions focused on specific technology areas, one on biometrics identity and advanced computing, and the other on expeditionary and red team assessment.

“The Office of National Laboratories, prior to the reshaping that Science and Technology has done over the last year, was focused on managing those five laboratories within DHS S&T and also managing our relationship with the Department of Energy national labs. Those functions still absolutely exist within the laboratories and academic centers,” Wells reported during a SIGNAL Media interview. “We’ve essentially added on to what have traditionally been ONL capabilities to include those other functions.”

The reorganization also affected the Homeland Security Advanced Research Projects Agency (HSARPA). “We created the Homeland Security Advanced Research Projects Agency around a mission center concept. So, HSARPA is the portion of S&T that’s responsible for delivering research and development to our components in support of their operational needs, and we’ve organized that into three different mission centers that are aligned with the various missions within the department,” Wells explained.

Overall, the changes help the labs and academic centers to better support HSARPA projects, he indicated. “What this new construct enables us to do is have HSARPA focused on managing research and development programs that deliver capabilities to components, while the laboratories and academic centers maintain our enduring capabilities that assist in delivering discrete capabilities through HSARPA projects.”

As early as 2024, officials began pursuing more unified research and development investments. “We decided that the best way to unify our investment approach was aligned with DHS missions, and so we embarked upon doing a functional continuity analysis to figure out the various functions we conduct across the directorate, the underlying statutory and regulatory reasons behind those, and how we more efficiently organize ourselves to make sure that we’re delivering return on investment in terms of mission capabilities.”

The next year, President Donald Trump’s administration initiated “a number of staffing efficiencies” across the federal government,” Wells noted, which resulted in S&T losing about 30% of its staff. “That further gave us some opportunity to realize efficiencies in the way that we were organized. Once we lost a certain number of federal employees through natural attrition, through a variety of efficiency programs in the federal government, this reshaping allowed us to realize the mission alignment that we were originally focused on, while also taking into account our streamlined staffing model.”

The reorganization “has allowed us to take advantage of the staffing that we have and align that with mission delivery in a way that’s most efficient for the number of people and the budget that we have,” he added.

The directorate has gone through several rounds of reshaping the leadership team. “I would say at this point, we have formed the leadership team down through the supervisory level, and we’ve asked each of our laboratories and divisions to conduct a staffing analysis to look at what missions and functions they are charged with delivering or performing, and how their current staffing supports that and what changes might we need to make in order to ensure we have adequate staffing within each of the divisions and laboratories.”

That analysis was expected to be completed in August, he said. “That’s the analysis that we’re going through now to inform any further movement within our existing staffing or any additional hiring actions we might need to make,” he said in July.

Wells said officials may “beef up” S&T’s research and development abilities. “We are certainly still going through making sure that our laboratory and academic capabilities cover the waterfront of the mission space and identifying gaps where we need to perhaps beef up laboratory capabilities or add or modify academic centers of excellence. Sure, there’s a ton to go there, but I think we’ve already realized a lot of the internal budgetary and communication benefits of the reshaping.”

Asked for specifics on potential beefing up efforts, Wells deadpanned: “That’s obviously not a technical term.”

Then he added that the directorate will continue taking stock of laboratory infrastructure and potential new enduring needs within the mission centers. “That beefing up may mean that we have a particular laboratory that can do more or different things than they currently do that are going to be persistent needs, and perhaps we need to invest in that,” he said. “It may mean that we need to add new laboratory capability. That may not mean we’re building a brick-and-mortar lab, but it may mean we need some enduring testing and evaluation capability, and perhaps we can take advantage of an interagency capability that already exists that we need to establish a memorandum of agreement to access. It may mean that we need to go back to the board and say, ‘Hey, we really have an enduring need here. Let’s go see if we can budget for that and make the argument that it is a good investment for DHS.’”

Ultimately, the reshaping will allow S&T officials to make more intelligent, clear decisions about which mission spaces they invest in, and why, and how that aligns with department and administration priorities. Additionally, it may help the directorate to deliver solutions more rapidly. “We are increasingly looking to adopt private sector solutions first. If there is a space where industry has already invested in a capability, we don’t necessarily need to reinvest in research and development of that capability. We really need to be aware of it, identify it and help our components quickly adapt it or configure it for their use, which can be a much more efficient and cost-effective way of getting them the capabilities they need.”

We decided that the best way to unify our investment approach was aligned with DHS missions, and so we embarked upon doing a functional continuity analysis to figure out the various functions we conduct across the directorate, the underlying statutory and regulatory reasons behind those, and how we more efficiently organize ourselves to make sure that we’re delivering return on investment in terms of mission capabilities.

articles.heading: An AI “mind-reading” tool can reconstruct what you’re looking at from a brain scan
articles.summary: Scientists hope it could be used to reconstruct a person’s inner thoughts, mental images, or even dreams.
articles.content:
An AI “mind-reading” tool can reconstruct what you’re looking at from a brain scan
Scientists hope it could be used to reconstruct a person’s inner thoughts, mental images, or even dreams.
A new AI tool can guess what you’re looking at just by analyzing your brain scans—and re-create that image with remarkable precision. It can go the other way, too, and predict a person’s brain activity based on what they’re looking at.
In the image above, for example, the left-hand image of each pair is what the user actually saw—and its right-hand counterpart is what the model reconstructed from the brain scan.
Michal Irani, who developed the tool with her colleagues at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, hopes her “mind-reading” tool will ultimately reveal more about how the brain works, and could perhaps be used to help locked-in people communicate, or allow scientists to re-create the content of dreams.
Judy Illes, a neuroethicist and professor of neurology at the University of British Columbia in Canada, who was not involved in the research, describes the work as “magnificent.” “The idea [of using this approach] to help people with neurologic conditions … therapeutically is tremendously exciting,” she says.
But other scientists warn that a similar approach could be used to reveal people’s inner thoughts and mental imagery, potentially without their consent. “The results seem very impressive,” says Tommy Sprague, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Santa Barbara. “But if there’s a way to surreptitiously extract information about what you’re thinking about, then …150 years of sci-fi can come true anytime, and that’s worrisome in a lot of ways.”
Peeking into the brain
Neuroscientists have been working for years on ways to use functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to reconstruct what people see and what’s going on in their minds. The first attempts produced images that were blurry and hard to make sense of. Advances in technology—both in the fMRI scans themselves and in the tools used to make sense of the results—have led to improvements over the years.
Irani and her colleagues started by analyzing publicly available brain-scan data. Other researchers had already collected scans from volunteers who were shown hundreds of images while they lay in fMRI scanners.
fMRI uses a giant magnet to track the flow of oxygenated blood through the brain. Brain areas that “light up” on the scans are thought to be those that are particularly active at any given moment. The results are not especially specific—in typical fMRI scanners, each highlighted “voxel” of activity covers around three cubic millimeters, containing around 16,000 neurons.
But Irani and her colleagues used newer datasets collected using scanners with a higher resolution—each voxel covered around one cubic millimeter of neurons, she says. Those datasets showed what the brain activity of volunteers looked like when they viewed various images.
Other teams have done this too, and several other tools have been used to re-create images from brain-scan data. But they’re not good enough, says Irani. Say a person saw a banana. These models can generate an image of a banana, but it would look different, she says. “It wouldn’t have the same structure, the same position.”
A better decoder
The researchers wanted to more closely re-create the images that had been seen. The first step was to train an AI model on already available data from eight people who each had been shown around 9,000 images while in a high-resolution fMRI scanner.
Crucially, their “brain decoder” has two branches—one to predict the structure of an image (where the colors are, for instance) and a second to predict its content (for example, a bunch of bananas on a plate). The predictions allow a diffusion model, a type of AI best known for creating video and images by gradually cleaning up a noisy mess of pixels, to produce a much more accurate representation of what the person saw.
But to improve the models they needed more data—far more than was actually available.
To get around this problem, Irani and her colleagues trained another model—an encoder that can predict brain activity from an image. The team then used the encoder and decoder together to improve both tools.
It works like this: Start with a new image of, say, a leopard. Then use the encoder to predict what someone’s fMRI brain scan would look like when the person saw that picture. The decoder is then used to reconstruct the image. At first, the reconstruction probably won’t look much like a leopard, says Irani. But repeatedly training the models this way eventually leads to dramatic improvements.
This approach also allows the team to train their models on as many images as they want, even images that have never been shown to a person in an fMRI scanner. Irani says that around 70% of the training data is from images that were not originally paired with fMRI scans.
By combining data from multiple studies, they were also able to identify brain regions that seem to share functions across all individuals. One region seemed to respond to images of food, for example, while another responded to images of sports. Irani, a computer scientist, says she is now working with neuroscientists “to see if we can actually use these tools that we’ve developed to really find out new things about the brain.”
The resulting “universal brain encoder” can work on a scan from a new person with minimal calibration. In other attempts, a tool has typically required about 40 hours of fMRI data on anyone new before it can be used to predict what that person is seeing. Irani’s decoder only needs one hour of data, she says. The finding was presented at the Cognitive Computational Neuroscience conference in New York last month.
That could make it valuable for neuroscientists studying the brain, says Sprague. “None of us can afford 40 hours of imaging for a new subject,” he says. “It’s something like $600 to $1,000 an hour.” Tools like this one could speed up research, he says.
State of the art
The encoder and decoder aren’t perfect. “Of course we have failures,” says Irani. Over a Zoom call, she pointed out an image of a cake that her tool reconstructed as a pile of three sandwiches, and another of a dog in a bathtub that was reconstructed as a similarly colored goat in a bathtub.
But they represent the state of the art. In a comparison test, the tool was found to be much better than previously described ones. “All in all, really we outperformed the others by a significant margin,” Irani says. “Mind reading” is a “cute, jazzy name” for what they’re doing, she adds.
Irani is now planning to move beyond images to video and audio. She wants to be able to reconstruct what people are thinking about or imagining, and the contents of their dreams. “That’s something we don’t have yet,” she says. “But we’re striving to achieve it.”
Such a tool might enable people who are “locked in” and completely paralyzed to communicate using their brain activity alone, she says. It could also help scientists unpick some enduring mysteries surrounding the inner workings of our minds, such as what PTSD flashbacks look like.
Advances like this inevitably raise questions about mental privacy. What if some bad actor could reconstruct someone’s thoughts or memories?
“If you’d asked me that 10 years ago, I’d have laughed a lot,” says Sprague. Getting a willing person to lie still in a scanner and actively engage with a research question is hard enough; imagine making someone do it involuntarily. But Irani and other scientists are working on similar approaches to decode brain activity from EEG—electrical brain activity measures collected via a cap of electrodes or even through headphones.
And as models improve, it will become even easier to analyze the brain activity collected this way. “We have to be a little more serious about the ethical considerations,” says Sprague. He thinks Irani’s approach would probably “work quite well” in predicting images that a person is thinking about but not looking at.
The move to EEG would be a “game changer,” says Marcello Ienca, a neuroscientist and philosopher at the Technical University of Munich, Germany. Once an EEG device has been calibrated to a user’s own brain, it could be relatively easy for companies to extract additional information from that person’s brain—potentially without consent. Ienca can also imagine some courts allowing mental image reconstructions as legal evidence.
“I have no doubt that this is, you know, well-intentioned research, but I think it’s also pretty obvious that it could be co-opted for … ethically and societally problematic commercial uses,” he says.
Irani acknowledges the potential for misuse with the use of EEG. But she’s not concerned for now. “I’m trying to think only of good things,” she says.
