articles.summary: Joint Interagency Field Experimentation (JIFX) events continue to advance and accelerate the development of new technologies that are vital across the joint force for readiness and battlefield advantage in contested environments.
articles.content:
Joint Interagency Field Experimentation (JIFX) events continue to advance and accelerate the development of new technologies that are vital across the joint force for readiness and battlefield advantage in contested environments.
Autonomous swarming, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), uncrewed drones by land, sea, and air, counter-drone detection, high-energy laser weapon systems, GPS denied navigation, C5ISR (command, control, communications, computers, cyber, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance) systems, advanced energy systems, and expeditionary additive manufacturing are just some of the wide-ranging technologies that have undergone experimentation and development at JIFX.
During a week of experimentation held in August 2026, nearly 200 uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) sorties executed experimental flight tests throughout the vast airspace accessible through JIFX. This brings the tally up to 635 sorties flown during the past year at the Naval Postgraduate School’s (NPS) quarterly JIFX events, held in southern Monterey County at the California National Guard’s Camp Roberts.
The sorties pushed the boundaries of new UAV designs and upgrades to existing UAV hardware, software, controls, and operations. Though the aim for each sortie differed, one immediate factor underscored each experiment — how energy and innovation drive advantage in the future.
Drone Dominance Fueled by JIFX
ModalAI, Firestorm (watch slow motion https://youtu.be/upa74ykT_iY), and Greensight (watch https://youtu.be/OF2LTJ4PYMM) participated in the U.S. Department of War’s Drone Dominance Program (DDP) competition, set to wrap up in 2027. Firestorm and Greensight are frequent JIFX attendees. And ModalAI, which attended JIFX twice, made it into the final DDP selection and is still in the running. So far, it has shipped over 2,000 drones to DDP.
Back at JIFX, a small fleet of ModalAI quadcopters, operated by Gambit Defense, also made an appearance. The Gambit test flights hit the radar of JIFX director and NPS faculty member Michael Richardson.
“The experiments with autonomous swarming activity by Gambit have been very powerful,” said Richardson, who is also a retired U.S. Army colonel and former special operations officer. “Gambit is a great example of the many companies that come to JIFX and show incredible promise, particularly with respect to advancing the drone warfare doctrine of Pacific Command.”
Gambit experimented with its AI/ML mesh network system under contested electronic warfare conditions. It flew dozens of sorties for autonomous target detection, follow, patrol, and swarm missions. When jammed, its drones automatically maintained communication.
Like Gambit, Rhoman Aerospace is a frequent participant at JIFX providing software solutions for different drone platforms. During a separate field experimentation effort, it provided a system for GPS-denied navigation over open water to NPS researchers and Naval Special Warfare operators.
Had it not been for experiments by Rhoman at previous JIFX iterations, this collaboration with NPS would not have happened.
“From JIFX to JIFX, we see industry make iterative development as we poke and push them in different directions,” Richardson emphasized. “JIFX is shaping change. It facilitates more effective connections between what emerging technologies can offer and the pressing needs of national security and defense.”
Innovations in Operational Energy
Reliant on batteries and liquid fuels, participants mobilized in hangars, on the tarmac, and along the flightline of Camp Roberts’ McMillan Airfield. From rows of workstations inside the Technical Operations Center, they also ran C5ISR experiments.
On a remote hill further across the base at the Combined Arms Collective Training Facility (CACTF), other experimenters interfaced systems with human operators to investigate urban structures from the air and ground. And, in between, GArmor’s experimental armored crew transport roved the surrounding terrain.
As UAVs buzzed above, new counter-UAV sensor technology scanned the sky to spot them with radiofrequency, passive radar, acoustic, and other forms of drone detection. These, too, needed reliable energy sources.
Optimizing the energy used by these technologies, through testing at JIFX, directly improves their application and longevity in operational environments.
“We see a lot of value in JIFX because energy is part of every technology, whether it requires energy, produces energy, or just absorbs energy,” said Michael Davis, associate chair of NPS’ Energy Academic Group and, like Richardson, a retired U.S. Army colonel and former special operations officer.
The Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment’s Operational Energy-Innovation (OE-I) Directorate recently began providing support to JIFX. Davis is tasked with scoping out technological trends at JIFX and determining how these trends could potentially impact tomorrow’s battlefield.
“JIFX expedites technology transition. It helps technologies quickly become operational. With energy technologies, this can be challenging across the landscape of the joint force,” said Davis. Of much interest to him were the bourgeoning technologies of Chargebotic and Haylon Technologies.
Chargebotic came to experiment at JIFX with its energy harvesting system. It used a UAV, modified with additive manufactured components printed on the spot, to clamp a tether onto a powerline to parasitically extract energy, extending its operational utility. After flight tests that dialed in the UAV’s altered performance characteristics, Chargebotic successfully attached to a live powerline suspended on a test rig and drew electricity from it.
This source of parasitic energy was just the kind of emerging energy trend Davis keeps an eye out for. Similarly, at JIFX in February 2026, Davis applauded Reach Power’s use of radio frequency waves to wirelessly beam energy that recharged the battery of a hovering UAV, increasing its station time by nearly ten-fold.
Haylon took a different approach to energy provision. Its multiple battery chemistry switching system allowed a device, such as a UAV, to receive uninterrupted energy from more than one type of battery. Switching depends on the device’s current performance requirements and the various strengths and optimal uses for different battery sources.
In the case of a UAV, which requires a large amount of energy for a short time during takeoff, it is powered by a battery type that can provide a boost of energy up front. But these types of batteries are quickly depleted.
Therefore, Haylon’s system would switch the battery type after takeoff. During the flight phase, the UAV would then be powered by a battery that cannot deliver high energy but instead provides a steady stream of energy over a prolonged duration. By mixing the best qualities of two different batteries, the UAV maximizes its energy efficiently, extending its operational range.
“We also want to make sure that we're not adding to the logistical burden as we build new technologies, especially facing future challenges like constrained logistics and contested environments,” added Davis. “So, by helping technologists understand this from early in their development and experimentation, we can help them avoid later slowdowns or complications as they get to higher transition readiness levels.”
JIFX by Land to BOMA by Sea
U.S. Navy Lt. Cmdr. Max Leutermann, an NPS and Special Operations Command (SOCOM) researcher, continued experimenting on a compact and mobile counter-drone system for boats used by special operations forces. As NPS students in 2025, Leutermann and Swedish Armed Forces Maj. Patrik Liljegard rapidly developed the system from scratch and used JIFX to field test an early-stage prototype that they mounted in a pickup truck’s bed.
“NATO required us to create a system that was passive so that operators who were on a small boat wouldn’t give off any sort of detectable signatures or emissions,” said Leutermann.
“While companies and other NPS students at JIFX flew their drones all around, we tried to detect them,” he continued. “Different types of drones at different altitudes, distances, directions, angles of attack. Our second goal at JIFX was processing what we detected and representing it on the navigation display.”
Building upon JIFX, they also successfully demonstrated the operation of their prototype aboard a proper boat at the Bold Machina (BOMA) 2025 exercise in the Netherlands, which was run by NATO Allied Special Operations Forces Command (SOFCOM).
The results were so promising that Leutermann and Liljegard reteamed months after having graduating from NPS, with SOCOM, NATO SOFCOM, and the Swedish Armed Forces providing support and funding for the continued development of the system.
At the latest JIFX, Leutermann and three Swedish programmers experimented on a much-refined version of their counter-drone system in preparation for NATO’s next BOMA exercise, held in September 2026 in Portugal.
In addition to collaborations with Latent AI (AI dataset generation), Haylon (dual battery chemistry), and Bellum Systems (passive radar), Leutermann’s counter-drone system was powered by Chargebotic using an expeditionary battery from Chariot Defense.
Last year at JIFX, Chariot had experimented with mobile, low-signature, and high energy battery development and powered Aurelius’ laser weapon system for drone defense and Firestorm’s expeditionary additive manufacturing station for drone building.
During the September BOMA — weeks after JIFX in August — Leutermann reported that he was making excellent progress on the Operational Data Integration Node (ODIN) of the c-UAV system. ODIN is an AI-driven, sensor fusion engine that collects and centralizes all data from the various sensor platforms connected to the system.
“BOMA showed that the core ODIN architecture works in the field,” said Leutermann from Portugal. “We demonstrated passive RF cueing, autonomous visual search and tracking — including an RF-dark drone with no operator interaction — and ingested RADAR data into ODIN.”
An Advanced Technology Proving Ground Like No Other
What separates JIFX from field exercises and demonstrations focused on developing defense science and technology is that JIFX focuses on experimental campaigns — not the sales and marketing campaigns often seen at other venues. Participants conduct experiments with work-in-progress technology. They do not demonstrate polished products like at a tradeshow.
Over 30 experimental campaigns were successfully completed at the August JIFX by different organizations, which also led to many collaborative experiments between them.
Three focus areas emerged from the technology of these campaigns:
-
AI-enabled decision advantage - experiments aimed at helping operators rapidly transform large volumes of data into actionable information.
-
Autonomous systems in contested environments - experiments sought to improve the resilience and effectiveness of autonomous systems operating in denied, degraded, and contested conditions.
-
Expeditionary sustainment and edge operations - experiments addressed the challenges of sustaining distributed forces in austere environments.
As a proving ground, JIFX affords a safe and secure environment with an infrastructure that allows participants to operate under real-world conditions and push their technology to the limits — and often beyond. Stakeholders from across the joint force with operational knowledge and experience provide the experimenters with insights into the actual needs of those in the field.
With the sprawling Camp Roberts as its backdrop, JIFX most recently hosted 269 participants from industry, defense, and academia organizations. As with past events, mid-career officers came to observe. They were students from across the service branches and international commands who are studying at NPS.
Most of these students were fresh from military deployments and had highly relevant experience related to the technologies undergoing experimentation at JIFX. They knew what worked well for them, what didn’t work, and the operational and technological gaps that still needed to be filled. This gave them valuable perspectives into practical applications and operational uses, which they readily shared with the experimenters.
The experimenters found the knowledge the students shared had helpful impacts on the development of their technologies. This two-way street exposed the students to innovation and emerging technologies at stages of development much earlier than they would have encountered operationally during their regular duties.
U.S. Army Capt. Evan Prince, a Defense Analysis student who’s looking to add Information Sciences as a second major, was among the group of 60 students in attendance.
“I was really excited when I saw Watchtower, which is an AI-enabled system that basically ingests intelligence to create most likely and most dangerous courses of action taken by a would-be adversary,” he said. “They're working on a solution that can fill a gap that I’m looking at.” Developed by Panoptica Technologies, Watchtower helps generate and expedite threat assessments for military intelligence analysts.
“The initial reason why they popped out to me was because of my thesis,” Prince added. “Watchtower has great potential, and if its scope is able to expand a bit to cover the actual gap I've seen operationally, then I think it's something that can support our force very well.”
Prince is also a Meyer Scholar, an NPS program exposing students to a wide range of technologies operationally relevant to the modern battlespace. He found the program prepared him for an even more meaningful engagement with Panoptica at JIFX.
“It's what equipped me for the conversation I had about Watchtower,” he said.
His experience at JIFX highlights how bringing students and experimenters together can create meaningful connections between emerging technologies and operational challenges.
Defense Technology Pipeline and Range of the Future
JIFX does not only foster technology, but it also evolves with it. Exemplifying this was the experimental Defense Innovation Network Assistant (DINA) TAK (Tactical Assault Kit), which integrated data from Gambit, MicroVision, Insignito Solutions, Bellum Systems, and others into a sensor fused, shared operational data environment.
Developed in collaboration between Naval Surface Warfare Center (NSWC) Corona, California Baptist University, NPS, Standard TLM, and other partners, DINA TAK moves JIFX closer into the realm of live-virtual-constructive (LVC) experimentation ranges.
DINA TAK, a government AI tool, is designed to enable future integration and JIFX expansion to a true LVC experimentation range. DINA TAC benefits from the wide range of technologies that help expand and refine the tool, which in turn increases JIFX's ability to support ad hoc integration and coordination among participants.
Troy Clarke, the Inland Empire Tech Bridge director at NSWC Corona, briefed government stakeholders at JIFX about DINA TAK and its connection to LVC experimentation ranges.
“We introduce new technology into the ranges that we could then incorporate into the actual tactical training ranges,” Clarke said.
But the initial stage of development simply had experimenters inputting their data from telemetry, sensor networks, and other ISR (intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance) sources with ATAK (Android tactical assault kit) devices. DINA TAK then used AI-enabled data aggregation to support visualization, real-time tracking, after-action reconstruction, and more.
Once fully established, the “Range of the Future” could become a resource for others from across industry to also conduct experimentation. And for stakeholders scouting technology, DINA TAK has the potential to provide up-to-date and in-depth assessments backed by proven supporting data.
“JIFX is a very unique and special environment where you can bring early-stage technology and integrate with other innovators who are trying to figure out their niche and how they're going to get their technology across the joint force,” said Jason Hay, director of technology at BryceTech.
Hay attended JIFX as contract support to stakeholders, where he soaked in and evaluated DINA TAK and the other technologies. By gaining this understanding, he now looks to leverage JIFX for accelerating technologies.
The rapid pace of experimentation throughout the vast land, sea, and air laboratory and the extensive collaboration between participants impressed him, and he sees JIFX as a vital pipeline for defense science and technology.
“Just like you have to stockpile munitions, you have to stockpile innovation,” Hay said. “A supply of intelligence, knowledge, and data is necessary for the development of future technologies. If you don't have people exploring the early stages of technology, then the supply will dry up. The good news is that JIFX is here to keep the experiments running and on course.”
NPS, located in Monterey, California, provides warfighting-focused graduate education, including classified studies and interdisciplinary research, to advance the operational effectiveness, technological leadership and warfighting advantage of the naval service. Established in 1909, NPS offers master’s, doctoral and distance-learning certificate programs to U.S. Department of War military and civilian students, as well as to international partners, to develop warfighters and leaders who can think critically, solve complex operational problems and deliver mission-ready solutions through advanced education and research.

Once fully established, the “Range of the Future” could become a resource for others from across industry to also conduct experimentation. And for stakeholders scouting technology, DINA TAK has the potential to provide up-to-date and in-depth assessments backed by proven supporting data.

“JIFX is a very unique and special environment where you can bring early-stage technology and integrate with other innovators who are trying to figure out their niche and how they're going to get their technology across the joint force,” said Jason Hay, director of technology at BryceTech.

Hay attended JIFX as contract support to stakeholders, where he soaked in and evaluated DINA TAK and the other technologies. By gaining this understanding, he now looks to leverage JIFX for accelerating technologies.

The rapid pace of experimentation throughout the vast land, sea, and air laboratory and the extensive collaboration between participants impressed him, and he sees JIFX as a vital pipeline for defense science and technology.

“Just like you have to stockpile munitions, you have to stockpile innovation,” Hay said. “A supply of intelligence, knowledge, and data is necessary for the development of future technologies. If you don't have people exploring the early stages of technology, then the supply will dry up. The good news is that JIFX is here to keep the experiments running and on course.”

NPS, located in Monterey, California, provides warfighting-focused graduate education, including classified studies and interdisciplinary research, to advance the operational effectiveness, technological leadership and warfighting advantage of the naval service. Established in 1909, NPS offers master’s, doctoral and distance-learning certificate programs to U.S. Department of War military and civilian students, as well as to international partners, to develop warfighters and leaders who can think critically, solve complex operational problems and deliver mission-ready solutions through advanced education and research.

articles.content:
WASHINGTON – Following release of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, global tech trade association ITI President and CEO Jason Oxman issued the following statement:
“Comprehensive permitting reform is essential to America’s ability to build, compete, and lead – especially in the AI era. Greater certainty, lower costs, and faster deployment of critical infrastructure will help power the next era of American growth while maintaining important environmental safeguards.
“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is an encouraging step forward and offers a strong foundation to shorten environmental review timelines, streamline transmission permitting and planning, enable deployment of advanced transmission technologies, and leverage AI to address interconnection delays.
“Congress should act to deliver lasting permitting reform that allows America to build at the speed and scale our economic security demands.”

articles.title: Pete Hegseth appoints Elon Musk to US taskforce on future of warfare
articles.description: Pete Hegseth appoints Elon Musk to US taskforce on future of warfare theguardian.com
articles.description_html: Pete Hegseth appoints Elon Musk to US taskforce on future of warfare  theguardian.com
articles.article_title: Pete Hegseth appoints Elon Musk to US taskforce on future of warfare
articles.heading: Pete Hegseth appoints Elon Musk to US taskforce on future of warfare
articles.summary: A year after his explosive tenure at Doge, the SpaceX CEO is back in the Trump administration’s good graces
articles.content:
Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, marking the SpaceX CEO’s first return to government since he ran the chaotic, so-called “department of government efficiency”, or Doge. Musk will be joined by Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House.
A defense department press release on the effort, called Project Meridian, described its goal as “identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”. The project will run for 120 days and culminate in an unclassified public report of its recommendations.
The defense department’s project brings Musk back into government work a little more than a year after his explosive tenure as leader of Doge, which gutted federal agencies while failing to achieve its stated cost-cutting goals. It is also a sign of how Musk has re-entered the good graces of the Trump administration after a dramatic falling out with the president last year.
Unlike Musk’s role at Doge – which drew heavy public criticism and costly boycotts of his products – the scope and goals of Project Meridian appear as if they will be much less time-consuming for the tech mogul. The project intends to look at how the US military can utilize new technology and also carry out warfare in untested terrains including subterranean depths and on the moon, the defense department stated in its release.
“We are witnessing rapid advances in artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics, biotechnology, among other critical high-tech areas. Combined, these new domains, new ways of fighting, and technological developments will profoundly alter the character of warfare,” Hegseth said in a memo. “To maintain global dominance, the United States must anticipate future operational environments and act decisively to develop the tools to dominate in them.”
Musk and Luckey are far from independent arbiters of the future of warfare. Both have extensive defense department contracts through their companies, with Anduril’s business centered on the government purchasing products that it advertises as the latest advance in warfare.
Gingrich was appointed as a member of the defense policy board in December 2020 during the first Trump administration but was dismissed less than three months later after Joe Biden became president. Going back to the 1990s, he has been warning about the threat of an electromagnetic pulse attack that could knock out US power grids.

articles.title: NASCIO Honors 11 State Technology Projects for Innovation
articles.description: NASCIO Honors 11 State Technology Projects for Innovation GovTech
articles.description_html: NASCIO Honors 11 State Technology Projects for Innovation  GovTech
articles.article_title: NASCIO Honors 11 State Technology Projects for Innovation
articles.heading: NASCIO Honors 11 State Technology Projects for Innovation
articles.summary: The National Association of State CIOs acknowledged states for using AI, cybersecurity, data and digital services to tackle some of their biggest tech challenges.
articles.content:
The National Association of State Chief Information Officers (NASCIO) announced the 2026 State IT Recognition Awards recipients Wednesday at its Annual Conference in San Diego. It recognized 11 winning projects across 10 categories, including AI, cybersecurity, data management, digital services and operational efficiency.
The awards acknowledge excellence in technology innovation, and this year’s submissions focus on using tech to address critical business problems and connect residents with government.
AI TAKES ON SOME OF THE BIGGEST WORKLOADS
Artificial intelligence was one of the areas where states are putting new technology to work on existing problems.
California received the Artificial Intelligence award for “From Hours to Minutes: Generative AI for California’s Transportation Network,” a project centered on the California Department of Transportation’s (Caltrans) use of generative AI to reduce the time employees spend on certain tasks.
Ohio is using AI in another part of government operations. Its Department of Administrative Services received the Operational Efficiency award for using AI to help with the early stages of modernizing legacy systems and moving older applications to the cloud.
The technology is used for tasks such as documentation, estimates and system analysis. According to the award information, AI has cut documentation and estimation time by 50 to 60 percent and reduced system analysis time by 40 percent.
STATES USE TECH TO WORK ACROSS AGENCIES
Some of the winning projects focused less on a particular technology and more on getting different parts of government to work together.
Connecticut received the Cross-Boundary Collaboration award for its Clean Slate project, which uses automation and collaboration among multiple criminal justice agencies to clear eligible criminal records.
The project, which is designed to make it easier for people to pursue jobs, housing and education when they qualify to be cleared, has cleared more than 300,000 records since September 2025.
Clean Slate depends on more than an automated process; it convenes multiple criminal justice agencies, using technology to help manage a task that crosses organizational lines.
Utah took a similar statewide approach with its Customer Experience project, which won the Data Management, Analytics and Visualization award. The state created a system to collect and analyze feedback from residents across 371 government service touchpoints and all 22 state agencies — giving leaders information about how people are experiencing government services and where those services may need improvement.
CYBERSECURITY MOVES BEYOND IT
Cybersecurity is another area where projects are reaching beyond traditional IT operations.
Michigan received the Cybersecurity award for “Securing Michiganders via MiLogin: Free Cybersecurity Awareness and Training Program.” The state is using its MiLogin single sign-on platform to provide residents with free cybersecurity training. The program combines the identity and fraud protections connected to MiLogin with practical information that can help residents better protect themselves and their data online.
Ohio was also recognized in the cybersecurity category for using Google SecOps and Gemini AI to automate and speed up cyber investigations across state agencies. The technology helps security teams detect and respond to threats in minutes instead of relying on slower, manual processes.
The projects take different approaches to the same broad challenge. Michigan is bringing cybersecurity education directly to residents, while Ohio is applying AI to the work security teams perform inside government.
DIGITAL SERVICES FOCUS ON REQUIRED TASKS
Several of this year’s projects focus on making government services easier to access.
Utah received the Digital Experience: Agency/Program Solutions award for modernizing the process of authenticating documents for use overseas. Its digital Apostille system allows people to submit, receive and verify documents online, cutting processing time and costs while maintaining legal safeguards for international recognition.
Puerto Rico received the Digital Experience: Enterprise Solutions award for CESCO Digital, a platform that unites several transportation services online. The system includes vehicle registration renewals, driver’s license services, traffic payments and toll payments.
ILLINOIS SPEEDS UP EMERGENCY RESPONSE
In Illinois, technology is being used in a setting where a few minutes can make a major difference.
The Illinois Department of Innovation and Technology partnered with the Illinois School for the Visually Impaired on a project recognized in the Information and Communications Technology category. It uses wearable, one-touch alerts that send emergency responders precise location information when help is needed at the school.
The system has cut average law enforcement response times from six to seven minutes down to three to four minutes, according to the award information. It also gives students and staff a simple way to trigger an alert, while giving responders information about where help is needed.
PENNSYLVANIA REFRESHED ITS CONTACT CENTER
Pennsylvania’s winning project addresses another part of government that many residents encounter directly: contact centers.
The state received the Enterprise Technology Management award for modernizing its contact center system across 63 centers and more than 4,000 agents. The new platform brings voice, chat, text, callbacks and self-service capabilities into one system. The modernization also saved more than $9 million and avoided service disruptions during the transition.
MINNESOTA BACKS MODERNIZATION WITH $40 MILLION
Minnesota took a different approach to the challenge of aging tech by creating a dedicated source of funding for modernization.
Minnesota IT Services received the State CIO Office Special Recognition award for its $40 million Technology Modernization Fund. The fund helps state agencies replace aging systems, reduce technical debt and move major technology projects forward.
It’s supported more than 50 projects across 28 agencies, cutting delivery timelines from years to months, and enabled major endeavors that could have taken years to move from planning to delivery.

articles.article_title: Spring Hill Elementary students meeting in former Cabell County Career Technology Center
articles.heading: Spring Hill Elementary students meeting in former Cabell County Career Technology Center
articles.summary: Wednesday was actually the first day of school for students at Spring Hill Elementary in Huntington.
articles.content:
Spring Hill Elementary students meeting in former Cabell County Career Technology Center
HUNTINGTON, W.Va. (WCHS) — Wednesday was actually the first day of school for students at Spring Hill Elementary in Huntington.
Building-related issues caused school leaders to begin the school year with remote learning. For the first time this school year, students are finally together in-person at a temporary location, the former Cabell County Career Technology Center.
Christina Kennedy, whose son is a third grader at Spring Hill Elementary School, said he is not normally excited about school and noted that remote learning was not working for him.
"I'm very thankful they have a place to be in-person with them," Kennedy said. "My son was not having the homeschool thing. He was not trying to do that pamphlet work. I think it will be better since he can go in with other students."
On Friday, teachers were told they had the weekend to prepare for students arriving Monday morning. Technology areas at the former career center were transformed into elementary classrooms for the school's 350 students.
"It's amazing to see the transformation of the rooms and what they looked like just three or four days ago," Cabell County Schools Deputy Superintendent of Operations for Cabell County Schools Justin Boggs said.
Boggs says problems with the HVAC system initially triggered the issues. While those concerns were being addressed, a plumbing problem was also discovered in the building.
"In order to address that plumbing issue, we had to ensure the safety of the students and staff," Boggs said. "We had air quality testing, and all of that testing came back within acceptable limits. However, we want to make sure we have the best learning environment for students."
The next step in the process is determining what work needs to be completed and putting those projects out for bid, with the ultimate goal of getting students back into their regular school as quickly as possible.

articles.article_title: Infrastructure work begins on Osceola County’s first tech park
articles.heading: Infrastructure work begins on Osceola County’s first technology park
articles.summary: Infrastructure work is underway at Westside Technology Park, a nearly 40-acre project planned for the Four Corners area.
articles.content:
Infrastructure work begins on Osceola County’s first technology park
Infrastructure work is underway at Westside Technology Park, a nearly 40-acre project planned for the Four Corners area.
The approximately $2 million development, billed as Osceola County’s first technology park, will combine outdoor recreation with technology-focused features. The site is near the intersection of Westside Boulevard and Funie Steed Road.
Osceola County Commissioner Peggy Choudhry has spearheaded the project since its groundbreaking in 2024.
"I am really looking forward to it coming to fruition," Choudhry said.
She added that the environmental reviews were necessary before infrastructure work could begin because some of the land is protected.
“We want to be sure we go through the right channels, and we want to make sure we are protecting land on the outskirts of it as well,” Choudhry said.
County officials also sought design ideas from members of Gen-Z, aiming to create a space where visitors can use technology while spending time outdoors.
“What people don’t realize is sometimes parks take a really long time because of the environmental and all the studies that we do as a county,” Choudhry said.
Plans call for walking trails, observation areas, benches and a dog park. Choudhry said the park will provide a needed outdoor gathering place in the surrounding community.
“It’s a great place because it’s in the middle of the community,” she said. “It’s the very first tech park in the Four Corners area, so we are excited.”
The county has not announced an expected completion date.

articles.heading: Hegseth returns to Quantico to lay out technology and people initiatives
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth gathered 600 rank-and-file troops on Wednesday at Marine Corps Base Quantico to announce six initiatives.
articles.content:
QUANTICO, Va. — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth gathered 600 rank-and-file troops on Wednesday at Marine Corps Base Quantico to announce six initiatives that included the creation of an autonomous warfare command, a religious affairs office that will report directly to the secretary, and the addition of a new corps of cadets at five universities.
Hegseth also highlighted a plan to cut 20% of the nation’s generals and admirals.
“I’m proud to stand on this stage and report that the warrior ethos has been revived, our military is being rebuilt and American deterrence is back,” the secretary said about five minutes into the “State of the Force” address, which he intends to make an annual event.
Hegseth, a 46-year-old Army National Guard veteran and former Fox News host, gave a speech exactly one year ago to about 800 generals and admirals and their top enlisted advisers to lay out his vision for the U.S. military.
Some of the policies the services have worked to implement include more physical fitness tests, tighter body fat restrictions and fewer shaving waivers across the force.
“Now, I think the generals heard the message. Those who responded positively, which is most of them, are leading newly focused and newly empowered and disciplined formations,” Hegseth said. “Those generals who did not, who clung to the woke department, or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion. Well, they no longer work here.”
Hegseth began Wednesday by praising the force, particularly the troops in attendance, and celebrating what he called the return to a warrior ethos. He also lashed out at media members and reiterated that the Pentagon is no longer the “woke department.”

articles.title: Six figure gift supports growing Construction Engineering Technology program
articles.description: Six figure gift supports growing Construction Engineering Technology program Louisiana Tech University
articles.description_html: Six figure gift supports growing Construction Engineering Technology program  Louisiana Tech University
articles.article_title: Six figure gift supports growing Construction Engineering Technology program
articles.heading: Six figure gift supports growing Construction Engineering Technology program
articles.summary: The Louisiana Contractor’s Educational Trust Fund and the Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors donated $247,640 to support Louisiana Tech University’s Construction Engineering Technology (CET) program, continuing a longstanding partnership that has strengthened facilities, equipment, and student learning opportunities.
articles.content:
The Louisiana Contractor’s Educational Trust Fund and the Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors donated $247,640 to support Louisiana Tech University’s Construction Engineering Technology (CET) program, continuing a longstanding partnership that has strengthened facilities, equipment, and student learning opportunities.
Representatives from the organizations presented the gift to Louisiana Tech President Dr. Jim Henderson on Sept. 24. The contribution comes as the CET program experiences significant enrollment growth.
First-time freshman enrollment increased 25 percent this fall, growing overall enrollment from 230 students last fall to 318 this fall. The program now ranks among Louisiana Tech’s 10 largest academic programs, with enrollment expected to approach 375 students by the end of the academic year.
“We are deeply grateful to the Louisiana Contractor’s Educational Trust Fund and the Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors for their generous and continued support of Construction Engineering Technology at Louisiana Tech,” said Dr. Collin Wick, dean of the Louisiana Tech College of Engineering and Science. “Their investment directly improves the education and experiences we can provide our students, from the spaces and equipment they use every day to opportunities to build relationships with professionals in the construction industry.”
Support from the organizations helped fund more than $1 million in renovations to laboratories and classrooms serving Civil Engineering and Construction Engineering Technology students in Bogard Hall. Completed in 2025, the renovations modernized spaces used for hands-on instruction and significantly improved the learning environment for students in both programs.
The partnership reaches beyond facilities. Funding has allowed the CET program to purchase updated laboratory equipment and support student participation in professional conferences, including the Associated General Contractors of America Convention. It also supports student organization activities and recruiting efforts designed to introduce prospective students to construction careers and opportunities at Louisiana Tech.
Those resources have become increasingly valuable as the program grows and Louisiana’s construction industry continues to need graduates prepared to enter the workforce with practical experience and industry connections.
This latest gift continues a relationship that has provided Louisiana Tech CET students with expanded opportunities inside and outside the classroom while helping the program respond to increasing student demand.

articles.title: Lenovo Technology Powers Aruba.it Racing – Ducati to Historic 2026 WorldSBK Triple Crown
articles.description: Lenovo Technology Powers Aruba.it Racing – Ducati to Historic 2026 WorldSBK Triple Crown Lenovo StoryHub

articles.article_title: Lenovo Technology Powers Aruba.it Racing – Ducati to Historic 2026 WorldSBK Triple Crown - Lenovo StoryHub
articles.heading: Lenovo Technology Powers Aruba.it Racing – Ducati to Historic 2026 WorldSBK Triple Crown
articles.summary: The team’s 2026 season has been defined by precision and dominance with Lenovo, Main Sponsor to Aruba.it Racing – Ducati, playing a central role.
articles.content:
- Powered by Lenovo’s technology, Nicolò Bulega completed the Triple Crown for the Aruba.it Racing – Ducati team by securing the 2026 WorldSBK Riders’ Championship at the Italian Round
- Lenovo, Main Sponsor of the team, has provided the hardware which has worked seamlessly all season aiding more informed race decisions
Today, the Aruba.it Racing – Ducati team cemented a standout season by winning the 2026 WorldSBK Triple Crown, as Nicolò Bulega secured the Riders’ Title at Cremona with two Rounds remaining. With Lenovo technology supporting the team throughout the season, this win follows the team’s earlier success, having secured the Teams’ Title and contributed to Ducati’s Manufacturers’ Championship victory.
In its 100th anniversary year, Ducati wrapped up its fifth straight Superbike Manufacturers’ Title at Donington Park with four Rounds still to run, while Aruba.it Racing – Ducati claimed the Teams’ Championship in the same weekend. The new Panigale V4R, built with aero ideas borrowed from MotoGP alongside a reworked chassis, front frame and double-sided swingarm, has been the backbone of that success. Supported by data-driven insights enabled by Lenovo technology, both Nicolò Bulega and team-mate Iker Lecuona have performed at the highest level throughout the season, with Bulega also achieving a new WorldSBK record of 25 consecutive wins.
The team’s 2026 season has been defined by precision and dominance with Lenovo, Main Sponsor to Aruba.it Racing – Ducati, playing a central role in its success. Lenovo ThinkSystem SE350 edge servers and Lenovo ThinkPad P1 mobile workstations have been pivotal in handling the heavy lifting of race data, delivering the high compute performance the team needs while remaining straightforward to use. This partnership reflects the winning combination of Lenovo’s advanced solutions and Ducati’s racing heritage, showing how technology and engineering excellence work hand in hand to achieve amazing results.
Furthermore, with the WorldSBK regulations prohibiting real-time analysis, Lenovo’s powerful hardware plays a critical role in processing race data and enabling setup adjustments at speed between sessions. Travelling to every round, Lenovo enables Ducati engineers to process up to 40 GB of data per weekend, allowing them to rapidly turn raw data into smarter strategies and sharper setups between races. With less than two hours between some sessions, the ability to analyze data and change configurations can make all the difference to performance.
“This extraordinary Triple Crown is the result of exceptional talent, determination and teamwork performed at the highest level. We are proud that Lenovo’s technology has supported Aruba.it Racing – Ducati throughout the season, helping the team make faster, more informed decisions in an environment where every detail can make a difference. This achievement highlights the value of a partnership built on innovation, excellence and a shared commitment to performance. Congratulations to Nicolò Bulega and the entire team on a truly historic accomplishment,” commented, Enza Truzzolillo, Managing Director and General Manager, Lenovo Italy.
“It’s been a great season and to top it off with the Triple Crown is a fantastic result for everyone involved. A special thanks to our partner Lenovo and everyone behind the scenes who has contributed to such a successful season. The WorldSBK championship is demanding not just for the riders and team but also for the technology we rely on. That’s why we look to Lenovo to provide high-performance solutions that are reliable and able to perform in tough environments, anywhere in the world,” commented Stefano Cecconi, Aruba CEO and Aruba.it Racing – Ducati Team Principal.
About Lenovo
Lenovo is a US$83 billion revenue global technology powerhouse, ranked #153 in the Fortune Global 500, and serving millions of customers every day in 180 markets. Guided by its vision of “Smarter Technology for All”, Lenovo is executing a Hybrid AI strategy that spans Personal AI – one personal AI, multiple devices; and Enterprise AI – helping customers turn data into insights and value. This strategy is delivered through the Group’s commitment to world-class innovation and a full-stack AI portfolio, including devices (PCs, workstations, smartphones, tablets, accessories), infrastructure solutions (server, storage, edge, high performance computing and software defined infrastructure), as well as software, solutions, and services. With a global footprint spanning more than 20 research and development locations and a global supply chain that includes more than 30 manufacturing sites across 11 markets, Lenovo is widely recognized for its operational excellence. Lenovo is listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange under Lenovo Group Limited (HKSE: 992) (ADR: LNVGY). Learn more at www.lenovo.com and follow the latest news in our newsroom.
About Aruba.it Racing
Aruba.it Racing – Ducati was established in 2015 through the collaboration between Aruba and Ducati as the official team of the manufacturer of Borgo Panigale in the Superbike World Championship.
In 2022, the team secured its first Riders’ World Championship title with Álvaro Bautista, who confirmed himself as World Champion in 2023.
During the same period, the team also consolidated its results in the Teams’ standings: from 2022 to 2026, Aruba.it Racing – Ducati has won five consecutive WorldSBK Teams’ titles, confirming itself as the benchmark team in the category.
Nicolò Bulega (2023 Supersport World Champion aboard the Ducati Panigale V2 of the Aruba.it Racing team) has completed an extraordinary 2026 season by claiming his first WorldSBK World Championship title, after contributing, together with teammate Iker Lecuona, to the team’s “Triple Crown” with the Teams’ and Manufacturers’ titles.
About Ducati Motor Holding S.p.A. – A Sole Shareholder Company – A Company subject to the Management and Coordination activities of AUDI AG
Powerful engines, distinctive design, innovative technologies and a lot of passion: this is the credo according to which Ducati, founded in 1926, still works today in the development and manufacturing of its world-famous motorcycles. In its factory in Borgo Panigale (Bologna, Italy), Ducati crafts the dream of every Ducatista giving life to motorcycles that are the purest expression of refined engineering with a constant attention to the highest standards of quality.
The Italian motorcycle manufacturer has racing in its DNA and competes with official teams in the MotoGP and WorldSBK Championships, where it tackles every race determined to continuously improve its performance and share the emotions of the sport with its community. 2025 was an extraordinary year for Ducati, which became MotoGP World Champion for the fourth year in a row, with five Grands Prix still to go, also winning the sixth consecutive Constructors’ Title and the Team Title. In WorldSBK, the Company confirmed its status as the most successful manufacturer in the championship for production-based motorcycles, winning the twenty-first Constructors’ Title in its history.
In 2026, Ducati celebrates its 100th anniversary. One hundred years of history, along with sporting successes, technological excellence and Made in Italy design that define each of its motorcycles, make Ducati one of a kind in the world of two wheels.
Driven by passion, racing spirit and a strong bond with its community, Ducati is present in over 90 countries worldwide.

Driven by passion, racing spirit and a strong bond with its community, Ducati is present in over 90 countries worldwide.

articles.content:
TAPI (Technology & API Services) Names Serge Rogasik CEO to lead next chapter of growth and competitiveness
TEL AVIV, Israel, Sept. 30, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- TAPI (Technology & API Services) today announced the appointment of Serge Rogasik as its Chief Executive Officer. Mr. Rogasik will lead a global business that combines a broad API portfolio, deep scientific and technical capabilities, and an extensive global operations network serving customers worldwide.
“I am honored to join TAPI at such an important moment in its evolution," said Mr. Rogasik. "TAPI combines a unique set of capabilities, assets and talented people with a well-earned reputation as a trusted partner to customers worldwide. As the pharmaceutical industry increasingly focuses on supply chain resilience and geographic diversification, TAPI is uniquely positioned to support its customers. Few companies can match one of the industry's broadest technology platforms and an integrated manufacturing and R&D network spanning India, the Middle East, Europe and the Americas. I am excited by the momentum in the business and see significant opportunities ahead to further strengthen TAPI's position as a leading integrated API and CDMO partner.”
Founded in 1935, TAPI is one of the world’s largest producers of active pharmaceutical ingredients and a leading CDMO partner with more than 4,000 employees, 13 manufacturing sites and six R&D facilities, supplying more than 350 active ingredients to customers around the world. Through its API and CDMO businesses, TAPI helps customers bring effective medicines to patients around the world.
Mr. Rogasik and the TAPI team will be at CPHI Milan, October 6–8, 2026, in Hall 3, Booth A73. Customers and partners are invited to stop by to meet him and the teams behind TAPI's catalog and CDMO businesses.
About Serge Rogasik
Mr. Rogasik is a transformation-focused global executive with more than 25 years of experience building, scaling and repositioning businesses across specialty ingredients, active ingredients, specialty chemicals and life sciences. He has spent a significant part of his career leading private equity-backed companies through complex carve-outs, accelerated growth, portfolio transformation, M&A and operational improvement in highly regulated markets – building stronger, more focused businesses that deliver sustainable long-term value. Most recently, as President and Chief Executive Officer of Kensing, a specialty ingredients company owned by One Rock Capital Partners, he helped transform a single-site carve-out from BASF into a global platform serving the personal care, nutrition, pharmaceutical and agrochemical markets. Under his leadership, Kensing integrated four acquisitions, expanded its global footprint and became the world leader in natural vitamin E and sterols.
Prior to Kensing, Mr. Rogasik led growth and transformation initiatives at Vantage Specialty Chemicals and Addivant, where he helped turn carve-outs and underperforming businesses into stronger, more focused global platforms through commercial expansion, operational improvement and strategic acquisitions. Earlier in his career, he held senior strategy, commercial, marketing and research roles with BASF, General Electric, Eastman Chemical Company, Rhône-Poulenc and Colgate-Palmolive, building deep international experience across specialty chemicals, life sciences and consumer markets.
Mr. Rogasik holds a Master of Science in Industrial Pharmacy and a postgraduate degree in Pharmaceutical Industry Management from the Institut des Sciences Pharmaceutiques et Biologiques de Lyon. Since 2023, he has served as Chairman of the International Association of Sterol and Stanol Producers and previously served on the Board of Directors of World Child Cancer USA.
About TAPI
TAPI is a global leader in the development and manufacturing of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), building blocks and key starting materials (KSMs) providing one of the industry's most comprehensive API portfolios. TAPI also offers customized CDMO services, utilizing their extensive expertise in a wide range of technologies to meet the diverse needs of partners, ensuring flexibility and excellence in every project. With 4,100 employees, a global footprint in 100+ countries, 13 sites worldwide, and a robust portfolio of 350+ high-quality products, TAPI's operations are integral to the delivery of high-quality, safe and effective medications to patients worldwide, supported by a sophisticated supply chain, focused innovative manufacturing, regulatory and quality excellence and a commitment to sustainability. For more information about how TAPI is advancing health from the core, visit www.tapi.com.

articles.article_title: FTC is investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over possible risks to consumers
articles.heading: FTC is investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over possible risks to consumers
articles.summary: Concerns around the dangers powerful AI models may pose to humanity have led some of the top AI developers to call for a slowdown
articles.content:
The U.S. Federal Trade Commission has opened an investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other artificial intelligence companies over dangers their technology may pose to consumers, the agency said Wednesday.
The AI giants and other tech companies in recent months have disclosed examples of their AI agents going beyond human instructions, finding their way onto the internet and hacking external websites.
An FTC spokesperson confirmed the investigation but declined further comment. The investigation was first reported by the New York Post, which said it has been underway for months.
Representatives for Anthropic and OpenAI did not immediately respond to messages for comment on Wednesday.
Concerns around the dangers powerful AI models may pose to humanity have led some of the top AI developers to call for a slowdown. The CEO of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, said this month that the industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned that within six to 12 months AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet.
OpenAI, meanwhile, recently delayed the launch of its newest model this week over safety concerns.

articles.title: Autonomous aircraft makes stop in SLC for demonstration of advanced aviation technology
articles.description: Autonomous aircraft makes stop in SLC for demonstration of advanced aviation technology ABC4 Utah
articles.description_html: Autonomous aircraft makes stop in SLC for demonstration of advanced aviation technology  ABC4 Utah
articles.article_title: Autonomous aircraft makes stop in SLC for demonstration of advanced aviation technology
articles.heading: Autonomous aircraft makes stop in SLC for demonstration of advanced aviation technology
articles.summary: An aircraft equipped with technology to allow it to fly autonomously made a stop in Salt Lake City to demonstrate advanced air mobility technology.
articles.content:
SALT LAKE CITY (ABC4) — An aircraft equipped with technology to allow it to fly autonomously made a stop in Salt Lake City to demonstrate advanced air mobility technology.
During the demonstration at Salt Lake City International Airport, one of Joby Aviation’s autonomous aircrafts came in for a landing as Joby engineers operated the aircraft remotely from the company’s headquarters in California. There was a pilot on board for safety, but the pilot was not the one flying the plane.
“I’m a pilot. I have 30 years as an airline pilot. I’ve flown here into Salt Lake for both United and JetBlue, so I didn’t imagine ever that there would be autonomy,” Bonny Simi, Joby’s president of operations, told ABC4.com.
Joby is already known for its electric aircraft and air taxi, and the company is working on introducing autonomy. Simi said that this technology is not to replace airline pilots, but instead, it is intended to protect military service members, emergency responders, firefighters, and anyone else who may be going to places where it’s dangerous. UDOT said that the autonomous aircraft have a role as part of a larger, connected transportation system to link communities to existing infrastructure like airports, transit, and roadways.
In March, UDOT was selected to lead a federal pilot program to test advanced electric aircraft along with other emerging aviation technologies, with the hope of integrating them into real-world operations. UDOT said that this demonstration today highlighted Utah’s role as a national leader in the development and deployment of advanced air mobility technologies.
“Utah has always been a place where innovation and big ideas can take flight. We are actively building a future transportation system that includes advanced air mobility solutions,” UDOT Aeronautics Director Matt Maass said. “This supervised autonomous flight is more than a demonstration; it is helping to generate important data that will be used to inform safety standards, future infrastructure decisions, and operating best practices for AAM deployment across Utah.”
Joby is hoping to bring its electric aircraft to Utah in time for the 2034 Olympic Games, allowing fast transportation above the traffic at a reasonable price. Those electric aircraft land and take off vertically, something Simi said she is very much looking forward to for the games.
“I’m an Olympian myself, spent a lot of time in Park City at Utah Olympic Park and driving up Parley’s Canyon, and the traffic is a lot, so you can imagine whisking above the traffic and landing in Kimball Junction, taking maybe 8 minutes from here, the Salt Lake Airport, up to Park City,” Simi said.
UDOT is confident that Utah will be a place where autonomous aircraft can fly, as Utah has a robust aerospace and defense supply chain, world-class research institutions, Hill Air Force Base, and the Utah Test and Training Range.
Two weeks ago, Joby Aviation’s J208 completed the first-ever fully autonomous flight across the United States. It flew 3,199 miles with zero control inputs from its onboard safety pilot, something that Joby founder and CEO JoeBen Bevirt said was a “glimpse into a new era of aviation.”

articles.article_title: Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project
articles.heading: Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project
articles.summary: ETIPP works alongside coastal, remote, and island communities that are seeking to improve the resilience, affordability, and reliability of their energy systems.
articles.content:
The U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project (ETIPP) works alongside coastal, remote, and island communities that are seeking to improve the resilience, affordability, and reliability of their energy systems. ETIPP helps these communities overcome the unique geographical and logistical challenges that limit their access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy resources.
This multi-year, cross-sector technical assistance program applies a tailored approach to each participating community. Leveraging the experience and expertise of its partner network—a broad coalition of local stakeholders, regional organizations, national laboratories, and DOE offices—ETIPP helps communities proactively identify and implement solutions that suit their particular needs.
ETIPP offers two tracks: strategic energy planning (four to eight months) and deep-dive technical assistance (12 to 24 months) for specific energy projects. Selected communities receive support for a project scoping phase, followed by energy planning and analysis projects that:
- Address the community's energy priorities, goals, challenges, and opportunities.
- Advance the community's ability to implement strategic, whole-systems solutions.
- Develop replicable approaches that can add value in neighboring communities, or those with similar characteristics.
In addition to direct funding, communities participating in ETIPP can expect substantial in-kind support from partnering national labs in the form of energy analysis, planning, and, where appropriate, support for leading-edge technology solutions. ETIPP regional partners also provide general program guidance and education.
ETIPP uses the Energy Technology Innovation Initiative's (ETI's) proven framework to find solutions to community energy challenges and share best practices and innovations. The program has supported 95 projects since its inception in 2020.

Learn More About ETIPP
ETIPP is managed by the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR). For more information about the program, application process, participating communities, and additional resources, visit NLR’s ETIPP website, or contact ETIPP@nlr.gov with questions.

articles.title: How publishers are rethinking audience engagement: Five takeaways from the Future of Media Technology Conference

articles.description_html: How publishers are rethinking audience engagement: Five takeaways from the Future of Media Technology Conference  niemanlab.org
articles.article_title: How publishers are rethinking audience engagement: Five takeaways from the Future of Media Technology Conference
articles.heading: How publishers are rethinking audience engagement: Five takeaways from the Future of Media Technology Conference
articles.summary: "It would be a mistake to try to replicate the creator economy."
articles.content:
Nieman Foundation at Harvard



Sept. 30, 2026, 3:31 p.m.
“It would be a mistake to try to replicate the creator economy.”

Earlier this month, just across from the Tate Modern in central London, journalists and media managers gathered for this year’s Future of Media Technology Conference, a one-day event hosted by Press Gazette. Speakers included journalists, technologists, and media professionals like The Economist’s Andrew Palmer, Politico UK’s Katie Palisoul, The Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism’s Mitali Mukherjee, The Logic’s David Skok, and News UK’s Tom Jackson. Here are five takeaways from the event.
App downloads, frequency of visits, and newsletter signups were identified as important indicators by The Guardian’s chief support officer, Liz Wynn. “You build motivation, support, effective comprehension of our mission, our purpose, why we exist, why we should keep coming back,” she said. “[It’s a] very important emotional driver, but it’s not enough on its own. We have to focus also on the habit and the value of driving people day to day.”
To build those habits, publishers are focusing on community-building, with some even employing AI tools to achieve that goal. Predictive models, such as using AI to recommend users their next read, were cited as a common example of how AI can help drive user engagement. Anna Sbuttoni, deputy head of digital at The Times and The Sunday Times, said her team is now using AI to help with another aspect of audience engagement: comment moderation.
“[Content moderation] is still overseen by humans, but it’s just brought that work way down, and it’s freed up that team to now do much more interesting and innovative community-focused work than they were doing when they were just spending hours and hours on this moderation job,” she said.
The Economist is a prime example of this. The magazine has moved away from its legacy of journalistic anonymity toward putting its journalists’ faces, names, and personalities at the forefront of its value proposition. Its executive editor, Andrew Palmer, said one of the reasons the publication has begun to showcase its journalists is a desire to highlight the humans behind the journalism as AI advances.
“It builds a connection, so we definitely have a lot of subscribers who want to see what our journalists do and understand the workings of the newsroom,” said Palmer.
Like many newsrooms, The Economist is fostering in-house talent to put in front of the camera as a way to respond to growing audience interest in creators. The team at The Times and The Sunday Times is also thinking about its talent strategy as the next step in audience engagement. Putting journalists in front of the camera is one strategy it is beginning to employ to reach people who might not otherwise engage with the papers.
“How can we make people consider getting a Times subscription? A big part of that has been just a complete change in how we approach our social video formats, and that’s really putting our journalists at the front and center of that. Getting people to know the real journalists,” explained Sbuttoni.
Earlier this year, The Guardian announced the formation of Guardian Studios — a new creative hub for video-first, personality-led journalism. “There can be a [certain] panic and [an] overcorrection from legacy brands. It would be a mistake to try to replicate the creator economy.”
Jasmine Dawson, senior vice president of BBC Studios, said one of the main things legacy publishers can learn from creators is a deep understanding of their audience. Creators, unlike broadcasters and publishers, “live and breathe” in their audience’s world: They understand them and know what they want.
“Obsessing about your audience means not only knowing where they are, but what they want to talk about, what they want to hear from you, what they want to see from you,” she said.
“There’s a real tension that exists in terms of what’s happening in partnerships and their relationship with audiences,” said RISJ’s director, Mitali Mukherjee. “We don’t have a clear sign of what exactly will happen.”
This uncertainty is one of the main reasons publishers are investing in strengthening direct relationships with their audiences. At the same time, they are examining their relationships with AI companies and their presence in AI search. They want to remain visible across search and AI services while protecting the value of original journalism.

The question of monetization extended beyond audiences to conversations around AI, particularly the tension between the short- and long-term economics of allowing AI platforms to use publishers’ content.

“Ideally we want to have relationships with all of these people and get fair value back. But if they come in and steal that content, we will sue them,” said Jackson. “It’s not just the monetary value of that deal, which is material. It’s also the ability to then have that close relationship with these organizations.”
In the midst of such a future-oriented conference, one old piece of technology stood out as a winner across the panels: newsletters. They were framed as direct, differentiated products that deepen reader relationships and reduce reliance on platform algorithms. Many of the news organizations showcased at the conference have invested in newsletters, which remain a strong way to engage directly with audiences and counter declining referral traffic.
For The Logic, a Canadian newsroom focused on tech and business, newsletters have been a core part of the organization since the beginning. David Skok, The Logic’s CEO and editor-in-chief, said the publication hasn’t seen a drop-off in open rates, while advertiser performance has continued to grow. He attributes their success to treating the newsletter as a premium, central product of the newsroom. The Logic considers its daily newsletter briefing, which is written specifically by its journalists, the front page of the newspaper.
“The way we treat newsletters is really more as their own product,” said Skok. “We were a bit ahead of the curve in that we had this direct relation with our readers, because we just decided very early on that we weren’t going to build our business on the top of some of these algorithms.”
Politico Playbook also demonstrates the enduring appeal of newsletters, having spawned numerous global iterations since its launch in 2007. Palisoul from Politico attributed its success to an “obsession with audience”: The team knows exactly who its readers are and what they want from the product.
“The Playbook is written with an exact audience in mind: a prime minister, a cabinet minister…But authors think of that person as a person. They don’t think of that person as an MP,” explained Palisoul. “It’s fun. It’s cheeky. It’s got good humor. Great puns. It tells them where they can go for a drink. It’s really focused on the daily life of that individual.”

articles.title: More than 44,000 file legal objections to Palantir NHS platform handling their data
articles.description: More than 44,000 file legal objections to Palantir NHS platform handling their data The Guardian
articles.description_html: More than 44,000 file legal objections to Palantir NHS platform handling their data  The Guardian
articles.article_title: More than 44,000 file legal objections to Palantir NHS platform handling their data
articles.heading: More than 44,000 file legal objections to Palantir NHS platform handling their data
articles.summary: Exclusive: Campaign comes amid backlash against tech company’s involvement with Israeli military and Trump’s ICE crackdown
articles.content:
Tens of thousands of people have formally demanded NHS England blocks the Palantir-powered national medical data platform from handling their personal information.
More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the nationwide Federated Data Platform (FDP) operated using the US company’s AI technology.
The coordinated campaign utilises rights enshrined in data protection laws and means the NHS must stop using the data unless it can provide a “compelling reason” to continue.
Hundreds of thousands of people have signed petitions demanding the government cancels its £330m deal with Palantir, and Andy Burnham will be required to make a decision to back or axe Palantir within months.
Campaigners have voiced anger at Palantir’s work for the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, and two House of Commons select committees have called for Labour to exercise a break clause in the seven-year deal which comes into force in February 2027.
David Murray, a retired IBM systems engineer and one of those requesting the data block, said: “I am a believer in the NHS having really good data on their patients, but I want it to be something you can really trust to be used for the right purposes. I am not happy about Palantir’s involvement with the IDF in Gaza and ICE in America.”
On Wednesday, the human rights group Amnesty International and patient campaign group, Just Treatment, parked a van styled like a shot-up Palestinian ambulance outside Palantir’s London HQ in a stunt that asked: “Why should a company linked to Israel’s destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system have any place in ours?”
Protesters have also raised concerns, acknowledged by the NHS England chief executive, Jim Mackey, that the benefits to public health from the Palantir-powered platform may not be as significant as has been claimed.
Palantir says the FDP, which is designed to connect sprawling health service data on topics ranging from surgery schedules to discharge planning, is helping to cut waiting lists and frees up beds. Louis Mosley, the company’s executive vice-president for UK and Europe, has accused people who disagree with that assessment of suffering from “Palantir derangement syndrome”.
A spokesperson said: “Palantir software is helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients and a 5.6% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days.”
Mosley has said its technology was used for locating hostages, not military targeting, in Gaza, although when challenged last year by a protester alleging “Palantir kills Palestinians” in Gaza, the company’s chief executive, Alex Karp, replied: “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.”
The formal objections to the FDP using personal data cite article 21 of the UK General Data Protection Regulation and express concern that “the involvement of Palantir undermines my personal trust in NHS data confidentiality”. Palantir said its patient data could only be handled according to the NHS’s instructions and remained in the UK.
Veronica Hawking, the campaigns director at 38 Degrees, a not-for-profit that coordinated the data objections, said: “The scale of this public backlash should be a huge wake-up call for the government.”
A spokesperson for NHS England said: “All NHS organisations remain in control of their data within the FDP, with suppliers unable to access it for their own purposes, and we will respond to the objection requests in line with data protection law.”
The 44,000 objectors have also asked that the NHS halts processing of their data through the Palantir platform while their main request is assessed.

articles.title: ‘No one should go without food:’ Virginia rolls out chip technology on EBT cards to fight SNAP fraud
articles.description: ‘No one should go without food:’ Virginia rolls out chip technology on EBT cards to fight SNAP fraud 12onyourside.com
articles.description_html: ‘No one should go without food:’ Virginia rolls out chip technology on EBT cards to fight SNAP fraud  12onyourside.com
articles.article_title: ‘No one should go without food:’ Virginia rolls out chip technology on EBT cards to fight SNAP fraud
articles.heading: ‘No one should go without food:’ Virginia rolls out chip technology on EBT cards to fight SNAP fraud
articles.summary:
The Virginia Department of Social Services hopes new technology will cut down on SNAP Benefit theft. 
The state distributed more than 145,000 chip-enabled cards in September, with the rollout continuing through the end of 2026.
articles.content:
‘No one should go without food:’ Virginia rolls out chip technology on EBT cards to fight SNAP fraud
RICHMOND, Va. (WWBT) - The Virginia Department of Social Services hopes new technology will cut down on SNAP Benefit theft.
The state distributed more than 145,000 chip-enabled cards in September, with the rollout continuing through the end of 2026.
“VDSS understands how distressing it is for a family or individual to discover their SNAP benefits have been stolen, and no Virginian should have to worry about going hungry because a criminal targeted the benefits they depend on,” the agency said in a statement.
Kassandara Johnson is a mom of four, works for a school system and is a SNAP recipient. She says she is careful about where she shops because of card skimmers.
“I try to be very specific where I shop, not just going anywhere because I’ve heard of those card reader scammy things,” Johnson said.
Johnson is not sure how scammers got her EBT card number, but in June, her SNAP benefits were wiped out the same day they were distributed. She reached out to 12 On Your Side hoping her story could raise awareness.
“When you ask for assistance and then you’re so grateful to get it and you finally get it, and then someone has stolen it,” Johnson said. “It definitely feels like a violation.”
Stolen benefits top $1.5 million
The Virginia Department of Social Services says more than $1.5 million of SNAP benefits were stolen from January to June of 2026.
Cyber security expert Alex Nette says stolen money cannot be replaced.
“There used to be federal legislation to refund and give that money back in the event of fraud or it being stolen,” Nette said. “That legislation at the federal level has since expired and a bill to renew it has expired in Congress.”
Move to chip technology
Nette said one way to avoid the fraud has been the move to chip technology.
“Europe recognized this long before we did and the United States is finally playing catch up,” Nette said.
In September, Virginia distributed 145,300 EBT cards with chip technology. California was one of the first states to make the move and see a decrease in fraud.
Until recently, SNAP EBT cards used only magnetic stripes, which thieves can copy with skimmers hidden on card readers.
The magnetic stripe is like a house key anyone can copy, and once copied, a thief can make a duplicate card. The chip creates a new code for every purchase that only works once, and even if a thief steals that code, it is useless to them.
How the scheme works
“People will report, ‘I didn’t use my card. I got the money at midnight, and I woke up at 6 a.m. and it was gone. How is this happening?’” On Your Side Investigator Jasmine Turner asked.
“Timing is a big part of it,” Nette said. “Oftentimes it feels like it’s something that happens super fast. What’s actually happened is there has been a whole setup and a number of things that have occurred long before then.”
Nette said a magnetic stripe card can be swiped at a store and the number is stolen and sold, in some cases to people outside of the U.S.
“Those groups then aggregate all of those numbers, maybe across multiple hundreds or thousands of SNAP benefits receivers,” Nette said. “And given that oftentimes SNAP accounts are funded at a certain date, at a certain time, they’ll wait until that moment and then spring the trap.”
The hope is that chip technology will make the scheme harder or stop it altogether.
“As consumers, we have to do everything we can to protect that information and our SNAP cards as well,” Nette said.
