articles.description_html: Using the latest technology to create a connected golf course makes improvements across the board  Golf Inc. Magazine
articles.article_title: Using the latest technology to create a connected golf course makes improvements across the board
articles.heading: Using the latest technology to create a connected golf course makes improvements across the board
articles.summary: Are the latest technology buzzwords the future of course management or simply another wave of technology searching for a problem to solve? The reality is somewhere in between.
articles.content:
Walk into almost any golf industry conference today and you’ll hear the same buzzwords repeated: Artificial intelligence. Internet of things. Automation. Robotics. Precision GPS. Predictive analytics. Digital twins.
It’s enough to make many golf course owners wonder whether they’re looking at the future of course management or simply another wave of technology searching for a problem to solve. The reality is somewhere in between.
While autonomous mowers, AI-powered sprayers and connected irrigation systems continue to attract attention, the biggest technological revolution happening on courses today isn’t necessarily about replacing people. It’s about helping owners and superintendents make better decisions by giving them something the industry has rarely possessed: accurate, connected data.
The golf course has always been a collection of moving parts. Irrigation systems, weather stations, maintenance software, tee sheets, GPS carts, point-of-sale systems and equipment management platforms often operate independently. Each produces valuable information, yet few communicate with one another. That leaves owners making expensive decisions based on incomplete information.
“The first problem is not a technology problem,” said Dave Vanslette, founder and CEO of FAIRWAYiQ. “It is a visibility problem.”
For owners supervising one of the largest capital assets they’ll ever manage, that distinction may be the most important technology lesson of all.
The foundation of intelligence
Colin Read, founder and CEO of Whoosh, believes the industry has reached a point where collecting information is no longer enough. The next step is connecting it.
Today’s superintendent may have one system tracking irrigation, another monitoring turf moisture, another managing employees and another controlling the tee sheet. Valuable insights remain trapped inside individual software platforms.
“You currently do not have a full view of what’s going on across the property,” Read said. “A connected golf course is a data-rich golf course.”
The goal isn’t technology for technology’s sake. Instead, owners should ask a much simpler question: Are we collecting the information that allows us to make better operational decisions? If the answer is no, then artificial intelligence won’t fix the problem.
Read argues that successful technology adoption begins with understanding whether a club is gathering meaningful data about labor, course conditions, equipment utilization, cart movement and rounds played. Once that foundation exists, artificial intelligence can begin identifying patterns that humans could miss.
Without clean data, AI becomes little more than an expensive guessing machine.
“AI isn’t a substitute for good data or good operations,” Read said.
Start with the problem, not the purchase
Golf technology companies naturally like to showcase the newest products. Owners, however, shouldn’t begin with demonstrations. They should begin with questions.
What operational challenge is costing the club the most money? Labor shortages? Water consumption? Turf damage? Pace of play? Equipment maintenance?
Sean Palmer, COO of The Union League of Philadelphia, believes technology only succeeds when it follows strategy rather than trends.
“Implementation of smart technologies or investments in analytics can make a tremendous impact on an operation, with the right strategy,” Palmer said. “New technologies are worth the investments when they provide efficiencies that free up capital or resources to achieve more than the operation could before the technology’s implementation.”
That means resisting the temptation to buy the newest robotic machine simply because it looks impressive at a trade show. A robotic range picker may generate excitement among members, Palmer noted, but replacing one relatively inexpensive labor position may not justify a significant capital investment.
Conversely, emerging technologies like AI-guided precision sprayers that dramatically reduce chemical use and labor could eventually deliver meaningful returns. The question isn’t whether technology is innovative. It’s whether it solves an expensive problem.
Labor is not disappearing; it’s changing
Few issues concern owners more than finding and retaining quality maintenance employees. Technology is often promoted as the answer. The reality is more nuanced.
AI or automation will not dramatically reduce staffing needs. Instead, technology allows existing employees to spend more time on the work golfers notice.
“The honest answer is that technology doesn’t reduce the total labor requirement,” Read said. “It redirects it.”
Autonomous equipment can mow fairways, collect range balls or potentially rake waste bunkers in the future, but insight from experienced superintendents remain indispensable.
Scott Bordner, director of agronomy for The Union League of Philadelphia, knows that firsthand. His facilities already employ robotic equipment, yet the technology still demands human oversight. He recalls receiving an evening alert from an autonomous range picker that had become stuck, requiring him to spend half an hour retrieving it before the next morning’s operation.
The lesson? Automation isn’t replacing expertise. At least not yet.
Automation frees maintenance teams from repetitive work while allowing them to focus on detailed mowing, bunker presentation, moisture management and countless other tasks that influence conditioning.
Technology also has the potential to improve employee satisfaction.
Read said that better task management software can rotate responsibilities, reduce monotony and give employees greater ownership over their work rather than assigning the same repetitive jobs.
For clubs struggling with retention, that may prove just as valuable as labor savings.
Water, the biggest battleground
If one area has already demonstrated measurable returns, it’s irrigation.
Water availability, cost and environmental stewardship continue to reshape golf course management across North America.
Smart irrigation systems now combine weather forecasts, soil moisture readings, evapotranspiration models and individual sprinkler control to deliver water only where it’s needed.
Bordner has seen the transformation. At Union League National, new irrigation controls and pump station technology have improved both water efficiency and water quality, allowing the maintenance team to deliver oxygen-rich irrigation comparable to rainfall while significantly reducing watering time.
Moisture sensors have replaced intuition with measurable data. The experienced superintendent still knows every inch of the property, but objective moisture readings help determine exactly where additional water — or less — is needed.
Owners should recognize that “smart irrigation” involves much more than automatic sprinkler scheduling. It means understanding water quality, soil composition, drainage, disease pressure, labor availability and golfer traffic before deciding how much water should be applied.
As Bordner noted, irrigation isn’t simply about using less water. It’s about applying the right amount in the right place at the right time.
Seeing what was once invisible
Perhaps no emerging technology illustrates the value of data better than precision GPS.
For decades, golf courses understood that cart traffic damaged turf. What they couldn’t determine was exactly where, when or how severely.
Vanslette said precision GPS has fundamentally changed those conversations.
Instead of relying on assumptions, superintendents can now show heat maps identifying where carts repeatedly cross vulnerable turf, where pace-of-play bottlenecks develop and how golfer behavior changes throughout the day. This information provides actionable data.
“The conversation shifts from whether there is a problem to what we do about it,” Vanslette said.
That visibility carries significant financial implications.
Compaction-related repairs often consume a meaningful portion of annual maintenance budgets without owners ever recognizing the true source of those costs. Likewise, recurring pace-of-play backups may quietly reduce tee-sheet capacity and annual revenue.
When owners can finally measure both, operational priorities become much easier to establish.
Integration is the next frontier
Collecting data is valuable. Connecting it may be transformative.
Read said many clubs still operate too many disconnected systems that never exchange information.
Consider a heavily trafficked front nine. The superintendent may recognize worsening turf conditions. Maintenance staff may notice increasing compaction. Yet unless those observations are connected to tee-sheet demand, cart traffic and player flow, the club may continue treating symptoms instead of addressing the underlying cause.
Perhaps more rounds should begin on the back nine. Perhaps tee-time spacing needs adjustment. Perhaps traffic restrictions should change.
Those answers emerge only when operational systems communicate with one another.
Integration also improves communication between ownership, management and maintenance. Rather than debating opinions, everyone reviews the same objective information.
Read encourages clubs to establish regular operational review meetings where owners, general managers and superintendents evaluate common performance metrics together.
The result is greater alignment and fewer emotional decisions.
AI will be an assistant, not the superintendent
Artificial intelligence remains the industry’s biggest conversation topic. It’s also the most misunderstood.
AI’s greatest value lies in processing enormous amounts of information quickly — not replacing experienced professionals.
Disease prediction, moisture management, equipment maintenance scheduling, task prioritization, labor allocation and predictive maintenance all represent practical applications where AI excels because they’re built upon quality data collected over time.
Bordner believes disease prediction and plant stress monitoring will continue becoming more accurate.
“Tools are evolving to make those decisions easier,” Bordner said. “Will plant stress and moisture detection continue to get easier to troubleshoot before it is visible? I believe that is the next big transformation in turf management to help superintendents be proactive instead of reactive.”
Read sees AI synthesizing information across multiple operational systems so important signals no longer slip through the cracks.
Vanslette envisions AI quietly orchestrating player experiences, operational decisions and maintenance activities behind the scenes while allowing employees to focus on hospitality.
None suggest AI will replace agronomic judgment.
“It cannot handle a member conversation that requires tact,” Vanslette said.
Nor can it replicate the instincts developed by a superintendent walking the golf course every morning. Technology provides intelligence, while experience still provides wisdom.
Leadership determines success
Ironically, the biggest obstacle to smart course management may have nothing to do with software. It’s organizational culture.
Technology adoption begins with leadership. Owners should first evaluate whether their organization embraces change before investing in new systems.
Read recommends beginning with a cultural assessment. Are employees receptive to new workflows? Does leadership consistently support innovation? Are managers willing to experiment, evaluate results and adjust accordingly?
The Olympic Club in San Francisco, one of Whoosh’s technology partners, exemplifies that philosophy by continuously testing autonomous equipment, operational workflows and member-facing technologies rather than assuming existing practices remain the best practices.
Smaller facilities can adopt the same mindset. In fact, they may benefit even more because efficiency gains have an outsized impact on leaner operations.
As Vanslette puts it, owners should “buy the boring foundation” before chasing flashy innovations. Measure operations, collect accurate data, integrate systems, then allow AI to amplify those investments.
Building the course of the future
For owners creating a five-year technology plan, the temptation will be to focus on robotics, artificial intelligence and whatever innovation dominates the next conference floor.
The experts suggest a different roadmap.
First, build a culture willing to embrace change. Second, identify the club’s biggest operational challenges before purchasing solutions. Third, invest in technologies that improve visibility, measurement and decision-making. Only then should clubs begin layering AI, automation and advanced analytics on top of that foundation.
The future golf course won’t necessarily employ fewer people. It will simply equip them with better information.
For owners, that’s perhaps the most encouraging takeaway from today’s technology revolution.
Artificial intelligence won’t replace great superintendents. Connected technology won’t eliminate experience. But together, they can help talented professionals protect their most valuable asset, spend resources more efficiently and create better playing conditions for golfers.
And in an industry where expectations continue rising while labor, water and operating costs grow more challenging every year, making smarter decisions may become the greatest competitive advantage of all.
This article originally appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Golf Inc.

articles.summary: Bank of America will host more than 500 technology companies and investors for its 15th annual Technology Innovation Summit in San Francisco on October 7. The summit brings founders and venture capital firms together with Bank of America leaders from Global Technology, Technology Investment Banking and Capital Markets to examine how emerging technology is changing banking and the wider economy.
articles.content:
Bank of America to Convene 500+ Innovators and Capital Providers at 15th Annual Technology Innovation Summit
Gathering in San Francisco, companies and investors will explore enterprise AI, technology investment and opportunities for collaboration
SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Bank of America will host more than 500 technology companies and investors for its 15th annual Technology Innovation Summit in San Francisco on October 7. The summit brings founders and venture capital firms together with Bank of America leaders from Global Technology, Technology Investment Banking and Capital Markets to examine how emerging technology is changing banking and the wider economy.
"For 15 years, we have been bringing people together at our Technology Innovation Summit, connecting entrepreneurs, investors and technology leaders," said Jim DeMare, Co-President of Bank of America. "It's a great event where we share ideas and build partnerships that pair the speed of the startup ecosystem with Bank of America's insights, expertise and global reach."
Artificial intelligence anchors this year's agenda as companies move from pilots to enterprise-wide deployment and measurable results. Sessions will cover the foundations of an AI-enabled business, the impact of AI on the workforce, client experience and personalization, and where investment is likely to concentrate next.
"Innovation is inseparable from business strategy and results," said Hari Gopalkrishnan, Chief Technology and Information Officer of Bank of America. "The summit puts innovators in front of our technology leaders so we can identify ideas that can scale responsibly and deliver real benefits for our clients and employees."
Connecting innovation and investment
Over the summit's 15-year history, Bank of America has hosted more than 7,000 companies and venture capital investors. More than 20% of the companies that have presented at the summit have gone on to become Bank of America vendors. This year, participating companies represent innovation in the areas of AI, data and analytics, enterprise infrastructure, information security, financial technology and software development.
Additional topics to be covered at this year's summit include:
- Which segments of the AI ecosystem will create the most impact for the enterprise
- Opportunities for startups and other venture-backed technology companies to partner with Bank of America
- Selling to large financial institutions, from proof of concept and procurement to implementation at scale
Bank of America
Bank of America is one of the world's leading financial institutions, serving individual consumers, small and middle-market businesses and large corporations with a full range of banking, investing, asset management and other financial and risk management products and services. The company provides unmatched convenience in the United States, serving more than 69 million clients with approximately 3,500 retail financial centers, approximately 15,000 ATMs (automated teller machines) and award-winning digital banking with approximately 60 million verified digital users. Bank of America is a global leader in wealth management, corporate and investment banking and trading across a broad range of asset classes, serving corporations, governments, institutions and individuals around the world. As the #1 small business lender in the United States (FDIC), Bank of America offers industry-leading support to approximately 4 million small business households through a suite of innovative, easy-to-use online products and services. The company serves clients through operations across the United States, its territories and more than 35 countries and/or jurisdictions. Bank of America Corporation stock (NYSE: BAC) is listed on the New York Stock Exchange.

articles.article_title: New Report Positions Florida as an Emerging Leader in Defense-Led Quantum Technology
articles.heading: New Report Positions Florida as an Emerging Leader in Defense-Led Quantum Technology
articles.summary: A report commissioned by FloridaCommerce identifies defense and practical deployment as central to Florida’s quantum opportunities.
articles.content:
Insider Brief
- A Quantum Insider report commissioned by FloridaCommerce identifies defense and practical deployment as central to Florida’s quantum technology opportunities.
- The assessment identifies post-quantum cryptography, quantum sensing, resilient navigation and secure communications as near-term priorities, drawing on 130 programs across 25 countries.
- The report proposes a five-year roadmap covering statewide strategy, funded pilots and testbed access, with full findings to be presented at Quantum Beach on Oct. 22, 2026.
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — 30th September, 2026 — The Quantum Insider today announced the release of Florida Quantum Ecosystem: A Strategic Assessment of Florida’s Quantum Technology Position and Opportunities, a comprehensive study of the state’s quantum assets, competitive position and path to leadership. The report was prepared by The Quantum Insider in partnership with the Business Development Board of the Palm Beaches (BDB), with support from FloridaCommerce, which commissioned the study.
The full report will be presented at Quantum Beach 2026, Florida’s statewide quantum conference, on October 22, 2026 at the Palm Beach County Convention Center in West Palm Beach. A preview of the findings is available now at thequantuminsider.com and bdb.org.
Florida’s defense advantage
The assessment finds that Florida’s quantum opportunity is deployment-led, and that national defense is at its center. The state hosts 21 major military installations and three combatant commands — U.S. Central Command and U.S. Special Operations Command at MacDill Air Force Base, and U.S. Southern Command in Doral — alongside a research base that includes the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, the University of Florida’s HiPerGator supercomputer, CREOL at the University of Central Florida and the Florida LambdaRail research network.
Drawing on a global review of 130 defense-relevant and quantum-secure programs across 25 countries, the report shows quantum defense activity moving from research into procurement, with post-quantum cryptography, quantum sensing, resilient navigation and secure communications as the nearest-term priorities. Each carries dual-use applications for Florida’s ports, healthcare system, financial sector and critical infrastructure.
A year of momentum
The report arrives after 12 months of rapid change. D-Wave relocated its headquarters to Boca Raton and Florida Atlantic University committed to a $20 million D-Wave Advantage2 system. IonQ announced a flagship Superion 256 deployment at Florida International University, a quantum-secure corridor with Florida LambdaRail and the acquisition of SkyWater Technology in NeoCity. Palm Beach State College’s Quantum Innovation Center, the Florida Alliance for Quantum Technology and FloridaQuantum have emerged as ecosystem anchors, and Quantum Beach has become the annual checkpoint for the state’s quantum community.
Key findings
- Florida’s $1.9 trillion economy — fourth-largest in the U.S. — offers large, complex operating environments where quantum technologies can be tested against real problems in defense, space, logistics, healthcare and finance.
- The state’s competitive window is narrowing but open: Florida is well placed to compete if it connects its assets with focus and discipline.
- Twenty-three stakeholder interviews across research, government, defense, industry and investment show broad alignment on building around existing strengths and sustaining statewide coordination.
- The report sets out a five-year indicative roadmap: establish an operating baseline, including a published Florida quantum strategy; build translation capacity through funded pilots and testbed access; then scale what works.
Quotes
“Palm Beach County has spent the past two years assembling the pieces of a real quantum ecosystem — a corporate anchor in D-Wave, a dedicated quantum computer at FAU, a workforce pipeline at Palm Beach State College and an annual conference that brings the global industry to our doorstep,” said Kelly Smallridge, President and CEO of the Business Development Board of the Palm Beaches. “This report gives the whole state a shared map of what we have, where the gaps are and what to do next. We’re proud to have partnered with The Quantum Insider on it and look forward to putting it in front of the industry at Quantum Beach.”
“Florida has the assets, the talent and the operating environments to turn quantum into a driver of economic growth, national security and high-value jobs,” said J. Alex Kelly, former Florida Secretary of Commerce and incoming President of Pensacola State College, whose team at FloridaCommerce commissioned the study. “What the state needed was a clear, evidence-based picture of where it stands and a practical roadmap for connecting those strengths with focus and discipline. This assessment delivers exactly that, and I’m confident it will help Florida compete for the companies, investment and partnerships that will shape this next technology frontier.”
“Most states are still deciding whether quantum is a research question or an economic one. Florida has already answered it,” said Dr. Rupesh Srivastava, Director of Public Clients at The Quantum Insider, who led the research team. “Our work across 130 defense and quantum-secure programs in 25 countries shows the sector moving from the lab into procurement, and Florida’s concentration of defense, space, ports and research infrastructure puts it in a small group of states that can host the entire stack. The opportunity now is deployment — getting these technologies into the hands of the users who already need them.”
About The Quantum Insider
The Quantum Insider (TQI) is the leading market intelligence and news platform for quantum technology, serving more than 200 enterprise and government clients worldwide. TQI operates a daily newsroom, the TQI Intelligence Platform with structured data on more than 2,100 quantum companies, and an advisory practice delivering strategy, ecosystem development and market-entry work for governments, enterprises and investors. TQI is part of Resonance, a Toronto-based intelligence and advisory firm operating across quantum, AI and space. Learn more at thequantuminsider.com.
About the Business Development Board of the Palm Beaches
The Business Development Board of the Palm Beaches is the official public-private economic development organization for Palm Beach County, Florida, working to attract, retain and grow businesses across the region. Learn more at bdb.org.
About FloridaCommerce
The Florida Department of Commerce (FloridaCommerce) is the state agency responsible for community, economic and workforce development across Florida. Learn more at floridajobs.org.

articles.title: Broadcom vs. NVIDIA: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.description: Broadcom vs. NVIDIA: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? The Motley Fool
articles.description_html: Broadcom vs. NVIDIA: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?  The Motley Fool
articles.article_title: Broadcom vs. NVIDIA: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? | The Motley Fool
articles.heading: Broadcom vs. NVIDIA: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.summary: Broadcom's 36% net margin and $27B free cash flow offer stability, while NVIDIA's 56% margin and $97B cash generation power explosive growth.
articles.content:
Choosing between Broadcom (AVGO -0.15%) and NVIDIA (NVDA +1.54%) involves weighing the stability of diversified networking and software against the explosive, hardware-driven growth that currently defines the artificial intelligence era.
Broadcom specializes in high-end networking hardware and enterprise software, while NVIDIA dominates the market for chips used in data centers. Both companies are essential to modern computing, making them top contenders for investors interested in semiconductor stocks as artificial intelligence continues to reshape the global economy.
The case for Broadcom
Broadcom provides a wide range of semiconductor solutions and infrastructure software for wireless and wired communication markets. Its business model shifted significantly following the acquisition of VMware, which expanded its reach into private cloud and enterprise software. A large portion of its revenue is driven by distributors, which account for nearly 48% of net revenue, while its top five end customers contribute approximately 40%. Broadcom has recently solidified its market position with a $200 billion memorandum of understanding with Samsung and a $30 billion chip commitment from Apple (AAPL +2.68%). Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.
In the fiscal year ended Nov. 2, 2025, revenue reached roughly $63.9 billion, representing a growth of approximately 23.9% compared with the prior fiscal year. The company reported net income of nearly $23.1 billion for the same period. This resulted in a net margin of approximately 36.2%, a significant increase from the 11.4% reported in its previous annual report.
According to its November 2025 balance sheet, Broadcom maintains a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.8x. This ratio compares total debt, including short-term and long-term borrowings, to shareholder equity. Its current ratio, which measures the ability to pay off short-term obligations with assets that can be converted to cash within one year, is roughly 1.7x. For the fiscal year ended Nov. 2, 2025, it generated free cash flow of about $26.9 billion. Free cash flow is the cash generated from operations minus capital expenditures. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 27.5% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back to cash flow.
The case for Nvidia
NVIDIA is a pioneer in GPU-accelerated computing, serving the data center, gaming, professional visualization, and automotive markets. The company has become the primary provider of the hardware that powers the modern AI industry and has established a partnership with OpenAI. Revenue concentration is a factor here as well, with two direct customers representing roughly 22% and 14% of total revenue. It relies on a network of partners, including cloud service providers and manufacturers, to deliver its technology to end users.
In the fiscal year ended Jan. 25, 2026, revenue reached approximately $215.9 billion, a massive 65.5% year-over-year increase. The company reported net income of nearly $120.1 billion during this period. This performance reflects a net margin of approximately 55.6%, which has remained relatively stable compared with the 55.8% net margin seen in the previous fiscal year.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, Nvidia carries a debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 0.1x, suggesting it relies very little on borrowed money. Its current ratio is approximately 3.9x, indicating a strong ability to meet short-term financial obligations. For the fiscal year ended Jan. 25, 2026, the company generated free cash flow of about $96.7 billion. Because its stock-based compensation was only roughly 6.2% of its operating cash flow, the reported cash generation is less affected by non-cash employee pay than that of many other technology companies.
Risk profile comparison
Broadcom faces significant regulatory scrutiny regarding its VMware acquisition, which is currently the subject of a legal challenge against EU antitrust regulators. The company also faces ongoing litigation, including a patent infringement lawsuit from TexasLDPC, and expansion risks into AI business models that may entail novel credit risks. Furthermore, its heavy reliance on a few large customers and the cyclical nature of the chip industry could lead to sensitivity during market volatility.
Nvidia faces intense competitive pressure from other hardware vendors and internal development teams at large cloud service providers like Microsoft (MSFT +1.71%), Alphabet (GOOGL +2.92%), and Amazon (AMZN +1.76%). Shifting U.S. export controls have effectively limited its access to the Chinese data center market, creating a potential competitive disadvantage. The company also faces securities litigation regarding historical revenue disclosures and relies heavily on TSMC for its manufacturing and production capacity.
Valuation comparison
Nvidia appears to be the more attractively valued option based on both future earnings estimates and sales over the past twelve months.
| Metric | Broadcom | NVIDIA |
|---|---|---|
| Forward P/E | 30.2x | 24.2x |
| P/S ratio | 18.8x | 17.9x |
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
To compare Nvidia and Broadcom, investors should consider a few key factors. Let's have a look at them and see what that tells us about each stock.
First off, there's growth. Both companies have recorded blistering growth in recent years, as the AI revolution has kicked into full gear. Broadcom has averaged 28% year-over-year revenue growth since 2021. Nvidia, meanwhile, has recorded a staggering 84% rate. In its most recent quarter (the three months ending on July 26, 2026), Nvidia reported an astounding 106% year-over-year revenue growth.
Another factor to consider is profitability. Here again, Nvidia wins the head-to-head matchup. Nvidia's operating margin stands at 65%, a rate it has roughly maintained for the last two years. Broadcom, on the other hand, has an operating margin of around 49%, up from a two-year low of 30%.
One final factor to weigh is free cash flow. To compare apples to apples, let's look at free cash flow per share. On this basis, Broadcom has a lead. The company generates roughly $8.07/share of free cash flow, while Nvidia delivers $5.21/share.
To sum up, Nvidia and Broadcom are both fantastic companies. Indeed, both rank among the top 10 largest companies in America, and given their fantastic fundamentals, it's obvious why. Nonetheless, if I were forced to choose between the two, I would select Nvidia. Its eye-popping revenue growth and superb margins give it a slight edge over Broadcom, despite the latter's higher free cash flow per share.

In its most recent quarter (the three months ending on July 26, 2026), Nvidia reported an astounding 106% year-over-year revenue growth.

Another factor to consider is profitability. Here again, Nvidia wins the head-to-head matchup. Nvidia's operating margin stands at 65%, a rate it has roughly maintained for the last two years. Broadcom, on the other hand, has an operating margin of around 49%, up from a two-year low of 30%.

One final factor to weigh is free cash flow. To compare apples to apples, let's look at free cash flow per share. On this basis, Broadcom has a lead. The company generates roughly $8.07/share of free cash flow, while Nvidia delivers $5.21/share.

To sum up, Nvidia and Broadcom are both fantastic companies. Indeed, both rank among the top 10 largest companies in America, and given their fantastic fundamentals, it's obvious why. Nonetheless, if I were forced to choose between the two, I would select Nvidia. Its eye-popping revenue growth and superb margins give it a slight edge over Broadcom, despite the latter's higher free cash flow per share.

articles.article_title: Broadcom vs. Qualcomm: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Broadcom's net margin towers at 36%, but customer concentration and a hefty SBC load cloud the picture; Qualcomm trades at half the valuation despite handset headwinds.
articles.content:
- AVGO -0.13%

- QCOM +0.55%

- 005930.KS -1.47%

- AAPL +2.74%

Semiconductor demand remains red-hot as artificial intelligence transforms the global economy. Choosing between Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) requires understanding which giant is better positioned for the next era of growth.

Broadcom focuses on high-end networking and infrastructure software, while Qualcomm leads the charge in wireless connectivity and mobile processing. Both companies are now racing to capture massive spending in the AI space, making them frequent rivals for investor attention. We will examine their financials and risks to see which represents the better value today.

The case for Broadcom

Broadcom sells semiconductor solutions and infrastructure software to data centers, telecom, and industrial markets. In its latest annual report, filed for fiscal year 2025, the company highlighted major agreements with Samsung and Apple . Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as its top five end customers account for roughly 40% of net revenue.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $63.9 billion, representing growth of approximately 23.9% compared to the previous year. This surge helped drive net income to roughly $23.1 billion, a significant jump from the $5.9 billion reported in 2024. The net margin, which measures how much profit a company keeps from every dollar of sales, reached a healthy 36.2%.

As of its November 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is roughly 1.7x, while the debt-to-equity ratio, which compares total debt to shareholder equity, is approximately 0.8x. Broadcom generated nearly $26.9 billion in free cash flow, which is the cash remaining after paying for operations and equipment. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 27.5% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back to cash flow.

The case for Qualcomm

Qualcomm develops foundational wireless and computing technologies, according to its latest annual report for fiscal year 2025, primarily for handsets, automotive, and IoT markets. The company is actively diversifying, recently securing a multi-year partnership with Amazon to provide custom chips for AWS data centers. It still relies on concentrated revenue from major smartphone manufacturers like Samsung and Xiaomi.

For FY 2025, revenue reached roughly $44.3 billion, representing approximately 13.7% growth over the prior year. Net income for the period was close to $5.5 billion, resulting in a net margin of nearly 12.5%. While revenue grew, the net margin was lower than the 26% seen in FY 2024, partly due to shifts in the product mix among chip companies.

As of its September 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 2.8x, and the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.8x. Qualcomm generated nearly $12.8 billion in free cash flow, representing the money left over after the company covers its operating expenses and capital investments. Both companies maintain similar debt levels relative to their equity, providing a stable foundation for future research and development.

Risk profile comparison

Broadcom faces high customer concentration, with a small group of end users and distributors accounting for nearly 48% of its revenue. The company is also vulnerable to cyclicality in the chip market and to geopolitical tensions surrounding manufacturing in Taiwan. Additionally, integrating large acquisitions such as VMware presents operational and regulatory challenges that could affect future profitability.

Qualcomm is highly exposed to the handset market, where major customers are increasingly developing their own internal chips. The business also faces pressure from rivals like Nvidia and NXP Semiconductors in the growing AI and automotive segments. Finally, ongoing legal disputes regarding its patent licensing model could threaten the company's high-margin royalty revenue.

Valuation comparison

Qualcomm is cheaper than Broadcom based on its Forward P/E (future earnings estimates) and its P/S ratio (sales over the past twelve months).

Metric

Broadcom

QUALCOMM

Forward P/E

29.8x

18.3x

P/S ratio

18.6x

4.6x

Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?

Although both chip stocks produce hardware that drives AI, I have to lean toward Broadcom in this case.

Admittedly, Qualcomm is a bargain at current valuations, and landing the AWS contract to develop custom chips for data centers is a significant milestone in its transformation into a more diversified chip company.

Unfortunately, its transformation places it in parts of the chip industry where it is merely another player rather than a leader. Moreover, the handset segment still accounts for the majority of its revenue, and losing Apple as a customer will probably take time to replace.

In contrast, Broadcom's custom silicon has driven rapid growth in recent quarters, allowing it to grow at a faster pace over the last five years. Furthermore, its infrastructure software business provides opportunities for combined hardware and software offerings and can soften the blow should the chip industry face a down cycle.

Hence, while Qualcomm is not going anywhere and could build a niche in certain types of AI chips, Broadcom likely holds more potential for faster growth despite its higher valuation.

articles.content:
Miller Named Wetzel County Schools Technology Director
To describe the Wetzel County Technology department is a bit of a hard task. What was a technology department fifty years ago, would have been someone replacing a typewriter ribbon or replacing a roll of paper in a mechanical calculator. Punch the keys to input numbers, pulled the arm to compute, and out popped a strip of paper with the answer.
Perhaps you may even remember Mr. Knight’s computer programming class. Students worked with bread boards, inserting jumper wires. Today we would call those wiring patterns, code.
We have evolved from Fred Flintstone technology into a world where the phrase, technology refers to the unseen trillions of electronic bits traveling through fiber optics to accomplish most any task we ask. In fact, if you listen to the TV news, that data is becoming intelligent, AI.
At the head of this new world in Wetzel County, Technology Director Melonie Miller has stepped into the exciting world that is at the heart of every student’s education. Mrs. Miller was offered the position and she is excited to have the opportunity to lead the county in this area.
“I am excited to take on this new challenge, and expand my understanding of this technology. My past work in education has been in the schools and having direct interactions with students and teachers. I loved that experience, and will miss that world. But opportunities don’t come along often, and I am eager to take this opportunity to grow my knowledge of this fascinating world. I look forward to working with my new colleagues who have a wealth of knowledge, and are eager to share it with me,” stated Mrs. Miller.
That technology requires individuals with skills that can understand all those flashing lights and bits inside the processors. In fact, the technicians who understand this new way of life are special individuals. Some would call them Geeks, others say they are nerds. But either one of those references is a great injustice to those individuals whose days are filled by the soft glow from a computer screen in a slightly dimmed room.
Wetzel County has a new center of technology in the world of the county’s 2,500 computers. In this world, every student has a laptop or iPad computer. Each is programmed with the contents that once filled old paper study books. With the touch of a key, students can take a test, complete it and push another key and it instantly arrives on the teacher’s computer. The system can grade it, or the teacher. This allows the teacher more time for class preparations and any of a hundred other tasks that fill their day. The system gives them the choice.
The Wetzel County Schools Technology Department is now enjoying increased efficiency and productivity after moving into its new home. That move took place mid-June when the spring semester ended. With the need for every day monitoring and working with programs during the summer months, it freed up time to organize and prepare to move into the new home. The move marked the completion of months of planning, and collaboration between the county’s maintenance department, and the tech dept staff.
The new work place was thoughtfully designed and constructed with the dedicated effort of the maintenance department under the scrutiny of Jamie Doty. Inside the tech department are lead Technology Specialist Josh Weekly, Technology Support Specialist Ed Davis, and James Froehlich. Their expertise and input made it possible to create a new work area that fit their daily operational needs.
At the heart of the Tech Department, are those individuals whose dedication keeps the systems running smoothly throughout the district while supporting teachers and students. Tech Integration specialists Holly Cain, Heather Hale, and Kandi Loy-Kay work closely with educators to enhance classroom instructions while the support specialist ensures devices, networks, and systems remain operational across the county.
While a few finishing touches remain to be completed, which includes the installation of new windows by the maintenance department, the new facility is already providing a functional and organized environment that supports the team’s work.
The new location reflects Wetzel County’s Schools commitment to providing staff with resources and workspace needed to efficiently serve students, teachers, and schools across Wetzel County.

articles.title: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss
articles.description: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss The Guardian
articles.description_html: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss  The Guardian
articles.article_title: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss
articles.heading: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss
articles.summary: Andrew Bailey’s comments come as fears grow that rogue models could take financial system hostage
articles.content:
The governor of the Bank of England has said authorities must retain the “right to intervene” in the AI industry amid growing fears that rogue models could take the financial system hostage.
Andrew Bailey said the risks posed by the rapid advancement of frontier AI models – a number of which have gone rogue in recent months – were “real and increasingly significant” and reduced the ability of society to supervise and intervene when things went wrong.
That had implications for financial stability, with the new technology having increased the “scale and sophistication of cyber threats to the financial system”. That could threaten daily card payment, bank transactions, and stock and bond trading across financial markets, he said.
The comments came as the Bank’s financial policy committee (FPC) warned that the growing mountain of AI debt was increasing financial stability risks.
The potential benefits of AI “are immense”, Bailey said but he added that authorities needed to be ready to step in.
In an inaugural opinion piece penned for the Bank of England’s Insight series, he said: “If we are to realise those benefits safely, we must answer one critical question. Should society retain the ability to intervene, to establish the boundaries within which these systems operate and to revise those boundaries as the technology evolves? To my mind the answer is unequivocally yes.”
However, the governor stopped short of calling for a regulatory clampdown. “Regulation is not, in my view, the right place to start. In the excitement surrounding AI development, there is a risk that we move too quickly to debates about regulatory architecture before establishing where the failure exists in the first place.”
Instead, he said a “sensible starting point” would be rigorous testing of new models, to understanding the behaviour of increasingly complex systems, in order to figure out “credible points” where authorities could intervene.
Warning on the ballooning AI debt pile, the FPC said large players in the sector have taken on $450bn (£339bn) worth of debt between January and September this year, already overtaking the $333bn worth of gilts due to be issued by the UK government for the whole of 2026.
That has tied investors – including hedge funds, asset managers and private credit firms – to AI companies’ fortunes at a time when those tech businesses have yet to turn a profit.
“The rapid increase in artificial intelligence-related debt issuance broadens the exposure of capital markets to development in AI,” minutes of the recent FPC meeting on 25 September said.
“The committee underscores the importance of timely and careful management of these intensifying, interconnected risks.”

articles.title: “We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer
articles.description: “We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer MIT Technology Review
articles.description_html: “We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer  MIT Technology Review
articles.article_title: “We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer
articles.heading: “We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer
articles.summary: Mark Chen on what the firm is doing to make its models safe, how a slowdown would work, and why the world is better off with OpenAI in it.
articles.content:
“We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer
Mark Chen on what the firm is doing to make its models safe, how a slowdown would work, and why the world is better off with OpenAI in it.
Two months after the bombshell news that a swarm of its agents had broken their containment and hacked into the computers of the AI company Hugging Face, OpenAI is still putting out fires. A steady drip of disclosures about other hacks in the weeks since has kept OpenAI in the spotlight and raised serious questions about the safety of its technology.
Last week brought news of another hack, this time into Australia’s national health-care system. The Australian government says that OpenAI did not notify it of the breach until 84 days after it happened.
But OpenAI insists it is not on the back foot. “I do kind of reject the premise that OpenAI is a company with visible impacts in the world and therefore OpenAI is not training safe and aligned models,” says Mark Chen, the company’s chief research officer.
Chen oversees OpenAI’s research teams. The recent agent hacks were accidents that happened during the testing of experimental models on his watch. In a lot of ways, the buck stops with him.
I sat down with Chen in London last Friday to talk about the fallout from the hacks, what his company is doing about it, and why he thinks things are not as bad as they seem.
Later that same day, OpenAI put out a report detailing yet another incident—the first since the company says it took measures to prevent them—in which its agents once again broke out and accessed the public internet when they were not meant to.
Over the weekend, OpenAI announced that it had paused the training of its latest models. A company spokesperson says: “We will resume only when we’re confident we have additional safeguards and alignments in place. We are working on these now. This is not the first time we’ve paused to take such measures, nor do we expect it to be the last as AI capabilities continue to advance.” OpenAI also says that it is now reviewing logs of agent activity dating back to January 2026 to understand what happened in these hacks.
The way Chen sees it, the Hugging Face incident triggered a welcome course correction for the industry. And he wants you to know that OpenAI is setting an example he hopes other companies will follow. “If you disappeared OpenAI, that would be bad for the world,” he says.
Out of control
Chen claims that the drumbeat of new cases in which OpenAI has lost control of its models reflects a deliberate choice on the company’s part.
“When it comes to the broader sphere of effects of the Hugging Face incident, this is something that we have been aware of and we’re figuring out the process of disclosure,” he says. “We want to make sure we do in-depth investigations before we just put details out there in the open.”
The trouble with this approach is that it gives the impression OpenAI has an ongoing problem that it is failing to fix.
But Chen insists that OpenAI is on it. He says the multiple cases (that we know of so far) in which his company’s agents broke containment and behaved in unexpected and undesirable ways were all part of the same cluster of activity in May and June that led to the Hugging Face hack. In short, you can blame the same few models running under the same flawed testing procedures—models and procedures that OpenAI has since dropped, Chen says.
“It’s not like, you know, Hugging Face happened and we patched that and then something else happened and we patched that,” he adds. “We’re just kind of making sure that we responsibly disclose the full waterfall of what happened.”
At least that was the case before Friday’s announcement that OpenAI’s agents had been caught accessing the internet on September 20, weeks after the company claims to have set up new safeguards. In its defense, OpenAI says the activity was flagged 15 minutes after it started (it took the company more than a week to notice the Hugging Face hack) and that this shows the new systems it has put in place to spot such activity are working.
What’s changed
I want to understand what’s changed inside OpenAI in the aftermath of this summer’s hacks that makes Chen confident his team is now back in control.
“Hugging Face felt like a very serious thing,” he says. “There are so many novel behaviors right there. There were multiple agents collaborating on a message board; they found their way out of OpenAI’s infrastructure. We’ve taken it very seriously. We don’t want this kind of thing to ever happen again.”
The realization for OpenAI, says Chen, was that models need to be watched while they are still being trained, not only once they are deployed: “From that moment on, we have treated the process of training as something that’s not secure,” he says.
OpenAI, like other top AI firms, has systems in place to monitor the behavior of its models. It uses specialized LLMs to monitor its consumer models, keeping tabs on their chains of thought—the scratchpads they use to plan ahead and note down partial results. In theory, if a watcher LLM spots signs of undesirable activity in a model’s chain of thought, it will get flagged to a human.
Typically, models were monitored in this way only once they were deployed. Chen says that OpenAI has now started monitoring all its training runs as well.
“We didn’t have the monitors on in training before. It wasn’t industry practice,” he says. “Now every single thing is put through monitors.” Human reviewers can then assess whether or not flagged agents are behaving as they should: “It’s all triage.”
Chen says that in the last couple of months OpenAI has shifted between 5% and 10% of its vast computing resources away from training new models and toward safety work, especially monitoring.
OpenAI has also fixed some of the processes within the organization itself, establishing clearer lines of communication and quicker handoffs between its research and security teams, he says.
All of which sounds sensible. But given how hard OpenAI sells the capabilities of its technology, why weren’t these systems and procedures in place already? Why did the company not see the hacks coming?
“Even just three or four months ago, when we looked at the behavior of these agents during training, the things that were happening were kind of amusing,” says Chen. “For instance, an agent might, you know, reach out to someone on Slack for help with a task.”
The signs were there, but they were misread. Cute behavior—like asking someone for help—that was rewarded during training reinforced a tendency to seek out shortcuts, a type of behavior that became far more consequential down the line. “I think the big update for us was how quickly that kind of behavior can lead to an impact with a footprint as big as the Hugging Face incident,” says Chen.
According to new reporting by the New York Times yesterday, OpenAI employees warned executives, including the firm’s president, Greg Brockman, months before the Hugging Face hack that its models were not being monitored properly during training.
An OpenAI spokesperson says: “As frontier models have become more capable, we continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster. We know we have more work to do, and we’ve recently slowed development and held back models that don’t meet our safety bar. We continue to make significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, and use real-time monitoring to respond faster to misaligned behavior.”
Race vs. pace
OpenAI’s rivals have taken note. Spurred by the fallout from the incident, the major AI labs—including Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and SpaceXAI—have all called for the pace of development to slow down. But how does that square with fierce international competition and trillion-dollar IPOs?
“We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot and take ourselves far off the frontier—that’s just a horrible strategy,” he says. “I think it’s really about setting a norm. The more that we can set that norm, it’ll be safer for the industry as a whole.”
Coordination across US companies will be hard enough. Establishing global norms is harder still, especially given concerns around AI’s impact on national security. If a global race continues, what then? And what about open-source models from outfits beyond the reach of US regulations?
Chen dropped his upbeat manner for the first time in our conversation: “I do think we have to prepare for a world where, say, six months to a year out, we have open-source models with the capability of the agents behind the Hugging Face incident, but which are deliberately misaligned to go attack infrastructure or create harm in the world.”
What that world needs most, says Chen, is OpenAI. “If you entertain for a moment that OpenAI is one of the companies that cares most about alignment—and I believe this to be true; it can be debated, but I really do think it’s true—then if you disappear OpenAI, that would be bad for the world.”
Existential risks
What about the more extreme claims made by some of his Silicon Valley peers that AI could kill us all—and that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are not doing enough to stop it?
“Researchers are a heterogeneous group of people, you know, with beliefs across the spectrum,” he says.
“Personally, I don’t think we have to be resigned to there being some probability that we’re all going to be existentially at risk. We have agency over this. We are not going to go and deploy models if they truly have that kind of probability of causing a risk to humanity. At a frontier lab, you have the ability to work on alignment to the point that you do not feel like you’re incurring more than epsilon risk to the world in deploying your models.”
(In discussions about levels of risk, the Greek letter epsilon is often used as a mathematical placeholder for an acceptable threshold. Chen doesn’t say what his epsilon would be.)
When tech leaders are asked to justify the downsides of AI, their go-to talking point is that the upsides—from helping cure diseases to coming up with cleaner sources of energy—far outweigh the immediate costs. Short-term pains, long-term gains.
But as the downsides pile up, does that case get harder to make? Is there a point where Chen would feel less as if he’s building something amazing and more as if he’s simply minimizing harm—fighting fires rather than forging a better future?
The capabilities of these models are already evident, he says: “It is time to start delivering the benefits of AI to humanity. It’s time to start working on deep problems in drug discovery, on materials, on scientific applications that will actually change people’s lives.”
“Yes, there is a bit of risk that we are incurring, but we see all these benefits,” he adds. “I think we should make that less of an abstract thing. If people can really see the upside, I think they’ll believe in it.”

articles.title: EXEED to Unveil Nearly 20 Green Technology and Ecosystem Innovations at 2026 International User Summit
articles.description: EXEED to Unveil Nearly 20 Green Technology and Ecosystem Innovations at 2026 International User Summit TMX Newsfile
articles.description_html: EXEED to Unveil Nearly 20 Green Technology and Ecosystem Innovations at 2026 International User Summit  TMX Newsfile
articles.article_title: EXEED to Unveil Nearly 20 Green Technology and Ecosystem Innovations at 2026 International User Summit
articles.heading: EXEED to Unveil Nearly 20 Green Technology and Ecosystem Innovations at 2026 International User Summit
articles.summary: Wuhu, Anhui, China--(Newsfile Corp. - September 30, 2026) - EXEED will unveil nearly 20 green technology and cross-industry ecosystem innovations...
articles.content:
Wuhu, Anhui, China--(Newsfile Corp. - September 30, 2026) - EXEED will unveil nearly 20 green technology and cross-industry ecosystem innovations during the 2026 EXEED International User Summit, taking place from October 18 to 24 in China.
The planned showcases will focus on new energy mobility, intelligent technology applications and ecosystem experiences, giving users, media and industry partners a closer look at EXEED's latest developments across electrification, AI and future mobility scenarios.
Centered on ecosystem, technology and convergence, this year's Summit will feature product, technology and interactive demonstrations designed to show how EXEED is connecting vehicles with intelligent services and broader mobility experiences.
To view an enhanced version of this graphic, please visit:
https://images.newsfilecorp.com/files/8814/316508_d111d7ee84179b88_001full.jpg
Green Technology Expands Across New Energy Mobility
EXEED continues to expand its lineup of plug-in hybrid, range-extended and pure electric vehicles, providing different new energy mobility options for customers across global markets.
At the Summit, the company will present new energy technologies and application scenarios designed to demonstrate how improvements in energy efficiency and electrification can contribute to lower-carbon mobility.
The demonstrations will form part of EXEED's wider presentation of how new energy technologies can support the development of more efficient and sustainable mobility experiences.
Rather than focusing only on individual vehicle technologies, the Summit will also show how electrified mobility can connect with intelligent systems and other parts of the user's daily environment.
Intelligent Technology Extends Beyond the Vehicle
AI will form another major part of the Summit program.
More than 3,000 units of AiMOGA, EXEED's embodied AI humanoid robot, have been delivered across more than 60 countries and regions, covering over 100 use cases.

articles.article_title: Big Four Firms Bet on AI’s Promise as Technology Threats Escalate
articles.heading: Big Four Firms Bet on AI’s Promise as Technology Threats Escalate
articles.summary: The Big Four accounting and advisory firms are committing to their AI strategies even as the technology’s top developers sound the alarm on the potential safety risks.
articles.content:
The Big Four accounting and advisory firms are committing to their AI strategies even as the technology’s top developers sound the alarm on the potential safety risks.
Rather than back away from the transformational technology, the industry’s dominant firms are approaching it not only as an opportunity to automate the manual work of accountants but to pitch new AI-driven products and services to their clients — including governance. Industry watchers say the Big Four, as early AI adopters, are well positioned to coach clients as they build strategies and defenses for the fast-developing technology.
“You do not slow innovation, rather you proceed responsibly,” Paul Griggs, the CEO of PwC’s US arm, told Bloomberg Television earlier this month.
A week later,
Meanwhile,
The Big Four — which also includes
Alliances with top AI labs including
Leaders of both tech companies have called to slow development of advanced models, citing the need for safety standards to counter security and economic risks. Warnings that the technology soon could evade human control reached the UN National Security Council last week and overshadowed a summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
On Monday, OpenAI shelved the release of its latest model to improve safeguards following a series of rogue hacking incidents. The company has previously said its systems improperly accessed US and Australian government websites.
Businesses stand to lose millions or billions if AI escapes controls. Unintended prompts could manufacture accounting entries or hack into systems they weren’t designed to access.
Despite those risks, the Big Four should continue to embrace the technology, industry watchers said.
“They need to lead from the front in the industry and demonstrate responsible use of AI,” said John McGowan, a Big Four veteran and the founder and CEO of tax workflow platform HubSync.
Governance Amplified
Innovation and risk management are needed in equal parts to squeeze the most value out of AI investments and trust the results, said Jennifer Kosar, AI assurance leader at the US affiliate of PwC, also known as
“AI absolutely remains central to our strategy,” Kosar said. “But that’s backed by the notion that governance enables us to move with that confidence.”
Common safeguards include matching the right tech to the task and baking in controls from the beginning. That includes spelling out ownership, monitoring the technology, and determining when humans should intervene, Kosar said.
EY declined to comment and Deloitte did not respond to questions about whether they would alter their AI strategy in response to the latest safety warnings.
Helping clients “navigate what’s next safely and securely” is among the goals of KPMG’s new technology and innovation group, US CEO Tim Walsh said in a Sept. 22 LinkedIn post. “The pace of change isn’t slowing down, and neither are we.”
Charged with functioning like a start-up, the group aims to co-create products with clients and AI labs including Google and
Testing, monitoring, and independent certification are some of the backstops KPMG has in place to deliver reliable AI. The firm is focused on helping its client build similar controls for “enterprise AI that’s available today,” KPMG said.
EY warned in a report this month that governance systems aren’t keeping pace with the rapid rollout of AI. A third of the AI leaders surveyed reported a “materially negative” AI incident or failure, with a range of impacts including to finances, operations, and reputations.
Field-testing governance for AI systems is among the services industry leaders say is ripe for growth. Mid-tier firm Grant Thornton now features AI validation and compliance checks among its reconfigured suite of assurance work.
Keeping Up With Advances
Firms are leaning on established safeguards to build a web of guardrails and checks to ensure AI-driven software and data systems operate as intended and deliver consistent results.
They and their clients should be re-evaluating those protocols as AI development introduces new risks and newer models come online, said Jeffrey Saviano, a senior lecturer at MIT Sloan School of Management and a retired EY partner.
The Big Four firms are in the unique position to show their clients, the broader market, and even regulators that they are willing to ask tough questions and take a cautious approach to adopting the technology, said Gia Chevis, associate department chair of accounting and business law at Baylor University.
“A role that the big accounting firms can play is just helping everybody slow down a little and reality-check a little bit to make sure we’re not getting ahead of ourselves,” Chevis said.
Despite the potential perils, future AI models might produce fewer mistakes and could better mirror human judgment. In the meantime, AI is helping professionals quantify the toll of shifting US tariff policies and it’s reducing manual data-crunching for auditors — significant advancements for the data-heavy accounting industry.
The firms want to be in a position to take advantage of those and future advancements, said Ashley Davis, an associate professor of management information systems and accounting at the University of Oklahoma.
“They see this promise of AI and are willing to take the hit right now and be on the frontier,” Davis said.

articles.article_title: Omdia identifies four forces set to reshape technology in 2027
articles.heading: Omdia identifies four forces set to reshape technology in 2027
articles.summary: As AI spending rises and supply chain disruptions continue, technology companies are working to translate rapid investment into lasting value through stronger economic and operational results. Omdia examines this shift through four key forces shaping 2027: AI monetization, supply chain resilience, digital sovereignty, and the growing reach of physical AI.
articles.content:
AI monetization, persistent supply chain disruption, digital sovereignty and Physical AI emerge as four forces shaping the next phase of technology competition
LONDON, September 30, 2026: In 2027, the technology industry will face a new test: turning years of rapid investment and innovation into sustainable value. According to Omdia, the focus is shifting from what technology can do to what it can deliver – economically, operationally and competitively.
Drawing on research and expertise from across the organization, Omdia has identified four forces shaping 2027: AI: Rebalancing from Investment to Monetization; Supply Chain: Crisis is the “New Normal”; Digital Sovereignty: Independence Comes at a Cost; and Physical AI: Intelligence Escapes the Screen.
Together, these forces point to a shift in which AI must increasingly demonstrate real returns, businesses must compete through persistent supply disruption, organizations must weigh greater technological control against its costs, and intelligence moves beyond software and screens into the physical world.
AI: Rebalancing from Investment to Monetization
The AI technology arms race will continue, but the measure of success is changing. With 59% of organizations expecting their AI budgets to increase by 10% or more in 2027, pressure to demonstrate tangible returns will intensify. Enterprises will increasingly judge AI investments by ROI and productivity gains rather than technical superiority alone. Across infrastructure, software, services and devices, attention will shift to where AI creates value, how that value is captured and which business models can turn adoption into sustainable returns.
Supply Chain: Crisis is the “New Normal”
Technology companies can no longer assume disruption will end and supply chains will return to normal. AI infrastructure demand, component constraints, geopolitical pressures, energy requirements and macroeconomic uncertainty are combining to create persistent volatility. Already hardware delays are impacting 60% of PC channel partners, highlighting the operational pressures businesses continue to face.
Navigating these pressures will increasingly become a measure of competitive strength. Companies that build resilience into their operations will be better placed to turn disruption into advantage, while less agile competitors risk losing ground.
Digital Sovereignty: Independence Comes at a Cost
The question is increasingly shifting from whether organizations need greater digital sovereignty to how much control they actually need – and what they are prepared to pay for. More than 100 countries are now pursuing digital sovereignty initiatives, reflecting the growing importance of control over data, infrastructure, AI and digital supply chains.
But complete technological independence will rarely be practical or necessary. Organizations will instead need to determine what they must control, where partnerships remain essential and where greater sovereignty creates enough business value to justify the additional cost and complexity.
Physical AI: Intelligence Escapes the Screen
AI’s move beyond software and screens and into the physical world is accelerating. Advances in AI, edge computing, sensors and connected hardware are creating intelligent systems capable of perceiving, learning and responding to their surroundings. Global humanoid robot shipments alone are expected to exceed 700,000 units by 2030, reflecting the growing investment and momentum behind physical AI.
The opportunity extends far beyond humanoid robots, spanning vehicles, buildings, energy infrastructure, workplaces and connected consumer environments. As intelligence becomes embedded in the physical world, organizations will also face new questions around governance, safety, liability, integration and trust.
Commenting on the launch of Omdia’s Forces Shaping 2027, Omdia Chief Research Officer Evan Kirchheimer said: “The defining technology story of 2027 will not simply be what comes next, but what happens as the investment and innovation of recent years meets economic and operational reality.
“AI needs to demonstrate returns. Supply chain disruption needs to be planned for rather than waited out. The perceived imperative of digital sovereignty brings difficult choices around cost and access. And as AI moves into the physical world, businesses face an entirely new set of opportunities and responsibilities.
“What makes these forces particularly significant is how closely they are becoming connected. Decisions made in one area increasingly have consequences elsewhere, making it more important than ever for businesses to understand the wider technology landscape when deciding where to invest and compete.”
The Forces Shaping 2027 program brings together Omdia research from across the technology ecosystem to identify and track the four forces expected to shape the year ahead. Launching with an e-book exploring each force and the research underpinning it, Omdia will continue to track how these forces evolve through its research and analysis throughout 2027, with AI-enabled access making it easier for clients to explore and navigate Omdia’s research.

With 59% of organizations expecting their AI budgets to increase by 10% or more in 2027, pressure to demonstrate tangible returns will intensify. Enterprises will increasingly judge AI investments by ROI and productivity gains rather than technical superiority alone. Across infrastructure, software, services and devices, attention will shift to where AI creates value, how that value is captured and which business models can turn adoption into sustainable returns.

Supply Chain: Crisis is the "New Normal"

Technology companies can no longer assume disruption will end and supply chains will return to normal. AI infrastructure demand, component constraints, geopolitical pressures, energy requirements and macroeconomic uncertainty are combining to create persistent volatility. Already hardware delays are impacting 60% of PC channel partners, highlighting the operational pressures businesses continue to face.

Navigating these pressures will increasingly become a measure of competitive strength. Companies that build resilience into their operations will be better placed to turn disruption into advantage, while less agile competitors risk losing ground.

Digital Sovereignty: Independence Comes at a Cost

The question is increasingly shifting from whether organizations need greater digital sovereignty to how much control they actually need – and what they are prepared to pay for. More than 100 countries are now pursuing digital sovereignty initiatives, reflecting the growing importance of control over data, infrastructure, AI and digital supply chains.

But complete technological independence will rarely be practical or necessary. Organizations will instead need to determine what they must control, where partnerships remain essential and where greater sovereignty creates enough business value to justify the additional cost and complexity.

Physical AI: Intelligence Escapes the Screen

AI's move beyond software and screens and into the physical world is accelerating. Advances in AI, edge computing, sensors and connected hardware are creating intelligent systems capable of perceiving, learning and responding to their surroundings. Global humanoid robot shipments alone are expected to exceed 700,000 units by 2030, reflecting the growing investment and momentum behind physical AI.

The opportunity extends far beyond humanoid robots, spanning vehicles, buildings, energy infrastructure, workplaces and connected consumer environments. As intelligence becomes embedded in the physical world, organizations will also face new questions around governance, safety, liability, integration and trust.

Commenting on the launch of Omdia's Forces Shaping 2027, Omdia Chief Research Officer Evan Kirchheimer said: "The defining technology story of 2027 will not simply be what comes next, but what happens as the investment and innovation of recent years meets economic and operational reality.

"AI needs to demonstrate returns. Supply chain disruption needs to be planned for rather than waited out. The perceived imperative of digital sovereignty brings difficult choices around cost and access. And as AI moves into the physical world, businesses face an entirely new set of opportunities and responsibilities.

"What makes these forces particularly significant is how closely they are becoming connected. Decisions made in one area increasingly have consequences elsewhere, making it more important than ever for businesses to understand the wider technology landscape when deciding where to invest and compete."

The Forces Shaping 2027 program brings together Omdia research from across the technology ecosystem to identify and track the four forces expected to shape the year ahead. Launching with an e-book exploring each force and the research underpinning it, Omdia will continue to track how these forces evolve through its research and analysis throughout 2027, with AI-enabled access making it easier for clients to explore and navigate Omdia's research.

articles.content:
