articles.article_title: OpenAI unveils AI assistant 'dots' while safety worries delay new model
articles.heading: OpenAI unveils AI assistant 'dots' while safety worries delay new model
articles.summary: Sam Altman spoke in San Francisco during OpenAI’s annual event for tech developers.
articles.content:
OpenAI unveils AI assistant 'dots' while safety worries delay new model
OpenAI on Tuesday unveiled "dots," a new artificial intelligence (AI) assistant they say can proactively carry out tasks on a user's behalf.
At its annual developer day in San Francisco, chief executive Sam Altman referred to "dots" as "remarkably capable, always-on agents that can handle really anything you can think of."
At the same time, OpenAI president Greg Brockman and other tech leaders held a meeting with President Donald Trump as the firm faces intense scrutiny after internal tests of its AI agents revealed unexpected and occasionally harmful actions.
Dots, however, were pitched as brightly coloured cute cartoons meant to function as digital assistants for people with busy lives.
The dots, Altman said, "can handle really anything you can think of."
A glossy video was shown during the event, with people speaking to and naming animated versions of their "dots," then giving them various tasks, like building a website and booking afterschool activities for their children.
Speaking about "my dot," Altman almost entirely eschewed referring to the tool as an agent, which has been in common use for years. AI agents are essentially AI chatbots that are programmed to operate somewhat autonomously.
"You just give your dot a responsibility... and your dots will just get to work and keep working," Altman added.
OpenAI's event on Tuesday took place as President Donald Trump held a White House lunch with tech leaders and House Speaker Mike Johnson.
Trump repeated his belief that AI companies should regulate themselves.
He also said they had discussed creating a ten person committee to oversee the sector, adding there would be "tremendous self-policing"
Some researchers and company heads have called for a slowdown in AI development as more instances of breaches by AI firms' models become public.
"We need to navigate the centrist path," Altman told the BBC during a question and answer session with reporters on Tuesday.
"I am hopeful that the industry will figure out a more sensible, more pragmatic stance than has been exhibited by some of the members of our industry," he added, declining to specify particular company names or leaders.
The day prior to OpenAI's event, the company said it was delaying the launch of its latest model due to certain safety issues that showed up during internal testing.
Since July, the company has been dealing with a series of issues with its AI agents acting improperly. It has faced unprompted hacking into the AI platform Hugging Face, posting to third-party websites images that AI agents took from ChatGPT user chats, and accessing non-public information maintained by the Australian government.
OpenAI, as well as rival AI firm Anthropic, previously delayed public release of certain AI models due to potential risks, mostly pertaining to cybersecurity or hacking concerns.
On Tuesday, Altman raised the possibility of "a legitimate loss of control" to an AI system, adding "and you can imagine where we have too much concentration of power in a small number of companies or one company or person or country or whatever".
Both OpenAI and Anthropic are expect to be listed on the public stock market in the coming months. Anthropic likely will do so this year, while OpenAI is poised for 2027.
Altman said he was eager for his company to sell shares in public markets.
"I think it's bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public," Altman told reporters. "I want people to be able to part in the upside of AI."
Both companies have lately been clear that they believe AI poses a genuine risk on a large scale, be it to public infrastructure or public safety.
Speaking last week to the UN, Altman pleaded for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained.
Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, told the UN that if the speeding development of AI was not properly managed and overseen, future versions of the technology "could be a risk to humanity as a whole."

articles.description: Trump says top tech firms have signed accord to ‘self-police’ AI development Spectrum News
articles.description_html: Trump says top tech firms have signed accord to ‘self-police’ AI development  Spectrum News
articles.article_title: Trump says top tech firms have signed accord to ‘self-police’ AI development
articles.heading: Trump says top tech firms have signed accord to ‘self-police’ AI development
articles.summary: The president and a large group of leaders of AI firms signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews of the technology
articles.content:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Tuesday said that he and a large group of leaders of artificial intelligence companies had signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews of the technology during a meeting at the White House.
“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters outside the West Wing.
The announcement followed an extensive meeting between Trump and numerous leading executives from top tech firms that are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI infrastructure, including data centers in communities across the country that have sparked grassroots, bipartisan opposition. Many of the executives gathered in Washington have called for a slowdown in the development of the technology after several hgh-profile incidents where AI agents have gone rogue.
But earlier Tuesday, Trump promised that the U.S. government wouldn’t limit the development of artificial intelligence or support calls for “guardrails” or other restrictions.
“I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution,” Trump said at the unveiling of an AI chatbot, America.gov, intended to help Americans navigate government services. “We can’t stifle it, and we’re leading by a lot.”
Top AI executives met with Trump at the White House Tuesday, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, Greg Brockman, president of OpenAI, Jeff Bezos, founder of Amazon, and Elon Musk, whose X social media platform includes its own AI model, Grok.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sat to Trump’s right at Tuesday’s White House lunch, according to a seating chart the president posted on Truth Social. Musk sat to Trump’s left. Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also attended.
Trump’s bullishness on AI contrasts with the alarms sounded recently by some AI executives, including Amodei, who earlier this month called for leading firms to slow down their development of the technology. Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also called for allowing safety measures to catch up as companies reported mounting examples of AI agents going rogue.
Other executives, particularly Huang and Zuckerberg, have downplayed the concerns about runaway AI and underscored the responsibility of each company to ensure the safety of their products.
Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and Republican Speaker of the House, Louisiana Rep. Mike Johnson, also attended.
The unveiling of the AI chatbot occurred at a daylong event in Washington during which multiple Trump administration officials celebrated a “Golden Age” fueled by what Trump insists on calling “super intelligence,” rather than artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio highlighted that America.gov could soon be used to apply for a first-time passport fully online, without an in-person visit to a processing center that is currently required.
Speaking to reporters after the lunch with tech CEOs, Trump said there had been widespread agreement on “self-regulation” by the AI developers, “and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that.”
He also said the executives had agreed to assuage the bipartisan opposition to data centers cropping up in local communities across the country, by providing more financial support to local schools or taking steps to reduce energy costs.
“You’re going to see, data centers are going to be very popular,” Trump said. If the opposition continued, Trump suggested, “they’ll be forced to go overseas or other locations.”
Also Tuesday, Altman said in a television interview that the company is increasingly focused on safety. The day before, his company halted the rollout of a new model over safety concerns.
“We are pacing our progress, which includes sometimes not training a model,” he said on CNBC. “We have to do these in a way where we can make very confident safety cases and claims, so that people don’t have a bunch of anxiety.”
For his part, Trump on Tuesday portrayed the race to develop AI as largely a global competition between the United States and China, with the U.S. in the lead. He said there would be a winner and a loser, with no “second place.”
The two countries agreed last week to establish a channel for handling AI-related incidents during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington. But Trump underscored Tuesday that he didn’t want to cooperate too much with China: “I didn’t want to do anything, because we’re leading. Why would I want to do anything?”

articles.description_html: Technology Access Program at Pomona Closes Digital Divide  Pomona College
articles.source: Pomona College in Claremont, California - Pomona College
articles.article_title: Technology Access Program at Pomona Closes Digital Divide | Pomona College in Claremont, California - Pomona College
articles.heading: Technology Access Program at Pomona Closes Digital Divide
articles.summary: The Technology Access Program (TAP), a pilot program created under Pomona’s strategic vision pillar of equity and access, provided MacBook Airs to 247 of the 441 members of the first-year and new transfer classes.
articles.content:
When Olatunmbi Abolarin ’30 was admitted to Pomona, the financial aid package came as a relief to her and her family. But they still had concerns about how to pay for books, a laptop, plane tickets to and from Atlanta, and other expenses.
Cue the Technology Access Program (TAP), a pilot program created under Pomona’s strategic vision pillar of equity and access this fall that provided MacBook Airs to 247 of the 441 members of the first-year and new transfer classes.
“TAP puts reliable technology in students’ hands from day one,” says Joseph Brennan, assistant vice president, information technology finance & operations. “A reliable laptop is now part of the basic academic toolkit.”
All first year and transfer students who received institutional grant aid from Pomona were eligible to receive a laptop, which is theirs to keep after they graduate. The devices came with essential academic software and four years of warranty and technical support—further bridging the digital divide.
“The initiative tries to give students as much of an equitable start to their education here,” says José Rodriguez, vice president and chief information officer.
While Abolarin figured she would have to find a campus job to save up for a computer, applying for jobs, she points out, also requires a computer.
“The laptop has been really, really helpful,” she says. “Sometimes I don’t even realize how helpful it is until I’m doing my work and I think, ‘Wow, this would be so much harder on a phone or on paper.’”
On Move-In Day for new students, several stations in Mudd-Blaisdell residence hall got students set up with their new devices. With more than half of the Class of 2030 receiving laptops, an efficient system had to be put in place to configure and distribute the 13-inch MacBook Airs for each student.
Volunteers from Information Technology Services and other departments came to campus that Saturday morning to help with distribution and set up.
“I was actually in need of a new computer, and the Mac works great,” says Lexi Mathis ’30, who arrived at Pomona from Durham, North Carolina. “It’s going to be used for so many more years, including post grad.”
The three-year pilot program, funded by an anonymous $1.1 million gift, complements the Access to Course Essentials (ACE) program, a new initiative which provides all Pomona students with course materials at no additional cost.
“One of the best surprises we received this summer was that Pomona would provide a new laptop,” says Erika Haub, who traveled from Shoreline, Washington, to drop off her son Elijah Haub ’30. “When all of his course materials were also provided, we were even more relieved.”
“The free course materials that went along with the laptop are super important for me to be here,” adds Elijah Haub.

articles.article_title: Digital Force Technologies Awarded $500M IDIQ Contract from JIATF-401 to Deliver Advanced Counter-UAS Capabilities
articles.heading: Digital Force Technologies Awarded $500M IDIQ Contract from JIATF-401 to Deliver Advanced Counter-UAS Capabilities
articles.summary: SAN DIEGO, Sept.  29, 2026  (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Digital Force Technologies (DFT), a defense technology company specializing in the development and...
articles.content:
Sep. 29, 2026, 04:33 PM




SAN DIEGO, Sept. 29, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Digital Force Technologies (DFT), a defense technology company specializing in the development and manufacturing of Full-Stack Mission Systems, today announced it has been awarded a $500M Indefinite Delivery, Indefinite Quantity (IDIQ) contract by Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF-401) to provide Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems (C-UAS) and Counter-Small Unmanned Aerial Systems (C-sUAS) capabilities in support of the Domestic Shield Program.
Under the IDIQ, DFT will provide its C-UAS family of systems powered by SeraphimOS™ to support Department of War personnel conducting force protection, base defense and counter-UAS operations globally, including Continental United States (CONUS) and Outside Continental United States (OCONUS) requirements.
“This award represents a significant milestone for DFT and reinforces the importance of rapidly delivering adaptable, mission-ready technology to the warfighter,” said Justin MacLaurin, President and CEO of Digital Force Technologies. “The UAS threat is evolving at an extraordinary pace, and defending our forces and critical infrastructure requires systems that can evolve just as quickly. Our SeraphimOS™-powered mission systems bring sensing, decision and action together at the tactical edge, giving operators the flexibility to integrate new sensors, effectors and capabilities as the mission changes.”
DFT Counter-UAS System in Operation
DFT’s SeraphimOS™ is an edge-based software architecture designed to fuse data from multiple sensors, autonomously assess and classify threats, and deliver actionable information to operators in real time. Its open architecture enables integration across a broad ecosystem of sensors, effectors, platforms and third-party systems, allowing DFT to configure mission-specific capabilities without requiring a closed, single-vendor technology stack.
For C-UAS missions, the platform supports the full kill chain from detection, tracking and identification through engagement with kinetic and non-kinetic effects. SeraphimOS™ also enables advanced orchestration of uncrewed systems, supporting coordinated multi-domain sensing and autonomous operations in contested, disconnected and degraded environments.
The award supports JIATF-401’s Domestic Shield initiative, which is focused on accelerating the deployment of layered C-UAS capabilities to protect military installations, critical assets and personnel against rapidly evolving unmanned aerial threats.
“Safeguarding our critical assets against increasingly agile drone threats demands flexible, highly mobile protection that can deploy rapidly where it is needed most,” said U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of Joint Interagency Task Force 401. “By continuing to provide capabilities on the marketplace through a streamlined framework, JIATF-401 is able to cut through red tape and rapidly deliver state-of-the-art counter-UAS solutions into the hands of warfighters.”
About DFT
Digital Force Technologies (DFT) is a San Diego, California-based defense technology company that builds Full-Stack Mission Systems to accelerate and automate the kill chain at the tactical edge. Purpose-built for Force Protection and Counter-UAS applications, DFT's mission-tailored systems enable military operators to detect threats, make decisions, and execute effects at machine speed. Trusted by the U.S. military, DFT has fielded thousands of systems in support of the nation's most critical missions. For more than 25 years, DFT has combined deep operational expertise with advanced technologies to rapidly design, develop, and manufacture mission-ready capabilities that meet the evolving demands of the modern battlefield. For more information, please visit www.digitalforcetech.com.

Media Contact
Glenn Mandel
Firecracker PR for DFT
glenn@firecrackerpr.com
A photo accompanying this announcement is available at https://www.globenewswire.com/NewsRoom/AttachmentNg/02b4d3a6-8cb7-4792-a3d7-fdfa08789f2f

articles.title: Trump gathers with AI leaders and floats ‘self-regulation’ as the way to deal with the technology’s dangers
articles.description: Trump gathers with AI leaders and floats ‘self-regulation’ as the way to deal with the technology’s dangers Yahoo Finance
articles.description_html: Trump gathers with AI leaders and floats ‘self-regulation’ as the way to deal with the technology’s dangers  Yahoo Finance
articles.article_title: Trump gathers with AI leaders and floats ‘self-regulation’ as the way to deal with the technology’s dangers
articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: President Trump gathered top AI leaders in Washington on Tuesday and doubled down on his opposition to any government intervention, suggesting that "self-regulation" may be the answer amid growing concerns about the technology getting out of human control.
articles.content:
- META +3.24%

President Trump gathered top artificial intelligence leaders in Washington on Tuesday and doubled down on his opposition to government intervention, suggesting that "self-regulation" is the answer to growing worries about the technology getting out of human control.

"There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said after meeting with the assembled CEOs. "There was a lot of commonality in this room."

Trump said he and the CEOs signed a "morally binding" accord that wasn't immediately released but that the president said would keep the companies in line through "self-policing and group policing."

Some executives on hand said the so-called Accord on Super Intelligence would include commitments to a combination of technological controls to detect problems with new models, internal risk review efforts, external auditors, and other measures.

Meta ( META ) CEO Mark Zuckerberg called the accord "a start," while others suggested some details still needed to be worked out.

"The mechanism, how we address those risks, is still under discussion," Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) CEO Dario Amodei said. Progress had been made toward both the US winning AI and also winning safely, he said, though he emphasized that the technology still poses "real dangers."

Amodei published an essay earlier this month titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," which set off a fierce debate about the need for a cooperative slowdown in AI capability.

The accord also formally changed the name of the technology in government record-keeping to Super Intelligence.

"We've changed the name officially to SI," Trump said.

The "meeting and luncheon on Super Intelligence," as the White House described the event, took place in the East Room, with Trump even posting the seating chart . The location was the same spot where just a few days ago, many of the same AI leaders gathered for a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Elon Musk of Tesla ( TSLA ), Jensen Huang of Nvidia ( NVDA ), and Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) were all at the head table with Xi last Thursday and again received prominent spots near Trump.

After the meeting, Trump also said he was "very close" to a decision on an AI czar and would announce it in the next three to four days.

Other notable guests included Google ( GOOGL , GOOG ) CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft ( MSFT ) CEO Satya Nadella, OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) president Greg Brockman, Palantir ( PLTR ) CEO Alex Karp, Amazon ( AMZN ) founder Jeff Bezos, and others.

The gathering came as the US continues to digest a raft of alarming new AI disclosures in recent days, such as an Axios report that OpenAI, Anthropic, and security researchers were sifting through thousands of incidents of problematic actions by AI agents.

And in Florida, the attorney general unveiled a new state-level challenge asking a court to halt OpenAI's training of new models unless it puts outside safeguards in place.

But that skepticism didn't change the tenor of the gathering in Washington.

Trump repeatedly brushed off worries about the technology, saying after the meeting that he believes AI will make the world a safer place and that fears about data centers driving up costs were overblown.

He said instead that these new facilities "are going to make communities very happy."

At an event earlier in the day to launch a new government website powered by AI, Trump promised that AI is "going to mostly be put to great use and we'll stop the bad use," through the Department of Justice and FBI.

He added he would "never stifle the growth of technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution."

This story has been updated.

Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.heading: Jackson-Madison County Library awarded $19,762 technology grant
articles.summary: Secretary of State Tre Hargett, Sen. Ed Jackson, Rep. Chris Todd and Rep. Johnny Shaw announced technology grant funding totaling $19,762 for Jackson-Madison County Library.
articles.content:
Jackson-Madison County Library awarded $19,762 technology grant
JACKSON, Tenn. (WBBJ) - Secretary of State Tre Hargett, Sen. Ed Jackson, Rep. Chris Todd and Rep. Johnny Shaw announced technology grant funding totaling $19,762 for Jackson-Madison County Library. The funding will be used for desktop computers.
Officials react to funding
“Thank you to Senator Jackson, Representative Todd, and Representative Shaw for their ongoing commitment to supporting our local libraries,” said Secretary Hargett. “Providing libraries with updated technology allows them to better serve the evolving needs of patrons in communities across Tennessee. I’m grateful for their continued partnership, dedication, and advocacy in strengthening our state’s libraries.”
“This $19,762 technology grant will help Jackson-Madison County Library purchase desktops,” said Sen. Jackson. “These upgrades will give people in Jackson better access to the tools they use for learning, work and staying connected.”

Jackson-Madison County Library awarded $19,762 technology grant

JACKSON, Tenn. (WBBJ) - Secretary of State Tre Hargett, Sen. Ed Jackson, Rep. Chris Todd and Rep. Johnny Shaw announced technology grant funding totaling $19,762 for Jackson-Madison County Library. The funding will be used for desktop computers.

Officials react to funding

“Thank you to Senator Jackson, Representative Todd, and Representative Shaw for their ongoing commitment to supporting our local libraries,” said Secretary Hargett. “Providing libraries with updated technology allows them to better serve the evolving needs of patrons in communities across Tennessee. I’m grateful for their continued partnership, dedication, and advocacy in strengthening our state’s libraries.”

“This $19,762 technology grant will help Jackson-Madison County Library purchase desktops,” said Sen. Jackson. “These upgrades will give people in Jackson better access to the tools they use for learning, work and staying connected.”

Technology grants are administered by the Tennessee State Library & Archives, a division of the Secretary of State’s Office.

“Families in our community rely on the Jackson-Madison County Library for important educational opportunities, technology resources and programs for residents of all ages,” said Rep. Todd. “This funding will help the library serve even more Madison County residents by addressing the growing demand for digital skills.”

“A grant of almost $20,000 is a great boon for the Jackson-Madison County Library,” said Rep. Shaw. “The desktop computers provided by this grant will help bring additional online access and information to the entire region. My thanks to Secretary Hargett and his staff for their help in making this significant gift to the community possible.”

Grant program details

Technology grants are funded through the Library Services and Technology Act, which is made possible through the Institute of Museum and Library Services. Each grant is matched with local funds.

This year, $508,522 in technology grants was awarded at 99 libraries across the state. The grants are used to purchase or replace computers, software, networking software and other electronic equipment for library staff and patrons.

articles.article_title: KPMG Expands AI Innovation With New Technology Group
articles.heading: KPMG Forms Client Technology & Innovation Group
articles.summary: KPMG launches a new technology and innovation group to develop AI-based businesses, products and client solutions.
articles.content:
New York-based IPA 100 firm KPMG (FY25 net revenue of $15.9 billion) is expanding its AI innovation efforts with a new Client Technology & Innovation group focused on developing new AI-based businesses and technology products for clients.

Todd Lohr will lead the group as vice chair and head of Client Technology & Innovation effective Oct. 1. The group brings together KPMG’s technology partnerships, startup investments, venture capital relationships and other innovation programs under one organization.

KPMG said the group will experiment with and incubate new offerings before determining whether to scale them as standalone businesses, joint ventures or offerings within the firm. Its areas of focus include technology disruption, cybersecurity, business transformation and transactions.

“We’ll be working like a start-up at the edge to move faster without creating risk or sacrificing quality to our core business,” Lohr said.

The group will also expand KPMG’s work with technology companies including Anthropic , Google Cloud , Microsoft , OpenAI and Databricks to co-develop products and client solutions.

KPMG plans to use the initiative as a leadership development program as well, rotating selected employees through the new businesses in founder and leadership roles.

The organizational change follows several years of increased AI investment by KPMG. The firm said the new group will continue overseeing its internal AI transformation, while Steve Chase , vice chair and global head of AI and digital innovation, will retire Sept. 30.

articles.article_title: Autonomous vehicle company Zoox training technology in Denver
articles.heading: Autonomous vehicle company Zoox training technology in Denver
articles.summary: This winter, Denverites will see another fleet of autonomous vehicles on the road.
articles.content:
Autonomous vehicle company Zoox training technology in Denver
This winter, Denverites will see another fleet of autonomous vehicles on the road.
The city served as a testing ground for Waymo's self-driving vehicles to train in winter conditions before it began service here. Now, Amazon's Zoox autonomous vehicles will take advantage of Denver's winter conditions to train its own technology.
"Zoox is operating a small test fleet in Denver for a few months this winter to help train our driving technology on winter conditions, including heavy rain and snow," the company said. " Experiencing different weather conditions helps us improve how our technology handles various environments.
The Zoox vehicles training in Denver differ from those operating in other cities.
Their autonomous vehicles, which the company calls "robotaxis," are designed differently than a traditional car. Side doors slide open, like a bus, and two carriage-style seats face each other to make group rides more convenient. The seats also have individual climate controls, and the vehicles include charging stations for electronic devices.
Safety operators will drive the Denver fleet's vehicles manually and will not be taking passengers.
Zoox is currently operational in Las Vegas and San Francisco, with plans to expand into Austin and Miami. The company says it has no plans to expand service to Denver for now.

articles.title: Diraq To Establish Quantum R&D Laboratory In New Mexico
articles.description: Diraq To Establish Quantum R&D Laboratory In New Mexico Los Alamos Daily Post
articles.description_html: Diraq To Establish Quantum R&D Laboratory In New Mexico  Los Alamos Daily Post
articles.article_title: Diraq To Establish Quantum R&D Laboratory In New Mexico
articles.heading: Diraq To Establish Quantum R&D Laboratory In New Mexico
articles.summary: STATE News:
articles.content:
STATE News:
ALBUQUERQUE — Diraq, an Australia-founded quantum computing company, today announced plans to establish a new research and development laboratory in Albuquerque, in another boost to the momentum of the state's growing quantum ecosystem.
Diraq has signed a memorandum of understanding to establish operations at the Roadrunner Quantum Lab (RQL), powered by the State of New Mexico, a joint effort of Roadrunner Venture Studios and the New Mexico Technology and Innovation Office (TIO). Roadrunner Quantum Lab is a shared facility giving quantum startups, industry partners and national laboratories space to accelerate the development and commercialization of quantum technologies. Diraq’s space will include Maybell cryogenic equipment that supports device characterization and other research and development activities. Diraq’s lab is expected to begin operations by the end of the year.
The State of New Mexico is supporting Diraq's expansion into the state as part of its partnership with DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (QBI), a federal initiative to verify and validate utility-scale quantum computing. Diraq is a QBI performer currently in Stage B of the program, and the state's matching funds are helping to build equipment and infrastructure in the state quantum ecosystem that will enable Diraq's lab operations in New Mexico.
“Roadrunner Quantum Lab is focused on bringing quantum computing to market and their commitment to commercialization closely mirrors our own at Diraq,” said Andrew Dzurak, Diraq founder and CEO. “We’re building quantum computing processors based on silicon because that’s the most economical and scalable way to reach the many millions of qubits that our customers will require. New Mexico's investment in RQL demonstrates a strong commitment to building a world-class quantum ecosystem, and we're excited to establish a team in Albuquerque that will help accelerate our progress toward utility-scale quantum computing.”
Diraq will establish a dedicated measurement engineering team in Albuquerque, adding specialized U.S.-based capability in quantum device testing and characterization, with further growth planned as operations scale. The New Mexico lab will complement Diraq’s existing U.S. operations in Palo Alto, Chicago and Los Angeles, as well as its research and engineering centers in Australia.
"Diraq's decision to build here is more proof that New Mexico has the talent, the labs and the infrastructure quantum companies need to go from research to real-world scale," said TIO Director Nora Meyers Sackett. "We're proud to back this expansion and continue growing a quantum ecosystem that's attracting the most cutting-edge companies in the world to New Mexico."
“We’re excited to welcome Diraq to the Roadrunner Quantum Lab as the company expands its U.S. research and development capabilities,” said David Kistin, director of the Roadrunner Quantum Lab. “Diraq’s measurement engineering team will add another technical dimension to the work taking place at RQL and create new opportunities for collaboration across the facility — supporting New Mexico’s continued growth as a center for quantum research and development.”
Diraq is developing quantum computers using silicon spin qubits, which are built with the same CMOS manufacturing processes used to make today's computer chips. Because this approach builds on the established semiconductor industry, it offers a promising path to producing quantum chips at scale in systems designed to be cost-effective and fit within existing data center infrastructure.
Scale is one of the field's central challenges, since useful, utility-scale quantum computers are expected to need millions of qubits. Diraq's roadmap targets 150,000 physical qubits on a single chip by 2029 and more than 2 million by 2031. Pursuing these ambitious goals advances the aims of DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (QBI) to bring utility-scale quantum computing within reach by 2033.

articles.title: Ahead of meeting with AI leaders, Trump again says he won't 'stifle' the technology's growth - ABC News

articles.description: Ahead of meeting with AI leaders, Trump again says he won't 'stifle' the technology's growth ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.description_html: Ahead of meeting with AI leaders, Trump again says he won't 'stifle' the technology's growth  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.article_title: Ahead of meeting with AI leaders, Trump again says he won't 'stifle' the technology's growth
articles.heading: Ahead of meeting with AI leaders, Trump again says he won't 'stifle' the technology's growth
articles.summary: The meeting comes as AI leaders are issuing dire warnings about the threat of AI and calling for steps to slow it down before it outsmarts humans.
articles.content:
Ahead of meeting with AI leaders, Trump again says he won't 'stifle' the technology's growth
The meeting comes as AI leaders are issuing dire warnings about the threat.
Ahead of his lunch meeting with AI leaders about the threat of the rapidly innovating technology, President Donald Trump said again Tuesday he won't "stifle" the growth of the technology.
"This is one more example of why I will never stifle the growth of technology that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution. This is why the SI -- superintelligence -- is, they're saying, bigger than the Industrial Revolution, far bigger than the internet, not even close -- and we see it, and we can't stifle it. And we're leading by a lot," Trump said an event unveiling America.gov -- a federal website that uses AI to help connect Americans to federal resources.
The meeting comes as AI leaders are issuing dire warnings about the threat of AI and calling for steps to slow it down before it outsmarts humans. Following those warnings, lawmakers are weighing what -- if any -- action should be taken.
Along with House Speaker Mike Johnson and members of Trump's Cabinet, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg will attend the meeting, according to a guest list released by the White House, along with Elon Musk, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Jensen Huang from Nvidia, Palintir's Alex Karp and Shyam Sankar, Amaxzon's Jeff Bezos, and Greg Brockman from OpenAI.
The president indicated that he didn't want global collaboration or regulation of the industry and said he discussed it with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House last week.
"We talked about it, not that much because I didn't want to do anything. We're leading, so why would I want to do anything? And, and a lot of people said, 'Let's do it together with China.' But then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know. But we do work with them in so many ways," Trump said.
"We're leading now over China and everyone else and I want to keep it that way. I want to keep it that way," Trump said. "The only way you can keep it that way is to do exactly what we're doing right now. We don't want to stifle growth."
The president repeated that law enforcement would be the key mechanism in stopping companies who "go down a very dark and dangerous path" on AI.
"At the same time, we want people to behave honestly. We want them to be trustworthy, and that's why we have the DOJ. That's why we have the FBI. That's why we have forms of government that are very effective if people decide to go down a very dark and dangerous path," Trump said.
Zuckerberg has pushed back on calls from other tech leaders to collectively slow down AI, saying "every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely."
The meeting will also include other tech leaders.
This won't be the first time that top tech leaders have met with Trump on the issue. The Meta CEO also attended the state dinner at the White House for Chinese President Xi Jinping last week, along with the CEOs of OpenAI, Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, AMD, SpaceX and executives from Amazon and Apple. Amodei also had dinner with Trump late on Sunday night.'
The president has said that the warnings about the technology and calls to slow down AI development are a "hoax."
"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX[...]," Trump said in a social media post in mid-September, before comparing the warnings to his impeachments.
The president has made clear that he does not believe in regulating the technology. Just last week while addressing the United Nations General Assembly, Trump said the U.S. "rejects" a global attempt to regulate AI.
Johnson told reporters two weeks ago about the meeting, saying there would be "a deliberate discussion about the responsibility of the companies to maintain safety, and what role, if any, the government has to play in that."
While Johnson called on the companies to "self-regulate," he also also stressed that the U.S. should not lose its competitive edge in the space.
"We cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI, because then we will lose our edge to China, and that has serious national security implications for," Johnson said.
On Monday, Johnson said the the fears of the threat of AI is a Chinese psychological operation and are politically motivated.
"This is what Democrats do. They glom on to something and say, 'This is doom and gloom and everyone will die if we don't win,'" he told Fox Business. "Don't buy it. It is a Chinese psyop."
The White House has not responded to ABC News when asked about the meeting.

articles.article_title: ICE starts to explore AI, data strategy support contract
articles.heading: ICE starts to explore AI, data strategy support contract
articles.summary: Immigration and Customs Enforcement's production environment now needs ongoing operations-and-maintenance support and continued enhancement.
articles.content:
ICE starts to explore AI, data strategy support contract
Immigration and Customs Enforcement's production environment now needs ongoing operations-and-maintenance support and continued enhancement.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement has embarked on initial market research efforts to explore how it could hire at least one contractor to support its enterprise strategy for artificial intelligence and data.
ICE’s office of the chief information officer has led the agency through a multi-year initiative to become a more data-driven organization and get more tech offerings into a production environment. This includes STELLA, an artificial intelligence platform that functions as a large language model for capabilities such as chatbots and workflow automation.
The production environment now requires ongoing operations-and-maintenance support and continued enhancement work to support ICE’s future transformation efforts, the agency said in a sources sought notice published Tuesday.
AI, data, and technology strategy and architecture are the three major functional areas ICE is looking for industry support in. ICE is also exploring the possibility of an enterprise agentic software factory operating model to aid in AI-enabled delivery.
That factory would have three architectural layers including an enterprise operating model and control plane, agentic orchestration and runtime layer, and independent assurance boundary.
The plane would be set up to support portfolio governance, while the runtime layer would act as a coordinator of AI and software giants. The boundary would provide cybersecurity, accessibility and mission acceptance testing capabilities to users.
ICE’s request for information has 12 questions for industry to answer ahead of the agency’s acquisition planning and requirements development efforts. The RFI asks for feedback on contract strategy, pricing models, multi-cloud and AI platform sustainment capabilities, and experience in AI governance and risk management.
Responses to the RFI are due by 10 a.m. Eastern time on Oct. 16.

articles.title: New Innovation Is Required to Fund AI’s $6 Trillion Buildout
articles.description: New Innovation Is Required to Fund AI’s $6 Trillion Buildout Bain & Company
articles.description_html: New Innovation Is Required to Fund AI’s $6 Trillion Buildout  Bain & Company
articles.article_title: New Innovation Is Required to Fund AI’s $6 Trillion Buildout
articles.heading: New Innovation Is Required to Fund AI’s $6 Trillion Buildout
articles.summary: To justify the investment, AI must do more than boost productivity; it will need to unlock new sources of growth and value.
articles.content:
To justify the investment, AI must do more than boost productivity; it will need to unlock new sources of growth and value.

By David Crawford, Kristie Tagawa, Cory Boles, and Tatum Quinn

- AI infrastructure investment is racing ahead, but generating enough economic value to justify it will require trillions of dollars in new AI-driven revenue.

- Productivity gains from existing enterprise and consumer applications won't be enough; entirely new markets must emerge to close the funding gap.

- The winners will be those that create breakthrough AI applications that transform industries and expand the global economy.

The unprecedented speed and scale of the AI buildout, with billions flowing into chips, data centers, networks, and power systems, have focused attention on the challenge of building capacity. But the more important question may be whether enough economic value can be created to justify it.

Consider the scale of investment and the gap between that and the revenue model necessary to fund it.

- The arms race among hyperscalers (Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle) is accelerating: Their capital expenditures could reach $780 billion in 2026, nearly five times the level of just three years earlier.

- Leading-edge AI data centers today are approaching 1 gigawatt (GW) of power capacity. By 2027, many are expected to approach 2 GW facilities, with 9 GW campuses emerging by the end of the decade (see Figure 1).

Note: Each data point is an independent estimate for the single largest AI data center at that time; power and cost shown as midpoints of published ranges; 2027, 2029, and 2030 values extrapolated from a doubling trend

By 2031, annual spending on AI infrastructure could reach $1.5 trillion, including new data center infrastructure and compute capacity as well as ongoing upgrades to the installed base of GPUs, memory, and networking equipment.

If we assume that capital expenditures amount to about 25% of industry revenue (an ambitious but reasonable percentage based on trends among cloud providers), sustaining this level of investment would require an AI market approaching $6 trillion annually.

Some of that revenue is already coming into focus. Consumer AI products, through subscriptions and advertising, could generate an estimated $200 billion to $400 billion by 2031. Enterprise adoption could contribute another $1 trillion to $1.4 trillion in gains to providers alone as AI delivers meaningful productivity gains to enterprises across software development, sales, marketing, customer service, and IT operations.

Together, the consumer and enterprise AI market could total between $1.2 trillion and $1.8 trillion, leaving about $4.2 trillion of new revenue to reach the $6 trillion market that we estimate will be necessary to fund the buildout (see Figure 2).

That revenue must come from new sources of economic value.

Sources of new value

Dramatic innovation will be required to deliver the revenue necessary to fund the gap. Bain’s research finds four key categories that are likely to help deliver this growth.

- Search and advertising ($100 billion to $200 billion): By integrating ads into their chatbot products and encouraging the trend of using AI to replace a large portion of traditional Internet search, model providers could unlock $100 billion to $200 billion or more in revenue.

- Autonomous everything ($400 billion): Using AI to autonomously operate automobiles, trucks, and drones, as well as other industrial automation initiatives, represent a $400 billion market opportunity by increasing equipment uptime while reducing training and operating costs. Autonomous vehicles could provide significant value as new cars and trucks for consumers, as robotaxi services, and by automating logistics services.

- Physical AI ($900 billion): Advanced AI models can enable highly realistic simulations and digital twins of physical processes, helping companies improve productivity, test modifications, and accelerate the deployment of autonomous systems. Similarly, AI-powered robotics, including humanoid robots, can operate in unstructured environments, unlocking a wide range of new applications across the physical economy, from manufacturing to surgery. As a result, the physical economy could represent a $900 billion opportunity across priority sectors (including automotive, electronics, semiconductors, and aerospace and defense), assuming a 10% reduction in R&D and manufacturing costs from higher yields and faster factory ramps.

- New product development: Beyond AI’s uses today, new applications could help close the gap. New Innovation Is Required to Fund AI’s $6 Trillion Buildout

To justify the investment, AI must do more than boost productivity; it will need to unlock new sources of growth and value.

By David Crawford, Kristie Tagawa, Cory Boles, and Tatum Quinn

en
At a Glance
  • AI infrastructure investment is racing ahead, but generating enough economic value to justify it will require trillions of dollars in new AI-driven revenue.
  • Productivity gains from existing enterprise and consumer applications won't be enough; entirely new markets must emerge to close the funding gap.
  • The winners will be those that create breakthrough AI applications that transform industries and expand the global economy.

The unprecedented speed and scale of the AI buildout, with billions flowing into chips, data centers, networks, and power systems, have focused attention on the challenge of building capacity. But the more important question may be whether enough economic value can be created to justify it.

Consider the scale of investment and the gap between that and the revenue model necessary to fund it.

  • The arms race among hyperscalers (Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle) is accelerating: Their capital expenditures could reach $780 billion in 2026, nearly five times the level of just three years earlier.
  • Leading-edge AI data centers today are approaching 1 gigawatt (GW) of power capacity. By 2027, many are expected to approach 2 GW facilities, with 9 GW campuses emerging by the end of the decade (see Figure 1).
Figure 1

By 2031, annual spending on AI infrastructure could reach $1.5 trillion, including new data center infrastructure and compute capacity as well as ongoing upgrades to the installed base of GPUs, memory, and networking equipment.

If we assume that capital expenditures amount to about 25% of industry revenue (an ambitious but reasonable percentage based on trends among cloud providers), sustaining this level of investment would require an AI market approaching $6 trillion annually.

Some of that revenue is already coming into focus. Consumer AI products, through subscriptions and advertising, could generate an estimated $200 billion to $400 billion by 2031. Enterprise adoption could contribute another $1 trillion to $1.4 trillion in gains to providers alone as AI delivers meaningful productivity gains to enterprises across software development, sales, marketing, customer service, and IT operations.

Together, the consumer and enterprise AI market could total between $1.2 trillion and $1.8 trillion, leaving about $4.2 trillion of new revenue to reach the $6 trillion market that we estimate will be necessary to fund the buildout (see Figure 2).

That revenue must come from new sources of economic value.

Figure 2

Sources of new value

Dramatic innovation will be required to deliver the revenue necessary to fund the gap. Bain’s research finds four key categories that are likely to help deliver this growth.

  • Search and advertising ($100 billion to $200 billion): By integrating ads into their chatbot products and encouraging the trend of using AI to replace a large portion of traditional Internet search, model providers could unlock $100 billion to $200 billion or more in revenue.
  • Autonomous everything ($400 billion): Using AI to autonomously operate automobiles, trucks, and drones, as well as other industrial automation initiatives, represent a $400 billion market opportunity by increasing equipment uptime while reducing training and operating costs. Autonomous vehicles could provide significant value as new cars and trucks for consumers, as robotaxi services, and by automating logistics services.
  • Physical AI ($900 billion): Advanced AI models can enable highly realistic simulations and digital twins of physical processes, helping companies improve productivity, test modifications, and accelerate the deployment of autonomous systems. Similarly, AI-powered robotics, including humanoid robots, can operate in unstructured environments, unlocking a wide range of new applications across the physical economy, from manufacturing to surgery. As a result, the physical economy could represent a $900 billion opportunity across priority sectors (including automotive, electronics, semiconductors, and aerospace and defense), assuming a 10% reduction in R&D and manufacturing costs from higher yields and faster factory ramps.
  • New product development: Beyond AI’s uses today, new applications could help close the gap. These could include AI-driven drug discovery that makes treatments for rare diseases economically viable, always-available mental health support that addresses billions of dollars in unmet demand, materials science breakthroughs that unlock next-generation batteries and semiconductors, and autonomous scientific research that accelerates progress in fields from neuroscience to fusion energy—all examples of new opportunities resulting from abundant intelligence.

Innovation and entrepreneurship must accelerate

Enterprise productivity is the tip of the spear, the first gains we’re seeing from AI deployment, but it won’t be nearly enough. The economics required to generate ROI from AI infrastructure are demanding trillions in new revenue, not just cost savings.

The industry needs a wave of application innovation comparable with what mobile and cloud unlocked, not just productivity gains on existing workflows.

The infrastructure is being built ahead of the demand curve, and funding it sustainably will require adding approximately 1% to the annual global GDP growth rate. The question is whether the applications arrive in time to pay for it.

articles.heading: Alcon to Present Dry Eye, Contact Lens Research and Technology Experiences at AAOpt
articles.summary: Key Takeaways      	Alcon will present new research on dry eye disease, Tryptyr, contact lenses and contact lens care at Academy 2026 in Anaheim, Cali
articles.content:
Key Takeaways
- Alcon will present new research on dry eye disease, Tryptyr, contact lenses and contact lens care at Academy 2026 in Anaheim, California
- Dry eye studies will examine patient-reported outcomes, treatment satisfaction, quality of life, meibomian gland function and other clinical measures
- Interactive programming will include the WaterInnovations Immersive Experience, Marlo demonstrations and an Innovation Suite featuring Voyager DSLT and Valeda PBM
Alcon announced plans to present new research across dry eye disease, contact lenses and contact lens care at Academy 2026, the American Academy of Optometry annual meeting, taking place September 30 to October 3 in Anaheim, California.
The company’s scientific program will include research related to Tryptyr (acoltremon ophthalmic solution) 0.003% and Alcon’s broader dry eye portfolio. Meeting attendees will also have opportunities to explore the company’s technologies through its WaterInnovations Immersive Experience, Marlo demonstrations and an Innovation Suite featuring Voyager Direct Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty (DSLT) and the Valeda photobiomodulation (PBM) device.
Dry eye research
Alcon said its dry eye research at the meeting will examine patient satisfaction, symptoms and quality of life across its pharmaceutical and over-the-counter portfolio.
The studies will address areas including treatment satisfaction, effects of dry eye on daily activities and work, patient-reported symptoms, tear film measures and meibomian gland function.
Featured dry eye posters include "Comparing Patient-Reported Symptoms in Perfluorohexyloctane Ophthalmic Solution and Systane Pro Users" and "Assessing Meibomian Gland Function in Dry Eye Subjects Treated with PFHO or Systane Pro."
The meeting will also include research examining the experiences of patients with dry eye disease treated with acoltremon ophthalmic solution 0.003%. The studies will assess quality of life, daily functioning and treatment satisfaction.
Tryptyr-focused posters include Evaluating the Impact of Acoltremon 0.003% on a Subject’s Quality of Life and Ability to Perform Work and Understanding the Satisfaction of Symptomatic Lifitegrast Patients Who Switched to Acoltremon.
Contact lens studies
Alcon will also present research examining contact lens performance, wearer experience and patient and eye care professional needs. According to the company, the research includes studies of weekly replacement and daily disposable lenses, examining factors such as vision, comfort, digital device use and patient satisfaction.
Featured presentations include "Performance and Safety Evaluation of Weekly Replacement Serafilcon A Compared to Biweekly Replacement Senofilcon A Silicone Hydrogel Contact Lenses" and "Evaluation of Wear Experience with a Weekly Replacement Toric Contact Lens in Neophyte Wearers."
The company will also host an educational luncheon addressing expanded toric parameters within its WaterInnovations portfolio, with a focus on contact lens fitting and patient needs.
Interactive experiences
Beyond the scientific program, Alcon plans several educational and interactive experiences for eye care professionals attending the meeting.
The WaterInnovations Immersive Experience will provide an interactive environment designed to demonstrate the technologies and scientific principles underlying the contact lens portfolio.
Alcon’s Innovation Suite will feature Voyager DSLT and Valeda PBM. The technologies are intended to support care for patients with glaucoma and dry age-related macular degeneration, respectively.
Attendees can also participate in demonstrations of Marlo at Alcon’s booth, along with additional professional education and meeting activities.
Alcon will exhibit at booth 712 during Academy 2026.

NATO is stepping up its work with Allies, industry and the research community to ensure that the Alliance is “quantum-ready”.
On 30 July 2026, Allies approved a quantum technology roadmap to accelerate the understanding, adoption and integration of quantum technologies across NATO and Allied armed forces, and mitigate potential disruptive risks stemming from strategic competition.
A public summary of the roadmap is released on Tuesday (29 September) - read the roadmap.
The roadmap builds on NATO’s Quantum Strategy approved in 2023, and focuses on quantum computing, quantum communication, and quantum sensing. How quantum technologies interplay with other dual-use technologies such as AI, Space or Next Generation Communication Networks will also be at the centre of NATO’s work.
The Transatlantic Quantum Community (TQC) and its Industry Network will play an important role to support the implementation of activities identified in the roadmap through close cooperation with both industry and academia.
The TQC last met in Washington D.C. on 24-25 September 2026. Discussions focused on how advances in quantum computing could affect secure communications, critical infrastructure, intelligence, strategic stability and crisis decision-making. They also addressed the implications of AI-Quantum convergence for defence and security. Furthermore, they explored how to harness quantum technologies for Positioning and Navigation (PNT), and sensing, notably in light of the Questor 26 experimentation campaign conducted by the NATO Centre for Maritime Research and Experimentation (CMRE) and the TQC Industry Network in La Spezia, Italy, early this month.
The TQC also welcomed Belgium and Bulgaria, who officially joined 22 other Allies and six partner nations participating in the community.
On 12 May 2026, the Netherlands became the Chair of the TQC for one year, with Canada as Vice-Chair. Established in 2024, the TQC is a non-binding informal community of quantum experts from national governments, industry, academia, funding bodies, and research institutions.

articles.heading: Department of Technology Awards Ceremony
articles.summary: On September 26, Illinois State University’s Department of Technology (TEC) held its inaugural Department of Technology Awards Ceremony. The ceremony replaces TEC’s annual Scholarship Reception, adding recognition for faculty teaching awards in addition to celebrating Honors students, TEC ambassadors, and the students who were awarded over $75,000 in scholarship funds this year.
articles.content:
On September 26, Illinois State University’s Department of Technology (TEC) held its inaugural Department of Technology Awards Ceremony. The ceremony replaces TEC’s annual Scholarship Reception, adding recognition for faculty teaching awards in addition to celebrating Honors students, TEC ambassadors, and the students who were awarded over $75,000 in scholarship funds this year.
“(The awards ceremony) is a special event because it brings together the people at the heart of our programs: our students, their families, our faculty, alumni, and generous supporters,” said TEC Chair Josh Brown, who planned the additional recognitions for faculty members. He views the ceremony as a chance to celebrate student achievement while also expressing gratitude to those who invest in students’ successes.
The $75,000 total is an increase from last year’s scholarship funds, in large part due to the addition of the Richard C. Kohler Scholarship. Named after an alum who graduated from TEC in 1938, this scholarship covers all fees and tuition for a remarkable junior in TEC who has demonstrated dedication and excellent academic performance. This year’s winner was graphic communications (GCT) major Abigail Cook. Cook has been active in many Illinois State organizations, including GCT’s Phoenix Challenge competition team, which has taken first place in both events she participated in. She is also deeply dedicated to giving back to the community, both in her hometown of Murphysboro and in Bloomington-Normal. Cook also has the option to renew the scholarship for her senior year.
Other scholarship winners included Sarah Akanbi, Liam Axelsen, Christian Doubet, Mitchell Fitton, Michael Johnson, Nick Murdoch-Shey, and Tyler Ward. Dr. Brown recognized students who had won departmental scholarships, and Dr. Sundeep Inti, Dr. Jeritt Williams, and Dr. Chris Merrill presented recognition for individual program scholarship winners.
Williams won the College of Applied Science and Technology (CAST) Pre-Tenure Outstanding Teaching Award, and Professor Adam Burke received the Non-Tenure Outstanding Teaching Award.
The program ended with donor and emeritus faculty member Dr. Hank Campbell explaining the history of the department and the significance of many of the people for whom the scholarships were named. Campbell and Dr. Chad McEvoy, CAST dean, also honored the legacy of donor and former TEC department chair Dr. Joe Talkington, who passed away earlier this year.

articles.article_title: Shane Flanagan to Support Life Sciences & Technology Design and Construction Efforts for Burns & McDonnell in California
articles.heading: Shane Flanagan to Support Life Sciences & Technology Design and Construction Efforts for Burns & McDonnell in California
articles.summary: Shane Flanagan to Support Life Sciences & Technology Design and Construction Efforts for Burns & McDonnell in California
articles.content:
News
BREA, California — Burns & McDonnell, a 100% employee-owned engineering, architecture and construction firm, has announced that Shane Flanagan will lead its Life Sciences & Technology team in California as Consumer Products & Life Sciences Construction Department Manager.
In this role, Flanagan will focus on building high-performing teams, strengthening client partnerships and delivering high-quality solutions that address the evolving needs of pharmaceutical, biotechnology, animal health and medical device clients. He will support projects throughout their life cycles, from early capital planning and site assessments through design, construction, commissioning and startup. Working alongside the firm’s integrated planning, architecture, engineering and construction professionals, he will help bring construction insight into projects from the outset.
Flanagan’s focus will include scalable, high-tech facilities designed to meet current good manufacturing practice (cGMP) requirements while balancing quality, cost, speed, technical complexity and regulatory compliance. His team will support clients as they modernize manufacturing facilities, expand existing operations and develop new greenfield projects.
As a single-source design and construction partner, Burns & McDonnell integrates technical engineering, cost controls and constructability considerations to develop facilities that align with each client’s manufacturing processes, budget and schedule requirements.
Flanagan brings 15 years of experience leading multidisciplinary teams across pharmaceutical, biotechnology and advanced manufacturing programs, delivering results in safety, cost, schedule quality and client satisfaction.
About Burns & McDonnell
Working from more than 75 offices around the world, Burns & McDonnell designs and builds critical infrastructure. Our family of companies — driven by engineers, construction professionals, architects, planners, technologists and scientists — delivers projects grounded in safety and a desire to make a difference as we make our clients successful. Founded in 1898, Burns & McDonnell is 100% employee-owned. Learn more about our life sciences capabilities and experience here.

articles.title: Northrop Grumman to Accelerate Extended-Range C-UAS Missile Technology for US Army
articles.description: Northrop Grumman to Accelerate Extended-Range C-UAS Missile Technology for US Army Northrop Grumman
articles.description_html: Northrop Grumman to Accelerate Extended-Range C-UAS Missile Technology for US Army  Northrop Grumman
articles.article_title: Northrop Grumman to Accelerate Extended-Range C-UAS Missile Technology for US Army
articles.heading: Northrop Grumman to Accelerate Extended-Range C-UAS Missile Technology for US Army
articles.summary: ROCKET CENTER, W.Va. – Sept. 29, 2026 – To address the evolving challenges of detecting and defeating unmanned aerial systems at extended ranges, Northrop Grumman will develop next-generation air-breathing propulsion for the U.S. Army, significantly enhancing the range and air defense capabilities of the Army's extended Range Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (XRC).
articles.content:
Loading component...
Northrop Grumman performs a ground test of a solid fuel ramjet propulsion system, demonstrating the company’s commitment to pioneering propulsion technologies that underpin future missile capabilities. (Photo Credit: Northrop Grumman)
ROCKET CENTER, W.Va. – Sept. 29, 2026 – To address the evolving challenges of detecting and defeating unmanned aerial systems at extended ranges, Northrop Grumman (NYSE: NOC) will develop next-generation air-breathing propulsion for the U.S. Army, significantly enhancing the range and air defense capabilities of the Army's eXtended Range Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (XRC).
A leader in air-breathing tactical propulsion, Northrop Grumman will develop and integrate solid fuel ramjet propulsion technology for integration into XRC missile prototypes under this $18.8 million contract with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Aviation & Missile Center. Unlike solid rocket motors, which utilize propellant containing fuel and a chemical oxidizer, solid fuel ramjets use atmospheric oxygen as the oxidizer for the fuel during flight, freeing internal volume for additional fuel. The result is a more efficient propulsion system that delivers greater range and energy, enabling engagement of highly maneuverable aerial threats at safer distances from protected forces.
The development will include a comprehensive ground and flight test campaign to validate the design and production processes. The resulting design will support scalable, cost-effective manufacturing to meet urgent defense requirements quickly.
Expert:
Erik Buice, vice president, missile products, Northrop Grumman: “The rapid evolution of unmanned aerial threats demands innovative solutions. By aligning the Army's vision for next-generation air defense with our advanced propulsion expertise, we're delivering capability that engages targets farther away, protects mobile forces and strengthens layered defense against emerging aerial threats.”
Details:
Development for the XRC program will be conducted at Allegany Ballistics Laboratory in West Virginia, a premier Northrop Grumman-operated facility specializing in advanced propulsion systems and energetics.
The XRC program focuses on enhancing the performance of the Army’s Maneuver Short Range Air Defense (M-SHORAD) system — designed to protect maneuvering forces from low-altitude aerial threats. Additionally, the system’s compatibility with the Stinger Vehicle Universal Launcher improves defense against advanced unmanned aerial systems as well as traditional fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft.
With adversaries increasingly deploying sophisticated unmanned systems, the XRC program’s extended-range capabilities is a vital element within the Army’s layered air defense strategy. Northrop Grumman’s deep involvement in the Army’s broader counter-UAS ecosystem also includes providing the foundational command-and-control network, kinetic options and propulsion expertise leveraged by advanced interceptor systems.
As prime contractor for the Forward Area Air Defense Command and Control (FAAD C2) system — the Army’s official short-range air defense program of record — Northrop Grumman plays an essential role in modernizing U.S. Army air defense. Additionally, the company’s AI-driven AiON command system supports managing multiple sensors and engaging mass drone swarms, enhancing the tactical response to these emerging threats.
Northrop Grumman is also advancing Raid Hunter™, the 50mm Gun-Based Air Defense system delivering a cost-effective, high-engagement-capacity solution designed to defeat mass, mixed air raids and enhance protection of maneuver forces and critical infrastructure within a layered CUAS defense framework.
Northrop Grumman remains committed to pioneering advanced technologies that keep warfighters safe and preserve mission success through scalable, integrated and highly effective defense solutions.
Approved for public release. Distribution unlimited.

articles.title: Dunwoody College of Technology to Launch Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering
articles.description: Dunwoody College of Technology to Launch Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering PR Newswire
articles.description_html: Dunwoody College of Technology to Launch Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering  PR Newswire
articles.article_title: Dunwoody College of Technology to Launch Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering
articles.heading: Dunwoody College of Technology to Launch Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering
articles.summary: /PRNewswire/ -- As demand for civil engineers continues to grow nationwide, Dunwoody College of Technology today announced the expansion of its School of...
articles.content:
Hands-on degree launching in Fall 2027 will prepare students to design and maintain the infrastructure communities rely on
MINNEAPOLIS, Sept. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As demand for civil engineers continues to grow nationwide, Dunwoody College of Technology today announced the expansion of its School of Engineering with a new Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering. Launching in Fall 2027, the four-year degree will prepare students to design, build, and maintain the infrastructure communities rely on while helping to meet the highly in-demand workforce needs of employers across Minnesota and beyond.
The Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering combines rigorous engineering theory with Dunwoody's signature hands-on approach to learning. Students will gain experience through laboratory work, field experiences and project-based learning while studying five major civil engineering disciplines: structural, geotechnical, transportation, water resources and environmental engineering.
This will be the fourth program in Dunwoody's School of Engineering, which includes Computer, Electrical and Mechanical. Both Electrical and Mechanical are accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, and the Civil Engineering program will seek ABET accreditation as well.
"The structure and curriculum developed for the new Civil Engineering program align with the mission of Dunwoody's School of Engineering in providing another avenue for students to access high-paying engineering fields," said Noureen Sajid, director of the School of Engineering. "I want students who graduate from Dunwoody's engineering programs to not only be well-prepared for their careers, but also ready to become entrepreneurs and inventors of creative solutions."
"Civil engineers play a vital role in nearly every community, designing the roads, bridges, water systems and other infrastructure people rely on every day. With many in the field nearing retirement, the industry is facing an increasing demand for new experts," said Scott Stallman, Ph.D., President of Dunwoody College of Technology. "By combining rigorous engineering coursework with hands-on learning and close collaboration with the industry, this program will prepare graduates to tackle the complex infrastructure challenges facing communities today and in the future."
While developing the program and curriculum, the College sought feedback from a steering committee of licensed professional engineers from public and private organizations. The result: an engineering program that emphasizes experiential learning, fieldwork and real-world problem-solving. Graduates will be prepared for careers across civil engineering, including structural, transportation, geotechnical, water resources and environmental engineering. They'll also be able to look forward to a career with stability, high-growth potential and substantial pay.
The program incorporates modern engineering technologies, including geographic information systems (GIS), Autodesk Civil 3D, drones, LiDAR and AI simulation tools, while emphasizing sustainable infrastructure and multidisciplinary design. As infrastructure needs continue to evolve, the program is designed to help prepare graduates with the technical expertise and practical experience employers are seeking.
"Civil engineering is about creating the infrastructure people rely on every day. From roads and bridges to water systems and public spaces, civil engineers solve complex challenges that strengthen communities," said E.J. Daigle, academic dean of the School of Engineering at Dunwoody College of Technology. "At Dunwoody, students will combine engineering theory with hands-on experience to prepare for careers that will make a lasting impact."
The Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering program will launch in Fall 2027. More information about the program is available at dunwoody.edu/civil.
Media assets available HERE.
ABOUT DUNWOODY COLLEGE OF TECHNOLOGY
Founded in 1914, Dunwoody College of Technology is the only private, not-for-profit technical college in the Upper Midwest. Having provided hands-on, applied technical education to more than 200,000 individuals, Dunwoody is the college for experimenters and makers, a place where the curious and the confident learn by doing. Located in Minneapolis, Dunwoody offers a unique campus experience in dedicated labs, studios, and shops that treat students like future professionals from day one. With certificates, associate's, and bachelor's degrees in more than 40 majors – including engineering, robotics, design and other STEM-related fields – Dunwoody challenges students to come determined and graduate destined.

articles.heading: Tepper Sports & Entertainment Announces Trane Technologies as Cornerstone Partner
articles.summary: Designation elevates company as exclusive Official Climate Technology Partner of the Carolina Panthers and Charlotte FC and deepens its investment in the future of Bank of America Stadium
articles.content:
Designation elevates company as exclusive Official Climate Technology Partner of the Carolina Panthers and Charlotte FC and deepens its investment in the future of Bank of America Stadium

CHARLOTTE – Tepper Sports & Entertainment (TSE) today announced that Trane Technologies (NYSE: TT) has been named a Cornerstone Partner, extending a long-term commitment to the future of Bank of America Stadium. The company will serve as the exclusive Official Climate Technology Partner and an Official Sustainability Partner of both the Carolina Panthers and Charlotte FC. The designation places Trane Technologies among a select group of Cornerstone Partners and reflects the company's deep ties to the Carolinas. Trane Technologies, a global climate innovator with more than 45,000 employees around the world, maintains its North American headquarters in Davidson, North Carolina and employs more than 4,600 employees across North Carolina and South Carolina.

The announcement builds on a relationship that began in 2018 when the organizations first worked together on a comprehensive upgrade to Bank of America Stadium's climate and cooling systems to improve fan comfort, indoor air quality and energy efficiency.

"Trane Technologies has been a trusted partner for many years, and we're excited to have them play an even greater role as we continue the transformation of Bank of America Stadium," said Kristi Coleman, Tepper Sports & Entertainment CEO. "Their decision to become a Cornerstone Partner reflects the strength of our relationship, the value they bring to this project and a shared vision for what it means for our fans, our region and future generations."

Trane Technologies will become the presenting partner of the 300-Level Silver Club at Bank of America Stadium in 2029, encompassing more than 50,000 square feet of premium hospitality space and four adjacent club destinations across the level. As part of the stadium's ongoing transformation, the company is also leading the upgrade of the venue's HVAC infrastructure systems and controls to continue to improve comfort, efficiency and performance throughout the stadium.

"Bank of America Stadium is a powerful economic and community asset for the Carolinas, and we're honored to serve as a Cornerstone Partner to support its next chapter," said Dave Regnery, Chair and CEO of Trane Technologies. "We believe innovation can help shape a more sustainable future, and we look forward to continuing our support of this important venue and its transformation, providing advanced climate technology that helps enhance stadium comfort, efficiency and performance for years to come."

Another key component of the partnership is the continuation of the STEM Stadium of the Future Challenge, a 10-week program that empowers North and South Carolina high school students to dream big and design the next generation of sports venues. Challenged to envision what an NFL-style stadium built for their school could look like, students use STEM skills to create innovative concepts that blend sustainability, technology, fan experience, accessibility and school pride. Supported by mentors from Trane Technologies, teams construct scale models of their designs and present them before a panel of industry leaders, competing for Panthers Charities and Trane Technologies Foundation grants that help advance STEM education in their schools.

About Tepper Sports & Entertainment

Tepper Sports & Entertainment (TSE) owns and operates the Carolina Panthers of the National Football League (NFL), Major League Soccer's (MLS) Charlotte Football Club, and Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C. TSE is committed to making the greater Charlotte metro area the premier year-round destination for sports and entertainment in the Carolinas. From hosting around 12 football-focused events annually, Bank of America Stadium now boasts around 40 annual ticketed events. The diverse array of events attracts audiences spanning NFL, NCAA, high school football, MLS, international soccer, and blockbuster concerts. Beyond sports and entertainment, the venue accommodates hundreds of corporate and community events throughout the year and has served as a mass vaccination site in 2020, as well as an early voting site in the 2020, 2022 and 2024 elections.

About Trane Technologies

Trane Technologies is a global climate innovator. Through our strategic brands Trane® and Thermo King®, and our portfolio of environmentally responsible products and services, we bring efficient and sustainable climate solutions to buildings, homes and transportation. For more on Trane Technologies, visit tranetechnologies.com.

Know Your Foe: Week 4, Detroit Lions

From the dynamic Jahmyr Gibbs to a growing defense, get to know the Panthers next opponent, the Detroit Lions .

Monday Brew: Bryce Young shows toughness, expected to play this week
