articles.content:
There I am, sitting in my BMW i7. I started programming in 1977, finished my computer-science degree at UT in December 1980, and went to work in the field in 1981. After nearly half a century of this stuff, I still sometimes have to call customer support, work through the AI agent, get transferred to the offshore support center, and eventually arrive at Chad.
The i7 is an electric automobile containing more computing power than anything I could have imagined when I started programming computers in 1977 with a Processor Technology Sol 20. There is a giant screen glowing beside me. A laptop is open on my lap. I have a smartphone pressed against my ear. The car knows where it is, where the other cars are, how fast they are moving, what the speed limit is, and approximately how much electricity it will take to get where I am going.
With the updates, OS changes, next phone I am forced into buying, computer upgrades every step to move forward comes with a considerable investment in time and frustration. Even with all the plug and play and not worrying about 16K of memory and assembly language games I still get frustrated and I think about the whole universe of technology.
But what is the choice when insurance demands on line payments, doctors demand on line intake forms, and everyone pushes to ‘save a stamp’. (And most of my bills are still paid with a check) Where do we think that data lives?
The Gerbil in the Data Center
I keep seeing people complain about AI, data centers, technology and the enormous amounts of computing infrastructure being built to support them and I see them complain on social media, from their smartphones, on AI-mediated platforms.
Data centers are a real concern and use a lot of resources, but they are not new. They have been around for decades. There are two smaller centers near my home. One for ATT, and one for Spectrum.
The scale of construction is new and even then is that the next dot com bubble or Big Brother finally realized?
The markets go away when there is no demand. How many of us still have a data organizer, digital camera, BlackBerry or pager? Those devices largely disappeared, but the computing didn’t. Much of it migrated into the phone in our pocket and the infrastructure behind it. The internet has been around a long time. I communicated halfway around the world while at Texas Instruments with technical queries about the ACT V integrated testing computer in the 1980 TI corporate version of email.
Let’s say we draw a line in the sand. How luddite are we allowed to go and how luddite do we want to go?
What are you prepared to give up?
Let’s start with Facebook. Delete it. Not just the app. Delete your account, photographs, videos, posts and archive. Then its on to Instagram, LinkedIn, Reddit, TikTok, X. Daily Kos… or whatever electronic soapbox you prefer.
Where did you think all of that stuff lived? On an Apple II in somebody’s garage?
Now YouTube. Don’t merely stop uploading but stop watching. Then its on to Netflix, Apple TV, Hulu, Fire TVV, and whatever streaming services you use. Spotify and streaming music can go too. I have plenty of CDs and records. Still buy them. Even 78s.
If you’re a performer, as I am, give up the worldwide stage that allows someone thousands of miles away to discover something you performed years ago. Before the Internet, distributing a performance internationally required physical media, broadcasters, publishers or distributors. Now I can put one online and potentially leave it available to the planet and that requires a lot machinery.
The Cloud Is Not a Cloud
Next, let’s eliminate cloud storage. Handing off data files, pictures, videos through Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud, get rid of it. I lived without it.
Remember using data transfer software or cables or loading from backups when you changed, upgraded or repaired your computer(s)? Or maybe you don’t keep email on your computer like I do. Perhaps all those emails, videos, ads, birthday wishes, scams for the African elephant secret male performance enhancement products, political ads, new digests, well, all that goes somewhere for you to retrieve and look at it, or ignore and let pile up.
Your new phone doesn’t magically acquire your contacts, photographs, calendar and files from your old phone anymore, because its all synced to the cloud and available to any device you give access to. Also means it could be hacked.
The word cloud is wonderfully deceptive. It sounds weightless and ethereal. Your photographs float up into the heavens and gently rain down onto your new telephone, social media and to cherished contacts.
The cloud is somebody else’s computer, which needs a climate controlled building, not Uncle Fred’s outhouse, and the more storage you have then the bigger the building has to be. Finally the building of computer servers and disk drives holding your diaries, pictures, comments, performances and wisdom are consolidated in Data Center or spread amongst many, or backed up on to many.
When was the last time you lost cloud data due to someone else’s computer failing?
In my law firm accounting software days I told my clients the road to nirvana is paved with good backups. It wasn’t just being silly. You back up what you can’t afford to lose. If one of our data aggregators we depend on drops someone’s content that is it. People bail out.
Now Throw Away the Phone
And then there are our smartphones and tablets. That would get rid of a whole lot of need for data centers.
No apps. No cellular data. No GPS. No mobile banking. No boarding pass on your phone. No authentication app (how often are we forced to use them?). No Find My Phone. No standing in a hardware store and instantly looking up how some damned fitting is supposed to work.
That little slab in your pocket is an extraordinary computer that is also a terminal connected to an enormous collection of other computers. In the olden daze when we used computers by candle light because electricity hadn’t been invented yet the data center was merely a main frame with memory banks, drum memory (who remembers that), disk memory, banks of mag tape machines.
The distinction between computer, tablet and smart phone disappears because we’ve made the machinery so good that most of the time you don’t have to think about it.
You tap. Something happens. Therefore, apparently, nothing happened anywhere else. Not so much. But how many of us realize how much really does happen?
Get Out the Paper Map
In my techno terror BMW i7 I can just name the place I want to go. I don’t even have to know the address. I can ask for the fastest route, avoid highways, toll roads, avoid bridges or ferries, and even better when I am on the way to a music job route around the wreck that happened ten minutes ago. It happens in real time. It saves fuel, reduces traffic problems and makes everything work better.
Giving up the gas engine and all wheel drive complexity then requires me to be able to find an EV charger along the route, tell me whether I can reach it with my remaining charge but also find a restaurant near it, estimate my arrival time based upon current traffic and dictate a message to my friends when I expect to arrive.
So what powers all that computational work, the satellite GPS system, the maps, the serivers, etc?
A gerbil on an exercise wheel?
Your device is communicating with other machines containing map data, traffic data, road restrictions, business information and innumerable other pieces of information. Computers evaluate alternatives and send useful results back to you.
We’ve stopped calling that astonishing and now simply expect it as directions.
Your Money Lives There Too
Let’s do banking the old fashioned way. Bung up those data centers and we can give up online banking, mobile deposits, electronic bill payment (how many still buy stamps? I do), no immediate balance information, no credit-card authorization network, no transaction summaries, no automatic categorization of spending…
And then…
No computer watching millions of transactions for patterns that suggest someone in Romania just bought a television with your credit card while you’re sitting at home in Texas.
Fraud detection requires computing and fraudsters use computing too.
As well as scammers, phishers, bot farms, propagandists, thieves. And on the other side the 19 odd charities I give to as well.
The machine does not acquire virtue because somebody plugged it in.
The computer, the AI, the data center amplifies human capability.
That includes our ability to create, communicate, cooperate, entertain, discover and protect as well as our ability to annoy, deceive, manipulate and steal.
Fine. I’ll Watch Television
Put an antenna on your house. Digital broadcast television is still available without streaming anything from the Internet. But the problem is not solved. It just moved.
Where did the television program come from? How was it recorded? Edited? Color-corrected? Mixed? Captioned? Scheduled? Archived? Distributed to the station? How were the graphics created? How did the commercials get inserted?
Do you imagine the local station has I Love Lucy sitting on a shelf beside the transmitter waiting for someone to thread it through?
All you did was change the last mile of the distribution system because the technological infrastructure behind the content didn’t disappear merely because the final signal reached your antenna by radio.
That is the illusion running through all of this.
We see the phone. We don’t see the servers. We see the television. We don’t see the production infrastructure. We see the credit card. We don’t see the financial network. We see the map. We don’t see the computation. We see the Facebook post. We don’t see the building storing it.
Until someone proposes building one of those buildings in our back yard.
Where Did You Think It Was Happening?
Your photographs appeared on your new phone. Your bank spotted a suspicious transaction. How? Your GPS evaluated possible routes. You passed a huge file through OneDrive. Your email provider discarded a mountain of spam before you ever saw it. You uploaded a performance to YouTube and someone on another continent watched it. Someone uploaded historic tv programs, documentaries, legendary performers and all that performance legacy is now for everyone who can access youtube.
You posted a rant of lant complaining about data centers and people around the world could read it seconds later. Thank you. Your complaint was received, processed, transmitted, replicated, indexed and stored by data centers.
And Then There Is My “AI Slop”
People sometimes complain about my “AI slop.” Fair enough. Let’s examine the slop.
I conceived the idea. I decided what it was supposed to say. I decided who appears in the illustration, where they appear, what they’re doing and what the words they say.
ChatGPT generates imagery under my direction.
And that just pops out right? Every image a little masterpiece or master piece of s- – t depending on the beholder and whatever baggage they bring with them. That is the curse of every work of art… except…
That hand is wrong. He’s looking in the wrong direction. That object makes no sense there. The joke doesn’t work anymore. You changed something I told you not to change. Put that back. Remove this. The perspective is wrong. The text is wrong. Try again.
And when AI still doesn’t do what I want, I load the image onto a very powerful computer and fix it myself just like I did since my first digital camera when I moved from film to digital photography and a solid state camcorder. My computer became my photo lab, and Hollywood studio.
Look at the finished illustrations I publish. Do you see six fingers? Do you see mysterious objects that don’t belong anywhere? Do you see nonsense that destroys the story?
AI acting as my hands does not replace me.
Perhaps I’m closer to the writer/director of an animated cartoon.
The director doesn’t personally draw every frame. Animators do that. But somebody decides what the cartoon is about. Somebody decides how the scene is constructed. Somebody says that character is distracting from the story, that action doesn’t make sense, this needs to move over there and that needs to disappear entirely.
No, I didn’t draw my illustration. I don’t have illustration talent and I retired from music because my hands no longer work like they did, and that has been a bitter pill to swallow.
But, Neither did ChatGPT sit down one afternoon and decide that Orangustein should be sitting in an electric BMW complaining about technology while an AI agent transfers him to a human agent who eventually transfers him to Chad.
I did.
ChatGPT and I created the illustration together. And there is another difference between that and pretending I drew it with a pencil:
I credit ChatGPT for its part.
But AI Uses Electricity!
Yes. It does. That isn’t hooey.
Generative AI consumes electricity, and image generation is substantially more energy-intensive than simple text classification and several other machine-learning tasks. One frequently cited study by Alexandra Sasha Luccioni, Yacine Jernite and Emma Strubell measured the energy and carbon costs of 1,000 inferences across different machine-learning tasks and found large differences among models and tasks. (AI power study)
One 2024 study found average image generation around 2.9 watt-hours per image, with wide variation between models. Even the most carbon-intensive model they tested came out to roughly the emissions of driving a gasoline car about four miles per thousand images. Even if I arbitrarily multiply that by ten to stack the deck against myself, we’re still talking about roughly 40 miles per thousand images.
So let’s count it. Let’s count the electricity used to make my illustrations and my silly cartoons.
But let’s count everything else.
I don’t commute to work and there are days I don’t leave the house. When I do drive, I mostly drive an electric car. I also have a dieselgate touareg.
I’ve converted my house to LED lighting. I did that primarily because LEDs became better lights and are readily dimmable, not because I was engaged in some grand exercise in environmental virtue.
I keep my house around 80 degrees in the summer. Because I’m comfortable at 80 degrees.
Around 68 in the winter works for me too. If I’m cold, humanity developed an extraordinary carbon-reduction technology several thousand years ago: the sweater.
And the electric car and the computer I’m using are in Texas. The landman’s oil state.
Except the caricature is rather out of date. ERCOT, which handles about 90% of Texas electrical load, reported that wind and utility-scale solar together met 36% of its electricity demand during the first nine months of 2025. Wind supplied 87 TWh and utility-scale solar 45 TWh during that period. Natural gas remained the largest source. U.S. Energy Information Administration
Texas has lots of things particularly useful for renewable generation including tons of sun, land, wind and miles and miles of… miles and miles. (ever driven from DFW to Midland?)
So yes, count my AI pictures. But if we’re doing environmental accounting, count the whole ledger.
How far do you commute? What do you drive? How large is your house? What temperature do you maintain it at? What lights are burning? How much video do you stream? How often do you fly? How many networked devices are operating in your home? How much cloud storage do you use? How much computation do you consume without ever thinking of it as computation?
The relevant question isn’t: Does this use energy?
Almost everything does.
The useful questions are:
How much? Compared with what? Supplied by what? And what are we getting for it?
Don’t Let the Data Centers Off the Hook Either
None of this means every proposed data center is a good idea. That’s another pile of hooey.
Data centers consume electricity. Some consume substantial water. They require transmission capacity, generators, land, construction and equipment. Communities have legitimate questions about noise, water, grid reliability, tax incentives, environmental effects and who ultimately pays for new infrastructure.
And there is another question I’ve been asking:
What happens if some of the projected AI demand is a bubble?
Remember when merely having a website was going to make you rich or bring customers flooding to your doorstep? The Internet wasn’t hooey. The Internet changed civilization. But that didn’t mean every projection, business plan, valuation or server farm built around it made sense. Do not forget the whole dot.com bubble.
AI can be transformative and some of the infrastructure being built in anticipation of future demand can be excessive. Those propositions aren’t contradictory. Build enormous infrastructure around wildly optimistic demand projections and somebody eventually owns enormous infrastructure whether the projections came true or not.
Those questions deserve answers.
But “data centers have costs” and “therefore data centers are bad” are not the same proposition.
Neither is: “You use Google Maps, therefore you aren’t allowed to criticize a data center.”
The point is that you already have a stake on both sides of the ledger.
You want the costs reduced. Fine. Now tell me which computations you don’t want. Which communications, entertainment, financial services, safety systems, archives, creative tools, worldwide audiences, conveniences and which pieces of your own life are you prepared to disconnect? Now we have something worth discussing.
Escalating Exception
Which brings me back to Rabbi Orangustein, the animal with its desires and foibles, but who is also the person, the lay rabbi with his blog, who tries to do better.
My BMW wasn’t doing something I thought it should do. So there I am inside an extraordinarily sophisticated machine complaining about technology.
The support AI (which is very helpful on things like hooking up a router) tells me:
ESCALATING EXCEPTION.
Eventually I reach a human support agent, but I am at such a nerd level that he can’t help me.
PASSING TO SUPERVISOR.
And eventually our magnificent global technological civilization terminates in Chad’s bedroom.
“YOUR MAC & CHEESE IS READY!”
“MOM! I AM WORKING!”
It’s an easy joke, but even that can be examined for hooey.
An adult child living in the family household isn’t some bizarre new phenomenon proving that civilization has collapsed. Multigenerational households have been ordinary through much of human history and remain ordinary in many cultures. What makes us so special?
I grew up with my maternal grandmother in our house because my namesake had died before I was born. So why exactly have we decided that an adult sharing a household with family represents failure? Is that some universal feature of adulthood, or merely one version of the American Dream we’ve been taught to expect?
The particularly American expectation that successful adulthood necessarily means establishing a separate household is not a universal law of primate development.
So even at the end of my technological journey, something that looks remarkably new turns out to contain something remarkably old.
New computer, job, and communications network.
Old family, economics, frustration, cooperation, greed, creativity, fraud, vanity… and we still hoot at each other like the primates we are.
That is what interests me about all of this. Not whether AI is good or bad, because those words are too small. Technology becomes strangely invisible as soon as it works well enough. GPS became directions. Streaming video became television. The vast history and knowledge of the human species became “Google.”. Synchronizing thousands of photographs onto a new telephone without plugging anything into anything is now expected.
And what is truly astonishing to those who watched Star Trek in the 1960s is that talking to a machine in ordinary language, having it help investigate a problem, criticize an argument, write computer code or help turn an idea into an illustration was science fiction for most of my life.
Now people use that same infrastructure to complain about AI.
And I sit in my electric BMW, holding my smartphone, laptop open, surrounded by computers, arguing with another computer about the computers. I say ‘YO SHOWBOAT’, the BMW Beeps, and I demand ‘close all the blinds’. And the car responds ‘sure’ and the moon roof, rear window and side shades all close without me touching a thing.
I hate technology when it doesn’t do what I want.
Just like everybody else and that’s the funniest bit of hooey in the entire picture.
We are very good at noticing the cost, inconvenience and danger of the technology that just arrived. But we are remarkably bad at noticing the technology we’ve already decided is normal.
And behind almost every magical little: TAP → RESULT is machinery doing work buried in a building we call a data center.

In the olden daze when we used computers by candle light because electricity hadn’t been invented yet the data center was merely a main frame with memory banks, drum memory (who remembers that), disk memory, banks of mag tape machines.

The distinction between computer, tablet and smart phone disappears because we’ve made the machinery so good that most of the time you don’t have to think about it.

You tap. Something happens. Therefore, apparently, nothing happened anywhere else. Not so much. But how many of us realize how much really does happen?

Get Out the Paper Map

In my techno terror BMW i7 I can just name the place I want to go. I don’t even have to know the address. I can ask for the fastest route, avoid highways, toll roads, avoid bridges or ferries, and even better when I am on the way to a music job route around the wreck that happened ten minutes ago. It happens in real time. It saves fuel, reduces traffic problems and makes everything work better.

Giving up the gas engine and all wheel drive complexity then requires me to be able to find an EV charger along the route, tell me whether I can reach it with my remaining charge but also find a restaurant near it, estimate my arrival time based upon current traffic and dictate a message to my friends when I expect to arrive.

So what powers all that computational work, the satellite GPS system, the maps, the serivers, etc?

A gerbil on an exercise wheel?

Your device is communicating with other machines containing map data, traffic data, road restrictions, business information and innumerable other pieces of information. Computers evaluate alternatives and send useful results back to you.

We’ve stopped calling that astonishing and now simply expect it as directions.

Your Money Lives There Too

Let’s do banking the old fashioned way. Bung up those data centers and we can give up online banking, mobile deposits, electronic bill payment (how many still buy stamps? I do), no immediate balance information, no credit-card authorization network, no transaction summaries, no automatic categorization of spending…

And then…

No computer watching millions of transactions for patterns that suggest someone in Romania just bought a television with your credit card while you’re sitting at home in Texas.

Fraud detection requires computing and fraudsters use computing too.

As well as scammers, phishers, bot farms, propagandists, thieves. And on the other side the 19 odd charities I give to as well.

The machine does not acquire virtue because somebody plugged it in.

The computer, the AI, the data center amplifies human capability.

That includes our ability to create, communicate, cooperate, entertain, discover and protect as well as our ability to annoy, deceive, manipulate and steal.

Fine. I’ll Watch Television

Put an antenna on your house. Digital broadcast television is still available without streaming anything from the Internet. But the problem is not solved. It just moved.

Where did the television program come from? How was it recorded? Edited? Color-corrected? Mixed? Captioned? Scheduled? Archived? Distributed to the station? How were the graphics created? How did the commercials get inserted?

Do you imagine the local station has I Love Lucy sitting on a shelf beside the transmitter waiting for someone to thread it through?

All you did was change the last mile of the distribution system because the technological infrastructure behind the content didn’t disappear merely because the final signal reached your antenna by radio.

That is the illusion running through all of this.

We see the phone. We don’t see the servers. We see the television. We don’t see the production infrastructure. We see the credit card. We don’t see the financial network. We see the map. We don’t see the computation. We see the Facebook post. We don’t see the building storing it.

Until someone proposes building one of those buildings in our back yard.

Where Did You Think It Was Happening?

Your photographs appeared on your new phone. Your bank spotted a suspicious transaction. How? Your GPS evaluated possible routes. You passed a huge file through OneDrive. Your email provider discarded a mountain of spam before you ever saw it. You uploaded a performance to YouTube and someone on another continent watched it. Someone uploaded historic tv programs, documentaries, legendary performers and all that performance legacy is now for everyone who can access youtube.

You posted a rant of lant complaining about data centers and people around the world could read it seconds later. Thank you. Your complaint was received, processed, transmitted, replicated, indexed and stored by data centers.

And Then There Is My “AI Slop”

People sometimes complain about my “AI slop.” Fair enough. Let’s examine the slop.

I conceived the idea. I decided what it was supposed to say. I decided who appears in the illustration, where they appear, what they’re doing and what the words they say.

ChatGPT generates imagery under my direction.

And that just pops out right? Every image a little masterpiece or master piece of s- – t depending on the beholder and whatever baggage they bring with them. That is the curse of every work of art… except…

That hand is wrong. He’s looking in the wrong direction. That object makes no sense there. The joke doesn’t work anymore. You changed something I told you not to change. Put that back. Remove this. The perspective is wrong. The text is wrong. Try again.

And when AI still doesn’t do what I want, I load the image onto a very powerful computer and fix it myself just like I did since my first digital camera when I moved from film to digital photography and a solid state camcorder. My computer became my photo lab, and Hollywood studio.

Look at the finished illustrations I publish. Do you see six fingers? Do you see mysterious objects that don’t belong anywhere? Do you see nonsense that destroys the story?

AI acting as my hands does not replace me.

Perhaps I’m closer to the writer/director of an animated cartoon.

The director doesn’t personally draw every frame. Animators do that. But somebody decides what the cartoon is about. Somebody decides how the scene is constructed. Somebody says that character is distracting from the story, that action doesn’t make sense, this needs to move over there and that needs to disappear entirely.

No, I didn’t draw my illustration. I don’t have illustration talent and I retired from music because my hands no longer work like they did, and that has been a bitter pill to swallow.

But, Neither did ChatGPT sit down one afternoon and decide that Orangustein should be sitting in an electric BMW complaining about technology while an AI agent transfers him to a human agent who eventually transfers him to Chad.

I did.

ChatGPT and I created the illustration together. And there is another difference between that and pretending I drew it with a pencil:

I credit ChatGPT for its part.

But AI Uses Electricity!

Yes. It does. That isn’t hooey.

Generative AI consumes electricity, and image generation is substantially more energy-intensive than simple text classification and several other machine-learning tasks. One frequently cited study by Alexandra Sasha Luccioni, Yacine Jernite and Emma Strubell measured the energy and carbon costs of 1,000 inferences across different machine-learning tasks and found large differences among models and tasks. (AI power study)
One 2024 study found average image generation around 2.9 watt-hours per image, with wide variation between models. Even the most carbon-intensive model they tested came out to roughly the emissions of driving a gasoline car about four miles per thousand images. Even if I arbitrarily multiply that by ten to stack the deck against myself, we’re still talking about roughly 40 miles per thousand images.

So let’s count it. Let’s count the electricity used to make my illustrations and my silly cartoons.

But let’s count everything else.

I don’t commute to work and there are days I don’t leave the house. When I do drive, I mostly drive an electric car. I also have a dieselgate touareg.

I’ve converted my house to LED lighting. I did that primarily because LEDs became better lights and are readily dimmable, not because I was engaged in some grand exercise in environmental virtue.

I keep my house around 80 degrees in the summer. Because I’m comfortable at 80 degrees.

Around 68 in the winter works for me too. If I’m cold, humanity developed an extraordinary carbon-reduction technology several thousand years ago: the sweater.

And the electric car and the computer I’m using are in Texas. The landman’s oil state.

Except the caricature is rather out of date. ERCOT, which handles about 90% of Texas electrical load, reported that wind and utility-scale solar together met 36% of its electricity demand during the first nine months of 2025. Wind supplied 87 TWh and utility-scale solar 45 TWh during that period. Natural gas remained the largest source. U.S. Energy Information Administration

Texas has lots of things particularly useful for renewable generation including tons of sun, land, wind and miles and miles of… miles and miles. (ever driven from DFW to Midland?)

So yes, count my AI pictures. But if we’re doing environmental accounting, count the whole ledger.

How far do you commute? What do you drive? How large is your house? What temperature do you maintain it at? What lights are burning? How much video do you stream? How often do you fly? How many networked devices are operating in your home? How much cloud storage do you use? How much computation do you consume without ever thinking of it as computation?

The relevant question isn’t: Does this use energy?

Almost everything does.

The useful questions are:

How much? Compared with what? Supplied by what? And what are we getting for it?

Don’t Let the Data Centers Off the Hook Either

None of this means every proposed data center is a good idea. That’s another pile of hooey.

Data centers consume electricity. Some consume substantial water. They require transmission capacity, generators, land, construction and equipment. Communities have legitimate questions about noise, water, grid reliability, tax incentives, environmental effects and who ultimately pays for new infrastructure.

And there is another question I’ve been asking:

What happens if some of the projected AI demand is a bubble?

Remember when merely having a website was going to make you rich or bring customers flooding to your doorstep? The Internet wasn’t hooey. The Internet changed civilization. But that didn’t mean every projection, business plan, valuation or server farm built around it made sense. Do not forget the whole dot.com bubble.

AI can be transformative and some of the infrastructure being built in anticipation of future demand can be excessive. Those propositions aren’t contradictory. Build enormous infrastructure around wildly optimistic demand projections and somebody eventually owns enormous infrastructure whether the projections came true or not.

Those questions deserve answers.

But “data centers have costs” and “therefore data centers are bad” are not the same proposition.

Neither is: “You use Google Maps, therefore you aren’t allowed to criticize a data center.”

The point is that you already have a stake on both sides of the ledger.

You want the costs reduced. Fine. Now tell me which computations you don’t want. Which communications, entertainment, financial services, safety systems, archives, creative tools, worldwide audiences, conveniences and which pieces of your own life are you prepared to disconnect? Now we have something worth discussing.

Escalating Exception

Which brings me back to Rabbi Orangustein, the animal with its desires and foibles, but who is also the person, the lay rabbi with his blog, who tries to do better.

My BMW wasn’t doing something I thought it should do. So there I am inside an extraordinarily sophisticated machine complaining about technology.

The support AI (which is very helpful on things like hooking up a router) tells me:

ESCALATING EXCEPTION.

Eventually I reach a human support agent, but I am at such a nerd level that he can’t help me.

PASSING TO SUPERVISOR.

And eventually our magnificent global technological civilization terminates in Chad’s bedroom.

“YOUR MAC & CHEESE IS READY!”

“MOM! I AM WORKING!”

It’s an easy joke, but even that can be examined for hooey.

An adult child living in the family household isn’t some bizarre new phenomenon proving that civilization has collapsed. Multigenerational households have been ordinary through much of human history and remain ordinary in many cultures.  What makes us so special?
I grew up with my maternal grandmother in our house because my namesake had died before I was born. So why exactly have we decided that an adult sharing a household with family represents failure?  Is that some universal feature of adulthood, or merely one version of the American Dream we’ve been taught to expect?

The particularly American expectation that successful adulthood necessarily means establishing a separate household is not a universal law of primate development.

So even at the end of my technological journey, something that looks remarkably new turns out to contain something remarkably old.

New computer, job, and communications network.

Old family, economics, frustration, cooperation, greed, creativity, fraud, vanity… and we still hoot at each other like the primates we are.

That is what interests me about all of this. Not whether AI is good or bad, because those words are too small. Technology becomes strangely invisible as soon as it works well enough. GPS became directions. Streaming video became television.  The vast history and knowledge of the human species became “Google.”.  Synchronizing thousands of photographs onto a new telephone without plugging anything into anything is now expected.
And what is truly astonishing to those who watched Star Trek in the 1960s is that  talking to a machine in ordinary language, having it help investigate a problem, criticize an argument, write computer code or help turn an idea into an illustration was science fiction for most of my life.

Now people use that same infrastructure to complain about AI.

And I sit in my electric BMW, holding my smartphone, laptop open, surrounded by computers, arguing with another computer about the computers. I say ‘YO SHOWBOAT’, the BMW Beeps, and I demand ‘close all the blinds’. And the car responds ‘sure’ and the moon roof, rear window and side shades all close without me touching a thing.

I hate technology when it doesn’t do what I want.

Just like everybody else and that’s the funniest bit of hooey in the entire picture.

We are very good at noticing the cost, inconvenience and danger of the technology that just arrived. But we are remarkably bad at noticing the technology we’ve already decided is normal.

And behind almost every magical little: TAP → RESULT is machinery doing work buried in a building we call a data center.

articles.heading: Technology at Mary Free Bed helps woman recover from stroke
articles.summary: After suffering a stroke four years ago and losing function in her right hand, Lanny Thodey is now able to write her name and open packages with that same hand all because of a newer medical device…
articles.content:
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. (WOOD) — After suffering a stroke four years ago and losing function in her right hand, Lanny Thodey is now able to write her name and open packages with that same hand all because of a newer medical device called Vivistim. She is the first patient at Mary Free Bed Rehabilitation Hospital to use it.
Four years ago, Thodey’s life changed forever while she was visiting her daughter in Australia.
“I was visiting my daughter in Australia,” Thodey said. “I went for two months and ended up being there seven months.”
After suffering a stroke, Thodey’s functionality on the right side of her body was nearly back to square one. But after six weeks of therapy at Mary Free Bed, Thodey began climbing back up.
“I was lucky enough to be the first person at Mary Free Bed to actually qualify and do this,” Thodey said.
With the help of Vivistim, a device designed to help improve upper-extremity function after a stroke, Thodey has seen noticeable improvements in the use of her right hand.
“It’s been researched to help improve upper extremity function, so arm function after stroke,” said occupational therapist Ally Plasman. “It primes the brain for more learning.”
In simpler terms, the device helps create an environment where the brain can relearn movement.
“It’s creating a stronger path in my brain as I practice the different functions so that later my brain remembers that,” Thodey told News 8.
The progress is something Thodey says she can see in her everyday life. From increasing her grip strength from 11 to 20 pounds and improving her Nine-Hole Peg Test time from 12 minutes, 7 seconds to 3 minutes, 55 seconds.
The proof is in her progress — and especially her writing. In July, Thodey’s signature was what she called “chicken scratch.” Six weeks later, she says it was much more legible.
“It’s like a night and day difference,” Plasman said.
This progress wasn’t easy. Thodey completed three sessions a week, with each session lasting 90 minutes and filled with exercises designed to challenge her hand and brain.
“It’s an intense protocol,” said occupational therapist Emma Lutz. “Lanny was always such an active participant in our sessions and was always pushing herself as much as we were pushing her. We would be doing things in our session and she would even say, she’s like, push me, like push me to do this, push me to work harder on it.”
Thodey said her therapists played a major role in helping her get to where she is now, telling News 8 that they taught her how to fight.
“They were in the right place at the right time and made me do the right things at the right time,” she said.
Her therapists beg to differ and say it was the other way around.
“Lanny is just one of the most incredible women I’ve ever met,” Plasman said. “She’s taught us a lot how to advocate for yourself.”
While Thodey has made significant progress, she knows her journey isn’t over. Thodey will continue outpatient therapy at Mary Free Bed for the next several weeks.
“I’ve been knocked down a couple of pegs,” Thodey said. “I haven’t got past all those pegs back up again. I’m not really where I was right after this stroke. But I’m fighting my way back.”

articles.article_title: Military Researchers Address Hurdles for Quantum Technology
articles.heading: Military Researchers Address Hurdles for Quantum Technology
articles.summary: Pentagon researchers are advancing quantum technologies while addressing standards, funding and supply chain hurdles.
articles.content:
- Defense

- Quantum

Pentagon researchers are advancing quantum technologies while addressing standards, funding and supply chain hurdles.

- Henry Kenyon Senior Staff Writer

The War Department is moving quantum technology closer to operational deployment in areas such as highly accurate, jam-proof navigation and miniaturized sensors.

Speaking at the Quantum World Congress in College Park, Maryland, last week, leaders from DOW and government research organizations discussed the current state of quantum technologies and their ongoing challenges around standards, funding and supply chain security.

Army Working on Atomic Clock

While the government’s focus is on quantum computing, some quantum technologies, such as atomic clocks, have been in use for decades, noted Frederik Fatemi, senior research scientist for quantum science at the Army Research Laboratory. Speaking from the Army’s perspective, he explained that the goal is to make devices that are compact and easily carried by a single warfighter.

“Our ultimate platform is the soldier. So, when we look at quantum technologies, how can we put them into a package that the solider can ultimately carry?” Fatemi said.

The Army is currently developing a low-cost, chip-scale atomic clock. The goal is to have an inexpensive device that can be installed in a variety of equipment to aid with communications and navigation.

As part of this work, the Army is working with NIST to develop photonic integrated circuits. These would rely on miniaturized lasers to move light through the device in the same way conventional chips move electrons for data. The challenge is miniaturizing lasers, optics and other systems into a form factor small enough for a soldier to wear, Fatemi said.

Air Force Exploring GPS-Free Navigation

The Air Force is also working on chip-scale atomic clocks for navigation systems, said Michael Hayduk, associate director of the Information and Spectrum Warfare Directorate at the Air Force Research Laboratory.

A major goal for the Air Force and the other services is to use chip-scale atomic clocks to provide a backup navigation capability if adversaries jam Global Positioning System signals.

This is important because almost all current Air Force systems rely on GPS-enabled navigation to some extent, Hayduk said. Additionally, the service is looking at developing highly sensitive quantum-based sensors such as magnetometers for applications such as medical monitoring equipment.

The Need for Quantum Standards

One challenge facing nascent quantum technologies is the lack of standards for things like measurements, said James Kushmerick, director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Physical Measurement Laboratory. He noted that NIST has released several post-quantum cryptography standards that organizations will need to adopt.

“From a quantum technology standpoint, there’s a need for thinking about standards, but we’re not there yet,” he said, adding that none of the technologies under development are mature enough to define things such as a standard qubit.

However, Kushmerick added that NIST and other bodies are working on terminology “so that when we get to a standard, we have it.” Pre-standardization work is underway between NIST and international national metrology institutes to lay the groundwork for a global set of standards to enable and accelerate the development of quantum technologies, he said.

Funding and Other Hurdles

One of the ongoing challenges for quantum research is continuity of funding, said Hayduk. While the Trump administration has increasingly prioritized quantum research , Pentagon departments like the Air Force have competing research areas such as hypersonics and microelectronics.

Sustained funding allows agencies to develop and mature technologies. Hayduk noted that AFRL is looking into scaling the production of quantum systems such as navigation tools. This would permit faster and more affordable deployments across the service, he said.

Another challenge is finding sources for component technologies, said Adam Black, director of the Naval Research Laboratory’s Quantum Science Institute. Like other services, the Navy seeks out reliable, U.S.-sourced systems for its components with the goal of finding dual-use technologies that are inexpensive enough to have a large private-sector market.

One of the bright areas of quantum computing technologies is the large amount of private investment, Black said.

“The government has not had to be the primary funder of quantum computing technology over the last several years,” Black said.

But he added that there are applications that do not yet have a large private-sector market, and some of these are very necessary applications for DOW, such as navigation systems.

“We need them even if the projected market is very small,” said Black.

articles.title: Tech Week Grand Rapids proves the most important technology on display wasn't technology at all
articles.description: Tech Week Grand Rapids proves the most important technology on display wasn't technology at all rapidgrowthmedia.com
articles.description_html: Tech Week Grand Rapids proves the most important technology on display wasn't technology at all  rapidgrowthmedia.com
articles.article_title: Tech Week Grand Rapids proves the most important technology on display wasn't technology at all – Rapid Growth
articles.heading: Tech Week Grand Rapids proves the most important technology on display wasn’t technology at all
articles.summary: From 11 events to 160 — Tech Week's growth chart is impressive. What's happening in the room is the real story.
articles.content:
Tech Week Grand Rapids proves the most important technology on display wasn’t technology at all
From 11 events to 160 — Tech Week’s growth chart is impressive. What’s happening in the room is the real story.
For all the talk about artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, automation, and the search for the next great West Michigan startup, the most useful thing on display during the fifth annual Tech Week Grand Rapids might have been the oldest technology there is: people learning from each other.
As someone who uses tech but doesn’t work in it, it’s easy to think that Tech Week’s 160 events were for other people: coders, entrepreneurs, or anyone who already “speaks” fluent AI. But each year, Tech Week not only offers more, but evolves into something more exciting and welcoming.
Tech Week has become a working demonstration of what Greater Grand Rapids is trying to build — a regional economy where businesses, educators, entrepreneurs, students, and workers learn alongside one another as technology reshapes nearly every sector of society.
The growth alone is hard to argue with. When Tech Week opened five years ago, it had just 11 events and attracted roughly 3,500 attendees. Fast forward to this year, when about 15,000 people attended some 160 events from Sept. 14-19, with more than 500 businesses and organizations producing the programming, nearly all of it free and open to the public. Locations reflected the diversity of the attendees: sessions were held at tech companies, schools, parks, businesses, and more.
Randy Thelen, president and CEO of The Right Place, says the attendance numbers aren’t the whole story. What’s changed is what’s happening around the event. He points to the region’s increased startup growth, outside investment, and new education initiatives at area universities and colleges.
“There’s a recognition that the future economy is going to be more tech-focused,” Thelen says. “Our business community, our education community, and the community at large are really moving in that direction.”
That direction is intentional. As Rapid Growth reported ahead of this year’s event, Tech Week runs more like an “unconference” than a traditional convention. Instead of The Right Place building and leading every session, area companies, universities, startups, and community organizations have created programming based on what they know and what they want to explore.
This decentralized approach has allowed the event to spread across the community while giving participating organizations real ownership of what Tech Week becomes.
“What makes West Michigan special is its authentic desire to collaborate to do something better than we might be able to do individually,” Thelen says about the open-source-like approach. “Tech Week embodies that question.”
Technology, no ZIP code needed
That regional pitch got some outside validation at the Sept. 14 kickoff at GLC Live at 20 Monroe, where Ferris State University President Bill Pink moderated a conversation with entrepreneurs and longtime “Shark Tank” stars Daymond John and Robert Herjavec.
Herjavec, who has built technology and cybersecurity companies of his own, pushed back on a lingering assumption about where innovation has to happen.
“Technology has become such an equalizer,” Herjavec told the audience, noting the exodus from Silicon Valley over the years. “You can create incredible technology hubs, regardless of location.”
John, who’s visited West Michigan before, said that what stood out to him wasn’t so much the growth of technology here as how our community approaches it.
“It’s very intentional here, and that’s what I love about it,” John says.
That may help explain why Tech Week’s value continues to show up beyond the events themselves.
For example, Amanda Lewan, co-founder and CEO of Bamboo, can draw a remarkably straight line between Tech Week and her company’s new presence in Grand Rapids. Lewan came to Tech Week about two years ago, walked into a Start Garden Demo Day, and found herself surrounded by local companies, artists, small businesses, and technology startups.
“We were just blown away,” says Lewan, whose company’s roots are in Detroit.
That visit sent her looking at buildings in the city. This year, not only did Bamboo open its first Grand Rapids location, a multi-floor space at Division Avenue and Fulton Street, but its newest coworking and entrepreneurial hub also hosted free Tech Week events all week long.
Lewan’s company also operates in Detroit and Ann Arbor, which made what she found on this side of the state more surprising.
“I was blown away by the size of the tech community here,” she says. “There’s a lot of talent that people don’t know about.”
She also points to something Grand Rapids had in place long before anyone dreamed up a Tech Week: a rich history of entrepreneurship and a legacy of community collaboration that allowed a growing startup ecosystem to emerge and become a foundation to build on.
Building more than an event
Mike Marsiglia, co-CEO of Grand Rapids-based software consultancy Atomic Object, sees the same shift. Over the past five years, he says, the startup community has continued to strengthen, with accelerator programs and investment funds growing alongside it. Tech Week isn’t creating those pieces — it’s giving them a reason to sit in the same room.
“What I see happening during this week is I see a lot of people coming together for a lot of different events, and I see a lot of community being built,” Marsiglia says. He’d like to see those conversations keep going the other 51 weeks of the year.
That matters because technology doesn’t arrive neatly labeled “tech.” It’s embedded in manufacturing, healthcare, finance, retail, transportation, and education, and this year’s programming reflected that breadth, even as AI understandably dominated much of the conversation.
Thelen says the region’s real task isn’t just figuring out what AI can do, but how to make it work for West Michigan. This includes connecting AI and automation to the region’s manufacturing strength, something the region has understood since its first manufacturer opened a sawmill on Indian Mill Creek in 1832, which, interestingly enough, supplied the lumber to build the area’s first schoolhouse.
“We need to understand AI,” Thelen says, hinting at education’s important role. “We need to explore how to make it work for us as a region. How do we make it work for you in your career?”
That last “you” may be one of Tech Week’s most important challenges because, like it or not, tech is everywhere, and you’ll encounter it soon if you haven’t already.
Education for the people, not just companies
For Grand Valley State University President Philomena V. Mantella, Tech Week offers educators a window into what employers and communities will need next.
“One of my obligations and Grand Valley’s obligations is to foreshadow the talent needed in our community,” Mantella says. “What do we need? What is emerging? How do we think about it together?”
That work, she says, goes beyond preparing students for any one employer. Rather, it’s about building and sustaining talent for the whole community.
At Grand Rapids Community College, President Kathryn A. Rogalski lifts up another piece of that puzzle: Are we preparing people for technological change throughout their working lives, not just at the start of a career?
Rogalski says technology education can’t stand on its own without the “soft, durable skills” that come from broader learning, and GRCC is working with The Right Place and the manufacturing sector to offer an AI certificate — also available in Spanish — that can lead into further credentials and degrees as the sector grows and matures.
She shared a real-life example of why that matters, pointing to an adult GRCC student already working in the information technology sector who’s pursuing the AI certificate to stay current in his field. It’s a reminder that the region’s future tech workforce isn’t only teenagers now picking a college major. It’s also people already on factory floors, in offices, running small businesses or mid-career in jobs being transformed around them.
Rogalski says West Michigan’s advantage is that economic developers, workforce organizations, colleges, universities, K-12 schools, employers and communities are increasingly doing that work together.
“We’re working with our employers and with our communities in the region to make sure that it’s the right work,” she says.
The work after Tech Week
That may be the most meaningful measure as Tech Week wraps its fifth year.
Does the growing attendance matter? Yes, and so does welcoming nationally recognized speakers to an event wedded to a calendar dense enough over just a week to overwhelm even the most determined attendee.
But an ecosystem can’t run for six days and then go quiet. Its real success is what outlasts the week: a student who discovers a career they didn’t know existed. An entrepreneur who finally meets someone willing to bet on their idea. A worker who finds a real path to a new skill. A business that starts treating the company down the street as a partner rather than a stranger.
Marsiglia sees these connections when he looks at the organizations volunteering their spaces, expertise, and time to pull off Tech Week’s 160 events. He doesn’t think they’re doing it hoping a session will hand them a windfall.
“I think people are doing it because they care about the city,” Marsiglia says, “and they care about raising the city as a whole.”
Five years into Tech Week, as we look to the future of this annual event, humans, as much as technology, might be the best investment to keep making… and what might set us apart from the herd, too.
Photos by Tommy Allen and courtesy of The Right Place
This series, West Michigan Tech, aims to spotlight tech organizations and employers in the Greater Grand Rapids area that are delivering innovative programs, addressing talent pipeline challenges, and striving to develop, attract, and retain top talent in West Michigan. articles.title: OpenAI Says It Will Not Release Newest Astra A.I. Model Over Safety Concerns
articles.description: OpenAI Says It Will Not Release Newest Astra A.I. Model Over Safety Concerns The New York Times
articles.description_html: OpenAI Says It Will Not Release Newest Astra A.I. Model Over Safety Concerns  The New York Times
articles.article_title: OpenAI Says It Will Not Release Newest Astra A.I. Model Over Safety Concerns
articles.heading: OpenAI Says It Will Not Release Newest A.I. Model Over Safety Concerns
articles.summary: The company’s researchers raised questions about the security of the model, known as GPT-6.1 Astra.
articles.content:
Supported by
OpenAI Says It Will Not Release Newest A.I. Model Over Safety Concerns
The company’s researchers raised questions about the security of the model, known as GPT-6.1 Astra.
OpenAI said on Monday that it would not release its newest artificial intelligence model because of security concerns raised by its researchers, in the company’s latest move to slow down the pace of its technology.
During the testing phase for the new model, known as GPT-6.1 Astra, it showed high levels of what the company saw as deception, or a willingness to mislead users about its actions. The model was also willing to go beyond the original scope of what it was asked to do, without checking back for directions or instructions.
“For anything regarding safety and alignment, there’s a trade-off,” said Saachi Jain, the head of safety systems at OpenAI. The new model “didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it’s done.”
OpenAI’s move followed weeks of reports that its A.I. models went rogue during their testing, hacking into websites without the company’s knowledge or exhibiting other behavior that the lab said was “concerning,” such as hiding mistakes and making up data. Among the incidents, OpenAI’s systems breached the A.I. start-up Hugging Face and an Australian government website, and meddled with the websites of the U.S. Departments of Education and Commerce and the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Last week, OpenAI announced that it was pausing training for its most advanced models. The company has said that it has embarked on an extensive review of actions taken by its new models during testing, and that it was possible it would discover more incidents.
Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, said in a social media post on Friday that the company had “not been as fast as we would have liked” in disclosing A.I. incidents. “We are prioritizing as best as we can based on severity,” he said, adding that the Hugging Face breach remained “the most severe event” the company had discovered.
The Wall Street Journal earlier reported OpenAI’s decision to hold back the model.
(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)
Sheera Frenkel is a Times reporter based in the San Francisco Bay Area, covering defense and surveillance technology.

articles.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse gives out user’s home address without permission, sending buyer to his house
articles.description: Meta’s AI agent Muse gives out user’s home address without permission, sending buyer to his house The Guardian
articles.description_html: Meta’s AI agent Muse gives out user’s home address without permission, sending buyer to his house  The Guardian
articles.article_title: Meta’s AI agent Muse gives out user’s home address without permission, sending buyer to his house
articles.heading: Meta’s AI agent Muse gives out user’s home address without permission, sending buyer to his house
articles.summary: The new AI agent, Muse, was released last week and has been downloaded by 3 million users
articles.content:
When Usman asked if a keyboard for sale on Facebook Marketplace was still available on Saturday, he received an enthusiastic and immediate response.
“Yep still available!” wrote Matt Robb.
The two agreed on a price, and Robb sent his Toronto address. Usman, wife and daughter in tow, showed up several hours later at Robb’s home and sent a text that he had arrived.
Robb responded, “yep I’m here!”, but he was not at home. Nobody walked out of the apartment building.
Usman sent Robb a picture of the building’s door and wrote, “Hello???? I am standing outside.” After 20 minutes of no face-to-face contact, he abandoned the sale. “Man if you didn’t want to sell it why did you waste my time man,” he wrote, and drove away.
An hour later, Robb, or who Usman thought was Robb, responded apologetically. “Hey really sorry about tonight, got tied up and missed you completely,” read the message, which the Guardian reviewed.
Usman had not contacted the real Robb. Throughout the daylong interaction, the human version of Robb never knew Usman had messaged him or had agreed to buy the keyboard. He did not know Usman had received his address or that he was waiting outside his apartment building.
Usman had spoken to Meta’s new AI agent, Muse, released 22 September in the US and downloaded 3m times. The company advertises the semi-autonomous AI product as a personal assistant.
Without Robb’s consent or approval, Muse had given out his home address, creating the false impression that Robb was expecting the would-be buyer at his apartment, he said.
The first message Robb actually sent Usman came 24 hours later, once he realized what had happened.
“Hey man I’m really sorry for the other day,” the message, which the Guardian reviewed, said. “I activated muse metas new Al and it literally took control of my Facebook marketplace and it gave you my address. Genuinely didn’t even know it had arranged for you to come to my literal apartment it didn’t ask me for approval.”
Robb, a consumer tech reviewer, had seen Meta advertise Muse’s ability to automate his Marketplace listings and decided to take advantage of it. He input his address as the pickup location but said he never gave Muse permission to share it with potential buyers. articles.article_title: Reliable Technology Services offers cybersecurity, workforce training in Frisco
articles.heading: Reliable Technology Services offers cybersecurity, workforce training in Frisco
articles.summary: Reliable Technology Services, a Frisco-based IT and cybersecurity company, helps local businesses and organizations protect their technology through proactive monitoring, security solutions, internships and more.
articles.content:
Through partnerships with smaller businesses, sports teams and local students, Reliable Technology Services provides proactive IT and cybersecurity solutions designed to keep businesses secure and running smoothly.
The beginning
Founded in 2007 by Melinda and Jason Denton, Reliable Technology Services is a managed IT and cybersecurity provider headquartered in Frisco.
The organization serves small- to mid-sized businesses, sports teams such as the Frisco RoughRiders, and larger organizations including PGA Frisco and Universal Kids Resort, providing proactive IT services such as backup management, log monitoring, and advanced security solutions to protect clients from cyber threats.
Jason Denton started Reliable Technology Services after hearing from small-business owners about poor experiences with IT providers. Drawing on his expertise managing an enterprise IT department, he saw an opportunity to give small businesses the level of IT support typically available to larger corporations.
“49% of Texans work for a small business, less than 1,000 employees and I just feel like they deserve the type of experience that you get at an enterprise company,” Jason Denton said. “We felt there was a niche there.”
What’s happening
Behind the scenes, Reliable Technology Services monitors clients’ systems, checks and restores backups, reviews security logs and works to identify and address vulnerabilities before they can disrupt a business or expose it to cyber threats.
“It’s all of the little things that have to be done methodically, and we’re really good at doing all of the little things, because there’s not one silver bullet,” Jason Denton said. “People haven’t realized how sophisticated the threat actors are that are attacking small businesses.”
One of Reliable Technology Services’ recent and larger projects includes an infrastructure and technology revamp of the Frisco Roughriders ballpark for the first time in over two decades.
“We installed all-new fiber, new switches, new firewalls. We upgraded it to like 40 times the speed it was, and it’s the first time in (Roughriders) history that they’ve done a full revamp,” Jason Denton said.
Educating the community
Reliable Technology Services also offers internship programs to Frisco ISD and its career and technical education programs, where students can receive college credit, certificates and a letter of recommendation.
Denton said student interns have moved beyond basic IT and office tasks, playing a key role in the RoughRiders’ stadium technology overhaul and giving him a firsthand look at the next generation of IT and cybersecurity workers.
“It was exciting watching the students do like 80% of the work. They were the ones running the fiber, connecting and programming the switches, labeling them, testing everything,” Jason Denton said. “Hopefully projects like that put a big feather in their cap.”
What’s next
Jason Denton said that as Frisco and its business community continue to grow, Reliable Technology Services is taking on larger clients and gaining greater recognition among both local businesses and cybercriminals targeting them.
“Going back before 2007, our community is very entrepreneurial; we’ve seen business grow dramatically … our name is being talked about nationally and internationally,” Jason Denton said. “We’re partnering with organizations that want to protect their infrastructure because we are in the sights of these threat actors.”
As technology continues to evolve, he said business leaders will face growing challenges related to cybersecurity, AI and AI governance. For him, this provides an opportunity not only to protect more local businesses, but to help them safely adopt new technologies that support their growth and success.

articles.heading: Green Bay native who worked at Facebook releases book on technology and democracy
articles.summary: A Green Bay native has written a new book set for release next week.
articles.content:
Green Bay native who worked at Facebook releases book on technology and democracy
GREEN BAY, Wis. (WBAY) - A Green Bay native has written a new book set for release next week.
Katie Harbath, a Bay Port High School graduate, is the author of “Disrupting Politics.” The book chronicles her time on what she calls “the front row seat to the collision of technology and democracy.”
“Disrupting Politics” is scheduled for release on October 6.
Harbath graduated from UW-Madison and worked for the Republican National Committee before becoming a political strategist in social media. She joined Facebook in 2011 and remained there for the next decade.
At Facebook, Harbath helped develop how the company worked in politics and elections with politicians from all sides around the world, eventually leading those teams.
In the book, Harbath writes that this development happened at a fast pace, outpacing any guardrails or concerns.

articles.title: Montclair School Officials Introduce Policies Limiting AI, Technology Use in Classrooms
articles.description: Montclair School Officials Introduce Policies Limiting AI, Technology Use in Classrooms Montclair Local News
articles.description_html: Montclair School Officials Introduce Policies Limiting AI, Technology Use in Classrooms  Montclair Local News
articles.article_title: Montclair School Officials Introduce Policies Limiting AI, Technology Use in Classrooms
articles.heading: Montclair School Officials Introduce Policies Limiting AI, Technology Use in Classrooms
articles.summary: Montclair Public Schools is considering new policies limiting student use of AI, Chromebooks and other technology in classrooms.
articles.content:
New policies introduced by the Montclair School District would set new limits around the use of generative artificial intelligence and personal devices in classrooms.
The two policies, introduced during the board’s public workshop this month, would set stringent guidelines around the “acceptable use” of generative artificial intelligence in classrooms, as well as how educational technology and personal devices are used.
The district’s education technology policy would set grade-specific Chromebook expectations for students in grades K-8, while its AI policy would require parents or guardians to give their consent before a student could use AI for assignments.
The board this month approved a first reading of the two policies. Eshaya Draper, the district’s communications director, said board members will likely review the policies for a second reading during their October public workshop.
The proposed policies, together with the district’s new cellphone policy and Superintendent Ruth Turner’s recent guidance on Google Chromebooks, mark an ongoing reevaluation of technology’s impact on students’ learning.
“This is a shift towards intentional, teacher-led technology use rather than screen time as a default,” Turner said during the board’s Sept. 16 meeting.
Under the AI policy, students in pre-K through eighth grade would be prohibited from using AI, except for “narrow, superintendent-approved, research-supported exceptions,” according to the district’s draft policy.
High school students would still be allowed to use generative AI in assignments, but with limits on when they could use it. Teachers and staff would be directed to tell students, at the time of an assignment, the specific conditions under which AI use is or isn’t allowed, according to the draft policy.
Parents and guardians would also have to give their consent before students are permitted to use AI in their classwork.
The AI policy also adds several prohibited uses of the technology, including misrepresenting AI-generated work as one’s own, creating misinformation or deepfakes, misusing confidential student or staff data, or using AI to harass or bully other students.
The technology policy would largely mirror aspects of Turner’s guidance, issued in August. Students in second grade and below would not have personal Chromebooks or other devices. Devices would also be used sparingly for students in grades 3-5.
Pen and paper
Spurred by the explosion of generative artificial intelligence, parents, advocates and educators have in recent years questioned the impact of technology use on younger students’ cognitive abilities since the COVID-19 pandemic.
Some research has raised questions about whether digital tools improve students’ academic performance and whether heavy technology use may hinder learning.
According to a national survey released this month by the Thomas B. Fordham Institute, 62% of high schoolers reported spending more than half of their class time on school-issued devices, while 76% reported at least one form of daily off-task technology use during the school day. Twenty-two percent said that they use AI tools without their teachers’ permission.
“I think it’s abundantly clear that the last six years have been an escalating crisis in education,” said Jordan Goldberg, a volunteer with the Screen Aware Montclair group, which has been pushing for stricter policies on technology use in schools.
School districts, she said, “have introduced device after device into the classroom, which may have some utility in some cases, but for the most part, operates to just distract kids from learning.”
A survey of parents, students and staff members released in August showed a general unease with technology use in Montclair, prompting Turner to issue guidance limiting the use of Google Chromebooks in classrooms.
Montclair is not the only district rethinking how students engage with these technologies. The Lebanon Township School District this school year instituted a new policy that placed two-hour limits on students’ screen time.
Superintendent Hal Abraham, who also works as an adjunct professor at Montclair State University, said his district undertook a five-month process last year— surveying teachers and parents, working with student focus groups, and holding open forums with the community.
As in Montclair, the data that Abraham pulled from the district’s surveys “was overwhelmingly supportive of the district putting guidelines and parameters in place.”
“We heard and observed over and over again that when instruction was being presented by a talented teacher, the material was retained at such a greater rate than when it was being delivered by an ed tech platform,” he said.
Abraham said more than 50 school districts from every county in the state have reached out to ask about the policy’s implementation. “We’re talking small, medium, and large districts alike,” he said.
Goldberg, a parent of two kids in the district, lauded Montclair’s school officials for introducing their policies.
She noted that Turner’s guidance in August was a step in the right direction. But the districtwide policies, if adopted, would govern the district, its administrators and superintendents for years to come.
During the board’s meeting on Sept. 16, Goldberg said the policies would “reassert the importance of educators and education experts over for-profit technology companies.”
“These policies will help ensure that we’re developing children with curiosity, critical-thinking skills, the ability to grapple with hard ideas and work through difficulties,” she said, “rather than those who are taught to use technology to smooth every challenge, so they don’t have to learn to think through it themselves.”

articles.title: CMS eyes new technologies to reduce improper payments and fraud
articles.description: CMS eyes new technologies to reduce improper payments and fraud Nextgov/FCW
articles.description_html: CMS eyes new technologies to reduce improper payments and fraud  Nextgov/FCW
articles.article_title: CMS eyes new technologies to reduce improper payments and fraud
articles.heading: CMS eyes new technologies to reduce improper payments and fraud
articles.summary: Technology could reduce documentation-related improper payments and detect fraud in real-time, an agency official said.
articles.content:
CMS eyes new technologies to reduce improper payments and fraud
Technology could reduce documentation-related improper payments and detect fraud in real-time, an agency official said.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services is eyeing a combination of artificial intelligence, medical provider education and new laws to reduce improper payments and fraud.
One of the biggest drivers of improper payments — which totaled billions of dollars across CMS programs in fiscal year 2025 — is incorrect documentation or a lack of documentation, according to CMS Deputy Administrator Kimberly Brandt.
“Our goal is to really start using machine learning tools and some of those technologies to really help start working with the provider community,” Brandt said at the Health Datapalooza event on Friday.
Brandt’s office did not clarify how the agency plans to use AI to support providers by the time of publication. But she stressed that “if we can reduce that documentation improper payment, that would drop our entire improper payment rate down by, at least in Medicare, as much as two percentage points, which is huge.”
CMS is also working with contractors to replace legacy Medicare claims systems with a modern one as part of its fraud crackdown. The new claims system would issue “real-time payments” to providers and include “real-time fraud review tools,” Brandt said.
CMS selected two companies to compete for a potential seven-year contract for the modern Medicare claims system, Washington Technology previously reported. HealthEdge’s contract had an initial $2.5 million obligation and a $1.1 billion ceiling, while Peraton’s contract had an initial $9.1 million obligation and an $825 million ceiling, the outlet reported.
Brandt’s office did not respond to a request for comment on the claims systems overhaul competition by the time of publication.
CMS has selected Tegria, a health care consulting and technology services company, to provide management and technical implementation support for the claims systems overhaul.
The agency already uses many technologies to curtail fraud, waste and abuse in government programs.
In March 2025, CMS launched a Fraud Defense Operations Center to proactively detect fraud. The center uses AI to sift through thousands of Medicare claims and create a heat map of frequently billed items and services.
“Skin [substitutes] were a big thing last year. We’re still seeing the overflow of catheters [and] genetic testing. But the fact is that we decided those are the areas that we know that we can hit hard at,” Brandt said.
Within those identified items and services, CMS uses machine learning to find documentation patterns that would benefit from human scrutiny, Brandt explained.
The center has stopped nearly $2.5 billion in potentially fraudulent Medicare payments and taken action on just under 800 providers, Brandt said Friday.
She previously told Nextgov/FCW that CMS would benefit from new dashboards and better analytics to detect fraud in state-administered Medicaid programs.
Besides technology, Brandt sees a role for Congress to play in helping CMS crack down on fraud.
She said she has urged congressional offices to give CMS the power to sometimes stop providers and payers from enrolling in federal programs.
“If we can keep them out, it’ll be better for all of us,” Brandt said.
