articles.article_title: Marquis Who's Who Honors Tara Kallstrom for Expertise in Information Technology
articles.heading: Marquis Who's Who Honors Tara Kallstrom for Expertise in Information Technology
articles.summary: September 28, 2026 -- Tara Kallstrom is recognized as a distinguished technology leader with over three decades of experience aligning technology, solution sales and services, and strategic partnerships to accelerate growth and deliver measurable business outcomes
articles.content:
ATLANTA, GA, September 28, 2026 /24-7PressRelease/ -- Tara Kallstrom has been included in Marquis Who's Who. As in all Marquis Who's Who biographical volumes, individuals profiled are selected on the basis of current reference value. Factors such as position, noteworthy accomplishments, visibility, and prominence in a field are all taken into account during the selection process.
Recognized as an expert in Information Technology, Mrs. Kallstrom has established herself as a distinguished technology leader whose career has been defined by business transformation, commercial innovation, and solution-led growth across the global technology industry. For more than three decades, she has helped organizations fundamentally transform the way they create value for customers by aligning sales go-to-market strategy, managed and professional services, partner ecosystems, and customer success around measurable business outcomes. Her ability to bridge business strategy with emerging technologies has earned the trust of executive leadership teams navigating changing markets, evolving customer expectations, and supported decades of technology innovation.
Unlike many technology executives whose careers are concentrated within a single discipline, Mrs. Kallstrom has built an uncommon breadth of leadership experience spanning product management, solution engineering, sales, business development, customer success, marketing, sales operations, professional services, strategic partnerships, executive leadership, and go-to-market strategy. This unique perspective has enabled her to help organizations through all stages of commercial transformation—from traditional infrastructure and enterprise hardware to cloud computing, hosted and managed services, professional services, recurring subscription business models, and Everything-as-a-Service (XaaS).
Throughout her career, organizations have brought Mrs. Kallstrom in to lead transformational initiatives during periods of growth, organizational change, acquisitions, global expansion, and evolving technology business models. She has consistently helped organizations move beyond transactional technology sales to consultative, solution-led businesses that integrate technology, services, and strategic partnerships into cohesive customer solutions. Her leadership has enabled organizations to modernize commercial operations, accelerate traditional resale and partner-led recurring revenue strategies, strengthen partner ecosystems, and deliver long-term customer value in increasingly complex technology markets and procurement options.
A defining characteristic of Mrs. Kallstrom's leadership has been her ability to bring together technology manufacturers, distributors, solution providers, professional sales and services organizations, executive stakeholders, and strategic partners around opportunities extending well beyond traditional bilateral relationships. By building collaborative ecosystems and supporting development of scalable co-sell, cross-sell, and solution strategies, she has consistently enabled organizations to solve larger business challenges while creating sustainable growth for customers, partners, and the businesses they serve. She is widely recognized for translating emerging technologies into practical business strategies that accelerate adoption, strengthen organizational alignment, and create measurable business outcomes.
Today, Mrs. Kallstrom serves leadership roles as Director of Cloud Channel Partnerships, including Channel Partner Services (CPS) and Solution Sales teams at PC Connection, Inc., (dba Connection) in the Technology Solutions and Services organization She drives the development, growth, and execution of strategic technology solutions, services, and channel partnerships which support Connection's customers and partners. She drives the organization's strategic business focused on expanding indirect referral services and solutions under the co-sell model for hosted and managed recurring subscription technology services. In this role, she is responsible for advancing this commercial strategy, business transformation, partner portfolio expansion expertise, solution-selling initiatives, executive alignment, sales enablement, and operational excellence across a diverse ecosystem of leading technology providers and service partners.
Working collaboratively across executive leadership, technical organizations, finance, operations, portfolio and offering management, sales and enablement, and strategic partner communities, Mrs. Kallstrom helps advanced technology solution sales organization's and their customers move beyond traditional resale toward comprehensive partner-led business solutions that integrate cloud, communications, cybersecurity, modern infrastructure, AI-powered technologies, and managed and professional services. Her work continues to strengthen Connection's ability to deliver outcome-based technology strategies while expanding recurring revenue opportunities and long-term customer success.
Recognizing that meaningful transformation extends beyond technology alone, she has also led the development of scalable sales enablement programs, partner engagement strategies, executive business planning, and cross-functional operating models that align internal organizations with evolving customer needs. Through these initiatives, she continues helping organizations embrace collaborative solution selling while expanding the role of strategic partnerships in delivering measurable business value.
Mrs. Kallstrom's leadership and contributions have been recognized throughout the technology industry. In 2025, she received the prestigious CRN Woman of the Year – Solution Provider Award, presented by The Channel Company, recognizing exceptional leadership and impact within the technology channel. She considers this distinction one of the most meaningful achievements of her career, reflecting not only her own leadership but also the collective success of the high-performing teams, colleagues, and strategic partners with whom she has collaborated throughout her professional journey.
She was subsequently recognized as a CRN Women of the Channel Honoree in 2026 and has also received Connection's Technology Solutions Circle of Excellence MVP Award in recognition of her leadership, innovation, and contributions to advancing commercial growth and strategic partner engagement.
These honors reflect a career dedicated not only to business performance, but to advancing the technology profession through collaboration, innovation, organizational transformation, and the development of future leaders.
Throughout her career, Mrs. Kallstrom has consistently been drawn to organizations navigating periods of significant growth, organizational change, evolving business models, and technology disruption. Rather than following a traditional career path within a single discipline, she intentionally built expertise across virtually every commercial function of the technology business—including sales, solution engineering, product management, customer experience, business development, operations, marketing, professional services, strategic partnerships, and executive leadership. This broad perspective has enabled her to understand not only how technology is developed and sold, but how organizations must evolve to deliver lasting customer value in rapidly changing markets.
Mrs. Kallstrom began her professional journey in 1994 building foundational experience in sales and customer engagement before advancing into increasingly strategic leadership roles supporting some of the world's most recognized technology organizations. Early in her career, she distinguished herself through her ability to bridge technical expertise with business strategy, earning opportunities that expanded beyond traditional sales leadership into solution engineering, customer success, operational transformation, and executive business development.
As Vice President of Sales and General Manager of e-Technology Corporation – now EMTEC - she assumed responsibility for a encompassing inside and field sales, customer support, managed services, professional services, marketing, and operational leadership pre-acquisition. Guiding multidisciplinary teams through periods of complete reorganization, she helped the organization's position by aligning new technical capabilities and services with expanded customer business objectives and building scalable playbooks under enhanced operating models that could improve execution and revenue growth acceleration across the business.
Her experience expanded further through executive leadership positions focused on customer experience transformation, enterprise consulting, and operational excellence. While leading customer care operations for Recall, North America — now Iron Mountain Incorporated —, Mrs. Kallstrom directed six customer contact centers serving enterprise customers across the United States and Canada. She championed initiatives that modernized customer engagement, improved operational performance, and elevated the overall customer experience through technology-enabled process improvements and organizational alignment.
Mrs. Kallstrom also broadened her strategic perspective through consulting engagements with KPMG, where she advised organizations on enterprise transformation initiatives, operational improvements, and merger and acquisition risk management. Supporting clients including BMW Manufacturing, she gained valuable experience helping executive leadership teams navigate complex organizational change while aligning technology investments with long-term business objectives.
Her international experience continued to expand through leadership roles supporting organizations across Europe, North America, and Asia-Pacific. Working with United Parcel Service, she contributed to sales operational and commercial initiatives throughout Europe, while subsequent management positions with Eyeota, EnVeritas Group — now EVG Media—, ScanSource, Intelisys, and CareAR— now ResolveGrid — further strengthened her expertise in global business development, cloud transformation, strategic partnerships, sales enablement, artificial intelligence, and recurring revenue business models.
Across each of these organizations, a consistent pattern emerged. Rather than simply leading teams or delivering revenue growth, Mrs. Kallstrom became known for helping organizations rethink how they engaged customers, enabled sales organizations, developed strategic partnerships, and brought increasingly complex technology solutions to market. She repeatedly helped shift businesses from transactional product sales toward consultative, outcome-focused engagement models that integrated technology, services, and long-term customer success.
This progression ultimately positioned Mrs. Kallstrom to become a recognized leader in commercial transformation, helping organizations navigate some of the technology industry's most significant shifts—from infrastructure and hardware to cloud services, managed and professional services solutions, and subscription business models, with comprehensive Everything-as-a-Service (XaaS) strategies. Each chapter of her career built upon the last, creating a uniquely broad executive perspective that continues to distinguish her leadership today.
Throughout more than three decades of leadership, Mrs. Kallstrom has earned a reputation as a technology leader who sees opportunities beyond conventional organizational boundaries. While many technology leaders excel within a single discipline, she has become known for connecting business strategy, advanced technology solution sales, services, partner ecosystems, and executive leadership into unified commercial strategies that create measurable value for customers and sustainable growth for organizations.
As the technology industry evolved from hardware-centric business models to cloud computing, managed services, artificial intelligence, and recurring subscription offerings, Mrs. Kallstrom consistently remained at the forefront of that transformation. She has helped organizations modernize their go-to-market strategies by shifting customer conversations away from products alone and toward broader business outcomes—enabling sales organizations to address operational efficiency, workforce productivity, digital transformation, cybersecurity, customer experience, and long-term technology roadmaps.
A defining characteristic of her leadership has been the ability to unite diverse stakeholders around shared objectives. Throughout her career, she has successfully brought together technology manufacturers, distributors, cloud providers, solution providers, consultants, executive sponsors, technical specialists, and customer leadership teams to develop solutions that no single organization could deliver independently. Her collaborative approach has helped organizations expand strategic partnerships, accelerate solution adoption, and create new opportunities that extend well beyond traditional supplier relationships.
Mrs. Kallstrom has become particularly recognized for helping sales organizations embrace consultative, solution-oriented and co-sell engagement models. Rather than focusing solely on individual technologies or transactional sales, she champions comprehensive customer discovery, cross-functional collaboration, and business outcome alignment. By integrating professional services, recurring technology solutions, strategic partnerships, and technical expertise into cohesive customer strategies, she has consistently helped organizations increase customer value while strengthening long-term relationships and commercial performance.
Equally important has been her commitment to building scalable organizations. Throughout her career, she has designed and led initiatives that improve operational alignment, strengthen executive governance, enhance sales enablement, and create repeatable frameworks that allow organizations to sustain growth long after individual initiatives have concluded. Her leadership reflects a belief that lasting success is achieved not through isolated accomplishments, but through creating systems, processes, and cultures that enable others to succeed.
Her experience spans both established global enterprises and rapidly growing technology companies, providing her with a unique perspective on organizational leadership across varying stages of business maturity. Whether supporting multinational corporations through enterprise transformation, helping emerging technology companies scale commercial operations, or leading strategic initiatives within complex partner ecosystems, Mrs. Kallstrom has consistently demonstrated an ability to translate innovation into practical business execution.
Beyond organizational leadership, Mrs. Kallstrom is widely respected as a mentor, collaborator, and advocate for professional development within the technology community. She has invested significant time developing future leaders, coaching sales professionals, enabling technical organizations, and fostering collaborative environments where individuals are empowered to grow both personally and professionally. Her leadership philosophy emphasizes accountability, continuous learning, intellectual curiosity, and the belief that the strongest organizations are built by developing people as intentionally as they develop business strategies.
Throughout her career, colleagues have frequently sought her guidance not only for her commercial expertise but also for her ability to navigate organizational complexity, build consensus among diverse stakeholders, and identify creative approaches to solving business challenges. Her thoughtful, relationship-centered leadership style has earned the trust of executive leadership teams, strategic partners, customers, and peers across the technology industry.
Mrs. Kallstrom's influence extends beyond individual business results. Her work has contributed to the broader evolution of how technology organizations engage customers, develop partnerships, and create long-term value through collaborative solution delivery. As emerging technologies continue reshaping the industry, she remains committed to helping organizations embrace innovation while maintaining a steadfast focus on the people, partnerships, and business outcomes that ultimately define sustainable success.
Throughout her career, Mrs. Kallstrom has believed that the greatest competitive advantage any organization possesses is its people. While technology continually evolves, she maintains that lasting success is built by developing leaders, fostering collaboration, embracing continuous learning, and creating environments where individuals are empowered to innovate, solve complex problems, and achieve shared goals. This philosophy has guided her leadership across every stage of her career and continues to shape the teams and organizations she serves today.
An active advocate for professional development, Mrs. Kallstrom has devoted significant time to mentoring emerging leaders, coaching sales and technical professionals, and advancing solution-oriented selling throughout the technology industry. She has designed executive workshops, sales enablement programs, certification initiatives, and strategic learning experiences that help organizations strengthen technical expertise while improving collaboration across business, sales, engineering, and partner communities. She believes that sustainable business transformation occurs when organizations invest as intentionally in developing people as they do in adopting new technologies.
Mrs. Kallstrom has also been an advocate for expanding opportunities for women in technology and leadership. Throughout her career, she has supported initiatives that encourage professional growth, mentorship, and greater representation within the technology industry. She has participated in organizations including the Alliance of Channel Women and has consistently championed inclusive leadership, believing that diverse perspectives strengthen innovation, improve decision-making, and produce better outcomes for customers and organizations alike.
Her contributions have earned recognition from both her peers and the industry. Beyond receiving the CRN Woman of the Year – Solution Provider Award and being named a CRN Women of the Channel honoree, she has been recognized internally for leadership excellence and has been a multiple-time recipient of President's Club honors throughout her career. While she values these achievements, Mrs. Kallstrom considers the development of future leaders, the success of the teams she has led, and the enduring partnerships she has built to be the most meaningful measures of professional accomplishment.
Over more than three decades, Mrs. Kallstrom has built a career defined not by individual technologies, but by helping organizations successfully navigate change. She has led through successive waves of transformation—including enterprise infrastructure, networking, cloud computing, managed services, customer experience modernization, artificial intelligence, recurring revenue business models, and strategic partner ecosystems—while maintaining a consistent focus on delivering meaningful business outcomes. Her broad executive perspective, combined with a collaborative leadership style and a passion for innovation, has established her as a trusted advisor to executive leaders, strategic partners, customers, and colleagues across the technology industry.
Looking ahead, Mrs. Kallstrom remains committed to helping organizations embrace emerging technologies while ensuring innovation is guided by sound business strategy, strong partnerships, and exceptional customer experiences. She believes technology creates its greatest value when it enables people to work more effectively, organizations to compete more successfully, and partnerships to accomplish what no single company could achieve independently.
Outside of her professional career, Mrs. Kallstrom enjoys travel, outdoor recreation, photography, golf, and exploring diverse cultures through both business and personal experiences. She values spending time with family and friends and believes that curiosity, lifelong learning, and meaningful relationships enrich both personal and professional life.

articles.content:
Envision Energy Accelerates the Evolution of Global Wind Technology with DNV Certification for TG Pro
HAMBURG, Germany, Sept. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Envision Energy, a global leader in green technology, has received Type Certification from DNV for its TG Pro (EN-206/8.35 60 Hz) wind turbine, marking an important milestone in the collaboration between the two companies and further validating the technical maturity and market readiness of Envision's next-generation wind turbine platform.
The certificate was presented during WindEnergy Hamburg 2026 by Mette Redanz, Vice President of Renewables Certification at DNV, and Yimin Lou, Senior Vice President and Chief Product Officer of Envision Energy. The ceremony underscored the role of independent certification and industry collaboration in supporting the development of advanced wind technologies.
Since its launch in 2024, the TG Pro (EN-206/8.35 60 Hz) has secured multiple orders in China and international markets and undergone extensive prototype and commercial validation. Built on Envision's Model TG Pro platform, the turbine combines a high-performance turbine architecture, optimized aerodynamic design and intelligent control technologies to improve energy capture and generation efficiency across a broad range of wind conditions.
The TG Pro platform is also designed for long-term reliability, with strengthened key components and engineering solutions tailored to demanding operating environments. Its validation process has included component testing, digital-twin simulation, multi-site prototype operation and commercial deployment, providing a comprehensive basis for evaluating the turbine's performance and reliability. The DNV Type Certification provides independent third-party confirmation that the turbine design meets applicable certification requirements.
"The continued advancement of our next-generation turbine portfolio is built on rigorous validation and real-world application." said Yimin Lou, Senior Vice President and Chief Product Officer of Envision Energy, "The DNV certification of TG Pro further demonstrates the maturity of the platform and its readiness to serve customers across diverse international markets. As renewable power systems evolve, Envision will continue to advance intelligent, high-performance and reliable turbine technologies for Future Energy Systems, enabling renewable energy to deliver greater value at scale."
"Independent certification provides an important foundation for confidence in wind turbine technology, helping manufacturers, developers and other stakeholders assess the performance, reliability and compliance of new turbine platforms. We are pleased to support Envision through the certification of TG Pro." added Mette Redanz, Vice President of Renewables Certification at DNV.
Beyond TG Pro, Envision is also showcasing its broader wind turbine portfolio at WindEnergy Hamburg 2026. Its EN-156/5.0 MW platform has received a Provisional Type Certificate from Bureau Veritas. The certification process was completed in less than five months, providing independent third-party assessment of the platform's design and technical capabilities as it moves toward broader commercial deployment.
Developed for the Asia-Pacific region, the EN-156/5.0 MW is being deployed at the Manar Wind Power Project in Sri Lanka, representing Envision's first utility-scale wind turbine order in the country. Featuring a 110-meter hub height and enhanced anti-corrosion specifications, the turbine is designed for demanding coastal environments characterized by high salinity and humidity. The combination of international certification and real-world project deployment demonstrates the platform's focus on reliability and environmental adaptability, supporting its application in Sri Lanka and other markets across the region.
Together, the two certification milestones demonstrate Envision's continued focus on rigorous engineering, independent validation and market-specific product development. Through collaboration with leading international certification bodies and customers across diverse markets, Envision is advancing wind turbine technologies that combine performance, reliability and adaptability for the evolving global energy system.
- End -
SOURCE Envision Energy

articles.content:

On September 23, Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MU ) received a major vote of confidence from Wolfe Research, which maintained an Outperform rating and a $1,500 price target on the stock following updated memory industry models. Citing sustained pricing strength, accelerated capacity expansion, and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) demand, Wolfe projects that Micron and SK Hynix could generate enough free cash flow to buy back up to 25% and 32% of their market caps, respectively, through 2027. If fundamental tightness extends into 2028, capital returns could exceed 50% of market capitalization, creating a substantial cash-flow-driven catalyst for shareholders.

You Might Also Want To Read: Jim Cramer Shared Why Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU)'s Shares Didn't Rise On Shortage News

Bull Case: Massive Free Cash Flow and Execution

Wolfe's 25% buyback projection aligns directly with Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU)'s unprecedented financial scale and structural customer alignment. In Q3 FY2026, Micron posted record results, generating $41.46 billion in revenue, $25.39 billion in operating cash flow, and $18.30 billion in adjusted free cash flow. Strategic Customer Agreements (SCAs), non-cancelable, take-or-pay commitments, now cover significant DRAM and NAND volume, locking in demand visibility, margin stability, and $22 billion in customer cash deposits and commitments.

Furthermore, rapid technology execution in 1-beta DRAM nodes and HBM4 ramping allows Micron to capture premium pricing across high-performance AI workloads. Backed by low leverage and $30.2 billion in total cash and marketable investments, Micron possesses the financial flexibility to fund major capacity expansions while easily supporting large-scale capital returns to shareholders.

Bear Case: Heavy Capital Burden and Cycle Vulnerability

Despite Wolfe's bullish multi-year cash flow projections, the primary risk to executing a 25% market cap buyback stems from memory market cyclicality and an escalating capital expenditure burden. Memory markets remain inherently cyclical; if pricing momentum cools before 2027, free cash flow conversion could shrink rapidly, restricting planned share repurchases.

Additionally, manufacturing complex HBM4 and 1-gamma nodes increases cost per bit and slows bit growth, making profitability heavily dependent on high selling prices rather than unit cost reductions. With net capital expenditures reaching $7.1 billion in Q3 alone and heavy ongoing investments required for fabs and advanced packaging, rising capital spending during an unexpected market slowdown could compress margins and impair long-term returns.

Don't Miss: Jim Cramer Named Micron Technology (MU) His Top Memory Pick

Conclusion

Wolfe's research highlights a powerful catalyst: Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU)'s surging free cash flow could unlock transformative buybacks through 2027. While cyclical downside, rising cost per bit, and heavy capex requirements remain persistent risks, Micron's record Q3 FY2026 cash generation and long-term customer commitments make its share repurchase potential difficult for investors to ignore.

While we acknowledge the potential of MU as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. articles.content:
Anthropic CEO Amodei to have dinner with Trump at White House
Private dinner will be the first one-on-one meeting between the two men, according to reports.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is set to dine one-on-one with US President Donald Trump at the White House.
The meeting on Sunday evening, confirmed by Trump, comes after months of open conflict between the artificial intelligence startup and the Trump administration.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Refugees in South Africa fear new attacks as September 30 deadline looms
- list 2 of 4Ben-Gvir releases video threatening to kill senior Hamas figure in jail
- list 3 of 4UK Foreign Secretary confronted by activists over Palestine Action ban
- list 4 of 4Ireland beats Israel 3-0 wearing black armbands to support Gaza
The private dinner would be the first one-on-one meeting between the two men, according to US media, including Axios, which first reported the dinner.
Trump confirmed the dinner on Sunday evening and reaffirmed his stance against slowing the pace of AI development.
Trump also reiterated his belief that new regulations would open the door for China to outpace the United States in AI advancement.
Although he acknowledged Amodei’s concern that going too fast on artificial intelligence could expand risks, Trump said it was more important for the US to maintain a technological edge over China.
“We’re about maybe a year and a half up on China,” Trump told Fox News while attending the Presidents Cup golf tournament in Illinois.
“We’re leading, and we’re building tremendous, trillions of dollars’ worth of places. And why should we give that up?”
The meeting comes two days after a federal appeals court upheld the Pentagon’s decision to classify Anthropic as a “supply chain risk”, which prohibits the US military from using its models.
The startup was sanctioned by the Trump administration after refusing in February to allow its tools to be used for fully autonomous weapons or domestic mass surveillance.
Trump also badmouthed Amodei, saying he was trying to be “a perfect little angel” after the Anthropic chief called for a pause in AI development.
Amodei was absent from the state dinner held for Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, attended by AI industry leaders, including Amodei’s rival Sam Altman of OpenAI.
Despite mounting calls to slow down AI development due to the risk of losing control of the technology, the US government believes that the sector’s major players – OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta – cannot afford to slow down for fear that China will gain the upper hand.
Trump and Mike Johnson, the speaker of the House of Representatives, are set to meet with leading AI executives on Tuesday.

articles.description_html: Arctic race heats up: how radar technology could transform naval operations in the polar regions | Newswise  Newswise
articles.article_title: Arctic race heats up: how radar technology could transform naval operations in the polar regions | Newswise
articles.heading: Arctic race heats up: how radar technology could transform naval operations in the polar regions
articles.summary: Advanced high-frequency (HF) radar could help navies and governments monitor the rapidly changing Arctic as climate change reduces sea ice and opens new shipping routes.
articles.content:
As climate change transforms the Arctic and opens new shipping routes, an internationally renowned physicist says advanced radar technology could play a key role in helping navies and governments monitor one of the world's most challenging and strategically important regions.
Adelaide University Adjunct Professor Stuart Anderson, from the School of Physics, Chemistry and Earth Sciences, has examined how high-frequency (HF) radar could support future US Navy operations in the Arctic by providing wide-area surveillance, ocean monitoring and communications support.
The Arctic is undergoing rapid change as rising temperatures reduce sea ice and increase access to waterways such as the Northern Sea Route and the Northwest Passage.
These changes are expected to drive growth in commercial shipping, resource extraction and fishing activity across the region. At the same time, strategic competition among nations is increasing, creating new security and operational challenges.
Professor Anderson recently presented a paper to the 2026 IEEE Radar Conference in Phoenix, Arizona, discussing how radar technology – already used successfully for ocean surveillance in Australia and other parts of the world – could be adapted to the Arctic’s unique environment.
According to Professor Anderson, who is also an Honorary Professor at University College London, keeping track of activities across vast and remote Arctic waters requires technologies that can monitor large areas continuously and provide timely information to decision-makers.
"Climate change is reshaping the Arctic environment and creating new opportunities as well as new risks," said Professor Anderson.
"As more vessels, infrastructure and nations become active in the region, there is a growing need for reliable systems that can help maintain awareness of what is happening across these enormous areas."
HF radar is already used in several countries for defence, maritime surveillance and ocean monitoring.
The long-range surveillance system uses high-frequency radio waves bounced off the Earth’s upper atmosphere to detect aircraft and ships far beyond direct line of sight.
Unlike many other sensing systems, HF radar can observe very large areas, operate continuously and provide information in near real time.
Professor Anderson highlights the potential for HF radar to detect and track ships, map ocean surface currents, and monitor sea conditions.
Emerging research also suggests the technology may be able to distinguish between different types of sea ice and estimate key characteristics, such as thickness and size of individual ice pieces, known as floes.
"Understanding the location, movement and nature of sea ice is critical for safe and effective operations in the Arctic," said Professor Anderson.
"HF radar has the potential to provide information that is difficult to obtain using existing systems, particularly over very large areas."
The technology could also assist communications.
Satellite coverage and environmental conditions can pose challenges, and due to the unpredictability of radio waves in the Arctic, HF radar systems may give operators a more reliable communication tool.
Professor Anderson said HF radar should not be viewed as a stand-alone solution, but as part of a broader network of sensors and monitoring technologies.
"No single technology can do everything," he said. "The greatest value comes when information from multiple systems is combined. HF radar can add unique insights that strengthen the overall picture and support better operational decisions."
Professor Stuart Anderson was on the original team that designed and developed the Jindalee over-the-horizon radar (OTHR) system in 1974, enabling the Australian Defence Force to monitor air and sea movements across several million square kilometres. That same technology is now being deployed in Canada after the Australian Government signed the nation’s largest ever defence export in June 2026, in a $2.5 billion deal.

articles.summary: GUANGZHOU, China, Sept. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The results of the 51st International Exhibition of Inventions Geneva have been announced. The project "Key Precision Manufacturing Technologies and Applications for Low-Loss Stator Cores Based on Ultra-Thin Amorphous Materials," co-developed with GAC Group, received the exhibition's highest distinction, the Gold Medal with the Congratulations of the Jury. The award is selected from Gold Medal winners and requires unanimous approval from the jury.
articles.content:
GUANGZHOU, China, Sept. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The results of the 51st International Exhibition of Inventions Geneva have been announced. The project "Key Precision Manufacturing Technologies and Applications for Low-Loss Stator Cores Based on Ultra-Thin Amorphous Materials," co-developed with GAC Group, received the exhibition's highest distinction, the Gold Medal with the Congratulations of the Jury. The award is selected from Gold Medal winners and requires unanimous approval from the jury.
For new energy vehicle users, range depends not only on battery capacity, but also on how efficiently every unit of energy is used. By applying ultra-thin amorphous material to the motor stator core, GAC reduces energy loss in the motor so that more power can be used to drive the vehicle. The Quark Electric Drive 2.0 motor equipped with this technology achieves a peak efficiency of 99.03%, while the electric drive system reaches a CLTC operating efficiency of 94.184%. With the same battery capacity, driving range can be extended by 30 to 50 kilometers, helping users go farther on the same amount of energy and enjoy greater confidence in everyday travel.
The technology has first been applied to models for the Chinese market, including the AION N60, 2027 AION RT and 2027 AION i60. As the technology continues to enter mass production, GAC will expand its application to more models, turning advances in high-efficiency electric drive technology into tangible efficiency and range benefits for users in everyday travel.

articles.title: Counties call for review of technology, jail billing process
articles.description: Counties call for review of technology, jail billing process WV MetroNews
articles.description_html: Counties call for review of technology, jail billing process  WV MetroNews
articles.article_title: Counties call for review of technology, jail billing process - WV MetroNews
articles.heading: Counties call for review of technology, jail billing process
articles.summary: More and more counties trying to come with creative ways to deal with rising costs.
articles.content:
MORGANTOWN, W.Va. — The coalition of counties auditing jail bills spearheaded by Monongalia County suspects mistakes and duplication in what they are calling an “antiquated process.”
Monongalia County Commission President Tom Bloom said each county has paid an outside entity to examine and compare the bills. The mistakes include not properly tracking an inmate after a conviction and transfer from the jail system to the state prison system, multiple counties paying for the same inmate, and the cost of maintaining outdated technology.
“As we went through and each county started to hire individuals to look through the bills, we saw that at times the bills were 10 to 30 percent incorrect,” Bloom said. “This is hundreds of thousands of dollars.”
The coalition contends there are three systems in the state, the Department of Correction and Rehabilitation, circuit courts, and magistrate courts that do not maintain a uniform system to manage the status of inmates. Bloom said counties receive jail bill information via fax machine, and one commission reported 500 pages of jail bill information had been transmitted over a single two-week period. The members of the coalition believe the state should improve the jail and prison inmate tracking system by moving to a computer-based system that can display and manage information in real time.
“There are programs like that, and we don’t understand why we’re using such an antiquated system that is not working; it is very clear,” Bloom said.
According to Bloom, more than 20 counties are behind in making jail payments, and some cannot meet the obligation at all. The coalition counties, he said, make up more than 50 percent of the total jail expenses billed to the counties.
“Any money we find goes back to the county to pay the people we had to hire,” Bloom said. “We shouldn’t be doing this. There needs to be a better system, and we believe we can work with them.”
State lawmakers would need to approve the additional cost to automate the inmate management system, and support from WVDCR commissioner David Kelly would be important. Coalition counties want to press Kelly, and lawmakers need to make the needed changes during the upcoming legislative session.
“We would like to have the process immediately revaluated and get a new computer program to improve accountability and everyone working together,” Bloom said.
For counties like Monongalia, changes adopted in 2023 with HB 3552 jail costs have increased more than 30 percent along with the suspected billing mistakes. The counties would like to see an expedited solution so they can accurately plan for jail costs and manage other financial priorities.
“We want to work with them so we can solve these problems,” Bloom said. “The problems are extremely troubling and severe, and when you consider the amount of money it’s costing us.”

articles.article_title: Walmart denies using personal info to set prices as it expands digital shelf labels
articles.heading: Walmart denies using personal info to set prices as it expands digital shelf labels
articles.summary: Walmart is aiming to assuage customers' fears about its new pricing technology as it rolls out digital price labels at its stores
articles.content:
Walmart denies using personal info to set prices as it expands digital shelf labels
Walmart is aiming to assuage customers' fears about its new pricing technology.
NEW YORK -- Walmart is aiming to assuage customers' fears about its new pricing technology as it rolls out digital price labels at its stores.
In a statement posted on the company's website, Walmart Inc.'s CEO John Furner vowed that the Bentonville, Arkansas-based retailer isn't using personal information like income, shopping history or a customer's willingness to pay to set prices, and it won't be doing so in the future either.
“We don’t set different prices based on who you are or the time of day, and we won’t,” Furner wrote Friday. “Whether you’re buying groceries or electronics on a hot afternoon or in a sudden rush for an item, it’s never a reason to charge you more.”
The pledge from Walmart comes as concerns are mounting from some shoppers, consumer advocates and lawmakers skeptical about the rollout of digital price labels by the discounter and other stores. Digital price labels are rapidly replacing paper shelf tags at U.S. supermarkets and let stores change prices instantly from a central computer instead of having workers swap out paper labels by hand.
Furner noted that Walmart is also holding its artificial intelligence shopping assistant Sparky to the same promise and won't be using the bot to raise a customer's price or hide lower-priced options that meet their needs.
Furner said such practices would violate the company's “every day low prices” business model.
He also noted that prices can change: Walmart lowers them when it can pass savings along, or sometimes raises them because an item costs more to buy or to transport, he said.
Walmart said in March that 2,300 Walmart U.S. locations already use digital shelves, and it expects this technology to be chain-wide within the next year.
Walmart executives have repeatedly said it uses electronic shelf price tags to help the retailer change prices consistently and match what rings up at checkout. It also saves workers time and reduces labor costs by replacing paper tags.
Last month, the Federal Trade Commission said that it's putting companies on notice that the practice of personalizing pricing could violate consumer protection laws. The agency said it does not have the legal authority to ban personalized pricing in all circumstances, but it issued a new bulletin that warned companies that they must disclose to customers how the personal information is being used to set a price.

articles.article_title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to have private White House dinner with Trump
articles.heading: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to have private White House dinner with Trump
articles.summary: President Trump and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei will meet on Sunday evening at the White House after the artificial intelligence industry leader raised concerns about the technology’s risks. T…
articles.content:
President Trump and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei will meet on Sunday evening at the White House after the artificial intelligence industry leader raised concerns about the technology’s risks.
The two will meet for dinner at the president’s residence, two sources familiar with the dinner confirmed to The Hill.
Trump in recent weeks has dismissed concerns from lawmakers and industry leaders about the risks of AI. Amodei, whose firm developed the Claude chatbot, was among those to call for a slowdown in development.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote in an essay earlier this month after one of his researchers resigned and said AI poses dire risks to humanity.
Amodei was not among the host of tech industry leaders to attend Thursday’s state dinner at the White House in honor of Chinese President Xi Jinping, a group that included OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.
Axios was first to report the scheduled meeting.
“President Trump has been clear: America will lead the world in Super Intelligence, while protecting American consumers,” a White House official told The Hill, referring to the president’s moniker for AI.
“We will drive innovation, strengthen American competitiveness, and ensure this transformative technology works for the American people,” the official added.
Anthropic has for months been mired in a legal fight with the Pentagon for months over its designation of the company as a supply-chain risk.
The District of Columbia Circuit Court of Appeals, in a 2-1 ruling, sided with the Defense Department on Friday. The federal appeals court allowed the Pentagon to continue designating the company’s technology as a national security risk.
“Confirmed: @AnthropicAI = Supply Chain Risk,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote on social media after the ruling. “The @DeptofWar does what is right for the Country and our Warriors.”

articles.heading: 2026 AIAA 30/30 Recipients Announced: Aircraft Technology, Integration, and Operations Category
articles.summary: AIAA has identified 30 exceptional young professionals who are advancing aerospace through technical achievement, innovation, and leadership. The 30/30 Program highlights individuals in their 30s who…
articles.content:
AIAA has identified 30 exceptional young professionals who are advancing aerospace through technical achievement, innovation, and leadership. The 30/30 Program highlights individuals in their 30s who are driving breakthrough research, advancing next-generation technologies, leading impactful programs and teams, and accelerating innovation across aerospace. They are presented in seven different technical categories. Meet the winners in our Aircraft Technology, Integration, and Operations Category below. And learn about the full list of 30 exceptional individuals at aiaa.org/get-involved/honors-awards/awards/30-30-recognition-program.
Aircraft Technology, Integration, and Operations
James “JP” Stewart
Senior Vice President of Product Development
Electra
James “JP” Stewart is a 31-year-old aerospace engineer and leader of note. As senior vice president of Product Development at Electra, he is responsible for all aspects of the company’s operations.
Stewart is transforming the future of flight through a new Direct Aviation paradigm for regional air mobility that gives people the freedom to travel from where they are to where they want to go, avoiding long drives and overburdened airports. Ultra-short takeoff and landing aircraft are the key enablers. Electra has successfully designed and flight demonstrated the world’s first two-seat EL-2 Goldfinch aircraft, which requires only a 150-foot runway for takeoff and landing. EL-2 proved the feasibility of an integrated system with blown-lift technology and hybrid-electric propulsion. As the EL-2 Program Manager, Stewart brought his exceptional technical expertise, practical insights, and impressive business acumen to bear on this successful endeavor. Stewart is now focused on developing the game-changing nine-passenger ultra-STOL EL-9 aircraft with entry into service in 2029.
Stewart is a 2026 AIAA Associate Fellow; a National Business Aviation Association 2024 Business Aviation Top 40 Under 40 award recipient; a 2021 Virginia Tech Alumni Emerging Leaders award honoree; and a 2016 Aviation Week 20 Twenties laureate. He is an active pilot and instructor, flying both sailplanes and powered aircraft. He has represented the U.S. Soaring Team four times in World Championships. Stewart earned a University Honors Bachelor of Science in Aerospace Engineering from Virginia Tech in 2018.
Evan Harrison
Senior Research Engineer and Division Chief
Georgia Institute of Technology
Evan Harrison has made significant contributions to the aviation field, particularly in aerospace systems safety, airworthiness certification, and model-based systems engineering (MBSE). At the Aerospace Systems Design Laboratory, his work bridges the gap between complex aircraft design and regulatory compliance.
One area of impact is Harrison’s research on advancement of model-based approaches for aircraft certification. Collaborating with agencies like FAA and NASA, he has developed frameworks to streamline noise certification and conduct regulatory gap analyses for novel, electrified powertrain aircraft. His research has provided foundational MBSE methods to support the airworthiness standards for innovative concepts like NASA’s X-57.
As an expert in vehicle- and system-level safety assessment, his research focuses on predicting and mitigating loss-of-control incidents for general aviation and evaluating the operational reliability of emerging urban air mobility and eVTOL vehicle designs. His safety frameworks and energy-based flight safety analysis methods have contributed to modern flight-data monitoring programs aimed at improving fixed-wing aviation safety.
He has also been impactful as an instructor for various undergraduate and graduate-level courses at Georgia Tech, educating the next generation of aerospace engineers about aircraft design, safety by design, and vehicle performance. Harrison contributes to the aerospace profession through his technical publications and active membership in the AIAA General Aviation Technical Committee and the Transformational Flight Technical Integration and Outreach Committee.
Through his research, teaching, and industry engagement, Harrison helps shape the future of safer, cleaner, and more efficient vehicle architectures.
Sang-A Lee
Graduate Research Assistant
Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University
Before the age of 30, Sang-A Lee has established herself as one of the leading emerging scholars in aviation safety and unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) research. As Lab Manager and principal research contributor on multiple FAA-sponsored ASSURE projects, she has helped secure and execute a portfolio exceeding $10 million in federally funded research focused on UAS traffic analysis, collision risk, remote identification, and airspace integration. Her work directly supports FAA efforts to safely integrate emerging aerospace technologies into the National Airspace System.
Lee’s innovative contribution includes her dissertation on aviation maintenance safety culture. Through the development of new frameworks examining trust, fear, and organizational influences on safety performance, she has introduced a human-centered approach to understanding and mitigating maintenance-related risk.
Her impact also extends beyond dissertation. Lee authored a 155-page FAA-sponsored gap analysis synthesizing 238 technical sources and has presented her work to FAA officials, industry leaders, military executives, and academic audiences. With 17 peer-reviewed publications, multiple first-author articles, and leadership of interdisciplinary research teams, she is shaping the future of aviation safety and advanced air mobility through research that is both scientifically rigorous and operationally relevant.
Max Z. Li
Assistant Professor, Aerospace Engineering
University of Michigan
Max Li is an emerging aerospace engineering leader whose work is shaping exciting advances in air transportation systems, including next generation air traffic management, aviation operations, airline and airport systems, and advanced air mobility. At the University of Michigan, Li has established a vibrant research program and the Laboratory for Air Transportation, Infrastructure, and Connected Environments (LATTICE) dedicated to air transportation system resilience, optimization, and decision-making under uncertainty – areas of critical importance to the future of air transportation. His work imaginatively addresses significant challenges, including how to make aviation networks more efficient, robust, adaptive, and capable of operating safely under uncertainty and disruption. Specific examples of his impactful research contributions include analysis of autonomous vehicle impacts on airport leakage and environmental implications, development of large-language-model-driven conversational agents for strategic air traffic flow management, and stochastically optimized distributionally robust ground delay programs using learning-driven airport capacity predictions.
Li’s extensive publication record includes more than 30 journal articles and more than 70 conference papers addressing a broad range of topics in air traffic control, air traffic management, network optimization, airline and airport operations, and advanced air mobility. He has built strong collaborations across academia, industry, and government with research projects sponsored by NASA, FAA, DARPA, MITRE, NSF, and Collins Aerospace. Beyond research, Li has taught hundreds of students at Michigan and contributed extensively to the aerospace community through editorial service, technical committee leadership, conference organization, and international engagement.
Aman Deep Tripathi
Product and Commercialization Lead
Wisk Aero
As Product and Commercialization Lead at Wisk Aero, a Boeing subsidiary developing autonomous eVTOL aircraft, Aman Deep Tripathi leads the market requirements and business case for the Generation 6 aircraft and Wisk’s future product strategy. His work sets the technical roadmap guiding 800+ engineers through a decade-long certification effort..
Tripathi co-authored the Wisk–Boeing and Wisk–Skyports Concepts of Operations for autonomous air mobility. These have become foundational references across the international AAM standards and policy community, informing efforts at NASA, FAA, and ICAO, and shaping how the industry integrates uncrewed aircraft into the airspace. He has also published research with multiple NASA divisions.
He also gives generously to the profession – serving on the Transportation Research Board’s aviation economics committee, advising ICAO’s AAM Study Group, reviewing articles for leading aerospace journals, judging the CES Innovation and Global AAM Awards, and authoring a case study for a University of Washington competition (350+ students), alongside several U.S. patent applications in autonomous flight.
Colleagues and supervisors say that what distinguishes Tripathi is range: he turns market demand into engineering requirements, financial cases, and operational concepts that others now build upon. He is a leader both today and in the future and his blend of technical depth and commercial impact continue to make an impact.

articles.heading: Austin Peay State University Joins Tennessee Technology Advancement Consortium
articles.summary: Clarksville, TN - Mike Wilson has spent 21 years learning how Austin Peay State University (APSU) works: where expertise lives, who knows what, and which
articles.content:
Clarksville, TN – Mike Wilson has spent 21 years learning how Austin Peay State University (APSU) works: where expertise lives, who knows what, and which people need to find one another.
Now, as Austin Peay State University becomes the newest member of the Tennessee Technology Advancement Consortium (TTAC), that knowledge has a new purpose.
A Launch Tennessee initiative, TTAC helps universities across the state move promising research toward commercial use. Wilson’s role as APSU’s first commercialization counselor is one part of what the partnership makes possible.
Wilson is meeting with faculty across campus, learning what they’re working on, and identifying projects that may have applications beyond the university. He can also draw on TTAC, Launch Tennessee, and partners across the state to help Austin Peay State University faculty assess their ideas and decide how, or whether, to pursue a commercial path.
“A lot of things we’re going to have to do here at Austin Peay State University are look at building cross-departmental, cross-college relationships,” said Wilson, director of APSU’s GIS Center, one of several research centers and innovation hubs across campus.
The opportunities created through Wilson’s work and TTAC extend beyond connecting individual researchers or departments.
“I think the real potential is found when our faculty’s expertise and passions for innovation are matched with marketplace opportunities,” said Dr. Chad Brooks, vice provost for research and dean of the APSU College of Graduate Studies.
New Connections across Tennessee
Clarksville’s growth has expanded Austin Peay State University’s role in the region, Brooks said, while its proximity to Fort Campbell has also opened a distinct set of research possibilities.
“Fort Campbell changes the kinds of questions we can help answer,” he said.
In July 2026, Launch Tennessee awarded Austin Peay State University a TTAC grant to support a National Security Innovation Commercialization Convening. The event will bring researchers together with military stakeholders, startups, and industry leaders working in defense and dual-use technology.
The university already has research to bring to the table. Through Austin Peay State University’s collaboration with EagleWerx at Fort Campbell, students and faculty have responded to problems identified by the military.
One result is P.R.I.S.E.M., a 3D-printed backup sight developed by undergraduate manufacturing engineering technology students.
But national security is only one part of a university growing in size and research capacity.
APSU has doubled its enrollment over the past 20 years, and grant funding reached nearly $17.8 million in fiscal year 2026, a university record.
“As Austin Peay State University has grown, we’ve attracted faculty with talents and research experience from across the country,” Brooks said. “Fort Campbell gives us a close view of what can happen when researchers work alongside people who need a problem solved. The exciting part is wondering where else that could happen. Some of our strongest commercial possibilities may come from faculty who have never thought of their work that way.”
A Path Beyond Discovery
Promising research can stall for surprisingly ordinary reasons on the path to market. A faculty member may not know whether to file a patent, how to pay for the next test, or which company might care.
Few universities have all the answers on campus. TTAC is built around that reality, giving its members a statewide network of commercialization expertise, funding, and industry connections.
“The research is already happening at Austin Peay State University. What hasn’t always existed is the infrastructure to support a promising idea after the grant or publication,” said Jennifer Skjellum, vice president of commercialization and director of TTAC at Launch Tennessee, the state’s public-private partnership for startups and innovation.
“TTAC’s shared-resources model and one-on-one guidance enable emerging research institutions to tap into commercialization tools that, until now, typically only R1 campuses could sustain,” she said.
But no two projects arrive with the same needs.
One may require an intellectual-property strategy; another, funding for a prototype, market research, or validation. TTAC supports those different stages through commercial assessment, proof-of-concept grants, and technology-maturation funding, she said.
That continuity matters because the people and questions surrounding an idea change as the work develops.
“The handoffs are where promising ideas can get lost,” Skjellum said. “A researcher shouldn’t have to start over every time the work reaches a new stage.”
But an idea can survive every handoff and still remain invisible to the people who could use it.
The Tennessee Innovation Exchange, or TNIX, addresses that problem at a statewide scale.
Companies can search faculty expertise, research assets, and technologies across participating universities.
A business looking for a researcher, specialized facility, or licensable technology no longer has to know which campus to search first.
TTAC gives Austin Peay State University a route into that system. TNIX can place APSU’s capabilities before companies, investors, public agencies, and researchers who may never have known where to find them.
“Austin Peay State University sits in a part of the state where research and real-world need are especially close together, with Fort Campbell right next door,” said Deputy Governor and Tennessee Department of Economic and Community Development (TNECD) Commissioner Stuart McWhorter. “Their addition to the TTAC network helps turn that proximity into opportunity for faculty and for Tennessee.”
Research through a Business Lens
As its statewide connections grow, Austin Peay State University is bringing more of the campus into its commercialization effort.
The College of Business is developing the Larry W. Carroll Entrepreneurship Center, where faculty commercialization will sit alongside student entrepreneurship and support for veterans and aspiring business owners. Dean Mickey Hepner intends the center to serve the university as a whole. Its advisory board will include representatives from STEM and other areas, and he expects it to work closely with Wilson’s centralized commercialization effort.
For Hepner, that connection matters because researchers and entrepreneurs are trained to recognize value differently.
“They’re thinking about the next discovery, the next journal publication, the next grant,” Hepner said.
An entrepreneurial perspective asks where the work could be applied, who might use it, and whether a market exists.
“It’s more like here’s the idea, and here’s the market,” Hepner said.
The next question for “Grasslandia”
Dr. Dwayne Estes has already shown how far university research can travel.
Estes, a biology professor and co-founder of the Southeastern Grasslands Institute, came to Austin Peay State University nearly two decades ago to study plants, teach, and train botanists. As his research revealed the disappearance of southeastern grasslands, he began questioning whether the traditional academic path was enough.
“I was becoming somewhat disillusioned with academia,” Estes said. “I didn’t feel like my publications alone, or the teaching of students alone, would solve the problem.”
He wanted to continue both while building something capable of addressing the problem on a larger scale.
What began with a $20,000 grant grew into an institute that Estes said has raised $45 million and now employs 60 people.
The experience taught him how to build partnerships, attract funding, and extend research well beyond campus. It did not teach him how to commercialize an idea.
That challenge has hit Estes’ Grasslandia project. Backed by $4 million from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and built with geospatial technology company Esri, the digital platform brings maps, historical records, biodiversity data, and ecological information about southeastern grasslands into one system.
Farmers, government agencies, corporations, and others will be able to use it.
One Grasslandia database contains roughly 18 million cells of information, Estes said, much of it drawn from scientists across the field and around the world.
“I won’t be here forever, and these other people won’t,” he said. “We need a system that helps transfer this knowledge.”
Estes sees commercial possibilities in Grasslandia, a name meant to evoke a “world of grasslands.”
He’s less certain about what form they could take.
“I do think there’s a lot of potential for commercialization in that,” he said. “It’s just I haven’t quite wrapped my head around it yet.”
He has never patented anything and doesn’t know how to approach that part of the process.
“I just don’t even know how to go about that next level,” Estes said. “But I think we’d like to explore, for sure.”
For Austin Peay State University, that may be the point.
The research, ideas, and ambition are already there.
Austin Peay State University is now building the connections to help faculty recognize where those ideas might lead and give them someone to call when they’re ready to find out.

Now, as Austin Peay State University becomes the newest member of the Tennessee Technology Advancement Consortium (TTAC), that knowledge has a new purpose.

A Launch Tennessee initiative, TTAC helps universities across the state move promising research toward commercial use. Wilson’s role as APSU’s first commercialization counselor is one part of what the partnership makes possible.

Wilson is meeting with faculty across campus, learning what they’re working on, and identifying projects that may have applications beyond the university. He can also draw on TTAC, Launch Tennessee, and partners across the state to help Austin Peay State University faculty assess their ideas and decide how, or whether, to pursue a commercial path.

“A lot of things we’re going to have to do here at Austin Peay State University are look at building cross-departmental, cross-college relationships,” said Wilson, director of APSU’s GIS Center, one of several research centers and innovation hubs across campus.

The opportunities created through Wilson’s work and TTAC extend beyond connecting individual researchers or departments.

“I think the real potential is found when our faculty’s expertise and passions for innovation are matched with marketplace opportunities,” said Dr. Chad Brooks, vice provost for research and dean of the APSU College of Graduate Studies.

New Connections across Tennessee

Clarksville’s growth has expanded Austin Peay State University’s role in the region, Brooks said, while its proximity to Fort Campbell has also opened a distinct set of research possibilities.

“Fort Campbell changes the kinds of questions we can help answer,” he said.

In July 2026, Launch Tennessee awarded Austin Peay State University a TTAC grant to support a National Security Innovation Commercialization Convening. The event will bring researchers together with military stakeholders, startups, and industry leaders working in defense and dual-use technology.

The university already has research to bring to the table. Through Austin Peay State University’s collaboration with EagleWerx at Fort Campbell, students and faculty have responded to problems identified by the military.

One result is P.R.I.S.E.M., a 3D-printed backup sight developed by undergraduate manufacturing engineering technology students.

But national security is only one part of a university growing in size and research capacity.

APSU has doubled its enrollment over the past 20 years, and grant funding reached nearly $17.8 million in fiscal year 2026, a university record.

“As Austin Peay State University has grown, we’ve attracted faculty with talents and research experience from across the country,” Brooks said. “Fort Campbell gives us a close view of what can happen when researchers work alongside people who need a problem solved. The exciting part is wondering where else that could happen. Some of our strongest commercial possibilities may come from faculty who have never thought of their work that way.”

But no two projects arrive with the same needs.

One may require an intellectual-property strategy; another, funding for a prototype, market research, or validation. TTAC supports those different stages through commercial assessment, proof-of-concept grants, and technology-maturation funding, she said.

That continuity matters because the people and questions surrounding an idea change as the work develops.

“The handoffs are where promising ideas can get lost,” Skjellum said. “A researcher shouldn’t have to start over every time the work reaches a new stage.”

articles.content_html:
Meadow is a unique phone made for the times you decide you would rather leave your smartphone behind. The device is only three inches square, with a touchscreen taking up most of its face and a deliberately short menu of things it can do. Calls and texts are there. So are maps and Uber. Spotify and Apple Music cover music, while tickets can be pulled up at the door to a concert or event.

It looks almost like somebody cropped a smartphone down to its useful corner. The proportions are chunky and a little odd, especially beside the long black rectangles we have grown used to carrying. Meadow runs on Android, though there is no open app store waiting to fill the screen back up again. The software comes with a fixed group of services chosen around getting somewhere, meeting someone, listening to something, then heading home.

images courtesy Meadow

the camera makes you wait

The camera is where Meadow gets more interesting. There is a rear lens and a tiny mirror beside it for framing a selfie, while the usual front-facing camera disappears altogether. You can still take photos and video, but they are sent away to sync later instead of appearing instantly for review on the screen.

It changes a familiar little gesture. Take the picture, put the phone away. There is no immediate zooming in, deleting, retaking or passing the screen around for approval. Meadow still gives you the photograph. It simply separates taking it from looking at it.

the small device works independently from a user’s primary smartphone

a second phone comes with a second number

Meadow has its own cellular connection and phone number, so it works independently from the smartphone sitting back at home. Service runs on T-Mobile in the US, with plans beginning at $15 per month. That makes the whole setup more involved than switching on a stripped-back mode on an iPhone, though the physical separation is also the point. The distracting device is somewhere else.

The first larger batch has now begun reaching preorder customers. Meadow enters a growing category of phones built around doing fewer things, but its design feels especially literal: take the pieces of a smartphone that help you move through a city and put them into a much smaller object. Meanwhile, everything else can wait.

articles.summary: Walmart is aiming to assuage customers' fears about its new pricing technology as it rolls out digital price labels at its stores.
articles.content:
NEW YORK – Walmart is aiming to assuage customers’ fears about its new pricing technology as it rolls out digital price labels at its stores.
In a statement posted on the company’s website, Walmart Inc.’s CEO John Furner vowed that the Bentonville, Arkansas-based retailer isn’t using personal information like income, shopping history or a customer’s willingness to pay to set prices, and it won’t be doing so in the future either.
Recommended Videos
“We don’t set different prices based on who you are or the time of day, and we won’t,” Furner wrote Friday. “Whether you’re buying groceries or electronics on a hot afternoon or in a sudden rush for an item, it’s never a reason to charge you more.”
The pledge from Walmart comes as concerns are mounting from some shoppers, consumer advocates and lawmakers skeptical about the rollout of digital price labels by the discounter and other stores. Digital price labels are rapidly replacing paper shelf tags at U.S. supermarkets and let stores change prices instantly from a central computer instead of having workers swap out paper labels by hand.
Furner noted that Walmart is also holding its artificial intelligence shopping assistant Sparky to the same promise and won’t be using the bot to raise a customer’s price or hide lower-priced options that meet their needs.
Furner said such practices would violate the company’s “every day low prices” business model.
He also noted that prices can change: Walmart lowers them when it can pass savings along, or sometimes raises them because an item costs more to buy or to transport, he said.
Walmart said in March that 2,300 Walmart U.S. locations already use digital shelves, and it expects this technology to be chain-wide within the next year.
Walmart executives have repeatedly said it uses electronic shelf price tags to help the retailer change prices consistently and match what rings up at checkout. It also saves workers time and reduces labor costs by replacing paper tags.
Last month, the Federal Trade Commission said that it’s putting companies on notice that the practice of personalizing pricing could violate consumer protection laws. The agency said it does not have the legal authority to ban personalized pricing in all circumstances, but it issued a new bulletin that warned companies that they must disclose to customers how the personal information is being used to set a price.

A federal judge's decision to restore White House access for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico has refocused attention on political media, putting Trump Media & Technology Group (DJT) and its Truth Social platform back under the spotlight.
Trump Media & Technology Group has seen its share price swing sharply, with a 22.03% 90-day share price return compared with a year-to-date share price decline of 33.62% and a 1-year total shareholder return that is down 46.01%, reflecting fading longer-term momentum despite short bursts of interest around political media headlines.

Trump Media & Technology Group has already handed holders a sharp 90 day rebound, while longer term returns remain deeply in the red. Has most of the easy upside been spent, or do the numbers still argue for more potential gains?
Preferred Price-to-Book Multiple for Trump Media & Technology Group: Is It Justified?
On the numbers, Trump Media & Technology Group trades on a P/B ratio of 2.5x, which screens as expensive against the broader US Interactive Media and Services sector on 1x, even though it looks cheaper than its closer peer set on 3.2x.
P/B compares the market value of the equity with the net assets on the balance sheet. For a media and social platform business like Trump Media & Technology Group, this ratio tends to reflect what investors are willing to pay today for intangible assets, the user base, and future monetisation potential rather than just physical or financial assets reported on the books.
The gap to the wider industry is large, which suggests the market is paying a premium relative to other US Interactive Media and Services stocks. Compared with the peer average closer to 3.2x, the P/B of 2.5x looks more restrained, yet the firm is still loss making with a reported net loss of $1,304.2m on only $4.5m of revenue and a return on equity that is deeply negative, which raises questions about how much of that premium is being driven by sentiment rather than current fundamentals.
Relative to the industry benchmark of 1x, the P/B multiple is materially higher, which is a strong signal that the valuation is rich versus the wider group, even if it sits below the 3.2x peer average that investors are paying for closer comparables.

Micron Technology (MU) Could Be 46% Undervalued As AI Memory Bets Face Earnings Test
Micron Technology (MU) heads into its fiscal fourth quarter update with sentiment running high, as investors weigh record gross margin guidance, multi year fixed price contracts, and progress on new 512GB DDR5 server memory.
Micron Technology’s momentum has been powerful, with a 30 day share price return of 16.02% and a year to date gain of 243.12%. The 1 year total shareholder return is very large at roughly 6x, signalling strong enthusiasm around AI driven demand and the upcoming earnings update, despite a softer 90 day patch where the share price fell 5.50%.
Scan beyond Micron Technology and see how other AI infrastructure suppliers are setting up into earnings with the curated 85 AI infrastructure stocks.
Micron Technology now trades with a very large one year return and record margin guidance already on the table. Does that backdrop still leave enough upside in the risk reward, or is most of the good news priced in before the valuation work even starts?
Most Popular Narrative: 46% Undervalued
The most followed Micron Technology thesis pegs fair value at $2,018 per share, well above the last close at $1,082.28. That gap is driving a view that the market is still discounting how central high bandwidth memory could be to Micron’s cash generation.
The primary engine driving Micron's forward revenue growth is the industry-wide transition to vertically stacked HBM4 architectures. The high physical complexity of HBM manufacturing introduces a steep 3x physical wafer consumption penalty over standard planar DDR5. This wafer penalty reduces the global supply of standard commodity memory, creating a persistent supply deficit. This structural tightness allows memory manufacturers to transition away from annual fixed-price agreements toward compressed monthly contracts with retroactive, spot-linked post-settlement clauses that are designed to maximize capital returns.
See why 138 investors see Micron Technology as 46% undervalued.
Result: Fair Value of $2,018 (UNDERVALUED)
Still, Micron Technology’s AI memory story depends on smooth 1-gamma and HBM4 execution and disciplined global capacity; any stumble here could quickly puncture that 46% undervaluation pitch.
Find out about the key risks to this Micron Technology narrative.
Another View on Micron Technology’s Valuation
That 46% undervalued narrative leans on a rich fair value per share. The SWS DCF model presents a different perspective, with Micron Technology trading above an estimated future cash flow value of $578.24, which appears overvalued within that framework.
Investors using cash flow driven models may ask whether current enthusiasm already leans too heavily on optimistic margin and growth assumptions, or whether the market is simply discounting the cyclicality risk that the DCF is attempting to capture.
