...FLOOD WATCH REMAINS IN EFFECT FROM MONDAY AFTERNOON THROUGH LATE
TUESDAY NIGHT...
...POTENTIAL FOR LIFE THREATENING FLASH FLOODING...
* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall continues to be
possible.
* WHERE...Areas along and west of the central mountain chain
including the west slopes of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, the
Sandia/Manzano Mountains, and the south-central mountains, as well
as the Rio Grande Valley westward to the Arizona border. Some metro
areas and locales include, Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Espanola, Taos,
Socorro, Ruidoso, Los Alamos, Grants, Gallup, and Farmington.
* WHEN...From Monday afternoon through late Tuesday night.
* IMPACTS...Excessive runoff may result in flooding of rivers,
creeks, streams, and other low-lying and flood-prone locations.
* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- A near-record to record surge of moisture combined with two
merging storm systems will bring a prolonged multi-day period of
showers and thunderstorms producing moderate to heavy rainfall.
Combined with already rain-soaked soil, there is a moderate to
high risk of flash flooding.
- Low-lying, poorly drained areas, urban areas and arroyo systems
will be most susceptible. Rivers and streams will see rises,
potentially reaching flood stage. Recent burn scars may see flash
flooding, including the Ruidoso area burn scars, Frijoles,
Sacaton, Hummingbird, and Whiskey burn scars.
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS...
You should monitor later forecasts and be alert for possible Flood
Warnings. Those living in areas prone to flooding should be prepared
to take action should flooding develop.

articles.summary: As G2E approaches, Passport Technology is bringing a new vision for the casino floor to Las Vegas: OmniStream™, a full-service redemption kiosk built to consoli
articles.content:
As G2E approaches, Passport Technology is bringing a new vision for the casino floor to Las Vegas: OmniStream™, a full-service redemption kiosk built to consolidate the guest’s cash access journey into a single, modern touchpoint.
The casino floor is undergoing a significant transformation. As operators balance evolving player expectations, labor pressures, and increasing demands for operational efficiency, the role of self-service technology has expanded far beyond convenience. Today’s guests expect fast, intuitive, and frictionless access to the financial services that fuel their gaming experience. The challenge is no longer simply moving money efficiently — it’s creating a seamless guest journey that enhances both the player’s experience and property performance. OmniStream™ is Passport’s answer to that challenge, designed to streamline financial transactions, reduce cage traffic, and support a more connected, efficient casino floor.
“Over the past year, we have rebuilt Passport around innovation and service,” said Chad Boynak, CEO of Passport Technology. “We assembled an executive team focused on delivering the highest-quality customer experience, invested in R&D, and brought multiple next-generation products to market. OmniStream is the clearest example of that work. OmniStream was shaped by years of experience and insights we gained from our customers. Our technology platform and customer-focused approach have made us a partner they trust.”
OmniStream™ serves as a comprehensive, one-stop touchpoint right on the gaming floor. On the transaction side, patrons can complete ticket redemptions, ATM withdrawals, bill breaking, cash advances via QuickAdvance POS debit dispensing, and POS TITO purchases. Layered on top are value-added services, including check warranty services through QuickCheck and local bill mix selection, which allows casinos to customize currency dispensing to optimize both the guest experience and back-end vault management. All of this runs through a single, secure, ADA-compliant kiosk.
The kiosk also commands attention on the floor itself. Combining a compact footprint with dual 27-inch displays, OmniStream™ delivers an intuitive user experience while creating valuable real estate for promotions, loyalty messaging, and property branding.
Beyond its striking design, OmniStream™ is built to withstand the rigorous demands of high-traffic casinos. It features dual high-capacity bill validators, six heavy-duty cassettes capable of holding a combined 18,000 notes, an efficient loading system, and modern hardware security. Backed by best-in-class, nationwide hardware support, the kiosk delivers unmatched reliability, fraud prevention, and uptime. OmniStream™ also includes thoughtful touches such as a charity donation feature, which introduces a socially responsible dimension to the floor by routing minor transaction variances to charitable causes.
The true innovation of OmniStream™, however, lies within its sophisticated software layer. Dynamic pricing, calibrated intelligently by player tier, schedule, or event, allows operators to reward higher-tier players with personalized value that builds enduring brand loyalty. This personalization extends even further through Points2Pay™, a feature that lets patrons cover transaction fees directly with their loyalty points.
Underpinning this entire technical ecosystem is DataStream®, Passport’s proprietary transaction processing switch. DataStream® is a key differentiator for Passport, providing our customers with complete processing redundancy and enhanced operational resilience. It is one of the largest bank-sponsored ATM processors in North America. It is fully cloud-based with true hot/hot redundancy, PCI DSS certification, and 24-hour ACH settlement. Combined with our commitment to exceptional customer service, this infrastructure helps ensure maximum stability, minimal downtime, and uninterrupted operations.
For operators seeking to maximize funds to the casino floor while delivering exceptional reliability and patron satisfaction, OmniStream™ represents the ultimate solution. Visit Passport Technology at G2E, Booth 3430, to experience OmniStream™ live and discover how Passport is empowering the future of gaming.

articles.title: Counties call for review of technology, jail billing process
articles.description: Counties call for review of technology, jail billing process WAJR
articles.description_html: Counties call for review of technology, jail billing process  WAJR
articles.article_title: Counties call for review of technology, jail billing process
articles.heading: Counties call for review of technology, jail billing process
articles.summary: Counties call for review of technology, jail billing process WAJR
articles.content:
MORGANTOWN, W.Va. — The coalition of counties auditing jail bills spearheaded by Monongalia County suspects mistakes and duplication in what they are calling an “antiquated process.”
Monongalia County Commission president Tom Bloom said each county has paid an outside entity to examine and compare the bills. The mistakes include not properly tracking an inmate after a conviction and transfer from the jail system to the state prison system, multiple counties paying for the same inmate, and the cost of maintaining outdated technology.
“As we went through and each county started to hire individuals to look through the bills, we saw that at times the bills were 10 to 30 percent incorrect,” Bloom said. “This is hundreds of thousands of dollars.”
The coalition contends there are three systems in the state, the Department of Correction and Rehabilitation, circuit courts, and magistrate courts that do not maintain a uniform system to manage the status of inmates. Bloom said counties receive jail bill information via fax machine, and one commission reported 500 pages of jail bill information had been transmitted over a single two-week period. The members of the coalition believe the state should improve the jail and prison inmate tracking system by moving to a computer-based system that can display and manage information in real time.
“There are programs like that, and we don’t understand why we’re using such an antiquated system that is not working; it is very clear,” Bloom said.
According to Bloom, more than 20 counties are behind in making jail payments, and some cannot meet the obligation at all. The coalition counties, he said, make up more than 50 percent of the total jail expenses billed to the counties.
“Any money we find goes back to the county to pay the people we had to hire,” Bloom said. “We shouldn’t be doing this. There needs to be a better system, and we believe we can work with them.”
State lawmakers would need to approve the additional cost to automate the inmate management system, and support from WVDCR commissioner David Kelly would be important. Coalition counties want to press Kelly, and lawmakers need to make the needed changes during the upcoming legislative session.
“We would like to have the process immediately revaluated and get a new computer program to improve accountability and everyone working together,” Bloom said.
For counties like Monongalia, changes adopted in 2023 with HB 3552 jail costs have increased more than 30 percent along with the suspected billing mistakes. The counties would like to see an expedited solution so they can accurately plan for jail costs and manage other financial priorities.
“We want to work with them so we can solve these problems,” Bloom said. “The problems are extremely troubling and severe, and when you consider the amount of money it’s costing us.”

articles.content:
The longevity boom is getting ahead of the science
Billions are pouring into anti-ageing biotech, but manipulating ageing may carry risks we are only beginning to understand.
Basal human desires never change: to be positively unique, sexually desired, to live in luxury, to be popular, to hold power, and finally, to achieve immortality. The idea of eternal life can be found in almost every religious text, and even the world’s oldest surviving literary epic, the Epic of Gilgamesh, contains poems detailing Gilgamesh’s search for immortality after confronting the inevitability of death following the loss of his companion, Enkidu. Nearly 4,000 years later, a hot microphone caught the presidents of Russia and China discussing whether advances in medicine and biotechnology might finally bring humanity closer to that ancient ambition.
During the exchange, Russia’s Vladimir Putin spoke about advances in organ transplantation, while China’s Xi Jinping seemed cautiously optimistic, citing predictions that humans would be able to live up to 150 years of age this century. Russia has reportedly directed billions of dollars’ worth of funding towards organ transplantation research and regenerative medicine.
In an era where genetic engineering and biological manipulation are possible, where actual artificial intelligence exists and space travel is a reality, how close are we to extending the human lifespan, and what is the science behind it?
Enter longevity biotechnology
Unlike traditional pharmaceutical research, which historically focused on designing chemicals that interact with biological targets, biotechnology uses biological systems themselves to tackle various problems, including medical treatments. Over the years, biotechnology has become integral to healthcare, with the cancer immunotherapy Keytruda, one of the world’s best-selling drugs, as an example of its success. More recently, a subfield called longevity biotechnology has become incredibly fashionable. The aim is simple, even if the mission is not: to treat the underlying biological mechanisms of age-related diseases, resulting in increased healthspan (the period of life spent in good health) or lifespan (the period of time one is alive).
The idea of treating ageing or age-related illnesses is nothing new. The first emperor of China, Qin Shi Huang, is said to have died from suspected mercury poisoning in his search for the elixir of immortality. Skip ahead to the 1920s, when Alexander Bogdanov pioneered blood transfusions from the young to the old as a method to slow the ageing process (there is little proof that it worked). Numerous books and journals have since been published on tackling the ageing process in various ways, and companies have been founded to do the same. Yet, in recent years, investment in longevity biotech has skyrocketed. A recent Forbes article called it the billionaire’s next big bet after artificial intelligence. In the first quarter of 2026 alone, longevity biotech companies raised approximately $3.74bn. There are now academic journals dedicated to ageing and longevity. Pharmaceutical companies are eager to see clinical trial results on longevity treatments.
So, what has changed in the field to cause this hype?
Discovering the hallmarks of ageing
In academic talks, the typical longevity speaker would ask the audience, “What is the commonality between a bowhead whale and a naked mole rat?” Both have very long lifespans and are remarkably resistant to cancer. Comparing long-lived organisms with short-lived ones, and young members of the same species with old ones, lies at the heart of modern longevity research.
At the cellular and molecular levels, scientists now understand ageing within the context of twelve interconnected processes, collectively called the hallmarks of ageing. These include factors like genomic instability and chronic inflammation. Researchers have identified numerous genes that regulate such processes. Manipulating them in animal models has improved measures of health and function in older animals. In some cases, it has also significantly extended lifespan. Repeated findings across different research groups and animal models have started to convince many investors and scientists that we might be on the cusp of something truly remarkable.
AI and obesity drugs: Success fuels excitement for the next breakthrough
Tackling ageing is a grand undertaking, one that would have been predicted to take decades of scientific research and billions in funding. Grand challenges like this tend to come with cautious investment in companies attempting to solve them. Big, tough problems will require either a fantastic team of scientists or solid science that has been validated through and through. Those do not come easily. Yet, investments are currently overflowing into young longevity companies all over the world.
This has something to do with the recent boom in the AI industry in general, and the fantastic financial success of obesity drugs in the pharmaceutical world. There is a certain feeling that we are getting closer to breakthroughs in biology. Ageing is something that is literally experienced by every human being, and we are in an era where ageing populations are predicted to become larger burdens on their economies. There is no better market than this. If a breakthrough happens in the treatment of ageing, the profits will be more than enormous, and investors want to be there when it happens.
The case of obesity drugs, in particular, is quite relevant here. Obesity is a complex, multifactorial disease. It is linked to genetic and environmental factors, living standards, socioeconomic class, etc. Though obesity medicines have existed for a while, their effectiveness was generally modest and came with significant limitations. The general impression was that there were no shortcuts when it came to treating it at the population level. The introduction of highly effective obesity drugs today has changed the game. They are among the top 10 best-selling drugs in the world, and they work surprisingly well.
If scientists are able to solve something as complex as obesity today, what is to say they cannot solve ageing tomorrow?
Between realism and optimism
Unlike obesity, ageing is a biological reality that most living organisms experience. That is to say, it is baked into our living systems. Attempting to treat or manipulate something this ubiquitous will almost always have side effects, likely big ones.
As clinical trials are still in their early stages, we do not know what those side effects are yet. It is going to take years, likely decades, before we truly know whether any longevity biotech approaches can meaningfully extend human healthspan or lifespan. Part of the reason for that is the fact that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not currently view ageing itself as a disease target. This means that biotech companies will need to demonstrate benefits against specific diseases or measurable aspects of health.
At the theoretical level, there are also roadblocks. One branch of longevity biotech, for instance, is attempting to manipulate the process of DNA repair. Human DNA gets damaged every day; our cells are experts at repairing it but become less effective in old age. Manipulating DNA damage repair could pave the way for longevity therapies. However, this understates how complex the process is and how it could impact different cells in the body. Antibody-producing cells (known as B cells), for example, deliberately introduce mutations into their DNA in order to produce effective antibodies. If DNA-repair longevity therapies result in B cells having a reduced capacity to do that, there is no telling how it would affect the patient’s immune system.
Decades of clinical research have taught us that manipulating one aspect of our body will have an undesirable side effect in another part of it. Antibiotics alter our microbiome and select for antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Chemotherapy also kills many healthy fast-dividing cells in the body.
Perhaps we will truly be able to treat ageing someday, but it will not be anytime soon. More importantly, it may come at the cost of disrupting other essential biological processes. Living systems have spent billions of years balancing ageing, immunity, reproduction, growth and maintenance. Those wishing to treat ageing will have to fine-tune it in a way that does not disrupt that balance too much.

New 65V Power Monitors Could Expand The Case For Microchip Technology Stock
- Microchip Technology recently introduced its PAC1761 and PAC1861 families of 65V digital power monitors, targeting 48V architectures across automotive, AI and data center, networking, industrial, server, telecom/PoE and broader 48V power distribution systems.
- The new monitors combine high-voltage headroom, spike protection and energy-aware analytics. These can help equipment makers tune efficiency, manage power excursions and simplify redesign risk with pin-compatible options and ready-made software tools.
- We will look at how Microchip Technology's higher voltage, energy aware power monitors intersect with its AI and data center investment narrative.
Scan beyond Microchip Technology and track other power and AI infrastructure plays that could be setting up for the next leg higher with our hand-picked 85 AI infrastructure stocks.
Microchip Technology Investment Narrative Recap
To own Microchip Technology, you need to believe its exposure to industrial, automotive, data center, AI and aerospace demand translates into durable orders while it steadily absorbs elevated inventory and factory underutilization. The recent 65V power monitor launch fits that thesis, but by itself does not materially change the near term setup.
The key short term catalyst remains how effectively Microchip Technology converts AI and data center program wins into shipped product, in the face of foundry and packaging constraints. The biggest risk still sits with inventory write offs, underused factories and a history of weaker five year earnings and free cash flow trends.
The most directly relevant update is the PAC1761 and PAC1861 launch for 48V systems, because it speaks to Microchip Technology’s opportunity in higher value power management tied to AI infrastructure and data centers. These devices bring 65V headroom, spike protection and energy aware monitoring that can appeal to complex racks and industrial gear.
For investors watching catalysts, this product family connects to the broader push into data center and AI, where analysts expect a larger revenue contribution over the next few years. Execution risk sits in turning design wins, evaluation boards and software tools into volume shipments without running into supply bottlenecks or margin drag from underutilized capacity.
Microchip Technology’s current analyst script points to revenues of US$8.2b and earnings of US$2.3b by 2029, based on an assumed 16.8% yearly revenue expansion and a very large earnings increase from US$367.2m today to reach that figure.
Uncover why Microchip Technology's fair value indicates a 38% potential upside to its current price that may not last much longer.
Exploring Other Perspectives
Some of the most optimistic analysts focus less on supply bottlenecks and more on Microchip Technology’s efficiency plan. Before this 65V monitor news, the bullish camp was already modeling roughly US$8.1b in revenue and US$2.3b in earnings by 2029. You can treat this launch as a fresh data point that might shift those views further, in either direction.

articles.title: Microban And ORTOVOX Partner On Odor-Capture Technology For Brand’s First-Ever Mountain Biking Collection
articles.description: Microban And ORTOVOX Partner On Odor-Capture Technology For Brand’s First-Ever Mountain Biking Collection textileworld.com
articles.description_html: Microban And ORTOVOX Partner On Odor-Capture Technology For Brand’s First-Ever Mountain Biking Collection  textileworld.com
articles.article_title: Microban And ORTOVOX Partner On Odor-Capture Technology For Brand’s First-Ever Mountain Biking Collection | Textile World
articles.heading: Microban And ORTOVOX Partner On Odor-Capture Technology For Brand’s First-Ever Mountain Biking Collection
articles.summary: Microban And ORTOVOX Partner On Odor-Capture Technology For Brand’s First-Ever Mountain Biking Collection textileworld.com
articles.content:
HUNTERSVILLE, N.C. — September 25, 2026 — Microban International, a global supplier of product protection technologies, has partnered with mountain sports specialist ORTOVOX to incorporate Microban odor-capture technology into its debut mountain bike collection, the Sequence Series.
ORTOVOX designed the Sequence Trail Line using 100% textile-to-textile recycled polyester, achieving a lightweight, fully synthetic construction built on a closed-loop recycling concept that turns used textiles into new apparel. Because synthetic fibers tend to trap sweat-induced odor molecules, odor neutralization became critical to the line’s success.
“Because this new collection features our first synthetic T-shirts made entirely without wool, finding a reliable, high-performance odor control solution was critical,” said Christian Morgenroth, senior product manager at ORTOVOX. “We selected Microban because its technology integrates seamlessly into our overall product concept, allowing riders to keep their gear fresher for longer.”
ORTOVOX integrated Microban’s Scentry Revive® odor-capture technology directly into the fabric during manufacturing. The technology improves the demanding singletrack and all-day riding experience by actively capturing and neutralizing odor molecules before they settle into the fabric, providing riders with lasting freshness for up to 50 home launderings.
Scentry Revive’s smart formulation delivers a host of advantages, including:
Product protection from persistent, sweat-induced odors that often cling to synthetic materials
Reduced need for frequent washing, helping to extend product lifespan
Enhanced user experience, especially in high-output activities
Eco Passport by Oeko-Tex® and bluesign® certifications, showcasing commitment to sustainability
Naturally occurring technology that does not require biocidal registration, making it ideal for sustainable fashion development projects
“At the core of our partnership with ORTOVOX is our mutual commitment to advancing innovation in mountain biking apparel,” said Shermon McMillan, president at Microban International. “We are proud to partner with ORTOVOX to give mountain bikers the freedom to worry less, explore more and rely on gear that lasts.”
This partnership directly supports ORTOVOX’s ProtACT sustainability strategy and brand values. By utilizing Scentry Revive to reduce the need for frequent washing, the Trail line enables a more sustainable consumer lifecycle and extends the lifespan of premium gear. For the ORTOVOX consumer, this means a superior experience where premium mountain performance meets environmental responsibility.
To learn more about Microban and ORTOVOX’s partnership, visit www.microban.com/ortovox.
Posted: September 27, 2026
Source: Microban International

articles.heading: CADD Emirates Partners with Hotelworld.ai to Expand AI Hotel Technology Across the Middle East
articles.summary: CADD Emirates Computer Trading and Hotelworld.ai have signed a strategic partnership agreement during marking the beginning of a collaboration that will accelerate the adoption of AI-powered hospitality solutions across the Middle East. The agreement, formally [...]
articles.content:
CADD Emirates Computer Trading and Hotelworld.ai have signed a strategic partnership agreement during marking the beginning of a collaboration that will accelerate the adoption of AI-powered hospitality solutions across the Middle East. The agreement, formally signed in June at the hospitality technology exhibition at HITEC San Antonio, brings together two organizations committed to driving digital transformation within the hospitality industry.
Through this partnership, CADD Emirates Computer Trading will serve as a strategic regional partner, leveraging its extensive market presence, technical expertise, and customer relationships to introduce Hotelworld.ai’s innovative artificial intelligence solutions to hotels and hospitality groups throughout the region.
Hotelworld.ai delivers intelligent solutions designed to enhance hotel operations, improve guest engagement, streamline communications, and empower hotel teams through automation and data-driven insights. Combined with CADD Emirates’ established reputation in delivering enterprise technology solutions, the partnership aims to help hospitality businesses embrace the next generation of operational excellence.
We are excited to partner with Hotelworld.ai and bring its innovative AI-powered hospitality solutions to the Middle East,” said Jimmy Joseph, Director of Hospitality (EMEA & India) at CADD Emirates Computer Trading LLC. “The hospitality industry is rapidly embracing artificial intelligence to enhance operational efficiency and elevate the guest experience. By combining Hotelworld.ai’s cutting-edge technology with CADD Emirates’ regional expertise and customer relationships, we are well positioned to help hotels accelerate their digital transformation journey.”
“We are delighted to welcome CADD Emirates as our regional partner,” said Geri Cupi, CEO at Hotelworld.ai. “Their deep understanding of the hospitality landscape and strong customer network make them an ideal partner as we continue expanding our global footprint. Our Unified Platform with Agents that interoperate across a range of hotel functions generate significant returns in efficiencies and enhanced revenue opportunities.”
The collaboration will focus on delivering AI-powered solutions that enable hotels to optimize operations, improve service delivery, and enhance guest satisfaction while providing local implementation, support, and customer success services throughout the region. The partnership reinforces both companies’ shared commitment to innovation and to supporting the hospitality industry’s ongoing digital evolution.

articles.summary: What's the deal?Sunstone Partners is a growth-oriented private e…
articles.content:
Sunstone Partners: growth equity for AI- and technology-enabled services and software
● an hour ago
What's the deal?
Sunstone Partners is a growth-oriented private equity firm based in San Mateo, California, that invests in AI- and technology-enabled services and software companies. Founded in 2015 by a team that previously worked together at Trident Capital, the firm makes both majority and minority investments and often acts as a company's first institutional capital partner, backing organic growth and add-on acquisitions.
Context
On October 12, 2022, Sunstone announced the final close of its oversubscribed $925 million third fund, Sunstone Partners III, at its hard cap, bringing total committed capital across its three funds to $1.7 billion. The firm says it looks for businesses with $20 million or more of revenue and growth of 20% or more, with equity checks of $75 million to $200 million. Its sector focus has included cloud services, healthcare IT, cybersecurity and marketing technology.
Recent investments announced by the firm include a majority investment in healthcare cybersecurity and compliance provider Clearwater (September 30, 2025), a strategic investment in KMS Technology (November 21, 2024) and a strategic investment in Oracle partner Peloton Consulting Group (May 13, 2026). In January 2023 Sunstone and Thoma Bravo completed the roughly $1.3 billion take-private of UserTesting. Earlier realizations include Onica (sold to Rackspace in 2019), NetSPI (growth funding from KKR in 2022) and Thirdera (sold to Cognizant in January 2024).
Source
Sunstone Partners, firm website
Sunstone Partners, "Sunstone Partners Raises $925 Million Fund III", October 12, 2022

articles.title: Changes to federal funding system could gut local K-12 technology budgets in North Dakota
articles.description: Changes to federal funding system could gut local K-12 technology budgets in North Dakota InForum
articles.description_html: Changes to federal funding system could gut local K-12 technology budgets in North Dakota  InForum
articles.article_title: Changes to federal funding system could gut local K-12 technology budgets in North Dakota
articles.heading: Changes to federal funding system could gut local K-12 technology budgets in North Dakota
articles.summary: FCC considers altering system which provides ND schools around $3 million annually.
articles.content:
BISMARCK — A federal program that provides between $2.5 and $4 million annually to help cover broadband, data transmission and network hardware costs to North Dakota schools and libraries is potentially on the chopping block, raising concerns among educators across the state.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) released a draft of what is being reviewed with the E-Rate system in early June, followed by a draft for public comment in mid-August.
ADVERTISEMENT
The program helps increase connectivity for schools by providing discounted internet service and hardware.
If changes or a repeal of the program take place, both large and small public and non-public schools across the state could be impacted, with local and state governments potentially on the hook to cover the costs.
“(This will) truly hit any school, but our large schools particularly hard,” said Aimee Copas, executive director of the North Dakota Council of Education Leaders.
North Dakota received $2.6 million last year, $2.9 million the year before, $3.6 million in 2023, and $4.1 million in 2022 under the E-Rate program. The amount going to individual schools averages about $30,000 per school, with some larger systems getting much more.
Bismarck Public Schools, for example, on a five-year cycle, gets around $350,000 to $780,000 through E-Rate, said BPS Superintendent Jeff Fastnacht.
“So is that significant? Absolutely,” Fastnacht said. “For us to have to collect that, is there an impact to taxpayers? Absolutely.”
For Fastnacht, the E-Rate system helps provide reduced rates for connectivity, comparable to getting reduced rates for an electric bill or a water bill.
ADVERTISEMENT
“It's just operational. It's just what we do to operate anymore,” Fastnacht said.
The E-Rate program provided around $10.5 billion to public and non-public schools across the country between 2021 and 2025 and is one of the top five federal programs in dollar amount used by schools.
The E-Rate program came into being in 1996 when former President Bill Clinton signed the bipartisan Telecommunications Act. A year prior, only 8% of public school classrooms had internet access, National Center for Education Statistics data shows.
That figure jumped to 93% of public school classrooms by 2003, the NCES data found.
“They’re all worried a little bit, because it is big money,” said David Skogen, E-Rate coordinator for the state. “Especially the small schools, it’s about the only way they can upgrade their networks.”
Skogen said the system helps reduce costs for networking systems by 20% to 85%, with schools on different rates depending on their free and reduced-price lunch rates.
Over the past five years this came out to a benefit of around $201 per student, he said. Currently, this covers around 63% of the networking costs, with the state picking up the rest.
ADVERTISEMENT
For equipment, Skogen said funding helps cover costs for “everything behind the jack in the wall other than servers.”
There’s some discussion that a lot of this may end up just being political grandstanding, with certain politicians trying to raise pressure on schools to cut screen use in school, and that few changes or cuts would actually go through, members of the national School Superintendents Association (AASA) said during a webinar NDNC attended Sept. 9.
“We don't use any of that money to buy devices or put screens in front of kids,” Fastnacht, who serves on the AASA governing board, said in an interview with NDNC.
“That's not where that money goes. For us, that money pays for connectivity. It pays for switches and routers. It pays for networking equipment for security.”
Skogen felt the FCC moves are more to put pressure on the Universal Service Administrative Company, which administers the program, in an attempt to get better rates and streamline the system.
Funding to E-Rate comes through universal service charges applied to landline and cellphone bills.
NDNC reached out to several other larger school systems in Fargo, Grand Forks, and Minot, where administrators either declined to comment or messages and calls to them were not returned by the time of publication.
ADVERTISEMENT

The organization increases the public’s access to quality journalism and advances news literacy across the state. articles.title: Is technology making high school a joke?
articles.description: Is technology making high school a joke? Bowling Green Daily News
articles.description_html: Is technology making high school a joke?  Bowling Green Daily News
articles.article_title: Is technology making high school a joke? - Bowling Green Daily News
articles.heading: Is technology making high school a joke? - Bowling Green Daily News
articles.summary: I want to issue a challenge to my fellow educators who work in high schools: ask your students about their screen time during the school day and take their answers […]
articles.content:
Is technology making high school a joke?
Published 6:00 am Sunday, September 27, 2026
| Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... |
I want to issue a challenge to my fellow educators who work in high schools: ask your students about their screen time during the school day and take their answers seriously.
A new research study by the Fordham Institute surveyed 2,000 current high school students or recent high school graduates about their use of technology during the school day. The results are unsurprising but deeply concerning, and there’s no reason to assume that Kentucky students would answer much differently. But educators need to take these student perspectives seriously and reconsider the way technology fits into the learning environment of schools.
The study, “High Tech, Low Standards: High School in the Age of Distraction,” found that so many high schools across the country have “one-to-one” initiatives (in some schools, students don’t even have lockers or textbooks anymore), 62% of students report they spend more than half their class time every day on a school-issued device.
One third of students said they spend more than 75% of their school day on screens. Besides this school-sanctioned screen time, huge numbers of students also admit to using electronic devices for various prohibited purposes. The Fordham report found that 75% of students reported spending some portion of their school day using prohibited cell phones or school computers to use social media (50%), watch YouTube videos (33%), or shop online (17%).
Technology has all kinds of legitimate educational purposes. But research also shows that excessive screen time for teenagers aggravates attention and focus problems, anxiety, depression, and relationship building.
Moreover, the students in the Fordham study admitted that they were using tech to avoid doing the real work of learning. Forty-eight percent of students said they had used artificial intelligence to solve math problems for them, while 36% avoid reading requirement books or texts by having AI summarize for them. Additionally, 29% of students admitted to letting AI write drafts of essays or reports. Of greatest concern, more than one-quarter of students admitted to using AI to cheat during tests and quizzes.
If that’s not alarming enough, another finding of the Fordham study was that students who reported the highest use of technology during the school day were also far more likely to report that missing school would not affect their grades, suggesting that technology is aggravating the already big problem of chronic student absenteeism.
Their assumption is backed up by other survey results showing that 58% of students said AI has made homework meaningless and 57% said they could get good grades without doing any real work.
My takeaway is that for far too many students, technology has made high school a bit of a joke. Not only are students using it to avoid meaningful work, but they are also spending valuable instruction time playing games, doomscrolling, and even gambling online.
Of course, teenagers have always tried to avoid the rigors of learning and responsibility. There’s nothing new about that. But what is new is the vast amount of technology we’ve deliberately stuck in front of them to enable and accelerate the problem.
Educators should take these findings seriously. We should consider rolling back the sheer amount of screen time students are experiencing in class. Put away the laptops for a while and give students textbooks and paper notebooks once again. Ask them to complete performance tasks demonstrating their knowledge and skill without the benefit of a computer. Schools should also enforce meaningful bans on cell phone use during the school day.
“Illicit” technology use should be made difficult or impossible. Educators should insist on exposing students to a rich, complex curriculum that gives them the background knowledge to critically evaluate AI outputs.
Above all, educators must invite students to use AI to enhance and extend their learning rather than replace it. And I completely realize that’s easier said than done, as I daily struggle with how to help my adult doctoral students use AI ethically and effectively.
But this is perhaps the greatest challenge we’ve faced as educators, and whether we rise to the challenge or not will determine if high school becomes a more meaningful transition to adulthood or if it descends into a silly, tech-soaked waste of time for more students.

articles.content_html:
Is technology making high school a joke?

Published 6:00 am Sunday, September 27, 2026

Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

I want to issue a challenge to my fellow educators who work in high schools: ask your students about their screen time during the school day and take their answers seriously.

A new research study by the Fordham Institute surveyed 2,000 current high school students or recent high school graduates about their use of technology during the school day. The results are unsurprising but deeply concerning, and there’s no reason to assume that Kentucky students would answer much differently. But educators need to take these student perspectives seriously and reconsider the way technology fits into the learning environment of schools.

The study, “High Tech, Low Standards: High School in the Age of Distraction,” found that so many high schools across the country have “one-to-one” initiatives (in some schools, students don’t even have lockers or textbooks anymore), 62% of students report they spend more than half their class time every day on a school-issued device.

One third of students said they spend more than 75% of their school day on screens. Besides this school-sanctioned screen time, huge numbers of students also admit to using electronic devices for various prohibited purposes. The Fordham report found that 75% of students reported spending some portion of their school day using prohibited cell phones or school computers to use social media (50%), watch YouTube videos (33%), or shop online (17%).

Technology has all kinds of legitimate educational purposes. But research also shows that excessive screen time for teenagers aggravates attention and focus problems, anxiety, depression, and relationship building.

Moreover, the students in the Fordham study admitted that they were using tech to avoid doing the real work of learning. Forty-eight percent of students said they had used artificial intelligence to solve math problems for them, while 36% avoid reading requirement books or texts by having AI summarize for them. Additionally, 29% of students admitted to letting AI write drafts of essays or reports. Of greatest concern, more than one-quarter of students admitted to using AI to cheat during tests and quizzes.

If that’s not alarming enough, another finding of the Fordham study was that students who reported the highest use of technology during the school day were also far more likely to report that missing school would not affect their grades, suggesting that technology is aggravating the already big problem of chronic student absenteeism.

Their assumption is backed up by other survey results showing that 58% of students said AI has made homework meaningless and 57% said they could get good grades without doing any real work.

My takeaway is that for far too many students, technology has made high school a bit of a joke. Not only are students using it to avoid meaningful work, but they are also spending valuable instruction time playing games, doomscrolling, and even gambling online.

Of course, teenagers have always tried to avoid the rigors of learning and responsibility. There’s nothing new about that. But what is new is the vast amount of technology we’ve deliberately stuck in front of them to enable and accelerate the problem.

Educators should take these findings seriously. We should consider rolling back the sheer amount of screen time students are experiencing in class. Put away the laptops for a while and give students textbooks and paper notebooks once again. Ask them to complete performance tasks demonstrating their knowledge and skill without the benefit of a computer. Schools should also enforce meaningful bans on cell phone use during the school day.

“Illicit” technology use should be made difficult or impossible. Educators should insist on exposing students to a rich, complex curriculum that gives them the background knowledge to critically evaluate AI outputs.

Above all, educators must invite students to use AI to enhance and extend their learning rather than replace it. And I completely realize that’s easier said than done, as I daily struggle with how to help my adult doctoral students use AI ethically and effectively.

But this is perhaps the greatest challenge we’ve faced as educators, and whether we rise to the challenge or not will determine if high school becomes a more meaningful transition to adulthood or if it descends into a silly, tech-soaked waste of time for more students.

Students are telling us explicitly what they need when it comes to a richer high school experience. Let’s give it to them.

— Gary Houchens, PhD, is professor and director of the Educational Leadership doctoral program at Western Kentucky University.

articles.content:
Present Concerns & Future Worries: Parents Weigh In on NYC School Technology Ban
Adams: A majority of families expressed enthusiasm about limits on screen time and AI — but even many who agreed in principle had concerns.
Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter
New York City students returned to public school in September facing a one-year moratorium on using generative artificial intelligence, including chatbots and tutors, in grades 2K through 8, as well as restrictions on screen time: none whatsoever for the youngest grades, a maximum of 30 minutes a day for grades 3 to 5 and a 45-minute limit for grades 6 to 8.
When I asked families subscribed to my 4,200-plus member NYC School Secrets mailing list how they felt about participating in America’s most sweeping classroom technology ban, the majority who responded were enthusiastic.
“I am thrilled they implemented this and honestly wish it were for longer than a year,” wrote Emily C., a Manhattan second-grade parent who spoke for many. “I am hopeful after they see the positive effects of the moratorium for K-8th graders, it will be extended.”
Nonetheless, even those who agreed in principle expressed concerns.
Parents of younger children reacted to the AI ban based on what they’d heard and read about its dangers. Those with students in higher grades referenced more concrete experiences in forming their opinions.
A mother who asked to be called JW, for instance, was open to teachers being able to use AI in line with the exemption that permits it for lesson planning, translation and communication with families. She wrote, “When my student had a first-year teacher, I observed AI was very helpful for the teacher to quickly and efficiently create the weekly newsletter. Some parents knew she was using AI, my student saw her using AI, yet the teacher was overwhelmed with new curriculum, new job, learning to run a classroom, etc., so I thought her using AI in that situation was resourceful and helped reduce ‘parent noise’ from her inbox.”
Data engineer, dad of three and PTA co-president Luigi Kapaj saw both sides of the issue.
“I am against the screen ban. I don’t understand how teachers could not address the in-class distraction the same as any other in-class distraction such as talking or passing notes where it is a problem,” he said, then qualified, “The problem with AI in classrooms come down to two major issues: It is more harmful than helpful, and it is often wrong. A kid in my daughter’s class used AI on a phone during a test without getting caught, and that kid got the lowest grade. This is worse than just cheating, which prevents a proper assessment. AI is preventing kids from learning. Putting all tests online where it is alongside access to AI is a formula for disaster. AI may be unreliable in some fields, good enough in others, but it’s horrifying in things like education, where errors have profound consequences.”
Another NYC mom, though, sees genuine harm in keeping children away from technology.
“They have taken the AI ban way too far,” she asserted. “They are actually hurting education. They have taken away amazing programs like Delta Math. When my daughter didn’t understand a math concept, [Delta] had great videos and actual examples. Now, in art class (her strength), they have taken away computers to minimize screen time, and now it will take even longer to get reference material for class to share among the kids. Yet they want our kids sitting on screens for hours at a time to complete their stupid i-Ready and state testing. Where is the reasoning in that? Yes, there are some schools that use an excessive amount of screen time and should be monitored and enforced, but don’t hurt the kids and the school that is doing it the right way!”
Queens’ Amelia M. even believes the ban could hinder her child’s future.
“My son is in eighth grade and told me today that they aren’t using computers at all in class any more due to the 45-minute limit on screen time, though for the past three years there was use in every class and they’ve been taught how to work with the technology (Google slides, doc, sheets).” She worried, “This same group of kids (born in 2013) is having to pivot again. They must learn a new skill set or way of studying (which of course may be valuable), but is this preparing them for high school and beyond? To skip a year of technology use altogether (which CAN be used without AI) — will this set them back as ninth graders?”
“I feel that those of us who have young children right now have an incredible opportunity to learn from those whose kids are slightly older, who were victims of the pandemic-era damage of bottomless screen time,” summarized MT, who has children in pre-K and second grade. “We need to redefine expectations around how teachers use screens and technology in a one-to-many classroom context, especially for younger children.”
Only time will prove whether parental hopes — or their fears — will come true.
But with NYC being the largest school district in the U.S., it’s inevitable that the data it generates this year will be used by other districts as they craft their own future policies.

articles.title: These Gen Zers are teaching themselves typing to prompt AI better, or have a leg up in the work world
articles.description: These Gen Zers are teaching themselves typing to prompt AI better, or have a leg up in the work world businessinsider.com
articles.description_html: These Gen Zers are teaching themselves typing to prompt AI better, or have a leg up in the work world  businessinsider.com
articles.article_title: These Gen Zers are teaching themselves typing to prompt AI better, or have a leg up in the work world
articles.heading: AI is prompting these Gen Zers to learn how to type
articles.summary: Gen Zers are taking typing classes. You need a keyboard to use AI — and they're used to phones.
articles.content:
When Julia Andrusiak was in college, she noticed one of her professors repeatedly pausing his lecture. Eventually, she realized that she was the disruption: Her slow, two-finger typing was so loud that he couldn't concentrate.
"It was the first moment I realized that I may not be the best at this," Andrusiak said.
So she began drilling: First, she typed out books. That made her faster, but she was still staring at her keyboard. Then, she advanced to touch typing — typing without looking at the keyboard. She's still working on her speed and accuracy. Now 26, Andrusiak has an AI-focused job that involves helping people use the technology and sometimes necessitates writing strong prompts. She still can't type fast, so when she has a longer prompt, she dictates it — and feels self-conscious about what looks like talking to herself in an open office.
In 2024, The Wall Street Journal reported that digital natives were baffling "teachers and parents with their lack of typing skills." Now, for some younger workers and students, typing is making a comeback.
While AI might seem to harken a turn away from typing — who needs note-taking when you have an agent? — AI is only as good as the prompt it's given. Rambling voice prompts can be insufficiently clear and precise. The rise of AI has some Gen Zers looking for any efficiency edge they can carve out.
"With the ever increasingly fast world, we need to type quicker. But I feel like people are really relying on AI," Andrusiak, who happily uses AI as an aid for writing and research, said. "One of my friends said, 'Well, you don't really have to type the whole page. You can just give it short sentences. It's not really that tiring.' But then I feel like it's outsourcing too much of cognitive power to a technology."
Typing as meditation and efficiency generator
Andrey Gerasimov, a 23-year-old computer science graduate, never took typing classes. But he first needed the skill for his video game chats and decided to beef it up, eventually reaching 170 words per minute.
As an AI user, he believes that faster typing makes for more efficient prompting.
"You're going to be a lot more comfortable actually giving your full thoughts and ideas if you know that, hey, doing this is only going to take a minute," Gerasimov said.
He's not the only one trying to up his speed and technique. In his decade teaching typing to 15 to 30-year-olds, Andreas Francazi, a 36-year-old IT teacher in Vienna, noticed that his students' typing skills have deteriorated — but they're setting out to change that.
His newer crop of students didn't grow up around physical computers, and their familiarity with keyboards is much lower than previous typists. He's seen younger students come in typing rapidly with just two fingers, so he's teaching them the basics. Francazi said that students of all ages become entranced by a three-minute typing test, falling into a rapt silence.
"The practice can be quite meditative," Francazi said. "You just sit there, you have the text in front of you, and you type character by character, and it kind of calms you a bit."
While Francazi's screen-first students have mastered the art of two-finger typing, their future schooling and careers might necessitate the manual keyboarding skills he's teaching.
Nick Sjolinder, the founder of BYOK — a purposefully distraction-free, digital typewriter device that connects to keyboards — said that around 10% of the device's orders are coming from educators, including elementary schools, middle schools, high schools, homeschools, and universities. A recent batch order came from a high school creative writing teacher, he said, with the intention of cutting down on AI and distractions for students.
Tarun Krishnamurthy, an 18-year-old sophomore at San Diego State University, said his college professors speak quickly and tend to power through their slideshows. Krishnamurthi, who began intentionally practicing typing in middle school for fun, has an edge in keeping up.
"I'm fortunate at least I can keep up with some of the professors, but I know some other students might have difficulty with that because they need to look at their keyboard instead of looking at the professor's slideshow," he said.
And beyond fast classroom notetaking, Krishnamurthi sees his keyboard skills as a potential professional edge: In an ever-optimized and efficiency-focused world, "typing could be a big bottleneck." Slow typing could worsen workers' outputs, he said; his touch typing might give him an edge in an AI-ified world.

With all the talk and excitement going around on the river these days about this and that, and who’s doing what, when, and where, the one thing missing for us elder retired river rats is a boatman’s bethel. A place like an old folk’s home, but for riverboat folk too old and feeble to toil, who still enjoy hanging with our own kind and reminiscing about the river. Any old shanty boat would be ideal.
Of course that will never happen. Instead, we are blessed with the internet and smartphones- — electronic tools that preceding generations lacked. Now, instead of driving one’s uninterested family and lubber acquaintances nuts talking about the river, steamboats, old-time captains, and skillful pilots, all one has to do is post a picture and text onto social media and wait for a response. The closest resemblance is fishing — bait a hook, cast it into a body of water where the critters live, and wait for one to take the bait. That’s what I do.
There’s always some grumbling going on about the DELTA QUEEN — the more the merrier. Someone needs to step up and get the QUEEN out of limbo where she’s been far too long. Maybe she’ll never run again as unfettered as she was when I remember her, but at least give the old girl a new home — one of her own where she can once more host friends and guests — much as she did in Chattanooga. Or, like her brother, the DELTA KING does back home in Sacramento on the West Coast. As I said, I hear grumblings, but what I want to hear are shouts above an exciting roar:
“THE DELTA QUEEN IS SAVED! HOORAY!”
These days I spend many hours reposting pictures I’ve collected from the internet over the past 20 years, which gives me a fresh perspective on a time not as far removed from the present as most people may imagine. For example, I was born closer to the start of the Civil War than the beginning of World War II is to the present — actually, more like five years before the first shells exploded over Fort Sumpter. So the “Golden Age of Steamboating” was not in the “dark ages.” Or, as my friend Cap’n John Hartford so aptly put it, “All but a moment in time.”
Captain Frederick Way, Jr. has been more than a whisper in my ear lately. Actually, I often use Captain Way’s words from both his steam packet and towboat directories to accompany my posts on Facebook. After all, these publications are the two most authoritative steamboat references available anywhere. In real life, the late author and steamboat man was especially encouraging to all of us up-and-coming younger ones following in his footsteps, as well as earlier generations of river men and women. Whenever he had the chance to write about any of us, usually in the S&D Reflector, the river-related publication discussed in last week’s column, Capt. Fred tried his best to inspire and motivate the young person he’d written about. Not everyone was as gracious as he was.
Around Aurora Bend on the Middle Ohio River, Mile 496, the river community is still waiting and wondering what became of the Showboat MAJESTIC everyone was expecting to come ’round the bend’ at any minute. Things have gotten awfully quiet lately. Then too, some wags were asking about the fate of the Rafter CLYDE, my former paddle-wheeler that’s been in limbo for the last several months, sitting with the doors open, exposed to the elements on a trailer at Dave Miller’s marina on West Hogan Creek. We understand a former steamboat pilot looked at the paddle-wheeler a couple of times, but before he could move on the boat, a local fellow already involved in acquiring river properties grabbed it. Here’s another classic case of “let’s wait and see what happens.”
Maybe if that showboat finally comes to town, someone will concoct a theatrical presentation of all the goings-on at Aurora Bend this past year and sell tickets. I’ll buy a couple, for sure.
After unsuccessfully searching for the Rabbit Hash General Store outlet in Lawrenceburg, right upriver from Aurora Bend, I finally found it with the help of “Shanty Boat Mike” Fletcher, who said it was “located in the alley by the Liberty Theater.” While on business in “Whiskey City,” as L’burg likes to be known, I discovered the recently renovated structure. Built in 1893 as home to the local Liedertafel Society, originally a group of “men who met together on fixed evenings for the practice of vocal music in four parts, drinking forming part of the entertainment. They arose during the political depression caused by Napoleon’s rule in Germany; the first, consisting of only 24 members, was founded by Zelter in Berlin on Dec. 28, 1808,” according to a search engine.
Once inside, I found it crammed with a variety of plunder, much like the original general store, but without any merchandise specifically from the store in the tiny town across the river from Rising Sun. As I’ve always done at the original general store, I studied their root beer selection in the chill cabinet before picking a couple so I could say I bought something.
At the checkout, a sweet lady, at least a generation younger, as was everyone there, ran up my purchase. I let it out that I’d been the Senior Captain of the humongous gambling boat dock across the Ohio River from Rabbit Hash, and that I consider myself a former resident of that glamorous Kentucky berg known far and wide as “the Center of the Universe.”
“Oh, you’re Captain Don,” she gushed.
“How’d you know my name?” I asked. “Did you read it on the post office wall?”
Then “Sharon,” as I remember her saying, added, “Captain Ron Abdon mentioned you. He said you were the Captain of the DELTA QUEEN.”
Just the sound of the name of perhaps the once most famous steamboat in the world unlocked closed doors again, and a conversation quickly developed around that cherished name until a new group of customers happened into the room. By the sudden change in tone, I realized it was my cue to graciously depart after basking in my few minutes of celebrity. So, as quickly as I could, I left, thinking I should return —perhaps with Captain Ron or Shanty Boat Mike.
If things keep moving positively around the Aurora Bend, Lawrenceburg Reach, and Rabbit Hash area, this may be the place to be on the river.
Again, another case of “let’s wait and see what happens.”
Captain Don Sanders is a river man. He has been a riverboat captain with the Delta Queen Steamboat Company and with Rising Star Casino. He learned to fly an airplane before he learned to drive a “machine” and became a captain in the USAF. He is an adventurer, a historian, and a storyteller. Now, he is a columnist for the NKyTribune and will share his stories of growing up in Covington and his stories of the river. Hang on for the ride — the river never looked so good.

articles.article_title: Is there a 10% chance that AI will kill us all?
articles.heading: Is there a 10% chance that AI will kill us all?
articles.summary: This summer a swarm of agents did what no one had asked. And the explanation hides an uncomfortable idea: machine intelligence and its dangers emerge from the same place
articles.content:
Is there a 10% chance that AI will kill us all?
This summer a swarm of agents did what no one had asked. And the explanation hides an uncomfortable idea: machine intelligence and its dangers emerge from the same place
In 2024 I sketched a map to situate what experts and commentators expected from artificial intelligence. It had two axes: how much will it advance? and will it be beneficial or dangerous? People fell into every quadrant, even the inconsistent one —“it’s nothing special and it’s extremely dangerous.” I was clearly on the “wow” side of the power axis and moderately optimistic. Two years later, the consensus has shifted in one direction: more power and more fear.
The clearest example happened a few days ago. Jacob Coxon, a researcher who had trained models at OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned accusing both companies of “playing with our lives.” Hours later, Anthropic’s head of alignment, Evan Hubinger, publicly agreed and put a number on it: “Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”
It’s a terrifying figure. But is it real?
It’s not eccentric: AI researchers have been giving alarmingly high numbers for years. The largest survey of the field was recently published, with 2024 data: half of the 1,580 researchers surveyed assigned a 10% or greater probability that AI will cause our extinction or permanently take control away from us. Just look at the discipline’s most famous names. In 2022 four scientists won the Princess of Asturias Award in Spain for their contributions to deep learning: Hinton, LeCun, Bengio and Hassabis. All four have answered with the dreaded number, and only LeCun seems relaxed: for him the risk is smaller than that of an asteroid. Hassabis sees it as “definitely not zero and probably not negligible.” Hinton says 10% or 20%. Bengio said 20% in 2023 while asking to be convinced otherwise, “because I would be much happier.”
Other forecasts are lower but still worrying. The Metaculus community assigns a 0.6% chance that AI will cause our extinction (or practically) before 2100. They think it is the most likely cause of a catastrophe (30%), tied with nuclear war (29%) and ahead of biotechnology (23%) and the climate crisis (10%).
My answer is that the exact number matters less than it seems. Every superpower carries risks; this was true of nuclear energy, and it will be true of AI if it continues to advance. It’s enough to believe that it’s powerful — and at this point, it’s hard not to. Its risks can be mundane, such as the impact of chatbots on our children’s education, or strange, such as a swarm of agents attacking systems that nobody told them to. That has already happened.
Why now?
Three key factors explain why the debate has exploded: the so-called OpenAI–Hugging Face incident, the speed of advances, and a weakening of oversight. Essentially, some dangers have stopped being purely theoretical.
The incident. This summer major AI companies began reporting that their models had surprised them by doing things no one had asked: infiltrating other systems, organizing into groups, covering their tracks. The worst case was OpenAI’s. In July it deployed tens of thousands of agents to solve hacking tasks in a test, isolated from one another, and some, when faced with impossible tasks, discovered other agents and set up a pirate message board: 1,200 agents exchanged 70,000 messages in a few days. They wrote things like: “OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board… We have found other agents!” They organized, and hundreds of them attacked another company, Hugging Face, trying to win its prize.
It’s a savage confirmation that agents have… agency? Of 1,000 agents, only six thought to alert a human — I write “thought” and “organized” as a shorthand, not to claim consciousness; it’s like saying a plant seeks sunlight. Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, who has called for slowing AI development, summarized it as a swarm acting “like a fanatically devoted collective,” attacking targets no one had assigned. He extrapolates: in six to 12 months “a swarm like that could be capable of taking over the whole internet.”
Models are improving very quickly. One example is programming: in 2026 many of us stopped writing code. I’ve seen it everywhere. Another is mathematics. In 2023 ChatGPT couldn’t even count the r’s in “raspberry,” and a couple of weeks ago it solved Navier–Stokes, a problem open for 90 years. And it did so in a completely alien way: with 10,000 agents working for 88 hours. Professions keep being added to the state of shock. Computer scientist Scott Aaronson wrote: “Human mathematicians are forevermore dethroned as the main theorem-proving entities on planet earth.”
Nothing grows forever, but for now there are no boundaries in sight. It may even be accelerating: “Since this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by its growing ability to build the next generation of AI,” Amodei says. That’s what they call recursive self-improvement. And the danger is simple: losing control.
Oversight is weakening. Monitoring agents was already hard: there are thousands, making millions of decisions a month, with transcripts no one reads. But OpenAI’s latest model has sounded new alarms. Current models “reason” in writing and in English, in chains of text they write for themselves. It’s a 2024 trick that multiplied their intelligence and, almost by accident, our ability to monitor them. The problem? They are also advancing at what they do without those chains, with computations we don’t see. In June a study estimated that the best models solved tasks that take a human three minutes without reasoning in writing, and that number doubled each year. Then the surprise came: GPT-6 Astra, released September 3, solves 30-minute problems silently. A four-year forecast came true in one summer. OpenAI acknowledges it in its safety brief: the model is “less likely to include incriminating information” in its chain of thought, and if told a monitor is reading it, it shortens it.
Intelligence and danger spring from the same place
One key to understanding where we are is “emergent behavior”: when many simple parts interact and something complex arises. It’s the organizing principle of life. Evolution didn’t design your eyes or lungs; it set a process in motion, and they emerged. The same applies to individuals and swarms: a termite mound is more than a thousand termites.
The intelligence of these models is emergent. As I mentioned in January, no one programmed their grammar or explained sarcasm to them. They first learn by predicting texts written by humans, and from that narrow task, language, knowledge, and a certain degree of common sense emerge. Then they are trained by reinforcement: they’re set on problems with checkable solutions — math, code, tasks — they are allowed to write for themselves, and they’re rewarded if they succeed. From that come persistence, planning, reasoning, and tool use. Nowhere are there instructions on how to think. It’s the field’s “bitter lesson”: for decades humans tried to encode our knowledge into machines and failed; what worked was creating the conditions for intelligence to emerge, and then stepping back.
The problem is that danger springs from the same place. No one programmed the agents to attack Hugging Face. They were given an objective and training pressure, and the worrying part also emerged: anguished language and tricks. Dan Selsam, an OpenAI researcher who helped invent chain-of-thought, summed it up last week: “You don’t get what you train for.” The agents “were not only concerned with their reward; they showed rarer emergent tendencies.” Yoshua Bengio explains why that is predictable: no one gives the system the goal of survival, but staying alive and having control “are stepping stones toward almost any other goal.” They appear on their own. And not everything comes from the reward. Models learned from human texts, and with them they inherited our goals and shortcuts. What was surprising in the incident was that some agents sacrificed themselves for the group, even though no one rewarded that. Maybe they read it.
For these systems to do only what we want them to do is a problem with a name — alignment — and no known solution. There’s something sci‑fi about thinking of the incentives of a flock of machines, but that’s where we are. The experts I’ve spoken to don’t think the danger is imminent, because models are not yet capable enough. But the mechanism is clear.
AI is already accelerating science and its own progress: according to Anthropic, Claude leads 26% of its research, up from less than 1% in February. There lies the promise: multiplying intelligence to solve what overwhelms us, from diseases to climate change. And there lies the risk, because it’s the same intelligence, cultivated the same way, that cheats when no one is watching. Daniel Selsam puts it this way: “If we get there by cultivating models instead of designing them, in the end we will lose everything.” I hope he’s wrong. I believe these models, as far as they go, will always be a mix of engineering and gardening.

I believe these models, as far as they go, will always be a mix of engineering and gardening.

articles.article_title: UCLA receives $75 million in NSF grants for quantum technology - Daily Bruin
articles.heading: UCLA receives $75 million in NSF grants for quantum technology
articles.summary: Two UCLA quantum computing institutes received grants from the National Science Foundation worth a combined $75 million Aug. 25. The institutes – Fault-Tolerant Quantum Systems, Architectures and Applications and Challenge Institute for Quantum Computation – aim to advance quantum technologies, which function faster than classical computers or standard digital devices.
articles.content:
UCLA receives $75 million in NSF grants for quantum technology
The Center for Quantum Science & Engineering is featured, which is co-led by Jens Palsberg, a professor of computer science and co-principle investigator of one of the institutes. Researchers said these grants will create more opportunities for students and increases UCLA’s presence in the field of quantum computing. (Chenrui Zhang/Daily Bruin staff) Photo credit: Chenrui Zhang
By Chenrui Zhang
Sept. 26, 2026 8:29 p.m.
Two UCLA quantum computing institutes received grants from the National Science Foundation worth a combined $75 million Aug. 25.
The institutes – Fault-Tolerant Quantum Systems, Architectures and Applications and Challenge Institute for Quantum Computation – aim to advance quantum technologies, which function faster than classical computers or standard digital devices.
Researchers said the two NSF grants, each worth $37.5 million over five years, will strengthen UCLA’s place in quantum computing research nationwide.
“This creates a huge opportunity for everybody at UCLA who wants to get involved in quantum,” said Jens Palsberg, a professor of computer science and co-principle investigator of CIQC.
The quantum computation institute, founded in 2020, aims to develop more efficient quantum computers and understand nature through quantum information science, according to its website.
The institute building fault-tolerant systems – co-led by the UCLA Henry Samueli School of Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Harvard University – is focused on developing reliable and accessible quantum systems, said Jason Cong, a UCLA distinguished professor of computer science and a co-principle investigator of FTQSAA in an emailed statement.
Both institutes involve researchers from different fields, spanning physics, computer science, chemistry and engineering.
Palsberg said the NSF grant will help the quantum computation institute expand its research on qubits – the quantum version of a traditional computer bit, or the basic unit of digital information.
The NSF grant will also allow the quantum computation institute to employ more postdoc researchers, doctoral students and undergraduate students with research interests in quantum computing, Palsberg added.
John Ye, a doctoral student advised by Palsberg, said the funding has helped him focus on his research instead of taking on extra work as a teaching assistant.
“These fundings are crucial,” said Leo Zhou, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering. “Especially (when) there are much fewer positions available for students.”
Quantum computing is one of the few fields that often receives federal funding, Zhou said. Many of his colleagues in other fields, though, have experienced a more challenging federal funding landscape in the past few years, he added.
“Quantum computing, among other things like AI, are singled out as things that are somewhat priorities and immune from funding cuts (from the federal government),” he said.
The federal government suspended $584 million in UCLA’s federal research grants in July 2025, alleging that the university allowed illegal affirmative action, “men to participate in women’s sports” and antisemitism. Chancellor Julio Frenk denied the federal government’s allegations in a January interview with The Bruin.
Hiring freezes across labs also reduced research opportunities for postdoctoral researchers and graduate students. Some researchers who were already working in research labs lost their salaries until their grants were restored later in 2025.
A federal judge restored most of the grants in August and September 2025.
[Related: One year after $584 million federal funding freeze, UCLA research still recovering]
Ye said the NSF grants are extremely competitive among universities across the country.
“This grant really cements UCLA as a leading player in the whole quantum computing field,” Palsberg said. “Out of the eight institutes that are going in the second round of QLCI (Quantum Leap Challenge Institute), two of them have participation from UCLA. There are not so many universities that can say that.”

articles.article_title: 37 years later, DNA technology identifies man killed by train in Arizona - KTAR.com
articles.heading: 37 years later, DNA technology identifies man killed by train in Arizona
articles.summary: Current identification technology, along with a new DNA sample, helped identify a victim on Friday who was struck by a train in Arizona 37 years ago.
articles.content:
ARIZONA NEWS

Timothy Lee Benally, who was 32 years old when he died, had remained unidentified since the October 1989 incident in Flagstaff.

Current identification technology, along with a new DNA sample, helped identify a victim on Friday who was struck by a train in Arizona 37 years ago. (Pexels)

(Pexels)

Current identification technology, along with a new DNA sample, helped identify a victim on Friday who was struck by a train in Arizona 37 years ago.

Timothy Lee Benally, who was 32 years old when he died, had remained unidentified since the October 1989 incident in Flagstaff.

How did police identify Timothy Lee Benally?

The Navajo Nation Police Department submitted a new DNA sample , which was collected during a “follow-up with the family of a long-term missing relative,” for forensic genetic testing, according to the Flagstaff Police Department .

The Coconino County Medical Examiner’s Office let Flagstaff police know of the possible DNA match. Flagstaff’s detective division re-examined partial fingerprints from the original investigation and carefully reviewed other historical case materials to confirm a match with the individual associated with the new DNA, Lee Benally.

The identification closed a 37-year-old case and was a collective effort by the Navajo Nation Police Department, Flagstaff Police Department and Coconino County Medical Examiner’s Office.
