articles.content:
OnStar turns 30: The technology and people behind every emergency response


2026-09-25











Thirty years ago, OnStar set out to answer a life-changing question: What if a vehicle could detect a collision and call for help when its occupants couldn’t?
OnStar helped pioneer Automatic Crash Response technology. Today, it continues to shape the next generation of connected vehicle experiences, from hands-free driving with Super Cruise to in-vehicle AI assistance.
Over the years, we’ve had the privilege of hearing from customers whose lives were changed by OnStar — personal stories of crashes survived, critical help received, and loved ones brought home.
GM is the only automaker with its own dedicated emergency call center. In 2025, OnStar Advisors responded to over a half a million emergency calls. Nearly 49,000 of those calls required emergency dispatch triage for medical, police or fire assistance.
Here are some of the moments that underscore the lasting impact of OnStar technology and advisors.
Help reaches an injured child after a serious collision
For Kari and her daughter Molly, a trip in their Chevrolet Equinox changed in an instant when they became involved in a devastating multi-vehicle crash. On Interstate 69 in Indiana, their SUV was rear ended by another vehicle before it collided with a semi-truck. The crash crushed the Equinox and left Kari unconscious.
Molly was injured and frightened in the passenger seat when she heard a voice. “I could hear somebody talking to me,” Molly recalled. “I looked around and saw OnStar on the screen.”
An OnStar Emergency Advisor had connected through the vehicle’s Automatic Crash Response system. She already had a clear picture of how serious the crash was through OnStar’s Injury Severity Prediction technology and was able to relay critical information that helped first responders better prepare before arriving on scene.
The Advisor stayed on the line with Molly until emergency crews arrived. During emergencies, Advisors rely on a technique they call “repetitive persistence,” giving clear instructions in a calm, steady, commanding voice. This approach helps callers stay focused when fear makes it difficult to process information. With younger callers, Advisors simplify things even further, breaking directions into small steps they can follow.
“We are the first first responders,” the Advisor said. “An experience like [the accident on I-69] makes me incredibly proud of my team, of our training, and of the vital role we play in public safety. It motivates me to keep showing up at my best for the next person who calls.”
Help after a Texas rollover crash

articles.content:
Subscribe




40

TRAVIS AIR FORCE BASE, Calif. – Phoenix Spark brought Team Travis Airmen together with 28 industry vendors to explore emerging technologies and potential solutions to military challenges during its annual Industry Day at Travis Air Force Base, Sept. 23, 2026.
Industry Day featured technologies focused on human performance and readiness, contested logistics, security and counter-drone capabilities, allowing Airmen to explore solutions for evolving mission needs.
U.S. Air Force Maj. Dustin Wallace, 60th Air Mobility Wing chief of innovation and Phoenix Spark director, described Industry Day as an opportunity for Airmen to connect directly with the companies developing military technology.
“I hope it gets Airmen thinking about technology as a solution,” Wallace said. “Maybe there is a better technology that would help you accomplish a mission faster or better, more effectively.”
For Airmen, Industry Day provided exposure to technologies beyond the systems they already use and an opportunity to see potential solutions to challenges they encounter while accomplishing the mission. For commanders, the event offered a look at capabilities that could support their units and inform how they use available resources.
Counter-drone technology was the primary focus of Industry Day, with 18 of the 28 vendors showcasing capabilities designed to defeat drone threats. The focus allowed Airmen to explore technologies aimed at protecting personnel in modern operating environments.
As technology continues to evolve, Industry Day gives Airmen a closer look at emerging capabilities and how they could contribute to accomplishing the mission more effectively. That exposure also places Airmen closer to the modernization process by encouraging them to consider new solutions to the challenges they face.
“I hope more Airmen are inspired to see what the realm of possibility is with cutting-edge technology,” Wallace said.

articles.article_title: At Climate Week, C&EN reporters found that technology is still seen as a solution to our climate problem
articles.heading: At Climate Week, technology is still a solution to climate change
articles.summary: 3 C&EN reporters offer their impressions from the annual New York City event
articles.content:
News
The latest chemistry news, including important research advances, business and policy trends, chemical safety practices, career guidance, and more.
Read More
New York City—C&EN reporters Craig Bettenhausen, Ana Georgescu, and Aayushi Pratap have been on the move across New York City this week for Climate Week NYC, an annual decentralized conference organized by the nonprofit Climate Group that featured more than 1,500 events this year. In some circles, investing in technology to reverse climate change is a lost cause, but not so at Climate Week. Here’s a sample of what our reporters saw and learned.
Monday
Craig: I got into New York City at noon and went straight to Climate Group’s Hub Live event.
It seemed premature to pick out a theme for a week of reporting in the first couple of hours, but resilience and its synonyms came up over and over again from the stage. Speakers from across the private, public, and nonprofit worlds agreed that the efforts worth backing in this time of climate change are those that can deliver risk-reducing benefits such as grid reliability, stable supply chains, and lower costs.
Less consensus was apparent on where that emphasis leaves efforts to actually minimize climate change. Some at the conference relegated it to the role of a secondary benefit, while others treated it as a core motivation in need of a more compelling business case. “We’ve got to change the narrative; we’ve got to be talking about why it makes energy more affordable, more available, and safer,” said Mindy Lubber, CEO of the sustainability nonprofit Ceres.
I stepped out to a nearby coffee shop called the Jolly Goat to meet with Marta Sjögren, co-CEO of the low-carbon cement start-up Paebbl. Coming off a series A funding round in the fall of 2024, the firm has already presold the entire 100,000-metric-ton-per-year output of its first commercial-scale plant before even announcing the site location, she said.
The firm will reach cost parity with conventional cement production around 2030, when European carbon emission limits and taxes are taken into account, Sjögren said, and that region is the firm’s focus for now. In the US, she said, the business conversations she’s having hinge on supply chain stability. Like oil, gas, and chemicals, cement materials have been disrupted by the war in Iran and the other global challenges to shipping in recent years.
Back at the Climate Group event, speakers from governments including Iceland, France, and Mexico brought up the opportunity their nations see to lead on cleantech. The future of manufacturing is energy-efficient technology that avoids reliance on unstable or unfriendly regions, Iceland prime minister Kristrún Frostadóttir said. Her country is well positioned to develop geothermal technology, including emerging versions that drill deeper to tap into superhot rock, she said. Nations that invest in cleantech now, Frostadóttir said, see the first benefits, and their citizens become the experts the world turns to.
Happy hours abound at Climate Week, and I picked two. One was the Carbon Removal Community Reception, where folks talked about removal techniques like direct air capture, reforestation, and biochar. I picked the second because the eye-catching name, “F*ck Doom Hour,” suggested an optimistic streak. After chatting on a rooftop about biological pesticide alternatives and the likelihood of new nuclear technology’s making an impact on the carbon footprint of chemical manufacturing, I hopped on a commuter train to my hotel, which was in Newark, New Jersey, because rooms in New York City proper were $550 or more per night.
Aayushi: It was clear on Monday that fall had officially arrived in New York City. So had delegations from across the world in town for the United Nations General Assembly, which was also happening. Men in black suits and ties, looking like they were straight out of a Federal Bureau of Investigation movie, could be seen guarding cars with tinted windows.
I hopped on the 1 train and headed to an event in the Chelsea neighborhood about climate solutions in Asia. Of the many events that were ongoing that morning, I picked this one for its intriguing description. "Asia is not simply a place where climate solutions need to be deployed. It is increasingly a place where they are being built," it said.
The folks there discussed their victories as well as the challenges of deploying climate solutions in their countries. Among them was Gaurav Godhwani, cofounder and CEO of an Indian company called CivicDataLab. He discussed how his firm is deploying an artificial intelligence–based platform that uses satellite images to predict the impact of climate disasters.
Tuesday
Craig: I spent the morning at PlanetHAUS, a showcase of sustainable food, home, and personal care goods spread out over several floors of an event space in the Flatiron neighborhood. The place was packed with people and concepts, but one that stood out was a pain au chocolat made with a butter substitute thermochemically synthesized from captured carbon dioxide by the start-up Savor. Tasting it, you would never know it wasn’t conventional dairy.
Next up was the Cool House, a tech showcase and symposium on climate control and related technologies. At least part of the air-conditioning and refrigeration world is preparing to adopt refrigerants including propane and isobutane instead of the fluorochemicals in wide use today. It will be the fourth major chemical shift since the late 1990s in response to concerns first about ozone depletion, then global warming, and now the accumulation of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).
From there, I went to a technology showcase put on by the cleantech accelerator Activate Fellowship. It more than filled a literal ballroom with early-stage chemistry entrepreneurs at booths pitching their start-ups to a crowd of investors and early adopters. The conversations showed a marked shift toward critical materials, energy security, and supply chain independence and away from climate change mitigation as an end unto itself.
I closed my day at Art into Action, an exhibit at the nearby Chart gallery that reflected on the climate and public health impacts of industrial methane leaks. The energy transition arts collective Light Hill Collaborative used data from methane-spotting satellites and cameras to name a top US methane-leaking corporation for every month of 2025, and it commissioned an original artwork for each. Small and midsize oil and gas companies led the pack, but the energy majors TotalEnergies and Occidental Petroleum were also represented on the gallery walls.
Aayushi: I spent Tuesday morning huddled in my apartment to listen to speeches by world leaders, including US president Donald J. Trump, at the UN General Assembly, which was happening live across town. Just days after tech leaders had raised the alarm on unchecked progress of AI, Trump dismissed their concerns. “The very same people who said we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming—a name since reborn to climate change because the planet was cooling, not warming—and nobody was dead,” he said.
One thing I have learned after nearly 7 years of living in Manhattan is that one should go to Times Square only if one must. And Tuesday evening I felt I must, so I made my way to a hotel near Times Square to attend a session called “The Hormuz Effect: Climate Action and Energy Security after the Iran War.”
A panel of experts discussed how the war has exposed the vulnerabilities of the global energy supply chain. Zainab Usman, a senior research scholar at the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, said that at least in the short term, the war will lead to diminished clean energy sources. Still unclear is whether the war will force nations to ramp up renewable energy capacity in the long term.
Ana: As the junior reporter at Climate Week, I gave myself a couple of themes to pursue—batteries and critical minerals—rather than attempt to be everywhere at once.
I hit the ground on Tuesday by attending a panel on community rights related to mineral supply security. It was a useful counterpoint to the conversations that took place the rest of the day about how the US can build the supply chains needed for an increasingly electrified economy.
I then headed uptown to the NYC Battery Symposium. The afternoon included a conversation with Audrey Robertson, assistant secretary of energy, leading the Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation at the US Department of Energy (DOE), followed by an innovator showcase and a panel on battery energy storage amid growing power demand.
Robertson put the supply chain problem in the context of defense procurement: the US Department of Defense mandated that US war fighters be equipped with US-based supplies, she said, “but it’s hard because we don’t have the supply chain right now.”

New York City—C&EN reporters Craig Bettenhausen, Ana Georgescu, and Aayushi Pratap have been on the move across New York City this week for Climate Week NYC, an annual decentralized conference organized by the nonprofit Climate Group that featured more than 1,500 events this year. In some circles, investing in technology to reverse climate change is a lost cause, but not so at Climate Week. Here’s a sample of what our reporters saw and learned.

Monday

Craig: I got into New York City at noon and went straight to Climate Group’s Hub Live event.

It seemed premature to pick out a theme for a week of reporting in the first couple of hours, but resilience and its synonyms came up over and over again from the stage. Speakers from across the private, public, and nonprofit worlds agreed that the efforts worth backing in this time of climate change are those that can deliver risk-reducing benefits such as grid reliability, stable supply chains, and lower costs.

Less consensus was apparent on where that emphasis leaves efforts to actually minimize climate change. Some at the conference relegated it to the role of a secondary benefit, while others treated it as a core motivation in need of a more compelling business case. “We’ve got to change the narrative; we’ve got to be talking about why it makes energy more affordable, more available, and safer,” said Mindy Lubber, CEO of the sustainability nonprofit Ceres.

I stepped out to a nearby coffee shop called the Jolly Goat to meet with Marta Sjögren, co-CEO of the low-carbon cement start-up Paebbl. Coming off a series A funding round in the fall of 2024, the firm has already presold the entire 100,000-metric-ton-per-year output of its first commercial-scale plant before even announcing the site location, she said.

The firm will reach cost parity with conventional cement production around 2030, when European carbon emission limits and taxes are taken into account, Sjögren said, and that region is the firm’s focus for now. In the US, she said, the business conversations she’s having hinge on supply chain stability. Like oil, gas, and chemicals, cement materials have been disrupted by the war in Iran and the other global challenges to shipping in recent years.

Back at the Climate Group event, speakers from governments including Iceland, France, and Mexico brought up the opportunity their nations see to lead on cleantech. The future of manufacturing is energy-efficient technology that avoids reliance on unstable or unfriendly regions, Iceland prime minister Kristrún Frostadóttir said. Her country is well positioned to develop geothermal technology, including emerging versions that drill deeper to tap into superhot rock, she said. Nations that invest in cleantech now, Frostadóttir said, see the first benefits, and their citizens become the experts the world turns to.

Happy hours abound at Climate Week, and I picked two. One was the Carbon Removal Community Reception, where folks talked about removal techniques like direct air capture, reforestation, and biochar. I picked the second because the eye-catching name, “F*ck Doom Hour,” suggested an optimistic streak. After chatting on a rooftop about biological pesticide alternatives and the likelihood of new nuclear technology’s making an impact on the carbon footprint of chemical manufacturing, I hopped on a commuter train to my hotel, which was in Newark, New Jersey, because rooms in New York City proper were $550 or more per night.

Aayushi: It was clear on Monday that fall had officially arrived in New York City. So had delegations from across the world in town for the United Nations General Assembly, which was also happening. Men in black suits and ties, looking like they were straight out of a Federal Bureau of Investigation movie, could be seen guarding cars with tinted windows.

I hopped on the 1 train and headed to an event in the Chelsea neighborhood about climate solutions in Asia. Of the many events that were ongoing that morning, I picked this one for its intriguing description. "Asia is not simply a place where climate solutions need to be deployed. It is increasingly a place where they are being built," it said.

The folks there discussed their victories as well as the challenges of deploying climate solutions in their countries. Among them was Gaurav Godhwani, cofounder and CEO of an Indian company called CivicDataLab. He discussed how his firm is deploying an artificial intelligence–based platform that uses satellite images to predict the impact of climate disasters.

Tuesday

Craig: I spent the morning at PlanetHAUS, a showcase of sustainable food, home, and personal care goods spread out over several floors of an event space in the Flatiron neighborhood. The place was packed with people and concepts, but one that stood out was a pain au chocolat made with a butter substitute thermochemically synthesized from captured carbon dioxide by the start-up Savor. Tasting it, you would never know it wasn’t conventional dairy.

Next up was the Cool House, a tech showcase and symposium on climate control and related technologies. At least part of the air-conditioning and refrigeration world is preparing to adopt refrigerants including propane and isobutane instead of the fluorochemicals in wide use today. It will be the fourth major chemical shift since the late 1990s in response to concerns first about ozone depletion, then global warming, and now the accumulation of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).

From there, I went to a technology showcase put on by the cleantech accelerator Activate Fellowship. It more than filled a literal ballroom with early-stage chemistry entrepreneurs at booths pitching their start-ups to a crowd of investors and early adopters. The conversations showed a marked shift toward critical materials, energy security, and supply chain independence and away from climate change mitigation as an end unto itself.

I closed my day at Art into Action, an exhibit at the nearby Chart gallery that reflected on the climate and public health impacts of industrial methane leaks. The energy transition arts collective Light Hill Collaborative used data from methane-spotting satellites and cameras to name a top US methane-leaking corporation for every month of 2025, and it commissioned an original artwork for each. Small and midsize oil and gas companies led the pack, but the energy majors TotalEnergies and Occidental Petroleum were also represented on the gallery walls.

Aayushi: I spent Tuesday morning huddled in my apartment to listen to speeches by world leaders, including US president Donald J. Trump, at the UN General Assembly, which was happening live across town. Just days after tech leaders had raised the alarm on unchecked progress of AI, Trump dismissed their concerns. “The very same people who said we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming—a name since reborn to climate change because the planet was cooling, not warming—and nobody was dead,” he said.

One thing I have learned after nearly 7 years of living in Manhattan is that one should go to Times Square only if one must. And Tuesday evening I felt I must, so I made my way to a hotel near Times Square to attend a session called “The Hormuz Effect: Climate Action and Energy Security after the Iran War.”

A panel of experts discussed how the war has exposed the vulnerabilities of the global energy supply chain. Still unclear is whether the war will force nations to ramp up renewable energy capacity in the long term.

articles.summary: MASSENA -- A Massena resident has raised further concerns about the village's decision to use Flock security cameras.    Village resident Marty Fowler submitted a letter to the village prior  …
articles.content:
Saturday, September 26, 2026 | St. Lawrence County, NY

Posted 9/25/26
MASSENA -- A Massena resident has raised further concerns about the village's decision to use Flock security cameras.
Village resident Marty Fowler submitted a letter to the village prior …
This item is available in full to subscribers.
To continue reading, you will need to either log in to your subscriber account, or purchase a new subscription.
If you are a digital subscriber with an active, online-only subscription then you already have an account here. Just reset your password if you've not yet logged in to your account on this new site.
Otherwise, click here to view your options for subscribing.
| Please log in to continue |
Posted


Village resident Marty Fowler submitted a letter to the village prior to the Sept. 15 regular board meeting, saying he was a veteran who served the nation to uphold American freedoms.
In his letter, Fowler said he, like many residents, "do not want to be passively tracked, monitored or logged by community funded networks."
"If the village leadership maintains that continuous surveillance is necessary for public safety and accountability, then that standard must apply equally to the government itself," Fowler wrote to the board.
He said residents were "not going to take this lying down," in reference to the installation of 13 Flock cameras throughout the village.
Fowler said he and other residents would track and monitor the installation of cameras, reporting them to sources like DeFlock, a popular website that tracks the use of numerous surveillance systems throughout the nation, including Flock and Motorola systems.
"If you choose to monitor us, your hardware will be fully exposed to the public," he said.
Fowler called for a "straightforward proposal," saying he felt it would be appropriate to also monitor the government much the same way citizens are monitored with the Flock system.
"If the government monitors them during their daily lives, then the public must be granted the same ability to watch you while you perform your public jobs," he wrote.
Fowler called for "reciprocal transparency" in his letter, noting he felt it was appropriate to include cameras to monitor the police station 24/7, along with administrative spaces, as well as the Mayor's office.
"If the government has nothing to hide from citizens, it should have no objection to being watched exactly like it's watching us," he wrote.
The letter drew a pointed response from Mayor Greg Paquin who took time to clarify the types of cameras in use by the village.
Though Flock has drawn significant scrutiny in recent months for numerous failures with its artificial intelligence and license plate reader systems, Paquin said those functions are not in use in the village of Massena.
Instead, the village opted for an agreement that provides surveillance systems that offer a live view with high resolution cameras that can be remotely controlled by police to move 360 degrees.
The cameras can be monitored on numerous electronic devices, including computers in the police station, as well in cruisers, on tablets and with cell phones.
Chief of Police Cody Wilson said the cameras would allow officers to more quickly and safely respond to a situation if they are able to get eyes on the scene prior to responding.
"It would allow for an appropriate response and would ensure we send the right resources to a given scene," he said earlier this year.
Paquin said the cameras are only to be used for criminal investigations and nothing further.
In the event another agency requires assistance, he said the police department would be asked for permission to view footage.
Paquin clarified that the footage would be released in the event of active, ongoing investigations but nothing more.
"This is nothing new. We are not part of that. I know there was a concern about other agencies using it," he said.
"If a police officer comes from Canton and came to us and said 'Hey we really don't like this guy. Can you see what he's up to?' No, we're not going to do that. That's not how this works," he said.
Paquin noted the system installed in the village does not have license plate reading systems, not facial recognition software or an automated ticketing system.
He also said the cameras are not monitored 24/7 by the police officers.
Wilson said the cameras are installed as a matter of "public safety and officer safety."
Signs will also be installed in the near future to mark the cameras for the public, though Paquin said they "are not hard to find at all."
Signs will be "well lit, placed appropriately and without obstruction to ensure visibility," he said.
In the works as well is a transparency portal, which will provide all information regarding the functions of the cameras, as well as statistics about the information gathered, along with policies and procedures that will govern the use of the cameras and footage obtained by the system.
Wilson said that portal is in the works and will be posted on the Police Department's website and social media platforms in the near future.

articles.summary: St. Louis County Executive Sam Page signed an executive order Friday that calls for a review of automated license plate recognition technology, or ALPR.
articles.content:
County Executive Page signs order to review license plate recognition technology
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (First Alert 4) - St. Louis County Executive Sam Page signed an executive order Friday that calls for a review of automated license plate recognition technology, or ALPR.
The order directs a review of ALPR technology, such as Flock cameras, that is used on county property. In a statement, Page said this is to focus on public safety while protecting people’s privacy.
This order follows Gov. Mike Kehoe’s recent executive order concerning safeguards for ALPRs. The order directs the county’s Department of Transportation and Public Works to conduct an audit of the cameras and review ALPR procedures.
The order also requests that the St. Louis County Board of Police Commissioners and the Police Department review their ALPR policies and make appropriate revisions where necessary to establish clear rules regarding ALPR use.
Page said the order takes effect immediately.

articles.title: Businesses expand AI’s cybersecurity uses as comfort with technology grows
articles.description: Businesses expand AI’s cybersecurity uses as comfort with technology grows Cybersecurity Dive
articles.description_html: Businesses expand AI’s cybersecurity uses as comfort with technology grows  Cybersecurity Dive
articles.article_title: Businesses expand AI’s cybersecurity uses as comfort with technology grows
articles.heading: Don't miss tomorrow's Cybersecurity industry news
articles.summary: Companies in the experimentation stage were less likely than established users to deploy advanced AI-powered defenses, a new survey found.
articles.content:
Dive Brief:
- Businesses are getting better at securing their AI systems as they spend more time using the technology, the advisory firm KPMG found in its latest quarterly AI survey.
- Accountability is also improving, according to KPMG’s Q3 report, with many organizations assigning responsibility for AI to a C-suite executive — including, in some cases, the CEO — or the executive committee.
- KPMG’s latest report also found that agentic AI use is growing.
Dive Insight:
One of the KPMG report’s key insights is that organizations’ AI maturity levels strongly influence how they use AI in the context of cybersecurity. Only 8% of organizations at the experimentation stage are deploying AI-assisted cyber defense technologies, for example, compared with 58% of organizations that have been using AI long enough to see returns on investment.
Among experimenters, 26% use AI only to monitor systems; among established users, the figure is 4%, reflecting organizations’ growing comfort with plugging AI into more security tasks over time. Established AI users were also more likely than experimenters to report spending some of their AI budgets on cybersecurity (71% versus 36%). Interestingly, established users were also more likely than experimenters to describe cybersecurity as a barrier to AI use (50% versus 34%).
As businesses see the threat landscape grow more complex, they are racing to update their cybersecurity strategies to account for faster-moving attacks. In KPMG’s latest report, 86% of organizations said they were “adapting their cybersecurity operating model for AI-accelerated threats.”
As part of the business community’s growing focus on AI governance, more than half (55%) of organizations reported operating an AI harness layer that incorporates a variety of technical controls to prevent AI from doing damage. Security and identity top the list of capabilities included in these harnesses (43% of organizations reported including those features), followed by data access controls (43%) and monitoring of AI outputs (41%).
But human controls also matter, and KPMG heralded the finding that 53% of organizations said they assigned AI responsibility to a senior executive. (Nearly one-quarter of organizations said they held their CEO or executive committee directly responsible for AI governance.) “A control layer without a named owner is a policy rather than a management system,” KPMG said in its report. “Accountability is what turns controls into decisions someone can be asked to explain.”
Security remains high on companies’ list of AI priorities. Human-AI collaboration tops the list, with 32% of respondents citing it, but responsible AI and security follow close behind with 30% each. All three of those figures increased by four percentage points between Q1 and Q3.
Agentic AI use is also growing, the report found: Nearly four in 10 respondents said they were either building or using multiagent systems, and 34% of organizations reported significant employee use of AI agents (up from 25% in Q1).
KPMG’s latest survey is based on interviews with 2,131 senior business leaders in 20 countries.

articles.title: Closing the Vision-to-Execution Gap: What the Archdiocese of New York Learned About Classroom Technology
articles.description: Closing the Vision-to-Execution Gap: What the Archdiocese of New York Learned About Classroom Technology Education Week
articles.description_html: Closing the Vision-to-Execution Gap: What the Archdiocese of New York Learned About Classroom Technology  Education Week
articles.article_title: Closing the Vision-to-Execution Gap: What the Archdiocese of New York Learned About Classroom Technology - SPONSOR CONTENT
articles.heading: Closing the Vision-to-Execution Gap: What the Archdiocese of New York Learned About Classroom Technology
articles.summary: Reliable classroom technology helps teachers teach without disruption, students explore ideas, and schools turn learning goals into action.
articles.content:
Every teacher has a vision for a lesson. Every student has a vision for something they want to build, compete in, or create. Every school has a vision for the kind of student it hopes to form. No matter the situation, teachers, students, and schools are constantly looking for tools that will better close the gap between what someone wants to do and what they can do.
Over the years, educators have turned to technology to close this vision-to-execution gap. Yet, flashy features do not always translate into practical use for students on a daily basis. Educators and students alike have become more discerning about their classroom technology. For example, 1:1 devices can be a great incentive for students, but they can also be a distraction. A gaming PC can foster teamwork and collaboration in eSports leagues but can also distract from homework and assignments. A webcam can be great for virtual participation, or it can contribute to screen fatigue and decreased attentiveness.
No longer are tech specs the best way to measure value for the classroom, student or school district. Rather, the best way to understand if your technology is useful for your students and educators is to understand how it will help execute your vision.
This pattern emerged clearly in a recent case study of the Archdiocese of New York’s rollout of ASUS devices across its schools, conducted in partnership with Archangel Education Technology.
The Educators’ Value: Instruction without Interruption
For Stephanie Alvarez, fifth-grade teacher at St. Philip Neri School, a valuable tech device is one that does not interrupt her teaching flow. Stephanie considers it a success if she can plan and execute a classroom lesson without technology interrupting her from things like lagging computers or browsers that crash mid-lesson. Tech that is deployed seamlessly allows her students to remain focused on learning while she can focus on teaching. Every minute she spends addressing tech issues represents time diverted from instruction. Across a classroom and a school year this adds up to a measurable amount of instructional time.
Technology that functions well is an underrated safeguard against educator fatigue. Devices that consistently work as intended remove a layer of daily stress that never appears on a tech spec sheet but directly support retention numbers. At the classroom level, reliable hardware is what allows teachers to execute their vision, and it protects both teacher and student success in the process.
The Student’s Value: Learning Under Real Conditions For students, the value of technology is measured differently. The students at St. Philip Neri offered their own perspective, describing that a device should be able to survive the bottom of a backpack or an accidental drop. Their devices should be able to withstand a bit of carelessness without having to fear it from breaking. A device that can’t withstand the ordinary chaos of being a student is not considered valuable to these kids. For the students, durable hardware is what closes their vision-to-execution gap.
From the student’s perspective, their tools enable them to understand and interact with the world differently. When a student is not afraid of breaking their device, that student uses it more freely and takes more creative risks. Taken further, a capable and durable device is often the first time a student has hardware good enough to attempt something ambitious, and the world opens up. They are able to envision building a robot, edit a video, compete in esports, or train a model.
The District’s Value: Institutional Scale
Sister Mary Grace Walsh, Superintendent of Schools for the Archdiocese, describes how the overarching goal of her school district is to positively form the whole person: mind, heart, and spirit. For her, technological value comes from tools that drive her mission and help engender the identity of her institution.
In practice, the archdiocese’s experience suggests this outcome is possible when the technology is reliable enough to recede into the background. Infrastructure that does not demand daily attention either lets her institution execute its mission at scale, or it becomes a daily distraction from that mission.
Closing the Vision-to-Execution Gap: The ASUS EmpowerED Hardware Grant Program
Teachers, students and administrators all understand that technology can either be a bottleneck or a tool to see a vision come to life. A single lesson can stall on a frozen screen. A single student’s ambition can stall on a device that cannot survive a backpack. An entire institution’s mission can stall on infrastructure that demands constant attention.
This is why ASUS is deploying its EmpowerED Hardware Grant Program. This month, ASUS is offering schools around the US the chance to deploy their vision across AI, robotics, esports, or media through their Grant Program. ASUS will award four schools a complete, twelve-station technology lab, configured for one of four focus areas. Each area corresponds to a kind of student dream that is currently waiting on the right tools:
- AI/STEM Labs: support the student who wants to explore artificial intelligence, data science, and emerging technologies.
- Gaming/Esports Labs: support the student who wants to compete, building teamwork and technical skill in the process.
- Media & Digital Creativity Labs: support the student who wants to tell stories through film, design, or content creation.
- Robotics Labs: support the student who wants to design, build, and program something that moves in the physical world.
Each winning school will receive ASUS notebooks or desktops and a full set of peripherals, ready to support a program rather than a single classroom.
Apply Now
Applications for the EmpowerED Hardware Grant Program are open to all U.S. K-12 schools and districts, including specialized labs, now through October 16, 2026.Schools can learn more and apply at asus.com/us/site/edu/grantprogram.

articles.title: Cedarville Stories: Rob McDole on Faith, Technology and the Future of AI
articles.description: Cedarville Stories: Rob McDole on Faith, Technology and the Future of AI Cedarville University
articles.description_html: Cedarville Stories: Rob McDole on Faith, Technology and the Future of AI  Cedarville University
articles.article_title: Cedarville Stories: Rob McDole on Faith, Technology and the Future of AI
articles.heading: Cedarville Stories: Rob McDole on Faith, Technology and the Future of AI
articles.summary: Cedarville Stories explores Rob McDole’s journey of faith, technology and AI, highlighting how biblical truth, discipleship and thoughtful stewardship can guide...
articles.content:
by User Not Found
As a new academic year begins at Cedarville University, technology and artificial intelligence continue to reshape the way people work, learn and communicate. On this episode of the Cedarville Stories podcast, Rob McDole, a leader in Cedarville’s Center for Teaching and Learning and an experienced voice on artificial intelligence, joins the conversation to explore AI through a biblical and educational lens.
Before discussing technology, McDole shares about his journey to Cedarville and the people who shaped his life. He reflects on meeting his wife as a Cedarville student and the influence of his mother and the godly mentors who invested in him when his father was largely absent during his childhood. His love of reading, learning, and technology began early, eventually leading McDole to choose Cedarville over a full-ride music scholarship at another college after discovering Cedarville’s early computer network, CedarNet.
McDole explains how his Christian faith shapes his understanding of innovation. Because God is the Creator, technological advancement, including AI, is not outside His sovereignty. Rather than responding to AI with fear, McDole encourages Christians to consider how technology can be used wisely to serve others and advance Kingdom purposes.
The conversation also addresses one of McDole’s primary concerns: humanizing AI. He cautions against treating AI systems as people or allowing their increasingly conversational nature to distort our understanding of what they are.
McDole discusses how AI has accelerated research, enabled simulations, and changed his own professional workflow, while also acknowledging the importance of setting boundaries and remaining attentive to real-world responsibilities.
Finally, the conversation turns to higher education. McDole explains why Cedarville is focusing on becoming AI-resilient rather than AI-resistant, emphasizing process over product and recognizing that education is about far more than earning a diploma. At its heart, Cedarville’s mission remains rooted in discipleship, biblical truth, and forming students in ways technology cannot replicate.
About Cedarville University
Cedarville University, an evangelical Christian institution in southwest Ohio, offers undergraduate and graduate residential and online programs across arts, sciences and professional fields. With 7,542 students, it is among Ohio's largest private universities and is ranked among the nation’s top five evangelical universities in the Wall Street Journal’s 2026 Best Colleges in the U.S. Cedarville is also known for its vibrant Christian community, challenging academics and high graduation and retention rates. Learn more at cedarville.edu.

articles.article_title: LPs Seek Stronger Technology Infrastructure From Managers | Chief Investment Officer
articles.heading: LPs Seek Stronger Technology Infrastructure From Managers
articles.summary: Customized and faster reporting is top of mind for limited partners, according to the CEO of fund administrator Gen II.
articles.content:
Institutional investors are becoming more discerning about the asset managers with whom they invest—in many cases seeking to do more with fewer groups. Limited partners increasingly seek out general partners that can deliver faster—and customized—private markets reporting,
A survey of LPs and GPs from fund administration firm Gen II Fund Services LLC found that LPs are less focused on their managers’ integration of new technology, including the latest artificial intelligence models and automation, and more focused on the outcomes that these technologies can drive and their benefits for LPs.
Gen II surveyed, in collaboration with the Harris Poll, 205 respondents, including 103 GPs and 102 LPs, from March 31 through April 8.
A Mismatch Between LPs and GPs
Steven Millner, co-founder and CEO of Gen II, notes that one of LPs’ most requested services—and a point of contention between them and their GPs—is faster reporting of results in private markets.
“Pretty much everyone I talk to in the LP space is really unhappy with the timeliness of reporting, [which typically is] 45 days on a quarter, 90 days on year-end,” Millner says. “That’s kind of a long-established precedent, but the reality is the LPs are very unhappy with that.”

articles.title: UMaine NSF-funded project to bring emerging technologies into rural Maine classrooms
articles.description: UMaine NSF-funded project to bring emerging technologies into rural Maine classrooms The University of Maine
articles.description_html: UMaine NSF-funded project to bring emerging technologies into rural Maine classrooms  The University of Maine
articles.article_title: UMaine NSF-funded project to bring emerging technologies into rural Maine classrooms - UMaine News - The University of Maine
articles.heading: UMaine NSF-funded project to bring emerging technologies into rural Maine classrooms
articles.summary: The University of Maine has received a grant from the U.S. National Science Foundation to give rural Maine teachers hands-on experience conducting research in artificial intelligence, quantum computing and microelectronics, which they will use to bring emerging science and technology into their own classrooms. The three-year project, which began Sept.…
articles.content:
The University of Maine has received a grant from the U.S. National Science Foundation to give rural Maine teachers hands-on experience conducting research in artificial intelligence, quantum computing and microelectronics, which they will use to bring emerging science and technology into their own classrooms.
The three-year project, which began Sept. 1, will provide 18 K-12 STEM teachers with research experiences alongside UMaine scientists and support them in turning what they learn into lessons for their students. The project is supported through NSF’s Robert Noyce Teacher Scholarship Program.
Nuri Emanetoglu, professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, is principal investigator. Susan McKay, professor emerita of Physics and Astronomy and a founder of the Maine Center for Research in STEM Education, or RiSE Center, is co-principal investigator.
The project combines UMaine’s expertise in emerging technologies with RiSE’s expertise in STEM education and teacher professional learning. Researchers will provide teachers with firsthand experience in advanced scientific research, while RiSE education specialists will help them translate those experiences into learning opportunities appropriate for their students.
“There are two parts to it,” Emanetoglu said. “One is exposing the teachers to the research projects and the state of the art in these fields. The second is translating that into an educational experience for their students.”
Each year, six teachers will be selected for the program. The first cohort will spend four weeks on UMaine’s campus in summer 2027 conducting research with Electrical and Computer Engineering and with Physics faculty and working with RiSE education research specialists. They will have an additional three weeks to continue their research and develop classroom materials.
“One of the really exciting parts is bringing together faculty who do research in these new, fast-moving fields while also tapping into the expertise of the RiSE Center at the University of Maine,” McKay said.
Teachers will work directly with UMaine researchers on projects involving AI, robotics, sensors, microelectronics and other advanced technologies. Depending on their research group, they could test AI models used to help robots recognize and grasp objects, study how microelectronic devices perform in extreme environments or work with microscopic devices used for scientific and biomedical applications.
The teachers will then draw from those experiences to develop learning opportunities appropriate for their students. A teacher could, for example, bring data collected through their research into the classroom and have students analyze it and determine what conclusions they can draw.
“They can really be part of an exciting research enterprise,” McKay said. “The beauty of having teachers design these kinds of learning experiences is that they know their students. They know what the students will know and what they’ll get excited about.”
Teachers will work in cohorts of six, allowing them to exchange ideas and provide feedback to one another. They will also test their lessons with fellow participants, their research group and RiSE team members before using the materials in their own classrooms. RiSE will continue supporting teachers throughout the school year as they refine their lessons and introduce new approaches in their classrooms.
The project focuses on teachers in rural, high-need Maine school districts, where students may have fewer opportunities to interact with scientists and engineers working in rapidly developing fields.
Emanetoglu said exposing students to areas such as AI, quantum computing and microelectronics can introduce them to new educational and career possibilities while helping prepare the workforce needed in strategically important areas of science and technology.
McKay said those opportunities could have implications beyond individual students and classrooms by contributing to Maine’s future economy.
“This is where innovation is going to come from in our economy,” McKay said. “There’s no reason why these sites of innovation can’t be in rural areas with good connections all over the world.”
Maine already has a long history in semiconductor manufacturing, Emanetoglu said, including semiconductor facilities in South Portland. Emerging fields such as AI, cybersecurity and robotics also can create opportunities that do not require proximity to a large manufacturing center.
“As long as you have a good internet connection, you could run that business anywhere in the state,” Emanetoglu said. “You could be doing that in Portland. You could be doing that in Fort Kent.”
The project brings together researchers from UMaine’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Department of Physics and Astronomy, Frontier Institute for Research in Sensor Technologies and RiSE Center.
The program is also designed so its impact can extend beyond the initial 18 teachers. Participants will have opportunities to attend conferences and share the research and instructional materials they develop with other educators. Returning teachers will also share their experiences with subsequent cohorts.
“This is a real opportunity for them to emerge as leaders in the STEM teaching field,” McKay said. “That’s exciting because it helps sustain the work that they’ve started.”
The project complements other UMaine efforts to strengthen STEM teacher leadership, particularly in rural communities. McKay said these types of professional development opportunities can also help retain strong teachers.
For Emanetoglu, long-term success would mean seeing the impact move from UMaine laboratories into Maine classrooms and, eventually, the state’s workforce.
“From the students’ perspective, it’s being exposed to these high-tech, high-impact areas and new career opportunities,” Emanetoglu said. “Hopefully, we’ll get some of them to come to UMaine or another institution where they can further study these areas.”
Contact: David Nordman, david.nordman@maine.edu

articles.content:
Mid-Coast School of Technology to host Open House, Career and College Expo
Event Date
Thursday, October 01, 2026 - 04:00 pm to 06:00 pm
ROCKLAND — Mid-Coast School of Technology invites students, families, community members, and alumni to attend its upcoming Open House + Career & College Expo on October 1, from 4 to 6 p.m., at its campus, at 1 Main St., Rockland.
Admission is free, and the event features giveaways, door prizes, and family-friendly activities throughout the evening. Additionally, the school's Bake Shop will be open during the event with items available for purchase.
Designed for middle schoolers, high schoolers, and adults alike, the Expo highlights career pathways, educational programs, and hands-on learning.
"School alumni are warmly invited to drop in, visit, reconnect with former teachers, and see how the programs and facilities have evolved," said MCST, in a news release.
Attendees can explore the building at their own pace with informal, self-guided tours to check out state-of-the-art labs, shops, and studios, as well as test interactive simulators, tools, and modern technology.
Event Highlights & Activities:
- Bake Shop Open: Stop by the student-run Bake Shop to purchase freshly made goods and support the program.
- Alumni Welcome: Former students are encouraged to stop by, reconnect with teachers, and share their career journeys with current and prospective students.
- Self-Guided Facility Tours: Walk around and explore specialized learning spaces, labs, shops, and creative studios at your own pace.
- Interactive Demos & Tools: Experience live CTE demonstrations, test out interactive simulators, and try hands-on equipment used in real-world industries.
- Early Pathway Exploration: Learn about program options available for 9th and 10th-grade students and explore technical careers before entering high school.
- Student & Mentor Connections: Meet inspiring high school students and ask them what the CTE experience is really like.
- Career & College Guidance: Connect with regional college representatives and employers, match personal passions to potential jobs, and receive guidance on certifications and job opportunities.
Grounding the event are Mid-Coast School of Technology's core values: Respect, Honesty, Responsibility, Courage, and Equality.
To learn more about the event, visit mcst8.org, call 207-594-2161, or follow Mid-Coast School of Technology on Facebook and Instagram at @midcoast.CTE.

Address
Mid-Coast School of Technology
1 Main St.
Rockland, ME 04841

articles.title: Advanced Micro Devices vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.description: Advanced Micro Devices vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? The Motley Fool
articles.description_html: Advanced Micro Devices vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?  The Motley Fool
articles.article_title: Advanced Micro Devices vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? | The Motley Fool
articles.heading: Advanced Micro Devices vs. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.summary: AMD trades at an 80x forward P/E while TSMC commands a 45% net margin, a stark contrast that frames the growth-versus-stability trade-off.
articles.content:
The artificial intelligence boom has transformed the chip industry into a high-stakes arena for investors. Choosing between chip designer Advanced Micro Devices(AMD +0.57%) and manufacturing giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing(TSM -0.01%) requires weighing innovation against industrial scale.
Advanced Micro Devices designs high-performance processors and accelerators that power data centers and gaming consoles. In contrast, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing operates as a pure-play foundry, manufacturing the actual chips that Advanced Micro Devices and its rivals design. These two giants are fundamentally linked, yet they offer distinct ways to play on the global demand for technology hardware.
The case for Advanced Micro Devices
Advanced Micro Devices designs high-performance computing products for data centers, gaming, and PC markets. The company provides specialized chips to major players, including Microsoft and Sony, which use its hardware in popular gaming consoles. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business. Additionally, the company maintains a strategic partnership with OpenAI to deploy massive amounts of graphics processing units (GPUs) for artificial intelligence. These products are essential for the semiconductor stocks that power modern technology.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $34.6 billion, representing a significant 34.3% increase over the prior year. This growth was accompanied by net income of approximately $4.3 billion. This level of profitability indicates a notable improvement over previous fiscal years, as the company captures a larger share of the high-end computing market. The net margin for the period was roughly 12.5%.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.1x. This ratio measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, with a lower number indicating less reliance on borrowed money. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to pay short-term obligations by dividing current assets by current liabilities, is approximately 2.9x. Free cash flow, calculated as cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was close to $5.5 billion in FY 2025. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 21.2% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
The case for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing is the world's largest pure-play foundry, meaning it manufactures integrated circuits designed by other companies. In its latest annual report, filed in early 2026, the company noted it served 534 customers across end markets, including high-performance computing, smartphones, and automotive. This business model allows it to benefit from the growth of the entire chip sector without being tied to the success of a single device or chip architecture.
In FY 2025, revenue reached close to $122.4 billion, representing a 32% increase over the previous year. Net income for the period was nearly $55.1 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly 45.0%. This exceptionally high level of profitability reflects the company's dominant position and its ability to maintain high pricing for its most advanced manufacturing nodes.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.2x. The current ratio is roughly 2.5x, indicating a strong ability to cover short-term liabilities. Free cash flow for FY 2025 was close to $32.2 billion, which the company uses to fund its massive research and development efforts and expand its global manufacturing footprint. The company maintains a healthy financial position while investing heavily in the next generation of lithography technology.
Risk profile comparison
Advanced Micro Devices faces intense competition in the data center and client markets from rivals such as Intel and Nvidia. The business is highly cyclical and sensitive to shifts in demand for artificial intelligence and gaming. Rapid technological changes can lead to product obsolescence and quickly impact revenue. Export control regulations and geopolitical tensions also pose risks to its supply chain. Furthermore, the company relies on a small number of manufacturing partners, creating vulnerability if those partners experience disruptions.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing operates in a highly capital-intensive industry. It faces risks associated with the massive costs of maintaining advanced manufacturing facilities. Geopolitical tensions also threaten its operations because a significant portion of its capacity is concentrated in a single geographic region. Additionally, any slowdown in the high-performance computing or smartphone markets could reduce demand for its services. The company also competes with other major foundries such as Samsung Electronics and GlobalFoundries for high-end orders.
Valuation comparison
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing appears cheaper on a multiples basis, while Advanced Micro Devices carries a premium for its specialized AI growth potential and software integrations. The Forward P/E ratio compares the current stock price to future earnings estimates, while the P/S ratio measures the stock price relative to sales over the past twelve months.
| Metric | Advanced Micro Devices | Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing |
|---|---|---|
| Forward P/E | 83.0x | 26.6x |
| P/S ratio | 25.1x | 16.4x |
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
As a longtime AMD shareholder, I remain bullish on the fast-growing company as it challenges Nvidia in its dominant business, AI accelerators.
NASDAQ: AMD
Key Data Points
However, I first bought AMD during the 2022 bear market, and a lot has changed since that time. Although the chip design companies like AMD tend to command higher earnings multiples, I have become increasingly concerned about valuations, especially AMD's 83.0 forward earnings multiple.
In contrast, fab companies like TSMC have historically traded at a discount. Nonetheless, I like that it dominates advanced chip manufacturing and claims 72.5% market share in the foundry business, according to TrendForce. Of the two companies, this makes it more critical to the semiconductor industry.
NYSE: TSM
Key Data Points
Additionally, it trades at less than 27 times forward earnings. While it is more expensive than in the past, it is a relative bargain to its counterparts. Although I continue to hold AMD stock, if I have to choose between these two stocks in the future, TSMC will likely be my choice.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.2x. The current ratio is roughly 2.5x, indicating a strong ability to cover short-term liabilities. Free cash flow for FY 2025 was close to $32.2 billion, which the company uses to fund its massive research and development efforts and expand its global manufacturing footprint. The company maintains a healthy financial position while investing heavily in the next generation of lithography technology.

Risk profile comparison

Advanced Micro Devices faces intense competition in the data center and client markets from rivals such as Intel and Nvidia. The business is highly cyclical and sensitive to shifts in demand for artificial intelligence and gaming. Rapid technological changes can lead to product obsolescence and quickly impact revenue. Export control regulations and geopolitical tensions also pose risks to its supply chain. Furthermore, the company relies on a small number of manufacturing partners, creating vulnerability if those partners experience disruptions.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing operates in a highly capital-intensive industry. It faces risks associated with the massive costs of maintaining advanced manufacturing facilities. Geopolitical tensions also threaten its operations because a significant portion of its capacity is concentrated in a single geographic region. Additionally, any slowdown in the high-performance computing or smartphone markets could reduce demand for its services. The company also competes with other major foundries such as Samsung Electronics and GlobalFoundries for high-end orders.

Valuation comparison

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing appears cheaper on a multiples basis, while Advanced Micro Devices carries a premium for its specialized AI growth potential and software integrations. The Forward P/E ratio compares the current stock price to future earnings estimates, while the P/S ratio measures the stock price relative to sales over the past twelve months.

Metric Advanced Micro Devices Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing
Forward P/E 83.0x 26.6x
P/S ratio 25.1x 16.4x

Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?

As a longtime AMD shareholder, I remain bullish on the fast-growing company as it challenges Nvidia in its dominant business, AI accelerators.

NASDAQ: AMD

Key Data Points

However, I first bought AMD during the 2022 bear market, and a lot has changed since that time. Although the chip design companies like AMD tend to command higher earnings multiples, I have become increasingly concerned about valuations, especially AMD's 83.0 forward earnings multiple.

In contrast, fab companies like TSMC have historically traded at a discount. Nonetheless, I like that it dominates advanced chip manufacturing and claims 72.5% market share in the foundry business, according to TrendForce. Of the two companies, this makes it more critical to the semiconductor industry.

NYSE: TSM

Key Data Points

Additionally, it trades at less than 27 times forward earnings. While it is more expensive than in the past, it is a relative bargain to its counterparts. Although I continue to hold AMD stock, if I have to choose between these two stocks in the future, TSMC will likely be my choice.

articles.article_title: The Biggest 3D Art & Technology Highlights From Gamescom 2026
articles.heading: The Biggest 3D Art & Technology Highlights From Gamescom 2026
articles.summary: Gamescom 2026 highlighted advances in ray-traced rendering, dense geometry, scalable asset creation, proprietary engines, and emerging AI-assisted 3D workflows.
articles.content:
The Biggest 3D Art & Technology Highlights From Gamescom 2026
Gamescom 2026 highlighted advances in ray-traced rendering, dense geometry, scalable asset creation, proprietary engines, and emerging AI-assisted 3D workflows.
Gamescom is primarily associated with trailers and playable demos, but the event also provides an enormous showcase for the technologies changing how games are made. This year’s most important 3D trends included more practical ray tracing, denser real-time geometry, increasingly specialized proprietary engines, and tools designed to shorten the journey from an idea to a usable asset.
NVIDIA introduced a second-generation transformer model for DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction. The new model reportedly has 35% more compute capacity and 20% more parameters, improving detail and temporal stability in ray-traced and path-traced games without substantially changing performance.
Gears of War E-Day
This is particularly important during motion, where limited ray samples can create ghosting, smearing, and unstable surfaces. Ray Reconstruction is still not a perfect solution to the compromises involved in real-time path tracing, but the update demonstrates how quickly neural rendering is becoming a standard component of modern graphics pipelines.
NVIDIA also highlighted RTX Mega Geometry through Gears of War: E-Day. The technology is intended to make ray tracing more practical in scenes containing enormous quantities of detailed geometry, allowing developers to combine dense assets, dynamic destruction, and sophisticated lighting more efficiently. For artists, this contributes to a broader shift in which more detail can survive the journey from source asset to playable scene.
At the asset-creation end of that pipeline, Tripo AI demonstrated how generative 3D tools are moving beyond producing isolated models and toward supporting wider production workflows. The company's current focus encompasses asset generation, optimization, team collaboration, pipeline automation, and exporting work into engines such as Unity.
Tripo P2.0, its latest breakthrough 3D-native foundation model, generates native quad meshes. Shown as a preview at Gamescom, Tripo P2.0 has since been officially released with a few concrete additions worth noting. It can produce up to four asset variations from one concept, giving artists and developers options to evaluate before investing additional production time. It adds a new Mesh Edit tool that lets a specific region of a model be regenerated without rebuilding the whole asset from scratch. The multi-view reference input enables an asset to be built from front, back, and side images rather than a single angle. Full details are available in Tripo's official P2.0 release announcement.
Moreover, the Tripo plus OpenAI's Astra workflow has drawn enthusiastic responses from users. A recent Tripo post showed a playable 3D game built in approximately four hours using Tripo-generated assets and fewer than 5,000 lines of code. It has demonstrated how anyone can use generative 3D tools like Tripo to create their own games or animations.
Engine development produced several other notable stories. Creative Assembly explained how its new Warcore engine allows Total War: Warhammer 40,000 to expand across planets and solar systems. Warcore improves rendering, asset manipulation, animation modularity, destruction, explosions, and the enormous volume of projectiles required by the setting. Its Havoc system helps communicate the physical impact of futuristic combat across unusually large battlefields.
Crystal Dynamics also revealed that Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis had to be rebuilt entirely from scratch in Unreal Engine 5 because no original source code remained. The project uses Nanite and Lumen alongside custom physics and animation technology, illustrating that adopting a general-purpose engine does not eliminate the need for substantial project-specific engineering.
4A Games
The game news itself was extensive, but the technical highlights were more focused. Metro 2039 won Best Visuals for its latest evolution of the 4A Engine, Control Resonant demonstrated Remedy’s Northlight rendering and destruction systems, and Gears of War: E-Day provided a practical showcase for Mega Geometry. Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis and The Witcher 3 Remastered also reflected the growing expectation that remasters and reimaginings should revisit animation, lighting, materials, and gameplay rather than merely increase resolution.

articles.title: UHealth Comprehensive Aortic Center: Advanced Expertise and Technology vs. Deadly Aortic Conditions
articles.description: UHealth Comprehensive Aortic Center: Advanced Expertise and Technology vs. Deadly Aortic Conditions South Florida Hospital News
articles.description_html: UHealth Comprehensive Aortic Center: Advanced Expertise and Technology vs. Deadly Aortic Conditions  South Florida Hospital News
articles.article_title: UHealth Comprehensive Aortic Center: Advanced Expertise and Technology vs. Deadly Aortic Conditions | Florida Hospital News and Healthcare Report
articles.heading: UHealth Comprehensive Aortic Center: Advanced Expertise and Technology vs. Deadly Aortic Conditions
articles.summary: UHealth Comprehensive Aortic Center: Advanced Expertise and Technology vs. Deadly Aortic Conditions South Florida Hospital News
articles.content:
The Comprehensive Aortic Center at UHealth is combining multidisciplinary expertise, 3D fusion imaging and minimally invasive procedures to treat complex aortic aneurysms and dissections.
Sept 24 2026 – The human body can be both sturdy and fragile. The heart beats around 100,000 times per day, vigorously sending blood through the aorta and other major arteries to feed oxygen and nutrients to various organs. Unfortunately, the aorta, which branches up from the heart and descends into the abdomen, bears the brunt of this pressure.
Sometimes it doesn’t hold up. The aortic wall can bubble out (an aneurysm) or even tear (a dissection).
Dr. Jean Panneton
UHealth—University of Miami Health System has recently boosted its ability to treat aortic diseases, recruiting two world-class surgeons to lead its Comprehensive Aortic Center. Co-directed by vascular surgeon Jean Panneton, M.D., and cardiothoracic surgeon Ciro Amodio, M.D., associate professor in the DeWitt Daughtry Family Department of Surgery at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, the center unites multiple disciplines to treat aneurysms, dissections and valve issues.
To complement the center, UHealth also opened a hybrid operating room, which leverages advanced imaging and other technologies to handle the most complex procedures. The end result is better care for patients with these urgent and often life-threatening conditions.
How Does a Hybrid Operating Room Improve Aortic Care?
Until relatively recently, catheterization procedures and open surgeries were separate specialties with distinct turfs. Working in catheterization labs, interventionalists or cardiologists leveraged minimally invasive techniques to treat arterial blockages, valve disorders and other issues. Surgeons conducted open procedures to perform bypass surgeries and repair aneurysms, dissections and other conditions.
But over the years, the distinctions between these disciplines have narrowed, creating the need for hybrid procedure rooms, where specialists can work side-by-side to simultaneously perform catheterization procedures and open surgeries. One of the hybrid room’s most important refinements is 3D fusion imaging.
“We take a CT scan of the patient and combine it with the fluoroscopy (moving x-rays), which give us 3D fusion imaging,” said Dr. Panneton, a professor in the DeWitt Daughtry Family Department of Surgery. “The images are so much clearer. It’s like night and day.”
Fusion imaging and other advanced technologies are giving cardiac and vascular teams the necessary tools to perform complex aortic reconstructions and provide care few other facilities can match. Recently, these tools helped surgeons at the Comprehensive Aortic Center perform complex procedures for the first time in South Florida.
New Aortic Procedures Available at UHealth
In April 2026, the U.S. Food & Drug Administration approved the NEXUS aortic arch stent graft, a safer way to repair aortic dissections and other high-risk aortic arch conditions.
“Because of our Comprehensive Aortic Center, we have tremendous expertise to take on these new procedures,” said Dr. Panneton. “This was the first Nexus implant in Florida, and it’s a less invasive way to do a total aortic arch replacement. It gives us a better way to repair aortic arch aneurysms, which tend to occur in elderly patients who are not necessarily good candidates for open heart surgery.”
Around the same time, Dr. Panneton performed another pair of minimally invasive procedures for the first time in Miami. These procedures rely on a technique called in situ laser fenestration, which was pioneered by Dr Panneton.
Using a catheter, a stent-graft is deployed inside the aorta to reline a blood vessel around an aneurysm or dissection. Then, surgeons use a laser to punch holes in the graft and reestablish blood flow to the important arteries that branch out from the aorta. These techniques recently helped two patients, one with a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm (a TAAA procedure) and the other an aortic arch aneurysm (a TEVAR procedure).
“We can do a thoracic endograft in the aortic arch, and we can revascularize the arch vessels, such as the subclavian artery (which sends blood to the arms and chest) and the carotid artery (which supplies the brain),” said Dr. Panneton. “We use the laser to revascularize them, and stents to reconnect them. It makes for a faster and more versatile procedure.”
What Could Minimally Invasive Treatment Mean for Recovery?
By combining intensive expertise and sophisticated technology, the Comprehensive Aortic Center is performing life-saving procedures many hospitals simply cannot provide. In addition, as new procedures and technologies come into play, the center will be well-situated to adopt them.
“We used to do open procedures for aneurysms and dissections, and people would spend two, three, four weeks in the hospital,” said Dr. Panneton. “Now people can go home two to four days after their procedures. These approaches are less invasive, safer and much easier on patients.”

articles.title: Teledyne and NASA advance hydrogen fuel cell technology
articles.description: Teledyne and NASA advance hydrogen fuel cell technology Engineering.com
articles.description_html: Teledyne and NASA advance hydrogen fuel cell technology  Engineering.com
articles.article_title: Teledyne and NASA advance hydrogen fuel cell technology - Engineering.com
articles.heading: Teledyne and NASA advance hydrogen fuel cell technology
articles.summary: The collaboration will help mature Teledyne’s Hydrogen Electrical Power System from TRL 5 to TRL 7 for space applications.
articles.content:
The collaboration will help mature Teledyne’s Hydrogen Electrical Power System from TRL 5 to TRL 7 for space applications.
Teledyne Energy Systems, Inc. has been selected to participate in NASA’s Announcement of Collaboration Opportunity, establishing a collaborative effort with NASA’s Glenn Research Center and Johnson Space Center to advance next-generation space power technology.
Under the Space Act Agreement, Teledyne Energy Systems and NASA will work together to mature the company’s Hydrogen Electrical Power System (HEPS), advancing the technology from Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 5 to TRL 7 for space environments. The collaboration supports NASA’s ongoing efforts to develop reliable, efficient power systems for future lunar and deep-space exploration missions.
HEPS is an advanced hydrogen fuel cell system designed to deliver efficient, air-independent power for demanding space applications. Building on decades of Teledyne heritage in space power systems, the technology is intended to support future lunar habitats, surface infrastructure, and other exploration systems that require dependable energy generation in harsh environments. The collaboration will leverage the technical expertise and facilities of NASA Glenn and NASA Johnson to help validate HEPS performance in relevant space environments.
As NASA continues to invest in technologies that will enable a sustained human presence beyond Earth, advanced energy systems remain a critical component of future mission success. Through this collaboration, Teledyne Energy Systems will continue to advance innovative power solutions that support exploration, scientific discovery, and the next generation of space missions.
For more information, visit teledyne.com.

articles.description: A wearable-to-implant wireless power transfer technology with variation tolerance Nature

articles.article_title: A wearable-to-implant wireless power transfer technology with variation tolerance - Nature Electronics
articles.heading: A wearable-to-implant wireless power transfer technology with variation tolerance
articles.summary: A wireless power transfer system that combines parity–time symmetric resonance and liquid metal-based receivers can maintain a transfer efficiency above 50%, even when under 30% strain and spatially misaligned, enabling reliable operation of untethered implantable bioelectronics.
articles.content:
Abstract
Advances in soft materials and device architectures have led to the development of fully implantable bioelectronic systems. However, reliable wireless power transfer for such systems remains challenging, particularly under dynamic physiological conditions. Conventional inductive coupling suffers from unstable power delivery due to coil misalignment, mechanical deformation and load impedance fluctuations, which disrupt the resonance. Here we describe a variation-tolerant wireless power transfer system that uses a nonlinear parity–time symmetric circuit. The system consists of a symmetric resonator pair formed by a wearable self-oscillating power transmitter and a liquid metal-based implantable receiver. A real-time feedback circuit in the transmitter provides automatic frequency adaptation, maintaining stable resonance against external disturbances. Moreover, the intrinsically stretchy receiver minimizes resistance-induced power losses during deformation. The power transfer efficiency remains above 50% under 30% strain and 30-mm misalignment. We illustrate the efficacy of the system in large animal models by performing wireless cardiac pacing and tachyarrhythmia termination under highly dynamic in vivo conditions.
