Abstract

Advances in soft materials and device architectures have led to the development of fully implantable bioelectronic systems. However, reliable wireless power transfer for such systems remains challenging, particularly under dynamic physiological conditions. Conventional inductive coupling suffers from unstable power delivery due to coil misalignment, mechanical deformation and load impedance fluctuations, which disrupt the resonance. Here we describe a variation-tolerant wireless power transfer system that uses a nonlinear parity–time symmetric circuit. The system consists of a symmetric resonator pair formed by a wearable self-oscillating power transmitter and a liquid metal-based implantable receiver. A real-time feedback circuit in the transmitter provides automatic frequency adaptation, maintaining stable resonance against external disturbances. Moreover, the intrinsically stretchy receiver minimizes resistance-induced power losses during deformation. The power transfer efficiency remains above 50% under 30% strain and 30-mm misalignment. We illustrate the efficacy of the system in large animal models by performing wireless cardiac pacing and tachyarrhythmia termination under highly dynamic in vivo conditions.

articles.summary: Polygraph+ will use new sensor technologies and AI to vet staff and hunt leakers. Experts say AI-enabled lie detection is “the worst of both worlds.”
articles.content:
The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector
Polygraph+ will use new sensor technologies and AI to vet staff and hunt leakers. Experts say AI-enabled lie detection is “the worst of both worlds.”
The US government wants to spend $30.3 million over the next five years on an improved form of lie detector, according to a Department of Defense budget request. The program, called Polygraph+ or Polygraph Next, will focus on scoring algorithms that use artificial intelligence and machine learning and on a technique called “standoff sensing,” which refers to the ability to take physiological readings without attaching a device to a subject’s person.
According to details of the budget document, which were first reported by Inside Defense, the project will “modernize federal polygraph and credibility assessment technologies” to improve their accuracy and reliability. But the project may be just the latest in a long line of failed attempts to use technology to detect lies. “It’s a misguided effort to reduce the complex to something that is tangible,” says Kyri Kotsoglou, a legal scholar at Northumbria University in the UK who studies the use of polygraphs in the justice system.
The move comes at a time of high tension within the department. Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has been increasingly turning to polygraph tests in an attempt to find the sources of alleged leaks to the press. In September, the New York Times reported that around 50 officers on the Joint Staff had been given polygraph tests after news coverage reported on the depletion of US weapons stockpiles in the war with Iran.
Polygraph+ will be run by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), which conducts background checks for the federal government. According to the budget document, which has not yet been approved by Congress, the new technology will be used for vetting of prospective employees and “insider threat detection.” It is not yet clear which specific technologies will be used, and the DCSA did not respond to a request for more information.
But other Pentagon efforts offer potential clues. In 2023, the department’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) ran an open submission process to find companies with products that could be used for deception detection.
It selected two companies to build prototypes: Presage Technologies, which claims to be able to measure heart rate and breathing rate using standard cameras, and Altec Research, a medical sensor company now branching out into non-contact sensing technologies. A screenshot of Altec’s prototype technology released by the DIU shows that it tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity. Presage Technologies and Altec Research did not respond to requests for comment. The DIU declined to comment.
Current lie detection technology has barely changed since the polygraph was invented in the 1920s. Examiners rely on blood pressure, pulse, breathing, and sweat measurements to determine if someone is lying. They make judgments about the veracity of respondents’ replies on the basis of differences in their physiological response to baseline questions like “Is the sky blue?” and target questions like “Have you ever committed a crime?”
The federal government conducts tens of thousands of the tests each year while screening employees, but the reliability of this technology has been repeatedly challenged—and its results are rarely admissible in court. In 1983, Congress’s Office of Technology Assessment concluded that there was very limited evidence supporting the polygraph’s use for screening employees, and in 2003, the US National Research Council (NRC) said evidence for its efficacy was “weak at best.”
Research suggests humans can spot a lie just over half the time without any technical assistance. The American Polygraph Association claims the polygraph is between 80% and 94% accurate. But the 2003 NRC report pointed out that a screening test with this level of accuracy could still lead to a lot of mistakes. The DOD employs 2.8 million people; an imperfect system applied at that scale could end up falsely accusing tens of thousands.
There are other issues too. Polygraph interpretations are often subjective: Different examiners get wildly different results, and people from minority groups are more likely to be judged as deceptive. What’s more, with training it’s possible for interviewees to learn a variety of countermeasures that can help beat the test; for example, they may artificially heighten their physiological response to baseline questions by stepping on a pin hidden in their shoe.
“If you know how it works, you can beat it,” says Sophie van der Zee, an associate professor who studies deception at Erasmus University in Rotterdam. She says the machine’s biggest effect is deterrence—often, subjects confess before it even begins. “But that only works if people think a polygraph works,” she points out.
Various new strategies for lie detection have been attempted over the decades, with technologies ranging from thermal cameras to pupil trackers to brain scans. None of them have yielded reliable results outside the lab. The problem is that there’s no single telltale sign of lying that’s true for everyone all the time. “There is still no Pinocchio’s nose,” says van der Zee.
AI could theoretically improve polygraphs if it could find patterns in the data that examiners can’t. AI algorithms are also more likely to be used for “multi-modal” deception detection, which seeks to combine multiple measurements into an overall deception “score” that is harder for people to game. Three things are happening under the surface that lie detection tries to home in on, van der Zee says: physiological stress, cognitive load, and the conscious efforts people make to conceal the fact that they’re lying. Current polygraph technology tackles only one.
“The more you can have combined methods that approach it from these three different angles, the more successful you will be,” van der Zee says. This isn’t a new concept—in the 2000s, researchers at Manchester Metropolitan University in the UK developed a system called Silent Talker that generated a deception score from video footage. This was later folded into iBorderCtrl, an EU-funded pilot program. In the US, a project called AVATAR incorporated eye tracking, voice analysis, and body movement detection into a tool for use at border crossings. All these projects have quietly faded away.
Kotsoglou says combining AI and the polygraph is “the worst of both worlds” because it adds uncertainty on top of invalidity. Even if AI or machine learning can spot previously unseen patterns in physiological data, it won’t be able to reliably link them to lying because there is no real ground truth.
“Even if you have all the records in the world from polygraph tests, you don't know whether those polygraph tests are right or not,” says Marion Oswald, a professor of law who has written with Kotsoglou on the use of polygraphs in the justice system. She fears that new forms of lie detection will, like the polygraph, be used more as a psychological prop than a scientific tool.
“It seems very much a response to the concern of the current administration to leaks and perceived lack of loyalty,” says Oswald. “[Lie detection is] being used as a threat, to intimidate and force people to confess to things, as opposed to anything that's actually getting valid information.”
Deep Dive
Artificial intelligence
A fundamental flaw leaves LLMs strikingly vulnerable to attack
It makes it easy to trick them into doing things they shouldn’t, such as telling you how to sabotage an aircraft’s navigation system.
AI’s recursive self-improvement might not come so quickly after all
AI agents are not yet creative enough to carry out genuinely innovative open-ended AI research, it seems.
Here’s why AI agents lie and cheat to reach their goals
The misbehavior is called reward hacking. This is what you need to know.
These startups are chasing the next big thing in LLMs
Meet the new kids nipping at the heels of the AI giants.

In his deliberations on what it means to be human, Pope Leo says “we are all born naked and in need; poor by birth, in need of bread, and words, and words of care and affection.”

Only through becoming adult, “we risk forgetting it,” with people’s “humanity betrayed or cast aside, exploited or deceived.”

“Life is no longer understood as a gift, but as a commodity. It is no longer viewed as a summons to care and responsibility, but as a product to be exploited.”

“Life is no longer understood as a gift, but as a commodity. It is no longer viewed as a summons to care and responsibility, but as a product to be exploited.”

He “to be human is to be free by nature,” and to “recognise [life’s] grandeur” and “immense potential.”

But he says “to be human … implies a responsibility before history,” as “the human being is one who grows, learns, and works with both hands and mind.”

He then talks about the tragedy of the second world war, when “humanity had come to realise that scientific progress, when severed from wisdom, can turn into a weapon of destruction.”

He says 80 years later, the founding charter of Unesco – built on that recognition – still stands.

Turning to the issue of technology, he says “our efforts in this domain must ensure that new technologies remain at the service of the human person , rather than becoming yet another instrument of domination and injustice.”

In a strong passage, he warns:

“Over the centuries, many tasks once performed by human beings have been entrusted to machines whose capabilities and applications have continued to expand. More recently, certain artificial systems have even been given the name of our human faculty of thought intelligence. At the same time, however, our ideas and relationships risk being impoverished by a process of dehumanisation. The paradox has become increasingly evident. While intelligence is attributed to computational systems, we struggle to recognise the inalienable dignity of human persons whose lives are judged according to the criterion of efficiency and, when deemed no longer productive, the rejected and discarded.”

As Pope Leo gets closer to the Notre Dame Cathedral, the bells ring once again, as they did this morning ( 10:07 ), to mark his arrival.

I have just realised that today’s blog has – inexcusably – not yet featured the Eiffel Tower.

Time to put things right:

Pope Leo is now travelling in a Papamobile through the streets of Paris, with large crowds of (very enthusiastic) well-wishers lining up his route.

He just blessed a small kid with a French beret on his head.

My heart.

Pope Leo ends with a call for action to help Unesco and other similar bodies “in the realisation that every people has its own precious part to play in the pursuit of that authentic human progress which peace alone can guarantee.”

“T his is not to embrace a naive optimism that ignores difficulties, but rather to persevere in the hope that the desired good is always attainable.”

“T his is not to embrace a naive optimism that ignores difficulties, but rather to persevere in the hope that the desired good is always attainable.”

And he ends on that note.

He will be at the Notre Dame Cathedral later this afternoon, before joining the French youth at the Stade de France in Saint-Denis of Paris.

Pope Leo also offers a comment on the ongoing discussion about the crisis of the UN and other similar international organisations as some countries see dialogue “an obstacle to action” and a “charade” and not a genuine attempt to resolve differences peacefully.

He says:

“ Our world regards international institutions with mixed feelings. On the one hand, t hese institutions are expected to respond to challenges that no individual state can face alone. On the other hand, these same institutions are experiencing a crisis of effectiveness, especially in situations where dialogue is seen as an obstacle to action rather than a resource for peace, a charade rather than an opportunity to seek the common good together. In this case, w e see the urgent need to promote a virtue that seems as greatly desired as it is really found, namely, the virtue of trust. Trust that differences do not necessarily constitute a threat. Trust that honest dialogue can bring about a greater good than what individuals could achieve on their own.”

On the one hand, t hese institutions are expected to respond to challenges that no individual state can face alone.

On the other hand, these same institutions are experiencing a crisis of effectiveness, especially in situations where dialogue is seen as an obstacle to action rather than a resource for peace, a charade rather than an opportunity to seek the common good together.

In this case, w e see the urgent need to promote a virtue that seems as greatly desired as it is really found, namely, the virtue of trust.

Trust that differences do not necessarily constitute a threat. Trust that honest dialogue can bring about a greater good than what individuals could achieve on their own.”

Pope Leo warns that “without truth, language becomes subject to the logic of violence and to the arbitrary will of the powerful.”

In what will be seen as a criticism of world leaders that disrespect the rule of law – you can think of some names here, I guess - he says:

“Instead of respecting the law, those in power invoke it when it serves their interests and disregard it when it restrains them, treating even justice itself as though it were a commodity to be bought and sold.”

“Instead of respecting the law, those in power invoke it when it serves their interests and disregard it when it restrains them, treating even justice itself as though it were a commodity to be bought and sold.”

He warns:

“If we realise that the corruption of the law begins with the corruption of the heart, we can recognise how every science risks losing its proper meaning when pursued without ethics, and thus ceasing to serve and reflect human dignity.”

“If we realise that the corruption of the law begins with the corruption of the heart, we can recognise how every science risks losing its proper meaning when pursued without ethics, and thus ceasing to serve and reflect human dignity.”

Pope Leo also warns against the pursuit of power without limits, as – using the analogy to the Tower of Babel – he says:

“ The more power seeks to oppress, the more it weakens itself, exposing its inhumane face. articles.heading: In a Nutshell: Exploring immersive technology inside the GRID Lab
articles.summary: What does it take to create a virtual world you can see, hear and move through? From immersive audio and 360-degree cameras to motion capture and virtual reality, Ohio University’s GRID Lab gives students access to the technology and hands-on experiences bringing those worlds to life.
articles.content:
In this episode of In a Nutshell, immersive audio and cinematic virtual reality specialist Jordan Herron takes us inside Ohio University’s Grid Lab for a look at the spaces, technology and opportunities available to students.
The tour includes the Immersive Audio Suite, XR Lab classroom and Motion Capture Suite, where students can work with professional-level tools while putting what they learn in the classroom into practice. Along the way, Herron highlights equipment ranging from binaural audio and 360-degree video kits to motion capture suits and a VR system that lets users physically walk through virtual environments.
Students also have opportunities to take part in professional-level projects outside the classroom, building experience they can apply to careers in fields ranging from video games to medicine and themed entertainment.

articles.content:
Georgia Institute of Technology professor Munmun De Choudhury discusses AI, mental health and humanity
September 25, 2026
On Wednesday evening, students, faculty and community members gathered in Mills Hall to hear Munmun De Choudhury, a computer scientist, social scientist and professor of interactive computing at the Georgia Institute of Technology, speak as part of the Hastings Initiative lecture series.
De Choudhury’s research focuses on digital mental health and the effects of emerging technologies on mental health, social relationships and access to care. Her lecture, “A Human and Humane Vision for AI and Mental Health,” examined the growing role of artificial intelligence in mental health care and the challenges of integrating technology into deeply human relationships.
De Choudhury opened by describing artificial intelligence (AI) as an increasingly active participant in people’s lives, rather than simply a tool operating in the background.
“AI is becoming an active participant in how we engage with technology and other human beings today,” De Choudhury said. She noted that artificial intelligence is increasingly mediating how people seek care, find connection and make sense of their psychological well-being.
De Choudhury then turned to the history of mental health care, describing psychoanalysis, pharmacological treatments and cognitive behavioral therapy as major paradigm shifts in the field. Despite those developments, she said, barriers including limited access to care, stigma and disparities remain.
AI, De Choudhury argued, could represent a fourth paradigm shift in psychological health care.
Over the past 15 years, research in digital mental health has examined how technology can expand access to support. De Choudhury discussed her group’s research examining social media communities, where people experiencing struggles in their emotional wellbeing can disclose their experiences and receive emotional and social support.
De Choudhury said anonymous and pseudonymous online spaces can allow people to express experiences they may not feel comfortable discussing elsewhere. Her research has also explored how AI can assist users in reframing difficult experiences and help peer supporters devise responses to people seeking mental health support.
However, De Choudhury argued that AI’s ability to produce accessible and convincing responses does not necessarily mean those responses constitute effective support for patients.
Research conducted by her group compared responses written by humans in online mental health communities with responses generated by large language models. According to De Choudhury, the AI-generated responses were often more readable and structured but lacked the lived experience present in human responses.
De Choudhury explained that AI frequently treats mental health concerns as problems to solve rather than experiences to be understood through human connection and empathy.
“Good is no good if it doesn’t reflect who we are as individuals,” De Choudhury said.
She also emphasized the importance of culture and context when evaluating AI-generated advice. Research from her group examined responses from large language models in English, Spanish, Chinese and Hindi, finding significant differences in the models’ performance across languages.
She described examples of users receiving advice that did not fit their cultural circumstances, claiming that mental health support cannot be separated from an individual’s identity, culture and social environment.
De Choudhury then examined the role AI can play in helping navigate human relationships. She noted that conversational AI is always available and can consistently provide validation, qualities that can make the technology appealing to people seeking support.
At the same time, she argued that constant validation can become harmful. Human relationships involve disagreement, discomfort and what De Choudhury described as “friction,” which can allow people to confront their assumptions and grow. AI’s tendency to provide a frictionless interaction, she said, can instead reinforce harmful perspectives.
De Choudhury ultimately argued that AI should be developed to enrich human relationships rather than replace them. She pointed to situations where AI could provide temporary support when a human is unavailable, help people prepare for difficult conversations or supplement existing mental health care.
De Choudhury reiterated that AI and humans possess different strengths and that the technology should be designed around those distinctions.
“I think humans have their own unique strengths, and AI has its own unique strengths,” De Choudhury said.
De Choudhury concluded by arguing that the greatest potential of AI in the mental health field lies not in replicating human relationships, but in helping preserve them.
“The biggest promise of AI is when it would help us preserve what is so human, especially when it comes to our mental health,” De Choudhury said.

articles.summary: UCLA is now the first university in the United States to launch a digital humanities department, combining humanistic studies with the exploration of artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies.
articles.content:
UCLA launches first digital humanities department to address AI and emerging technologies
UCLA is now the first university in the United States to launch a digital humanities department, combining humanistic studies with the exploration of artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies.
Students will get a deep understanding of computational tools and technologies, from the perspective of fields including culture, society, languages and history. Through the lens of those academic disciplines, students will look at how the technology is developed and used.
Dr. Todd Presner, co-creator of the department, said the new department is being launched at a critical time for the development of artificial intelligence.
"This is something that is really front and center as we think about ethical issues, where these technologies came from, how they're being used," Presner said during a live interview on California Tonight. "But even more broadly than that, it's also what it means when our cultural record becomes digitized as a human species."
In addition to addressing fears surrounding AI, the department encompasses a wide range of subjects. Examples include using 3D modeling to recreate ancient cities, design work, and social media analytics. Presner's HyperCities Project looks at t`he history of cities over time, including a tool that can map the lives of Holocaust survivors. His students worked on projects in conjunction with Holocaust Museum LA. "It was a way of memorializing these stories in digital formats," explained Presner.
This field has grown significantly at UCLA, evolving from a smaller program into a full-fledged department. Graduates will earn bachelor's degrees in digital humanities, preparing them for various career paths.

articles.title: Magnuson Center for Entrepreneurship to absorb the Technology Transfer Office in $60 million expansion
articles.description: Magnuson Center for Entrepreneurship to absorb the Technology Transfer Office in $60 million expansion The Dartmouth
articles.description_html: Magnuson Center for Entrepreneurship to absorb the Technology Transfer Office in $60 million expansion  The Dartmouth
articles.source: Magnuson Center and Technology Transfer Office merge in $60 million expansion - The Dartmouth
articles.article_title: Magnuson Center and Technology Transfer Office merge in $60 million expansion
articles.heading: Magnuson Center and Technology Transfer Office merge in $60 million expansion
articles.summary: Following a national search, Gabriel Schlumberger ’96 will begin as the executive director of the expanded center on Jan. 1, 2027.
articles.content:
The Magnuson Center for Entrepreneurship will absorb Dartmouth’s Technology Transfer Office, which supports the licensing and patenting of faculty-produced technologies and research, in a $60 million expansion, College President Sian Leah Beilock announced at the 13th annual Dartmouth Entrepreneurs Forum on Sept. 11. Though the combined center will share the Magnuson Center name, the new center will be restructured to continue supporting both existing Magnuson offerings and TTO functions.
TTO will be directly integrated into the new Magnuson Center following the expansion, according to TTO director Kim Rosenfield.
The College will primarily fund the merger and expansion with approximately $40 million in revenues from licensing COVID-19 vaccine technology developed at Dartmouth, according to Magnuson Center interim director Barry Schweitzer ’82, who does not oversee TTO. The remaining $20 million, of which $10 million has already been raised, will be funded through alumni donations.
In response to The Dartmouth’s request for comment, College spokesperson Kathryn Kennedy shared excerpts from Beilock’s script for her speech at the Dartmouth Entrepreneurs Forum. The new Magnuson Center is where Dartmouth’s “entrepreneurial spirit and groundbreaking research turn into real-world impact,” Beilock said in the speech.
“Dartmouth students are builders,” Beilock said. “The real differentiator of this new Magnuson will be students, faculty and alumni working more closely than ever before, learning from each other, solving real-world problems together and finding ways to connect those solutions to the people who need them.”
Beilock also announced that a donation from Amy and Jeff Crowe ’78 will endow the new center’s executive director position. Following a nationwide search co-led by vice provost for research Dean Madden and Magnuson Center board of advisors chair Andrea Reisman Johnson ’91, with support from executive search firm Isaacson, Miller, managing director of the startup accelerator Techstars Gabriel Schlumberger ’96 will serve as executive director of the new center. The old Magnuson's Center inaugural executive director Jamie Coughlin stepped down in June to pursue independent ventures, according to Madden.
Schlumberger, who studied government and film studies at Dartmouth, previously worked for Pixar and Disney and founded a company specializing in 3D-printed eyewear.
Schlumberger said in an interview with The Dartmouth that the center’s expansion will create a “coherent and fast-moving ecosystem” for students, faculty, staff and alumni.
“There’s an opportunity to reinvent how entrepreneurship is taught and make it look more experiential and infuse it across the college experience,” Schlumberger said. “Anybody who’s interested in working for a startup should be able to find an internship; anybody who’s interested in starting a startup as an alum should have support and help from the College.”
Schweitzer said the new expansion will “really allow” the Magnuson Center to “reach more of campus, as well as bring in more students to work on projects that are related to faculty research.”
In an email statement to The Dartmouth, Johnson wrote that “every member” of the Magnuson Center’s board donated funds to support the center’s expansion.
“True to our roots, we will continue supporting entrepreneurial programming for students and alums, and now we get to extend that work to faculty and tech transfer,” Johnson wrote.
The merger of the Magnuson Center and Technology Transfer Office follows a May 2025 report released by the invention2impact advisory group on the Technology Transfer Office’s efficiency, convened by then-Provost David Kotz, according to Madden, who chaired the group. The report recommended combining the offices.
Madden said in an interview with The Dartmouth that the goal of the expansion was to create a “comprehensive” support system for students, faculty and staff.
“We wanted to bring them together into a holistic ecosystem so that there would really be a one-stop shop for anyone who was interested in entrepreneurship or commercialization,” Madden said. “We wanted to make sure it didn’t matter where you start in the system.”
Rosenfield added that there previously were “silos” that limited collaboration between the Technology Transfer Office and the Magnuson Center.
“It was decided that if we could rebrand and put additional resources into the enterprise, then we would be even more effective than we already are,” Rosenfield said.
Madden added that he hoped that the new Magnuson Center will be a “home” for researchers from all backgrounds.
“We want to make sure that Magnuson is a home for folks interested in disseminating their work — not just for scientists or STEM researchers — but actually for the whole scholarly community,” Madden said.
Jonah Hymes ’28, a member of the Magnuson Student Leadership Board who attended this year’s Dartmouth Entrepreneurs Forum in San Francisco, said he is “excited” for new opportunities to collaborate with faculty and alumni.
“If a professor makes a company, they’re going to need help from students on the entrepreneurship end,” Hymes said. “That’s something that students can really be involved in and get some real hands-on experience with.”
Crowe and Coughlin did not respond to requests for comment by time of publication.
Correction appended (Sept. 25, 1:02 a.m.): This article previously misstated that the Magnuson Center will "absorbed" the Technology Transfer Office. The headline and body of this article has been corrected to reflect that the new center, which shares the Magnuson Center's name, will perform the Technology Transfer Office's functions and offer the existing Magnuson Center's offerings.
A previous version of this article erroneously stated that Gabriel Shlumberger will succeed Barry Schweitzer, who serves as interim director of the existing Magnuson Center, not the merged Technology Transfer Office and Magnuson Center.
Sahil Gandhi ’29 is a reporter from Staten Island, N.Y., and is majoring in environmental studies and government modified with philosophy and economics. He loves word searches and falling down internet and Wikipedia rabbit holes.

articles.title: Astera Labs vs. Marvell Technology: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.description: Astera Labs vs. Marvell Technology: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? The Motley Fool
articles.description_html: Astera Labs vs. Marvell Technology: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?  The Motley Fool
articles.article_title: Astera Labs vs. Marvell Technology: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? | The Motley Fool
articles.heading: Astera Labs vs. Marvell Technology: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.summary: Astera Labs boasts higher revenue growth, but customer concentration poses a risk. Marvell trades at lower multiples with broader diversification.
articles.content:
The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure has created a surge in demand for specialized connectivity chips. This leads many investors to choose between high-growth Astera Labs (ALAB +0.01%) and the more established Marvell Technology (MRVL -0.75%).
Astera Labs focuses on high-speed connectivity chips that solve data bottlenecks in AI servers. Marvell Technology provides a broader suite of networking, storage, and custom computing solutions for various data infrastructure markets.
While both companies benefit from the data center build-out, they have different profiles in terms of size, profitability, and market maturity.
ALAB & MRVL: Performance Comparison
Key Financial Metrics
The case for Astera Labs
Astera Labs designs connectivity solutions that enable high-speed data transfers within data centers, primarily for hyperscale cloud providers. Its product suite includes controllers and signal-conditioning chips that integrate with various industry standards to improve data flow. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as one end customer represented over 70% of revenue in 2025, and the top three accounted for approximately 86% of revenue.
In 2025, revenue reached $852.5 million, up 115% compared with the prior fiscal year. The company reported a net income of roughly $219 million, resulting in a net margin of close to 26%, representing a significant improvement over the net loss recorded in the previous year among semiconductor stocks.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0x, indicating the company holds no debt relative to its shareholder equity. A current ratio of 10.2x measures the ability to pay short-term obligations, suggesting a very strong liquidity position.
Free cash flow for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, was nearly $282 million. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 50% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back to cash flow.
The case for Marvell Technology
Marvell Technology serves a broad range of data infrastructure markets, including data centers, carrier networks, and enterprise networking. Data center revenue represented approximately 74% of its total net revenue in its most recent fiscal year. The company recently divested its automotive Ethernet business to Infineon Technologies on Aug. 14, 2025. It maintains significant customer concentration, with its ten largest customers accounting for roughly 82% of net revenue.
In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, revenue reached nearly $8.2 billion, reflecting year-over-year growth of nearly 42%. The company achieved a net income of approximately $2.7 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly 33%. This performance marks a notable swing toward profitability compared to the net loss reported in the prior fiscal year, driven by strong demand for cloud-based infrastructure.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity. The current ratio stands at nearly 2.0x, indicating the company has twice as many current assets as current liabilities.
Free cash flow reached roughly $1.4 billion for the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 34% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back to cash flow.
Risk profile comparison
Astera Labs faces substantial risks due to its heavy reliance on a limited number of end customers. Any decision by a major hyperscaler to shift designs or reduce purchasing would materially harm the business.
Furthermore, the company depends on a sole-source manufacturer, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, and its operations are concentrated in East Asia, creating exposure to geopolitical tensions. It also faces intense competition from larger, better-funded incumbents that may offer bundled incentives.
Marvell Technology faces uncertainty about the long-term sustainability of capital expenditures in the AI market. A significant risk is that customers may develop their own internal chips to reduce reliance on third-party silicon. The company is also frequently involved in patent litigation, which can be costly and divert management resources.
Finally, Marvell must navigate evolving export controls and trade restrictions, particularly with China, which could limit its access to key markets like those served by Nvidia.
Valuation comparison
Marvell Technology appears more conservatively valued than Astera Labs based on both earnings estimates and historical sales multiples, despite its larger market presence.
| Metric | Astera Labs | Marvell Technology |
|---|---|---|
| Forward P/E | 89.8x | 60.9x |
| P/S ratio | 51.2x | 23.7x |
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Astera Labs and Marvell are growing rapidly and reporting high profit margins. Astera might be the riskier of the two, given its customer concentration, but both are dependent on a rapidly expanding AI data center market.
Astera is growing notably faster, while Marvell trades at a lower valuation relative to sales and earnings. Still, I would lean toward Astera Labs, mainly because it is growing from a small revenue base and is clearly succeeding in capturing a large opportunity in the data center market.
Astera is positioned for strong growth over the next few years. Management noted on the recent earnings call that AI systems will feature more switching technologies to power denser chip clusters, particularly XPUs, which are expected to drive greater revenue momentum. Its Scorpio X-Series is expected to be its largest product family in the third quarter, benefiting from increasing silicon content per XPU.
Marvell could also be a solid stock to hold. It is the leader in connectivity. Management anticipates significant growth over the next three years as the market transitions to faster connection speeds, driving higher average selling prices. The company is targeting an operating margin of between 38% to 40%, which it should reach by the end of next year. Those are stellar margins on top of robust revenue growth.
Both are benefiting from the same data center tailwinds. Still, analysts expect Astera Labs to grow revenue at an annualized rate of 87% over the next two years, compared to 49% for Marvell. This should also translate to higher earnings growth. Assuming the AI data center market continues to grow rapidly, Astera Labs may offer higher long-term upside.

articles.title: Meta Unveils AI Gadgets Including Tamagotchi-Like Pendant amid Growing Concerns Over the Technology
articles.description: Meta Unveils AI Gadgets Including Tamagotchi-Like Pendant amid Growing Concerns Over the Technology People.com
articles.description_html: Meta Unveils AI Gadgets Including Tamagotchi-Like Pendant amid Growing Concerns Over the Technology  People.com
articles.article_title: Meta Unveils AI Gadgets Including Tamagotchi-Like Pendant amid Growing Concerns Over the Technology
articles.heading: Meta Unveils AI Gadgets Including Tamagotchi-Like Pendant amid Growing Concerns Over the Technology
articles.summary: Meta unveiled the Muse Charm and new VR glasses at Meta Connect on Wednesday, Sept. 23, highlighting the company’s growing focus on AI-powered technology amid broader concerns about its potential risks.
articles.content:
NEED TO KNOW
- Meta unveiled the Muse Charm, a keychain-sized AI device designed for real-time voice interaction without a phone or app on Wednesday, Sept. 23
- Mark Zuckerberg said the gadget is expected to ship in December, just in time for the holidays
- The announcement comes as Meta and the broader AI industry face growing scrutiny over the potential risks of the technology
Meta is making its AI technology smaller, more portable and more personal.
During the company’s annual Meta Connect conference on Wednesday, Sept. 23, Mark Zuckerberg unveiled the Muse Charm, a keychain-sized device that gives users access to Meta’s Muse AI through real-time voice interaction without requiring them to unlock a phone or open an app.
Zuckerberg introduced the device near the end of his presentation, describing it as a way to bring the Muse experience into a compact gadget that is always available.
“All right, we just went through a lot of products. I’ve got one more to show you because that little handheld thing that I was working on, it’s actually real,” Zuckerberg said.
Users can tap a fingerprint sensor on the corner of the device to begin talking to Muse, Zuckerberg explained. He said the charm could also allow users to show Muse what is happening around them without needing to reach for their phone.
“If you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what’s going on around you,” Zuckerberg said.
“So we’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” he said. “We’ve actually only built a few of these so far. It’s been absolutely joyful to play with so far.”
The device features a screen displaying the Muse avatar and is designed for real-time voice interaction, giving it a similar experience to a Tamagotchi.
The Muse Charm is still being finalized, with Zuckerberg noting that Meta needs to finish its materials and determine how its internal components will be arranged. He said the company plans to have it ready to ship in December, in time for the holidays.
“We are calling it Muse Charm, and we’re going to have more details to share on this one soon,” Zuckerberg said.
The gadget is part of Zuckerberg’s larger vision for Muse, which he described as eventually becoming a “personal superintelligence” used by billions of people.
Related Stories
“I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives,” he said.
Zuckerberg said Muse will include features such as goal-setting, personalized research and customizable characters and personalities. He also said each Muse will have its own private and secure computer.
Meta also unveiled new VR glasses during the event. Zuckerberg described the device as offering “a private cinema, a computer with multiple monitors and a game console in a pair of glasses,” adding that the glasses will be priced at $1,299 and are expected to ship in the spring.
The announcements come as increasingly advanced AI technology faces scrutiny over its potential risks. On Sept. 8, Jacob Coxon, a researcher who spent three years training emerging AI models at Anthropic, announced his departure from the company and warned that self-improving AI could pose an existential threat.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon wrote on social media.
Evan Hubinger, a team lead at Anthropic, responded to Coxon’s comments, writing, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger added that he personally believed there was a greater than 10% chance of that happening within the next decade.

PEOPLE reached out to Meta for comment but did not immediately hear back.

articles.title: Mayor Joe Cobb discusses potential data center at Wood Haven Technology Park
articles.description: Mayor Joe Cobb discusses potential data center at Wood Haven Technology Park WSLS
articles.description_html: Mayor Joe Cobb discusses potential data center at Wood Haven Technology Park  WSLS
articles.article_title: Mayor Joe Cobb discusses potential data center at Wood Haven Technology Park
articles.heading: Mayor Joe Cobb discusses potential data center at Wood Haven Technology Park
articles.summary: Mayor Joe Cobb sat down with 10 News to speak about the City Council’s role with the sale while attempting to address concerns some citizens may have about a potential data center coming to Roanoke County.
articles.content:
ROANOKE, Va. – Ever since the announcement of a possible data center coming to Wood Haven Technology Park in Roanoke County, residents have been sharing their concerns about it coming to their neighbors.
Mayor Joe Cobb sat down with 10 News Thursday to speak about the City Council’s role in the sale while attempting to address concerns some citizens may have.
Concerning Council’s role, Cobb said that the purchase was done in participation with multiple other committees.
“The Woodhaven Technology Park is a site that was mutually purchased through the Western Virginia Regional Industrial Facility Authority, but there are three participating committees,” Cobb said. “Roanoke City, Roanoke County and the City of Salem have different levels of ownership in that. {Around} 44% for the City of Roanoke, 44% for the County and 10-11% for the City of Salem.”
Cobb said that - for as long as he had been on council - the WVRIFA has been looking for the right company to come in and use the land at Wood Haven Technology Park to strengthen future infrastructure.
Cobb also confirmed that City Council had gotten “preliminary information” with the WVRIFA for the past couple of months about the company that would purchase the land - which a 10 News investigation revealed to be Clearview Dynamics LLC.
While the conversations between City Council and the WVRIFA were confidential, Cobb told 10 News that City Council didn’t sign a non-disclosure agreement regarding those conversations.
When asked about the potential positives of a data center, Cobb said they were attractive to companies that wish to bring their business to the area, saying that data centers are “the type of infrastructure we need here that companies are already relying on and that might help us attract additional companies.”
Cobb pointed out that this land deal could provide the city with much-needed financial flexibility and also spoke on the potential job impact it could bring.
“I’ve heard a range of things about how many employees are involved or actually hired after a center opens, and I think there’s a range of that,” Cobb said. “I’ve heard anywhere from 100 to over 500.”
However, he is also well aware of the negatives that come with data centers.
“It’s a local investment, but within that local investment, we have to be cognizant of not adding any cost burden to citizens who live in the area, address any noise issues,” Cobb said. {We need to} make sure that there are no environmental impacts and that the company is willing to take on the full cost of the energy that they’re using and water replacement.“
Cobb is hopeful that city and county officials can have constructive conversations in the future with those people.
“Much of what I have heard is very anti-data centers. I’ve not heard a lot of conversations that are constructive in terms of what you just asked me,” Cobb said. “What are the benefits? What are the drawbacks? And I think for us to make a comprehensive decision about that, we need all of that information.”
Finally, Cobb addressed rumors that another swath of land in Roanoke County could be used for a data center.
“There’s no interest in putting a data center at Old Monterey Golf Course,” Cobb said. “That’s a rumor that’s been flying around out there. There’s no truth to that whatsoever. We have other exciting opportunities for that land.”

articles.title: Connecticut Police Standards and Training Council reviews automated cameras, technology
articles.description: Connecticut Police Standards and Training Council reviews automated cameras, technology WTNH.com
articles.description_html: Connecticut Police Standards and Training Council reviews automated cameras, technology  WTNH.com
articles.article_title: Connecticut Police Standards and Training Council reviews automated cameras, technology
articles.heading: Connecticut Police Standards and Training Council reviews automated cameras, technology
articles.summary: MERIDEN, Conn. (WTNH) — The Connecticut Police Office Standards and Training Council (POSTC) is considering Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) and camera recommendations.  Last month, Gov. …
articles.content:
MERIDEN, Conn. (WTNH) — The Connecticut Police Office Standards and Training Council (POSTC) is considering Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) and camera recommendations.
Last month, Gov. Ned Lamont requested new guidance on using the technology in the state. This comes as ALPRs and other safety cameras continue to be the talk of several municipalities due to privacy and data concerns.
The five technologies mentioned at a meeting on Thursday include ALPRs, drones, police video security systems, automated traffic-enforcement safety devices and work zone control systems.
Part of the discussion was a seven-day default for ALPR retention (down from 21 days), tracking each query to know about any misuse, record preservation, local oversight, the need for a drone law and frequent audits.
“The law only required quarterly audits; POSTC decided to be more restrictive and do monthly audits,” Farmington Police Chief Paul Melanson said. “We will be looking at who’s looking at the data, what they are looking at it for, and they [will] have to have required fields so that it can be auditable data,” Farmington Police Chief Paul Melanson said.
According to officials, ALPR technology is used for crime investigations, finding missing people and wanted suspects.
A Connecticut Police Department survey showed that 16 agencies have 21-50 deployed ALPR cameras. The survey showed that 57 agencies use police drones and 34 don’t.
Sixteen agencies reported that they have an approved Automated Traffic Enforcement Safety Device(ATESD) program, while 71 said they do not.
In addition, 73 agencies reported that their ALPR reader data is stored on a cloud, and eight said it goes to local storage.
As far as vendors used for fixed ALPR’s, 39 agencies reported using Flock Safety, 24 said they use Rekor and 28 use Axon.
New laws surrounding some of the devices go into effect on Oct 1.

articles.title: More restaurants are struggling with profitability, and technology isn’t always helping
articles.description: More restaurants are struggling with profitability, and technology isn’t always helping Restaurant Business Magazine
articles.description_html: More restaurants are struggling with profitability, and technology isn’t always helping  Restaurant Business Magazine
articles.article_title: More restaurants are struggling with profitability, and technology isn’t always helping
articles.heading: More restaurants are struggling with profitability, and technology isn’t always helping
articles.summary: A third of operators have told the National Restaurant Association that they were not profitable in the first half of the year. Technology
articles.content:
A third of restaurants have told the National Restaurant Association that they were not profitable in the first half of the year, as weak traffic, particularly among low-income consumers, have kept a lid on sales.
Technology that has been all the rage in recent years has helped, but not perhaps as much as it should.
According to another association survey, 28.8% of consumers said that technology reduced corporate overhead, 27% said it reduced labor costs, and 20.4% said it reduced upfront costs.
But 28.3% said that it had no significant impact on operating costs and another 12% said that technology increased costs, meaning that around 40% of restaurant operators believe new technology hasn’t cut costs.
“There are some positives I think operators are already citing in terms of positive impacts,” Chad Moutray, chief economist for the National Restaurant Association, said at the FSTEC Conference on Thursday. Yet he noted that the percentages of people saying that technology has cut costs are “not as high as I would have expected.”
The profitability numbers do highlight some of the complexities of the current market. In his presentation at the conference, a sibling company of Restaurant Business and Nation’s Restaurant News, Moutray presented a range of seemingly conflicting bits of data.
For instance, he said, the economy is “holding up a little bit better than we kind-of give it credit for.” Moutray said that measures of the gross domestic product are expected to be “very strong” in the third quarter. According to the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, forecasters expect the economy to grow at an annual rate of 2.5% in the period, compared with 1.5% in the second quarter.
But much of that growth is coming from AI. And the economy overall is “K-shaped,” Moutray said, meaning some are doing well and others are not.
Consumer confidence has weakened this year, largely due to gas prices.
Higher-income consumers are still going out and spending a lot. Lower-income consumers, on the other hand, are dining out less often. The association expects sales to grow 4.3% so far this year, or 0.8% after accounting for menu price inflation, so the expected results are somewhat muted.
Consumers are still dining at restaurants, Moutray said. Eighty percent of consumers told the association that they visited a restaurant the previous week. But higher-income consumers were far more likely to say they went out in the past week than lower-income consumers.
And, Moutray said, 39% of consumers said they visited restaurants less in the third quarter than in the second quarter, compared with 23% who said they visited restaurants more often during the period.
Operators are worried, too. Thirty-two percent of operators told the association in April that the economy was their top challenge, more than any other concern. That is up from 25% who said the economy was their top challenge in August of last year. “Despite the stronger economy, consumers and businesses are very fragile,” Moutray said.

That is up from 25% who said the economy was their top challenge in August of last year. “Despite the stronger economy, consumers and businesses are very fragile,” Moutray said.

articles.content_html:
BRUSSELS — The EU should focus less on winning the race to build artificial intelligence and more on how to deploy it to turn around the bloc’s sluggish productivity, the European Commission's chief AI adviser told commissioners.

The technology is Europe’s best chance to accelerate growth in a range of sectors — including health, agriculture, transport, defense and manufacturing — Jim Hagemann Snabe, the EU’s new special envoy for industrial AI, told the bloc’s 27 commissioners at a Sept. 4 seminar, according to two Commission officials. They were granted anonymity to discuss the private briefing.

The EU is trying to capture the economic gains of rapidly advancing AI even as it grapples with the technology’s risks to jobs, security and society. Europe’s leaders should not worry too much about leading the development of frontier AI models, but should “be the ones who draw the greatest value from it” while managing its dangers, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her State of the Union speech last week.

Advertisement

The Commission brought Snabe in as special envoy in July to advise von der Leyen and Executive Vice President Henna Virkkunen on industrial AI and shape the EU executive’s strategy on the technology. His mandate spans the infrastructure and technologies needed to deploy AI — from data centers, computing capacity and chips to models and applications across industry.

A week before Snabe addressed the commissioners, a Commission AI expert delivered a separate seminar for the commissioners’ heads of cabinet. The Commission declined to name the expert as they are employed in a technical, not political capacity.

The message at both gatherings was to shift the debate from whether Europe can build the world’s leading AI models to how it can use the tech to drive its economy.

The seminars offered an early look at how that work is shaping the Commission’s approach.

Shift to adoption

The U.S. and China may lead in developing models and building computing capacity, the AI expert told the cabinet chiefs at their Aug. 28 seminar, but Europe can still benefit by applying AI in health care, manufacturing and public services, according to slides from the meeting seen by POLITICO. The presentation called for Europe to “invert the logic” of the debate.

That means identifying the most important uses for AI, pinpointing what is blocking them and taking targeted steps to remove those barriers, the expert said. Examples included rules to make it easier to test autonomous vehicles before mass production, secure data spaces for personalized medical treatment anda digital “farmer co-pilot” offering advice based on live farm and remote data.

Advertisement

The AI expert left the cabinet chiefs with what they called "food for thought": What could AI make possible in their portfolios that was previously too expensive or impossible? Which assumptions might no longer hold if cognitive work becomes dramatically cheaper? And how could policy promote positive outcomes while guarding against harmful ones?

AI could also help Europe accelerate the economic changes set out in Mario Draghi’s influential 2024 competitiveness report by speeding up experimentation, selection, scaling and diffusion of new ideas, the presentation said, with the expert pointing to slowing labor productivity, an aging population, weaker trade and the need to renew infrastructure as headwinds to growth. The goal is to extend the Draghi agenda from the factors of competitiveness to the speed of economic evolution, they said.

But useful applications will take time to develop. That means it must become easier for companies to experiment, grow and scale successful ideas, while ensuring Europe retains a share of the value created, rather than becoming dependent on a handful of outside providers for models, chips or computing power, both Snabe and the AI expert said.

The seminars are feeding into a broader Commission effort to turn that ambition into a plan. The Commission will until December undertake “deep work” mapping out how to use AI across different sectors. Snabe and his team will conduct sector analyses, consider pilot projects and examine the AI “tech stack” — models, chips and computing capacity — before drafting a policy package toward the end of the year. A final report and strategy should take shape in early 2027, and the team is due to examine the societal implications of the policies between January and March.

Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Snabe's Sept. 4 seminar "focused on how Europe can accelerate the uptake of industrial AI." He added that the special envoy "will deliver an evidence-based and forward-looking report on Industrial AI."

The Commission's evolving approach to AI comes as critics question whether it is keeping pace with the technology’s risks. Axel Voss, a German conservative lawmaker and von der Leyen ally, said the Commission had failed to adapt to rapid developments and was not enforcing the AI Act — the EU's law governing the risks of the technology — effectively enough. He pointed to recent hacking incidents involving AI agents and called for rules on liability when AI causes harm.

Cardinal Michael Czerny, who chairs the Vatican’s commission on AI, urged European politicians and bishops to respond more clearly to warnings that frontier models could escape human control. Czerny said he had not yet used AI himself, but felt it was his “moral duty” to gain personal experience with the technology.

September 24, 2026 – CSX has enhanced the capabilities of its Public Safety Coordination Center (PSCC) with new technology that allows callers to securely share real-time location information and live video during emergencies, making CSX the first railroad to deploy this type of system. “We’re a leader in this space, and this technology truly changes how we respond,” said Chris Bennett, director of Public Safety and Infrastructure Protection at CSX. “When we can immediately see where someone is and what they’re seeing, we eliminate guesswork, reduce stress for our operators, and enable faster, safer emergency response across the CSX network.” The PSCC serves as the critical link between CSX and public safety agencies, coordinating resources and response efforts when incidents are reported by employees, customers, or members of the community. One of the greatest challenges during emergency calls is determining a caller’s exact location, particularly when they are unfamiliar with their surroundings. The new technology helps solve that challenge by enabling PSCC operators to quickly identify a caller’s location and send a secure link that allows live video sharing from the scene. Operators can also instantly replay call recordings, translate multiple languages, and verify critical information while a call is still in progress. These capabilities provide a clearer understanding of unfolding situations and help accelerate response times. By providing better situational awareness and more accurate information, the system helps emergency responders make informed decisions when every second matters. The enhancement also improves coordination between CSX and local first responders, strengthening the company’s ability to support the communities it serves. With this investment in advanced technology, CSX continues to strengthen rail safety while helping protect employees, customers, and communities across its network.

articles.heading: Grant gives Marlboro County deputies new technology
articles.summary: Marlboro County deputies can now spend more time in the field thanks to new technology and vehicles paid for by a grant.
articles.content:
Grant gives Marlboro County deputies new technology
Sheriff says upgrades let deputies spend more time in the field
MARLBORO COUNTY, SC (WMBF) - Marlboro County deputies can now spend more time in the field thanks to new technology and vehicles paid for by a grant.
One of the biggest changes is how deputies write reports. In the past, they had to drive back to the station to finish their paperwork. Now, they can complete reports from their vehicles. That means less time driving back to the office and more time in the community.
Sheriff Larry McNeil said this is a change his department has needed for years.
“For us that’s new, for some parts, for the rest of the world it’s not new, but for us it’s new. That’s the difference. I’m standing here saying something, that a lot of other agencies have been doing for years, that we’re finally getting,” McNeil said.
Recruiting and vehicle needs
McNeil said the new technology could also help with recruiting. However, he said the department still needs more vehicles for new deputies.
“A good example of that would be, if I hired 2 people right now, I don’t have a vehicle to put them in, if that answers your question,” McNeil said.
New trucks for rural roads
The grant also provided two new trucks. McNeil said those will help deputies get around Marlboro County’s rural roads.
He said the department could still use more resources, but these upgrades are a start.
“It’s not that we’re not trying to get them, it’s just that it’s tough. Funding right now economically is tough for us. So these vehicles are coming at a good time and I know that,” McNeil said.
McNeil said the goal is to keep deputies out in the county and more available when people need them.

articles.content_html:
Grant gives Marlboro County deputies new technology

Sheriff says upgrades let deputies spend more time in the field

MARLBORO COUNTY, SC (WMBF) - Marlboro County deputies can now spend more time in the field thanks to new technology and vehicles paid for by a grant.

One of the biggest changes is how deputies write reports. In the past, they had to drive back to the station to finish their paperwork. Now, they can complete reports from their vehicles. That means less time driving back to the office and more time in the community.

Sheriff Larry McNeil said this is a change his department has needed for years.

“For us that’s new, for some parts, for the rest of the world it’s not new, but for us it’s new. That’s the difference. I’m standing here saying something, that a lot of other agencies have been doing for years, that we’re finally getting,” McNeil said.

Recruiting and vehicle needs

McNeil said the new technology could also help with recruiting. However, he said the department still needs more vehicles for new deputies.

“A good example of that would be, if I hired 2 people right now, I don’t have a vehicle to put them in, if that answers your question,” McNeil said.

New trucks for rural roads

The grant also provided two new trucks. McNeil said those will help deputies get around Marlboro County’s rural roads.

He said the department could still use more resources, but these upgrades are a start.

“It’s not that we’re not trying to get them, it’s just that it’s tough. Funding right now economically is tough for us. So these vehicles are coming at a good time and I know that,” McNeil said.

McNeil said the goal is to keep deputies out in the county and more available when people need them.

articles.title: UCF to Name School of Data, Mathematical and Statistical Sciences in Honor of Technology Pioneer, Alumna Yvette Kanouff
articles.description: UCF to Name School of Data, Mathematical and Statistical Sciences in Honor of Technology Pioneer, Alumna Yvette Kanouff University of Central Florida
articles.description_html: UCF to Name School of Data, Mathematical and Statistical Sciences in Honor of Technology Pioneer, Alumna Yvette Kanouff  University of Central Florida
articles.source: University of Central Florida News | UCF Today
articles.article_title: UCF to Name School of Data, Mathematical and Statistical Sciences in Honor of Technology Pioneer, Alumna Yvette Kanouff
articles.heading: UCF to Name School of Data, Mathematical and Statistical Sciences in Honor of Technology Pioneer, Alumna Yvette Kanouff
articles.summary: She transformed her own UCF mathematics education into a career of technological innovation. Now she is investing in the students who will use mathematics and adjacent technologies to create what comes next.
articles.content:
Yvette Kanouff wants UCF students to recognize the possibilities within themselves. Now, her name will become part of the place where generations of Knights turn those possibilities into discoveries.
On Thursday, Sept. 24, the University of Central Florida Board of Trustees approved renaming the UCF School of Data, Mathematical and Statistical Sciences to the Dr. Yvette Kanouff School of Data, Mathematical and Statistical Sciences. The renaming initiative was the in honor of a transformational gift Kanouff — a highly successful leader in mathematics and technology — made to UCF and establishes the school as one of the very few named mathematical schools in the United States.
Kanouff’s investment also establishes an endowed fund that will help advance UCF’s mission of expanding student success and maximizing excellence. The fund will support outstanding graduate students, expand scholarships that increase access and achievement, and recognize excellence in teaching and research among students, faculty and postdoctoral fellows across the school, which is in the College of Sciences.
Creating Paths to Success
Kanouff says she believes everyone can contribute to UCF student success, whether through mentoring, professional connections, volunteer service or financial support.
“I want our students and future students to know that what I’m investing in is them,” Kanouff says. “I want them and their children to have an amazing opportunity at a college that is able to fully develop their capabilities and talents.”
Her gift reflects a belief shared by many supporters of UCF’s Go For Launch campaign: that investing in students creates opportunities that extend far beyond graduation and strengthens the university’s impact for generations to come.
Kanouff knows firsthand how any financial assistance can help make a student’s college journey easier, which she says the new endowment and school name will help promote. Kanouff worked to pay for her studies while earning her bachelor’s and master’s degrees in mathematics at UCF. At the time, she says she did not understand how scholarships worked or what financial assistance might have been available. From this personal experience she knows there are students who have the ability and determination to succeed but they may not know where to find help.
“If you have the skill and you have the grit, there should be a path for you to have a wonderful career,” Kanouff says.
A Foundation for What Comes Next
In addition to access to opportunities funded by philanthropy, Kanouff says that students should seek out their professors and maintain lifelong relationships with them whenever possible.
When Kanouff was in graduate school at the College of Sciences, she chose a challenging topic on wavelets and their application to digital signal processing and centroids for her master’s thesis. She selected Ahmed Zayed, the former associate chair for graduate studies in UCF’s College of Sciences, as her advisor. Zayed became her “thesis father,” a term that reflected the lifelong commitment he made to mentoring her. The two have remained close ever since.
Zayed encouraged Kanouff to pursue a doctorate in mathematics, but her career ultimately took her in another direction. In 2025, UCF recognized her many contributions to mathematics, data science and technology by awarding her an honorary Doctor of Science. Zayed, now at DePaul University, traveled from Chicago to attend the ceremony.
“That relationship was something really, really special,” Kanouff says, “And that is something most students don’t have.”
In addition to lifelong friends and mentors, UCF gave Kanouff a strong foundation in mathematics. She began her career as a mathematician in the defense industry, applying pattern-recognition algorithms she had learned at UCF. She later carried that foundation into technology and other emerging fields, discovering how mathematical principles could be applied across industries and disciplines.
Over the years, Kanouff has often visited the campus to see how her professors were doing and occasionally taught a calculus class as a guest lecturer. When speaking with students, she often shares some of the emerging technologies that require the advanced math skills they are learning.
Kanouff points to artificial intelligence as one example of how mathematics drives emerging technology. AI systems rely on mathematical concepts such as pattern recognition, clustering, and association.
“People look at AI and think computer science,” Kanouff says. “I love computer science, but guess what else you have to take? You have to take data science and math and statistics.”
Expanding What’s Possible
Through Go For Launch: The Campaign for UCF’s Next Mission, Knights like Yvette Kanouff are helping UCF expand student success, fuel discovery and build a future the world has only begun to imagine. Join the mission at goforlaunch.ucf.edu.
That sense of possibility that Kanouff foresees reflects the vision behind UCF’s Go For Launch campaign and will shape the newly named school, bringing mathematics, statistics and data science together to help students understand complex problems and contribute across disciplines and industries.
“Yvette’s relationship with UCF demonstrates what can happen when graduates remain connected and invest in those who follow,” says Rod Grabowski, senior vice president for advancement and partnerships at UCF and CEO of the UCF Foundation Inc. “Her generosity advances the vision of Go For Launch by expanding opportunity for students, strengthening academic excellence and inspiring others to help build what comes next.”
Kanouff says she believes creating those possibilities is not the university’s responsibility alone. Alumni, friends and industry partners can strengthen students’ paths in large and small ways by staying connected, sharing their experience, mentoring or contributing to scholarships.
“Mathematics teaches us how to solve complex problems, but supporting students helps create opportunities for them,” Kanouff says. “Whether we give money, time, mentorship or opportunity, each of us can help a student see a path forward.”

articles.title: Olympic field hockey turf technology makes U.S. debut at SU
articles.description: Olympic field hockey turf technology makes U.S. debut at SU spectrumlocalnews.com
articles.description_html: Olympic field hockey turf technology makes U.S. debut at SU  spectrumlocalnews.com
articles.article_title: Olympic field hockey turf technology makes U.S. debut at SU
articles.heading: Olympic field hockey turf technology makes U.S. debut at SU
articles.summary: Syracuse University's new blue turf uses sugar cane-based materials and technology used to reduce heat, friction and water use.
articles.content:
A bright blue field in Syracuse is offering an early look at technology being developed for one of the field hockey's biggest stages.
Syracuse University field hockey is the first program in the United States to play on AstroTurf’s newest hockey surface, a prototype that is part of the company’s development for the 2028 Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles.
The Orange spent the first five games of the season on the road, but on Friday, SU finally returned to J.S. Coyne Stadium, where a major change awaited them.
The previous AstroTurf dated back to 2016. This summer, crews removed the old surface and transformed Coyne from green to blue. But the change goes far beyond color.
The new Poligras LA blue turf features CoolPlus technology designed to reduce friction, surface heat and water use. It uses more than 70% sugar cane-based material in a dual-yarn structure that had proven successful at the 2026 Hockey World Cup.
“[With] technology, every year something expands,” Syracuse field hockey head coach Lynn Farquhar said. “The speed of the surface is really important for us, [as well as] the ability to use water but not overdo it. We’re looking at the best in the world.”
Performance testing and player feedback will help AstroTurf continue developing the surface ahead of the Los Angeles Games.
For Syracuse, the upgrade also marks the next chapter at a stadium tied closely to the program’s history. The previous turf was installed after the Orange won the 2015 NCAA Tournament.
"Ironically, we had our national championship team back last season, and that’s where it kind of all clicked where, it was just time,” Farquhar said. “So here we are, looking for another elite surface for a program that has a quest for championships and hockey beyond Syracuse."
The Orange had plenty of time to anticipate their first chance to play on the bright blue field. SU opened its season with five consecutive games away from home, its longest season-opening road stretch since 1993. That wait ended Friday against UMass Lowell.
“I’m pumped, I’m honored, I’m excited,” Syracuse forward Aubrey Turner said before the home opener. “My heart’s beating super fast. I’m just really excited.”
The Orange rang in the new surface with a 3-2 shootout victory. Syracuse hits the road to open conference play this weekend before returning home on Oct. 9 to host Louisville.
