articles.summary: A sleep support device that encourages users to record moments of their day is among the projects from Georgia Institute of Technology.
articles.content:
Sleep supporting emotional wellbeing device among projects from Georgia Institute of Technology
Dezeen School Shows: a sleep support device that encourages users to record valuable moments of their day is among the projects from students at Georgia Institute of Technology.
Also featured is a compact bike that can store groceries, and a smartphone game to help improve understanding of sustainability.
Georgia Institute of Technology
Institution: School of Industrial Design
Courses: Master in Industrial Design Project and Product Development and Innovation
Tutors: Leila Aflatoony, EunSook Kwon, Herb Velazquez, Wayne Li, HyunJoo Oh and Kevin Shankwiler
School statement:
"The School of Industrial Design at Georgia Tech prepares students to address complex societal and innovation challenges through the integration of design, research and technology.
"As one of the world's leading research universities, we view industrial design as a discipline that generates knowledge and creates solutions.
"Our students and faculty explore the relationships among people, technology, society and business, using research to inform innovation and improve lives.
"Through collaboration across disciplines, students learn to navigate complexity and create solutions that are technically feasible and socially meaningful.
"Our programmes combine the creative foundations of design with research, technological fluency and interdisciplinary collaboration. Students learn to understand human needs, translate insights into action and develop meaningful solutions.
"The School of Industrial Design offers bachelor's and master's degrees, and our new PhD in integrated design and computing. Our programmes are recognised as human-centred technology design STEM degrees.
"The inherently interdisciplinary nature of design thinking and design research, combined with students' diverse academic and professional backgrounds, creates an educationally rich environment of interdisciplinary collaboration.
"Our curriculum fortifies the designer's role in humanising connections between people and technology, with a focus on the areas of interaction design, healthcare design, service design, product design and user-experience research."
Fresh! Bicycle by Aiden Soriano, Futa Kakinuma, Han Zheng, Leif Horn and Vu Ly
"The Fresh! Bicycle is a novel electric bicycle that transforms into a shopping platform.
"By enabling the bike to fold to nearly half its size, we address the issue of excessive lateral space when parked. This compact form makes Fresh! easier to store, park and navigate within tight urban environments.
"Fresh! streamlines shopping into a simple in-and-out experience. Instead of leaving products exposed, the bike keeps groceries safe, visible and directly in front of the rider.
"Fresh! affords freedom to move between stores or to a picnic without constantly loading and unloading items, expanding use beyond a single grocery trip."
Students: Aiden Soriano, Futa Kakinuma, Han Zheng, Leif Horn and Vu Ly
Course: Product Development and Innovation Studio II
Tutor: Kevin Shankwiler
Ducati Pen by Vu Ly
"'In lightness, my strength,' is Ducati's motto, embodying its relentless pursuit of style, sophistication and performance.
"The Ducati Trio Draft translates superbike architecture into an advanced three-in-one multi-pen and pencil."
Student: Vu Ly
Course: Product Development and Innovation Studio I
Tutor: Kevin Shankwiler
Mobster Wet/Dry Vac for Ridgid by Yhali Sheba
"The Mobster Wet/Dry Vacuum for Ridgid presents a unique and innovative 'upside-down' concept for job site cleaning.
"By moving the motor to the bottom of the unit, the drum can be modularised to fit varying capacities.
"Additionally, the Mobster has a trash hatch on the lid, allowing workers to toss in debris that may be too big for a vacuum hose to handle."
Student: Yhali Sheba
Course: Product Development and Innovation Studio I
Tutor: Kevin Shankwiler
Cadence Bicycle by Aisling Mahony, Estelle Cole, Serena McGuinn and Yhali Sheba
"Cadence is an electrically-assisted shared-use bicycle that incorporates music to build community.
"With an adaptive digital audio system, it allows you to mix music with friends and other bikers as you ride. Cadence transforms the experience of bike rental, taking it from transportation to a journey riders look forward to.
"Additionally, Cadence enables ride adaptability with the inclusion of a rear seat and fold-down footrest, allowing riders to use the bike beyond their ride during standstill moments and retaining it throughout the whole trip."
Students: Aisling Mahony, Estelle Cole, Serena McGuinn and Yhali Sheba
Course: Product Development and Innovation Studio II
Tutor: Kevin Shankwiler
Pik Bicycle by Arya Deshmukh, Cierra Langer, Kesiah Munyaruganda and Mia Wood
"The Pik Bicycle began as an exploration of shared mobility and became an argument for belonging. By treating the bike as a canvas rather than a commodity, we designed a system that adapts to people, stories and cities in motion.
"This project shows that shared transportation doesn't have to feel anonymous.
"Pik is built around choice and adaptability, reflecting how riders pick their mode – solo, shared or cargo – while the lighting system enables personal expression.
"Combined with ride documentation, the brand turns each trip into a personal and memorable experience. Your Pik is a piece of you."
Students: Arya Deshmukh, Cierra Langer, Kesiah Munyaruganda and Mia Wood
Course: Product Development and Innovation Studio II
Tutor: Kevin Shankwiler
Scrapling by Feiyang Liu
"Scrapling is a hybrid mobile game designed to help people understand sustainability through everyday interaction.
"The core concept centres on by-product circulation – the idea that materials often considered waste in production systems still hold value and potential.
"In the game, industrial by-products are personified as collectable characters called Scraplings. Each Scrapling represents a real-world by-product (e.g., wood residue, fly ash, whey) and interacts with the player through short dialogue-based quiz questions."
Student: Feiyang Liu
Course: Master in Industrial Design Project
Tutor: EunSook Kwon
Email: fliu358[at]gatech.edu
Oris by Vedant Kulkarni
"Oris reframes outdoor safety as a continuous, ambient layer of protection rather than a reactive tool of last resort. The device monitors movement, heart rate and location, initiating an alert sequence if prolonged inactivity is detected during a trek.
"This escalating model, progressing from haptic check-in to emergency beacon, transforms Oris from passive monitor to active guardian."
Student: Vedant Kulkarni
Course: Master in Industrial Design Project
Tutor: Herb Velazquez
Email: vkulkarni71[at]gatech.edu
Co Auronix by Yuanxiang Guo
"Co Auronix is an aftermarket control accessory for touchscreen vehicle human-machine interfaces that enables more convenient long-form audio listening and control while driving.
"Co Auronix demonstrates how a dedicated tangible interface can reduce visual demand, support safer driver behaviour and enhance the overall in-car listening experience.
"This design contributes to the broader discussion of automotive human-machine interaction by presenting an alternative to touchscreen-dominant systems, emphasising the value of tactile interaction for emerging in-car media experiences."
Student: Yuanxiang Guo
Course: Master in Industrial Design Project
Tutor: Wayne Li
Email: yuanxiangguo97[at]gmail.com
OrthoCore by Ruijie Jin
"Access to effective rehabilitation is limited by high costs, workforce shortages and insufficient therapy intensity, while existing robotic systems remain inaccessible due to their expense and complexity.
"OrthoCore presents an open-source modular rehabilitation robotics platform that integrates robotic joint modules, a guided parametric interface and customisable 3D-printed components to support personalised therapy."
Student: Ruijie Jin
Course: Master in Industrial Design Thesis
Tutor: Leila Aflatoony
Email: rjin71[at]gatech.edu
Somna by Yunhao Hua
"Somna proposes a reimagined sleep-support device as a day-night emotional anchor system that bridges daytime awareness and nighttime support.
"Rather than functioning as a passive sound masker, the system encourages users to intentionally record meaningful environmental moments during daily routines.
"These self-curated sounds are later replayed during periods of nighttime rumination, fostering a sense of familiarity, emotional grounding and continuity in lived experience.
"By transforming everyday auditory moments into personalised emotional anchors, the design supports subtle, non-clinical emotional regulation and redefines the role of sleep-aid sound devices from functional tools to experience-driven companions."
Student: Yunhao Hua
Course: Master in Industrial Design Project
Tutor: HyunJoo Oh
Email: yhua67[at]gatech.edu
Partnership content
This school show is a partnership between Dezeen and Georgia Institute of Technology. Find out more about Dezeen partnership content here.

articles.title: HHS Seeks Public Input on Wireless Technology Safety, Scientists Urge Caution
articles.description: HHS Seeks Public Input on Wireless Technology Safety, Scientists Urge Caution AIP.ORG
articles.description_html: HHS Seeks Public Input on Wireless Technology Safety, Scientists Urge Caution  AIP.ORG
articles.article_title: HHS Seeks Public Input on Wireless Technology Safety, Scientists Urge Caution
articles.heading: HHS Seeks Public Input on Wireless Technology Safety, Scientists Urge Caution
articles.summary: A call for the public to share their experiences on the health impacts of wireless technologies has raised eyebrows among scientists.
articles.content:
A cell tower on the island of Solta at sunset.

Viola Lopes / AP Images

The Department of Health and Human Services is asking scientists, clinicians, industry groups, and members of the public to weigh in on the potential health effects of electromagnetic fields and radiofrequency radiation from technologies including cell phones, Wi-Fi, wearable devices, and 5G. The request for information, published Sept. 21, will be used to examine existing safety standards and make recommendations to reduce unnecessary exposure, as well as assess the state of the science and identify priority areas for future research. The deadline to submit comments is Oct. 21.

“Wireless technologies are part of daily life, and our science must keep pace,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. in a press release, stating that the White House’s 2025 MAHA Strategy directed HHS to examine this issue, and “we are acting on that directive,” encouraging the public, as well as experts, to respond.

HHS’s focus on inviting people to share anecdotal evidence of the health effects they believe may be associated with RF/EMF exposure has drawn concern from researchers, with scientists telling FYI that such accounts should not be treated as equivalent to evidence from controlled studies and systematic reviews.

What the science says

Multiple scientific reviews and assessments, including by the World Health Organization and the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection, have concluded in the last decade that radiofrequency radiation exposure below recommended exposure limits is unlikely to cause adverse health effects. The Federal Communications Commission has said no scientific evidence establishes a causal link between wireless device use and cancer or other illnesses.

However, the WHO’s International Agency for Research on Cancer classified radiofrequency electromagnetic fields as “possibly carcinogenic to humans” in 2011 based on limited evidence suggesting cell phone users may have an increased risk of brain tumors — a designation that still stands today. An IARC advisory group recommended reevaluating this classification in 2024 to consider new human and animal cancer studies.

Organizations that have drawn links between wireless radiation and health issues, such as Children’s Health Defense, Environmental Health Trust, Environmental Health Sciences, and Tech Wellness, have all encouraged people to respond to HHS’s RFI. No scientific membership organizations appear to have publicly shared the call for comments.

The National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements told FYI that, while it does not plan to respond to this RFI, it will be providing a response to a separate request for comment from the Federal Communications Commission, which was also published this month and covers similar themes. That FCC request stems from a 2021 court ruling that ordered the agency to better explain its decision to retain its existing radiofrequency exposure limits.

Scientists question RFI’s focus on personal experiences

David Savitz, professor emeritus of epidemiology at Brown University, said that given the continued public concern about the potential health impacts of EMF exposure — particularly the relationship between radiofrequency exposure and child health outcomes — research in this area “may be of value as a service to the public even if it is unlikely to identify adverse health effects.” He does not, however, see this as a research priority “relative to many other more promising and urgent matters.” Savitz said that, for example, research on the collateral effects of digital devices, such as the mental health and behavioral effects of social media, “is a more compelling concern.”

The RFI’s focus on personal anecdotes is questionable, Savitz said, noting it is “hard to imagine how that would be helpful in addressing the scientific evidence or regulatory standards.” He continued, “If there is an interest in the public perception, a more methodical survey of such perceptions could be informative, but individual reports of health experiences is sure to elicit a very large number of anecdotal reports without any scientific value.”

Kenneth Foster, professor emeritus of bioengineering at the University of Pennsylvania, expressed concern that HHS may give anecdotal responses to the RFI undue weight in their considerations. The public should be able to comment on these issues, he said, but the evidence they provide should be synthesized into existing knowledge about the health hazards of EMF through well-conducted systematic reviews that consider the quality of the evidence.

“Making public health decisions on the basis of unfiltered, albeit very deeply felt, opinions of the public can lead to very bad advice - witness what is happening with vaccines,” Foster said.

Foster said he does not see any urgent unanswered questions about health effects from RF exposure below current safety limits. If the federal government does fund more work in this area, it should emphasize high-quality confirmatory studies rather than adding more exploratory studies to an already large and uneven literature, he said. Areas that could merit further research include electromagnetic hypersensitivity; the cognitive effects of screen time, particularly in children; and the potential hazards of brief, very high-energy radiofrequency pulses, he continued. Foster plans to respond to the RFI as a member of the IEEE Committee on Man and Radiation.

articles.article_title: Columbia College Enforces First-Of-Its-Kind Technology Ban — Here’s What We Know
articles.heading: Columbia College Enforces First-Of-Its-Kind Technology Ban — Here’s What We Know
articles.summary: Columbia College has officially banned electronic devices in all literature humanities and contemporary civilization courses.
articles.content:
Columbia College Enforces First-Of-Its-Kind Technology Ban — Here’s What We Know
Columbia College has officially banned electronic devices in all literature humanities and contemporary civilization courses.
Columbia University's undergraduate liberal arts college will make the unprecedented move beginning this fall, according to a report from the Columbia Spectator.
"I think the ban is an opportunity to make it a place of greater intentionality," said associate professor of Jewish and Israel studies, Clèmence Boulouque. "It might be a moment of 'eat your veggies,' and students might be disgruntled, but this is also what we think the humanities should set the standard for."
The new policy comes as Columbia continues to study the impact of generative AI on college students, and although the institution's music humanities department has had a device ban since 2025, this is a first-of-its-kind policy for the school's flagship first- and second-year core curriculum (Core) classes.
Why Was the Prohibition Recommended?
In Spring 2026, Boulouque, alongside English and comparative literature professor Dennis Tenen, co-chaired a faculty working group that examined AI's role in the core curriculum.
They recommended a ban after rounds of surveys with both students and faculty members.
"You can imagine valid pedagogical reasons to use technology in the classrooms, and we don't want to prevent people from doing that," said Tenen, referring to instructors who may require students to annotate a PDF as a group. "Obviously, instructors still have the freedom to use it in smart ways."
Leveling The Playing Field
Although the device ban has yet to be announced publicly, a spokesperson for Columbia College said the policy is provisional for the 2026-27 academic year and was communicated to instructors, who were also given recommended language for their class syllabi before the start of the current fall semester.
"For many years, my syllabi have included a strong encouragement not to have laptops in class," said Chloë Kitzinger, an associate professor of Slavic languages who teaches literature humanities. "I'm actually really glad to have this kind of coursewide policy now because I think it really does level the playing field."
For now, Columbia College will continue to provide accommodations for students registered with the disability services office and plans to discuss the full scope of the AI working group's recommendations with the faculty committee that governs the core curriculum.
Will Other Departments Adopt The New Policy?
According to Boulouque, it would be harder to get "Frontiers of Science," along with other science-based classes, to support the technology ban. She also noted how computer use for art humanities students made sense when tools like zoom could help them to study works of art up close.
Undergraduate writing program director Nicole Wallack warns that this program is not a "one-size-fits-all set of principles for all of its sections and instructors" as the nature of writing and the course itself vary. She also said some may believe device-free classes are identical to being AI-resistant, which is not always the case.
Others believe they are definitely linked.
Currently, Columbia offers faculty and staff free access to advanced models of Claude, ChatGPT, and Google Gemini, except for student access to Gemini within Google Docs, despite faculty concerns.
In August 2026, Columbia's law school implemented a new policy allowing students to use AI as a "learning aid"; however, it prohibits using the technology for the content they submit.
"We all know that there are Columbia students who rely on AI for assignments. Is that the kind of people we want to be when we grow up?" said Richard John, a member of the working group on AI in the Core who teaches contemporary civilization. "Is that the kind of people that we want to interact with?"
He added, "Here's a particularly egregious example: I have discussion posts, and I will ask questions in class. There are classes in which a student will actually look at an electronic device, punch in some letters, and get a discussion post answer. That's very insulting to the instructor, and we heard quite a lot about that."
At this time, Columbia joins the University of Chicago and the University of California – Berkeley as higher education institutions that have implemented some sort of technology ban for students.

articles.heading: Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: One commands massive customer contracts but bleeds cash. The other faces customer concentration but boasts superior margins.
articles.content:
- APLD -0.62%

- IREN -1.91%

- CRWV +3.72%

As the race for artificial intelligence infrastructure intensifies, investors are looking for the next big winner. Should you bet on Applied Digital (NASDAQ:APLD) or IREN (NASDAQ:IREN) for your portfolio?

Both companies are evolving from legacy crypto roots into powerhouse providers of high-performance computing and data center services. While they share a similar mission of powering the AI revolution, their contract structures and growth trajectories differ significantly. This comparison breaks down their financials and business models to help you decide which stock fits your strategy.

The case for Applied Digital

In its latest annual report, Applied Digital highlighted its design and operation of digital infrastructure for AI and cloud workloads, positioning it among tech stocks focused on North American data centers. The company primarily focuses on its AI Factory campuses, where the flagship Polaris Forge 1 site is fully contracted to CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV). Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as a single entity drives a huge portion of revenue.

In FY 2026, revenue reached nearly $611.3 million, representing growth of roughly 183.7% compared to the previous year. This massive surge was driven by the expansion of its high-performance computing segments. The company reported a net loss of close to $244.0 million, resulting in a negative net margin of approximately 39.9%, a metric that shows what percentage of revenue remains as profit after all expenses.

As of its May 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio is 4.0x, indicating the company has four dollars in current assets for every one dollar in short-term liabilities. The debt-to-equity ratio, which compares total debt to shareholder equity, is roughly 2.9x. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 245.5% of operating cash flow, meaning reported cash generation is heavily inflated by this non-cash add-back.

The case for IREN

According to its latest annual report, IREN is building next-generation data centers and AI cloud infrastructure while transitioning from legacy Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) mining. It recently secured a five-year, nearly $9.7 billion contract with Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) for data center capacity. Additionally, IREN signed a five-year cloud services agreement worth roughly $3.4 billion with Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) to support its ongoing expansion.

In FY 2026, revenue reached close to $707.0 million, which is an increase of roughly 41.1% over the prior year. The company reported a net loss of nearly $702.6 million, leading to a negative net margin of approximately 99.4%. This reflects the complex nature of transitioning between two energy-heavy business models and managing the associated growth costs.

According to its June 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 3.6x, which suggests it has sufficient short-term assets to cover its immediate obligations. The debt-to-equity ratio is close to 1.9x, showing the company uses nearly two dollars of debt for every dollar of equity. Free cash flow for the year was roughly negative $2.2 billion as the company scales its future infrastructure offerings.

Risk profile comparison

Applied Digital faces significant customer concentration, making it highly dependent on a small number of partners. It requires intensive capital and relies on frequent debt or equity financing to fund its projects. Most operations are concentrated in North Dakota, exposing the business to localized infrastructure risks and potential asset obsolescence from rapid technological shifts.

IREN struggles with financial instability, evidenced by its significant net loss in FY 2026. The transition from legacy Bitcoin mining to AI Cloud Services carries operational strain and potential regulatory scrutiny regarding energy usage. High leverage with nearly $7.98 billion in total debt and reliance on hardware suppliers like NVIDIA, Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL), and Supermicro add further layers of risk.

Valuation comparison

Applied Digital offers a lower P/S ratio based on sales over the past twelve months.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?

I'd go with IREN, though Applied Digital is doing interesting things in its own right. Applied Digital beat revenue estimates in its most recent quarter, a contract with CoreWeave provides long-term revenue visibility, and the company is building AI data center capacity at a rapid pace. For investors comfortable with early-stage risk, it is worth watching.

But IREN's transformation from Bitcoin miner to AI cloud infrastructure company is one of the more striking pivots in the market right now. It reported $4 billion in contracted annual recurring revenue for its 2026 capacity and has Microsoft as a customer. Nvidia has officially certified IREN as a reference-quality cloud provider for its most advanced chips, essentially giving it a stamp of approval that the company knows how to operate AI infrastructure at the highest level.

Both companies are losing money and spending heavily to build out infrastructure, so this is not a space for the faint of heart. But for a patient investor willing to sit through the volatility, IREN's contracted revenue base and blue chip customer relationships are a more solid foundation to build on over time.

According to its latest annual report, IREN is building next-generation data centers and AI cloud infrastructure while transitioning from legacy Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) mining. It recently secured a five-year, nearly $9.7 billion contract with Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) for data center capacity. Additionally, IREN signed a five-year cloud services agreement worth roughly $3.4 billion with Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) to support its ongoing expansion.

In FY 2026, revenue reached close to $707.0 million, which is an increase of roughly 41.1% over the prior year. The company reported a net loss of nearly $702.6 million, leading to a negative net margin of approximately 99.4%. This reflects the complex nature of transitioning between two energy-heavy business models and managing the associated growth costs.

According to its June 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 3.6x, which suggests it has sufficient short-term assets to cover its immediate obligations. The debt-to-equity ratio is close to 1.9x, showing the company uses nearly two dollars of debt for every dollar of equity. Free cash flow for the year was roughly negative $2.2 billion as the company scales its future infrastructure offerings.

Risk profile comparison

Applied Digital faces significant customer concentration, making it highly dependent on a small number of partners. It requires intensive capital and relies on frequent debt or equity financing to fund its projects. Most operations are concentrated in North Dakota, exposing the business to localized infrastructure risks and potential asset obsolescence from rapid technological shifts.

IREN struggles with financial instability, evidenced by its significant net loss in FY 2026. The transition from legacy Bitcoin mining to AI Cloud Services carries operational strain and potential regulatory scrutiny regarding energy usage. High leverage with nearly $7.98 billion in total debt and reliance on hardware suppliers like NVIDIA, Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL), and Supermicro add further layers of risk.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?

I'd go with IREN, though Applied Digital is doing interesting things in its own right. Applied Digital beat revenue estimates in its most recent quarter, a contract with CoreWeave provides long-term revenue visibility, and the company is building AI data center capacity at a rapid pace. For investors comfortable with early-stage risk, it is worth watching.

But IREN's transformation from Bitcoin miner to AI cloud infrastructure company is one of the more striking pivots in the market right now. It reported $4 billion in contracted annual recurring revenue for its 2026 capacity and has Microsoft as a customer. Nvidia has officially certified IREN as a reference-quality cloud provider for its most advanced chips, essentially giving it a stamp of approval that the company knows how to operate AI infrastructure at the highest level.

Both companies are losing money and spending heavily to build out infrastructure, so this is not a space for the faint of heart. But for a patient investor willing to sit through the volatility, IREN's contracted revenue base and blue chip customer relationships are a more solid foundation to build on over time.

articles.description: Advanced transmission projects get $1.9B in DOE funding Utility Dive
articles.description_html: Advanced transmission projects get $1.9B in DOE funding  Utility Dive
articles.article_title: Advanced transmission projects get $1.9B in DOE funding
articles.heading: Don't miss tomorrow's electric utility industry news
articles.summary: The department expects the projects will add 23 GW in grid capacity and will come online in “record time” to improve the existing transmission system.
articles.content:
The U.S. Department of Energy plans to offer $1.9 billion to help fund 31 grid-improvement projects that are expected to add 23 GW of capacity to the transmission system, it said Thursday.
DOE expects the project sponsors will reconductor or rebuild more than 1,500 miles of transmission lines and add grid-enhancing technologies across nearly 21,000 miles of transmission lines.
The funding from DOE’s Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades, or SPARK, program was enabled by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.
“These selected SPARK projects put advanced transmission technologies to work, modernizing critical infrastructure, maximizing the capacity of existing lines, and unlocking more than 20 GW of additional grid capacity,” DOE Office of Electricity Assistant Secretary Catherine Jereza said in a press release.
Instead of building new transmission corridors, which can take decades, using advanced grid technologies will deliver “massive” grid upgrades in “record time,” DOE said.
“By maximizing existing rights-of-way, the selected projects will eliminate congestion bottlenecks and avoid expensive greenfield construction — lowering operating costs to help reduce consumer electricity bills,” the department said.
In total, DOE expects project sponsors will contribute about $3.4 billion for the planned infrastructure, bringing the total spending to $5.3 billion.
The project selections grew out of a mid-March DOE solicitation that focused on grid resilience, smart grid and grid innovation programs.
Utilities DOE selected for funding include Alabama Power, Duke Energy Carolinas, Eversource Energy, Kit Carson Electric Cooperative and PPL Electric, according to a summary of the selected projects.
At least two planned projects are designed to bolster transmission links between the Eastern and Western interconnections, which currently have a limited capacity to exchange electricity.
The Colorado Energy Office is sponsoring a $1.2 billion project that would deploy advanced transmission technologies to “expand interregional transfer capability, improve system reliability, enhance operational flexibility, and strengthen grid resilience across Colorado, Texas, and neighboring regions,” according to DOE’s project summary.
And the Oklahoma Office of Management and Enterprise Services is spearheading the $832 million “Three Corners Connection” project, which aims to create a high‑capacity link between the Southwest Power Pool in Oklahoma and the Western Electricity Coordinating Council in Colorado, according to the summary.

articles.title: A new neurobiology center in Vermont aims to democratize brain-mapping technology
articles.description: A new neurobiology center in Vermont aims to democratize brain-mapping technology The Boston Globe
articles.description_html: A new neurobiology center in Vermont aims to democratize brain-mapping technology  The Boston Globe
articles.article_title: A new neurobiology center in Vermont aims to democratize brain-mapping technology - The Boston Globe
articles.heading: A new neurobiology center in Vermont aims to democratize brain-mapping technology
articles.summary: Davi Bock helped lead a landmark study mapping the brain of a fruit fly. Now he wants to expand access to the technology at new center housed at the University of Vermont.
articles.content:
BURLINGTON, Vt. — In the years since Davi Bock helped lead a team of neuroscientists to map the brain of a fruit fly, many of his peers have set their sights on ever-larger brains: those of zebrafish, mice, and even humans.
Bock has a different ambition. Rather than focus on a single complex organ, he wants to harness the technology — a massively powerful microscope and the means to process the reams of data it produces — to map many smaller structures. And he wants to make it widely available to scientists tackling their own research projects.
“It’s just that there’s so many more things to look at, and there’s so much demand across the biosciences,” said Bock, an associate professor of neurology at the University of Vermont’s Larner College of Medicine. “Let’s point this new kind of flashlight across the range of biology.”
To that end, Bock is building a national observatory here to increase access to the state-of-the-art technology. On Thursday, the University of Vermont announced it secured $19 million from the National Science Foundation to power the project.
The five-year grant will help Bock acquire the equipment and design the processes necessary to map anything from a single-celled organism to hair follicles to lungs.
“The rule in biology is that when we look at the structure of a thing, we tend to be able to have insights and form hypotheses about how the thing works,” he said.
About $16 million will go to Bock’s lab at UVM, while the remaining $3 million will fund computing work at the University of California San Diego to handle the data the microscope produces.
Kirk Dombrowski, vice president for research and innovation at the University of Vermont, called the National Science Foundation funding a boon for an institution that isn’t known for cutting-edge research infrastructure.
“We’re really excited about what this facility will be able to do for the life sciences and what we’ll be able to build around it at UVM,” he said.
The project is possible, Dombrowski said, because Bock, a leader in the emerging field of “connectomics” — the detailed mapping of connections within a nervous system — just happens to want to live here.
Bock grew up in Vermont and was inspired to pursue a career in science while working as a lab tech at UVM. After stints at Harvard and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute in Virginia, Bock decided to move home with his young family. They now live in Glover, the tiny Northeast Kingdom town best known for hosting Bread and Puppet Theater, the leftist art collective.
“It feels good in a way to bring some of the top-shelf science that we can do now back to UVM,” Bock said.
That science was developed during the decadelong effort to create a high-resolution model of a fruit fly’s brain. Bock and his colleagues hardened the brain and then sliced it into more than 7,000 ultrathin sections. They used a high-resolution electron microscope to capture millions of images, which supercomputers turned into three-dimensional models.
The fruit fly brain was by far the most complex organ mapped at the time, involving hundreds of feet of wiring connecting hundreds of thousands of neurons. Scientists hope that by studying such systems, they might learn lessons applicable to human brains and, among other things, develop cures for nervous system disorders.
The work informed a series of landmark studies published in the journal Nature in 2024.
Now, Bock aims to use that technology to support four pilot projects at UVM’s new observatory. One involves studying how a parasite causes toxoplasmosis, a disease commonly spread through kitty litter and contaminated food. Another will compare retinal circuitry in different species to understand how visual systems navigate various environments — for example, how a shark moves through murky or clear water.
Bock expects these projects will stress-test the technology and inform how it can be used at scale in a wide range of research. That could lead to yet another round of funding to expand the capacity of the UVM observatory.
“I think it’ll be a great hub for disseminating and democratizing access to this kind of capability,” he said.
Even beyond the scientific applications, Bock said, there is an aesthetic aspect to the work — and the remarkable 3-D images it produces.
“The natural world is beautiful, and it turns out that when you look at the microscopic scale, it stays beautiful and shows you surprising and delightful things,” he said. “There’s a pleasure in seeing the unexpected and the new in this sort of micro-world that we are made out of.”
Paul Heintz can be reached at paul.heintz@globe.com. Follow him on X @paulheintz.

articles.summary: The Marlboro County Sheriff’s Office is receiving more than $868,000 in federal funding to upgrade technology
articles.content:
by Tonya Brown

The Marlboro County Sheriff’s Office is receiving more than $868,000 in federal funding for technology upgrades, aging vehicle replacements and new law enforcement equipment.

U.S. Rep. Russell Fry presented the $868,040 in funding Thursday at the sheriff’s office in Bennettsville. The money is expected to help upgrade records, dispatch and jail management systems and provide deputies with body-worn cameras and other technology.

MARLBORO COUNTY, S.C. (WPDE) — The Marlboro County Sheriff’s Office is receiving more than $868,000 in federal funding to upgrade technology, replace aging vehicles and purchase new law enforcement equipment.

U.S. Rep. Russell Fry stopped at the sheriff’s office in Bennettsville on Thursday to formally present the funding secured through Community Project Funding.

Fry’s office said the Marlboro County Sheriff’s Office will receive $868,040 for technology and equipment upgrades.

The funding is expected to help modernize records, dispatch and jail management systems, replace aging vehicles and equip deputies with body-worn cameras and other technology.

MORE: Development company to host Q & A on future of former Georgetown steel mill site

The project stems from a funding request Fry submitted for fiscal year 2025.

In Frye’s request to congressional appropriators, he said the money would be used for an emergency backup generator, police cruisers, ballistic vests, body-worn cameras and other technology upgrades.

He added the upgrades would improve communication among law enforcement agencies and strengthen efforts to combat the possession and distribution of fentanyl and other illegal drugs in Marlboro County.

In his funding request, Fry described the project as an appropriate use of taxpayer money because of its potential to improve technology integration and communication among agencies.

The funding is part of federal money secured for community projects in South Carolina’s 7th Congressional District.

articles.heading: Black Book Announces Top Medical Group Technology and Services Vendors as Physician Practices Accelerate 2027 Technology, AI and Outsourcing Decisions
articles.summary: Pre-MGMA attendee survey finds staffing pressure, payer administration, fragmented technology and demand for measurable ROI reshaping purchasing priorities for independent and corporate-owned medical groups
articles.content:
Black Book Announces Top Medical Group Technology and Services Vendors as Physician Practices Accelerate 2027 Technology, AI and Outsourcing Decisions
Pre-MGMA attendee survey finds staffing pressure, payer administration, fragmented technology and demand for measurable ROI reshaping purchasing priorities for independent and corporate-owned medical groups
San Antonio, TX, September 24, 2026 (Newswire.com) - Physician practices, medical groups and ambulatory organizations are entering 2027 with a more urgent technology agenda centered on reducing administrative labor, improving revenue-cycle performance, consolidating fragmented workflows and determining where artificial intelligence and outsourcing can produce measurable operating gains, according to new Black Book Research findings released ahead of the MGMA Annual Conference, September 27-30 in San Antonio.
Black Book is also announcing and reintroducing its highest client-rated medical group technology, software and services categories for 2026 while completing a new series of 2027 Medical Group Practice Technology Client Satisfaction Awards covering emerging physician-enterprise priorities including value-based care technology and outsourcing, outsourced practice management, AI-enabled practice operations and technology-enabled administrative services.
The combined findings are designed to provide physician executives, practice administrators, MSOs, independent groups and corporate-owned practices with a clearer view of where their peers are directing technology and operating investments entering 2027.
Medical Groups Enter 2027 Under Intensifying Operational Pressure
In a September 2026 Black Book preconference flash survey of 1,184 physician-practice executives, administrators, finance leaders and technology decision-makers, respondents identified staffing constraints and payer-related administrative work as the two most immediate operating challenges affecting technology decisions.
Among the nearly eleven hundred unique Medical Practice respondents:
- 82% cited staffing shortages, labor costs or difficulty maintaining experienced administrative teams as a major operational concern.
- 89% identified payer administrative requirements, prior authorization, reimbursement complexity or claims follow-up among their most significant sources of avoidable work.
- 94% reported rising operating expenses without comparable growth in reimbursement.
- 91% identified denials, payment delays or revenue-cycle productivity as a 2027 improvement priority.
- 58% said disconnected systems, duplicate entry or weak integration between applications continue to create material staff inefficiency.
- 72% reported that recruiting and retaining qualified revenue-cycle, billing, scheduling or administrative personnel has become more difficult during the past 12 months.
- 79% identified cybersecurity, technology resilience or third-party technology risk as an increased executive concern.
The findings suggest that technology selection is becoming less centered on feature expansion and more focused on whether a product or service eliminates work that practices can no longer afford to perform manually.
"The technology conversation in medical groups has shifted from what a system can do to what work the organization can actually stop doing after it is implemented," said Doug Brown, Founder of Black Book Research. "Practices are facing simultaneous labor, reimbursement and administrative pressures. The technology or outsourcing investment that matters in 2027 is the one that produces a measurable operational result."
What Medical Groups Expect to Buy in 2027
Technology spending intentions remain strong, but Black Book found purchasing priorities increasingly concentrated around applications with identifiable labor, cash-flow or patient-access effects.
Among organizations planning significant technology or outsourcing investments through 2027:
- 70% expect to acquire, expand or replace revenue-cycle automation, billing or claims-management capabilities, with either software or outsourced services.
- 32% are evaluating AI-enabled administrative or clinical workflow applications.
- 37% are prioritizing patient access, scheduling, digital intake or patient communication technology.
- 41% expect new investments in value-based care technology, analytics or outsourced VBC support.
- 78% are reviewing cybersecurity, managed IT or infrastructure services.
- 16% are considering additional outsourced administrative or revenue-cycle functions.
- 13% are evaluating provider workflow, documentation or specialty clinical-system improvements.
- 19% expect to add or expand analytics, financial intelligence or practice-performance management capabilities.
- 11% anticipate a major practice-management or EHR replacement evaluation.
Artificial intelligence has moved rapidly onto physician-practice purchasing agendas, but respondents remain selective. 96% of AI evaluators within medical groups said integration with existing EHR, practice-management and revenue-cycle systems will be a major buying criterion, while 89% said they will require a defined operational or financial performance measure before expanding an AI implementation.
Purchasing Timetables Are Compressing for High-Priority Projects
The survey also indicates that practices are moving faster on targeted automation and outsourcing projects while remaining cautious about large platform replacements.
Among organizations expecting a material technology or services purchase during the next 12 months:
17% expect to make a selection or contract decision by the end of the first quarter of 2027, 20% expect a decision during the second quarter, 33% anticipate purchasing during the late second half of 2027 and 17% remain in early evaluation without a defined acquisition date. Smaller workflow products, AI applications and outsourced services are generally moving through purchasing cycles faster than EHR or practice-management replacements.
Conversely, 78% of organizations considering replacement of a major core platform reported that their evaluation process has lengthened compared with their previous major technology purchase, reflecting concerns about migration, implementation burden, interoperability, training and disruption to physician productivity.
Integration Has Become a Primary Technology Issue
Physician practices continue to add specialized applications, but technology fragmentation is increasingly influencing buying decisions.
Among surveyed technology decision-makers, 93% said they would favor a solution capable of working effectively with their existing technology environment over an application requiring significant additional interfaces or manual reconciliation.
The leading technology concerns entering 2027 are: interoperability and application integration; migration and implementation burden; AI governance, accuracy and human oversight; cybersecurity and third-party access; duplicate data entry and fragmented workflows; insufficient reporting across disconnected systems; vendor responsiveness and implementation resources; and the ability to quantify ROI within the first year.
70% of respondents said a documented implementation and migration approach now materially influences vendor selection, while 85% said technology proposals increasingly require a measurable first-year productivity, financial or staffing outcome.
Independent and Corporate-Owned Practices Share Priorities but Differ in Scale
Black Book found substantial overlap between independent and corporate-owned practices but differences in how technology investments are justified. Independent groups were more likely to prioritize immediate administrative labor reduction, collections improvement and simplified vendor management. Corporate-owned practices, MSO-supported groups and larger physician enterprises placed greater emphasis on standardization, centralized analytics, cybersecurity, integration across multiple locations and enterprise-wide operating visibility.
Black Book 2026 Client-Rated Medical Group Technology Leaders
Against this purchasing backdrop, Black Book is reintroducing several previously published 2026 client-satisfaction leaders relevant to physician practices and medical groups.

Black Book Announces Top Medical Group Technology and Services Vendors as Physician Practices Accelerate 2027 Technology, AI and Outsourcing Decisions

Pre-MGMA attendee survey finds staffing pressure, payer administration, fragmented technology and demand for measurable ROI reshaping purchasing priorities for independent and corporate-owned medical groups

San Antonio, TX, September 24, 2026 (Newswire.com) - Physician practices, medical groups and ambulatory organizations are entering 2027 with a more urgent technology agenda centered on reducing administrative labor, improving revenue-cycle performance, consolidating fragmented workflows and determining where artificial intelligence and outsourcing can produce measurable operating gains, according to new Black Book Research findings released ahead of the MGMA Annual Conference, September 27-30 in San Antonio.

Black Book is also announcing and reintroducing its highest client-rated medical group technology, software and services categories for 2026 while completing a new series of 2027 Medical Group Practice Technology Client Satisfaction Awards covering emerging physician-enterprise priorities including value-based care technology and outsourcing, outsourced practice management, AI-enabled practice operations and technology-enabled administrative services.

The combined findings are designed to provide physician executives, practice administrators, MSOs, independent groups and corporate-owned practices with a clearer view of where their peers are directing technology and operating investments entering 2027.

Medical Groups Enter 2027 Under Intensifying Operational Pressure

In a September 2026 Black Book preconference flash survey of 1,184 physician-practice executives, administrators, finance leaders and technology decision-makers, respondents identified staffing constraints and payer-related administrative work as the two most immediate operating challenges affecting technology decisions.

Among the nearly eleven hundred unique Medical Practice respondents:

  • 82% cited staffing shortages, labor costs or difficulty maintaining experienced administrative teams as a major operational concern.
  • 89% identified payer administrative requirements, prior authorization, reimbursement complexity or claims follow-up among their most significant sources of avoidable work.
  • 94% reported rising operating expenses without comparable growth in reimbursement.
  • 91% identified denials, payment delays or revenue-cycle productivity as a 2027 improvement priority.
  • 58% said disconnected systems, duplicate entry or weak integration between applications continue to create material staff inefficiency.
  • 72% reported that recruiting and retaining qualified revenue-cycle, billing, scheduling or administrative personnel has become more difficult during the past 12 months.
  • 79% identified cybersecurity, technology resilience or third-party technology risk as an increased executive concern.

The findings suggest that technology selection is becoming less centered on feature expansion and more focused on whether a product or service eliminates work that practices can no longer afford to perform manually.

"The technology conversation in medical groups has shifted from what a system can do to what work the organization can actually stop doing after it is implemented," said Doug Brown, Founder of Black Book Research. "Practices are facing simultaneous labor, reimbursement and administrative pressures. The technology or outsourcing investment that matters in 2027 is the one that produces a measurable operational result."

What Medical Groups Expect to Buy in 2027

Technology spending intentions remain strong, but Black Book found purchasing priorities increasingly concentrated around applications with identifiable labor, cash-flow or patient-access effects.

Among organizations planning significant technology or outsourcing investments through 2027:

  • 70% expect to acquire, expand or replace revenue-cycle automation, billing or claims-management capabilities, with either software or outsourced services.
  • 32% are evaluating AI-enabled administrative or clinical workflow applications.
  • 37% are prioritizing patient access, scheduling, digital intake or patient communication technology.
  • 41% expect new investments in value-based care technology, analytics or outsourced VBC support.
  • 78% are reviewing cybersecurity, managed IT or infrastructure services.
  • 16% are considering additional outsourced administrative or revenue-cycle functions.
  • 13% are evaluating provider workflow, documentation or specialty clinical-system improvements.
  • 19% expect to add or expand analytics, financial intelligence or practice-performance management capabilities.
  • 11% anticipate a major practice-management or EHR replacement evaluation.

Artificial intelligence has moved rapidly onto physician-practice purchasing agendas, but respondents remain selective. 96% of AI evaluators within medical groups said integration with existing EHR, practice-management and revenue-cycle systems will be a major buying criterion, while 89% said they will require a defined operational or financial performance measure before expanding an AI implementation.

Purchasing Timetables Are Compressing for High-Priority Projects

The survey also indicates that practices are moving faster on targeted automation and outsourcing projects while remaining cautious about large platform replacements.

Among organizations expecting a material technology or services purchase during the next 12 months:

17% expect to make a selection or contract decision by the end of the first quarter of 2027, 20% expect a decision during the second quarter, 33% anticipate purchasing during the late second half of 2027 and 17% remain in early evaluation without a defined acquisition date. Smaller workflow products, AI applications and outsourced services are generally moving through purchasing cycles faster than EHR or practice-management replacements.

Conversely, 78% of organizations considering replacement of a major core platform reported that their evaluation process has lengthened compared with their previous major technology purchase, reflecting concerns about migration, implementation burden, interoperability, training and disruption to physician productivity.

Integration Has Become a Primary Technology Issue

Physician practices continue to add specialized applications, but technology fragmentation is increasingly influencing buying decisions.

Among surveyed technology decision-makers, 93% said they would favor a solution capable of working effectively with their existing technology environment over an application requiring significant additional interfaces or manual reconciliation.

The leading technology concerns entering 2027 are: interoperability and application integration; migration and implementation burden; AI governance, accuracy and human oversight; cybersecurity and third-party access; duplicate data entry and fragmented workflows; insufficient reporting across disconnected systems; vendor responsiveness and implementation resources; and the ability to quantify ROI within the first year.

70% of respondents said a documented implementation and migration approach now materially influences vendor selection, while 85% said technology proposals increasingly require a measurable first-year productivity, financial or staffing outcome.

Independent and Corporate-Owned Practices Share Priorities but Differ in Scale

Black Book found substantial overlap between independent and corporate-owned practices but differences in how technology investments are justified. Independent groups were more likely to prioritize immediate administrative labor reduction, collections improvement and simplified vendor management. Corporate-owned practices, MSO-supported groups and larger physician enterprises placed greater emphasis on standardization, centralized analytics, cybersecurity, integration across multiple locations and enterprise-wide operating visibility.

articles.article_title: PLACE Adds Maxwell To Growing Mortgage Technology Stack
articles.heading: PLACE Adds Maxwell To Growing Mortgage Technology Stack
articles.summary: PLACE has acquired mortgage technology provider Maxwell, adding a platform used by more than 400 financial institutions as the real estate technology company pushes deeper into mortgage lending and the infrastructure surrounding it.
articles.content:
PLACE has acquired mortgage technology provider Maxwell, adding a platform used by more than 400 financial institutions as the real estate technology company pushes deeper into mortgage lending and the infrastructure surrounding it.
Maxwell facilitates more than $130 billion in annual transactions and touched nearly 10% of mortgage origination transactions in 2025, according to PLACE. The Denver-based fintech provides point-of-sale technology, business intelligence, fulfillment, diligence, and private-label origination services.
Maxwell becomes part of a PLACE organization that has been steadily expanding across mortgage lending, real estate services, and title — giving the company an increasingly broad position across the homebuying transaction.
“Maxwell is fundamentally aligned with the PLACE vision of a simpler, more connected real estate transaction,” PLACE CEO and co-founder Ben Kinney said. “The mortgage experience is a critical point to build trust with consumers.”
Mortgage Becomes A Bigger Piece
The acquisition follows a series of moves that have expanded PLACE's presence in mortgage and financial services.
Earlier this month, PLACE appointed former Better president and COO Chad Smith as CEO of Envoy Mortgage and president of PLACE's Mortgage and Financial Services division. PLACE said at the time that the appointment was intended to deepen Envoy's integration into its broader homeownership platform and accelerate growth of its mortgage business.
Envoy is a full-service national mortgage lender. PLACE has said its broader platform connects mortgage, real estate, title and escrow, property management, and other home services.
PLACE is already putting some of those connections in front of consumers. Its mortgage calculator, for example, was developed in collaboration with Envoy and allows consumers to connect with a mortgage professional to seek prequalification. The disclosure on the tool identifies Envoy as a PLACE affiliate while telling consumers they are not required to use the lender.
Maxwell gives PLACE another route into the mortgage business — this time through technology and services supplied to outside lenders.
Maxwell says its technology covers much of the origination process, including POS, processing, underwriting, closing, quality control, and due diligence. Its private-label operation also allows institutions to outsource mortgage origination using Maxwell's technology and nationwide infrastructure.
More Than An Acquisition
The Maxwell deal also follows PLACE's August acquisition of Radian Group's Real Estate Services business, which included due diligence, REO asset management, brokerage, and valuation services.
Radian simultaneously agreed to sell its title business to PLACE. That transaction remains subject to regulatory approvals and is expected to close in the fourth quarter.
Together, the transactions are assembling capabilities across several stages of a housing transaction: real estate, mortgage lending, mortgage technology and fulfillment, valuation, and due diligence, with title and settlement expected to join the mix if the Radian transaction closes.
For originators and lenders, that makes the Maxwell acquisition more consequential than a stand-alone fintech purchase. PLACE isn't simply adding another mortgage product to its portfolio. It is assembling businesses that operate at multiple points between finding a home and closing the financing, while simultaneously building relationships with both real estate professionals and financial institutions.
PLACE's own mortgage strategy reflects that approach. The company currently markets its lending platform to mortgage professionals around technology integration, referral relationships, compliance, marketing, and automation.
And PLACE indicated Thursday that the expansion isn't necessarily finished.
What Changes
For Maxwell's existing lender customers, the companies are emphasizing continuity.
PLACE said customers will continue receiving the same Maxwell platform and support, with no disruption to existing contracts, services, or relationships.
“The real estate market has dramatically evolved over the last 10 years since we launched Maxwell,” Maxwell CEO and co-founder John Paasonen said. “By doubling down on deeper connectivity between the real estate transaction and the mortgage transaction, under one platform, PLACE and Maxwell will enable lenders of all sizes to unlock a powerful synergy that makes consumers the center of the homeownership journey, no matter what brokerage or lender they choose.”
Maxwell has itself been expanding its technology beyond the traditional mortgage POS. In March, it launched an Encompass Automation Suite designed to automate workflows between the POS and LOS. In August, Maxwell partnered with Ardley to connect lead-generation technology with its POS, with the companies pitching the integration as a way for lenders to generate additional volume from their existing customer bases.
PLACE said Maxwell's addition will allow it to scale its financial services business and more closely connect the mortgage and real estate sides of its platform. PLACE says its existing ecosystem touched more than 100,000 real estate transactions in 2025.

articles.content:
Coast Guard R&D Center Honored for Technology, Innovation Work
The U.S. Coast Guard Research and Development Center (RDC) in New London, Conn., received the Coast Guard Unit Commendation for work spanning emerging technologies, unmanned systems, communications and search and rescue.
The award recognizes the RDC’s service from June 2023 through February 2026, a period in which its 82 military and civilian personnel executed 189 high-priority research projects and delivered 105 mission-critical products to Coast Guard operators and program offices.
Among the center’s most visible projects was the maritime integration of proliferated low-Earth orbit satellite communications. In 2023, RDC deployed the first fully functional underway Starlink terminal aboard polar icebreaker USCGC Healy (WAGB-20), including software and motion-compensation parameters enabling operation above 74 degrees north latitude. The evaluation helped drive broader deployment of broadband connectivity aboard Coast Guard cutters.
RDC also developed and fielded Counter-Uncrewed Aircraft System capabilities and conducted demonstrations integrating uncrewed air and maritime systems with operational Coast Guard assets. Trials in Caribbean trafficking corridors provided real-time intelligence to operations centers, while subsequent work examined UxS applications for northern border enforcement and reconnaissance.
Search-and-rescue research included testing the geo-fencing accuracy and over-water reliability of maritime public warning systems. Working with the U.S. Navy, RDC also conducted thermal-chamber and human-immersion trials to improve physiological data used by the Probability of Survival Decision Aid, enhancing warm-water survival-time predictions.
The center additionally developed a cloud-based R&D test environment to accelerate software prototype transition and led fleet-mix studies supporting the Coast Guard’s developing 30-year shipbuilding acquisition strategy.

articles.article_title: B.A.S.S. continues 50/50 technology format for 2027 Elite Series - Bassmaster
articles.heading: B.A.S.S. continues 50/50 technology format for 2027 Elite Series
articles.summary: BIRMINGHAM, Ala. — Following a successful debut that delivered compelling competition and strong fan engagement, B.A.S.S. announced today that the Progressive Bassmaster Elite Series will continue using the same forward-facing live sonar structure...
articles.content:
BIRMINGHAM, Ala. — Following a successful debut that delivered compelling competition and strong fan engagement, B.A.S.S. announced today that the Progressive Bassmaster Elite Series will continue using the same forward-facing live sonar structure introduced in 2026.
The 2027 season will again feature a split between tournaments in which live sonar is permitted and tournaments where live sonar is not allowed. A coin flip will determine the technology designation for each tournament on the 2027 schedule. The results will be revealed live during the Bassmaster Coin Flip Show on Tuesday, Oct. 6 at 10 a.m. CT.
In additional news, for the first time ever, the Bass Pro Shops Bassmaster Classic will also be included in the Coin Flip Show. The 2027 Classic field will be the first composed primarily of anglers who qualified under the 50/50 technology rule, making it a natural extension to apply the same format to the World Championship of Bass Fishing. One coin flip will determine the live-sonar rules for the next two Classics: If the 2027 Classic is designated a non-live-sonar event, the 2028 Classic will allow live sonar, and vice versa. This ensures consecutive Classics will showcase both styles of competition.
“The first season of the 50/50 format showed us that great competition is not defined by a particular style of fishing,” said B.A.S.S. CEO Chase Anderson. “Our anglers were challenged to demonstrate their versatility, and our fans embraced the opportunity to watch and learn from both forms of competition. Continuing the format in 2027 allows us to celebrate innovation while preserving the broad range of skills that has always defined the Bassmaster Elite Series. With the success of this structure in the Elites and because it is how our 2027 Classic contenders qualified, it was a natural fit to continue the framework and allow a coin flip to determine the format for the 2027 Classic.”
The 2026 season produced record-setting audience engagement and demonstrated the appeal of both sides of the format. Lake Guntersville, where live sonar was not permitted, was the most-viewed Elite event of the regular season, generating more than 21 million minutes viewed across B.A.S.S. digital platforms. The season finale at the St. Lawrence River, where live sonar was permitted, ranked second with more than 20 million minutes viewed.
The two events could hardly have been more different in setting, species and strategy, but fans responded enthusiastically to both. Guntersville highlighted traditional decision-making, shallow-water instincts and the ability to adapt as conditions changed. The St. Lawrence showcased the precision, boat control and interpretation of electronics utilized to locate and catch roaming smallmouth.
Together, the results reinforced the purpose of the 50/50 format: to test the complete skill set of the world’s best bass anglers while giving fans access to a wider variety of strategies and educational content.
“Fans loved both tournaments and learned from both events,” Anderson said. “That is exactly what we hoped this structure would accomplish. It created different challenges for our anglers without diminishing the excitement of the competition.”
The 2027 schedule is positioned to deliver an equally diverse test. From the vegetation and heavyweight largemouth of Lake Okeechobee and the Kissimmee Chain of Lakes to the current-driven fisheries of the Sabine and Mississippi rivers, the season will challenge anglers across dramatically different environments. Stops at Lake Fork, Lake Seminole, Santee Cooper Lakes and the Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway will add more opportunities for traditional and technology-driven approaches, while Lake St. Clair will provide a late-season smallmouth test.
Regardless of which events fall on either side of the format, the 2027 Elite Series will once again reward adaptability, decision-making and execution while giving fans two distinct ways to experience — and learn from — the highest level of professional bass fishing.
Be sure to tune in to the live Coin Flip Show on Bassmaster.com, 10 am CT on Oct. 6.

A coin flip will determine the technology designation for each tournament on the 2027 schedule. The results will be revealed live during the Bassmaster Coin Flip Show on Tuesday, Oct. 6 at 10 a.m. CT.

In additional news, for the first time ever, the Bass Pro Shops Bassmaster Classic will also be included in the Coin Flip Show. The 2027 Classic field will be the first composed primarily of anglers who qualified under the 50/50 technology rule, making it a natural extension to apply the same format to the World Championship of Bass Fishing. One coin flip will determine the live-sonar rules for the next two Classics: If the 2027 Classic is designated a non-live-sonar event, the 2028 Classic will allow live sonar, and vice versa. This ensures consecutive Classics will showcase both styles of competition.

“The first season of the 50/50 format showed us that great competition is not defined by a particular style of fishing,” said B.A.S.S. CEO Chase Anderson. “Our anglers were challenged to demonstrate their versatility, and our fans embraced the opportunity to watch and learn from both forms of competition. Continuing the format in 2027 allows us to celebrate innovation while preserving the broad range of skills that has always defined the Bassmaster Elite Series. With the success of this structure in the Elites and because it is how our 2027 Classic contenders qualified, it was a natural fit to continue the framework and allow a coin flip to determine the format for the 2027 Classic.”

The 2026 season produced record-setting audience engagement and demonstrated the appeal of both sides of the format. Lake Guntersville, where live sonar was not permitted, was the most-viewed Elite event of the regular season, generating more than 21 million minutes viewed across B.A.S.S. digital platforms. The season finale at the St. Lawrence River, where live sonar was permitted, ranked second with more than 20 million minutes viewed.

The two events could hardly have been more different in setting, species and strategy, but fans responded enthusiastically to both. Guntersville highlighted traditional decision-making, shallow-water instincts and the ability to adapt as conditions changed. The St. Lawrence showcased the precision, boat control and interpretation of electronics utilized to locate and catch roaming smallmouth.

Together, the results reinforced the purpose of the 50/50 format: to test the complete skill set of the world’s best bass anglers while giving fans access to a wider variety of strategies and educational content.

“Fans loved both tournaments and learned from both events,” Anderson said. “That is exactly what we hoped this structure would accomplish. It created different challenges for our anglers without diminishing the excitement of the competition.”

The 2027 schedule is positioned to deliver an equally diverse test. From the vegetation and heavyweight largemouth of Lake Okeechobee and the Kissimmee Chain of Lakes to the current-driven fisheries of the Sabine and Mississippi rivers, the season will challenge anglers across dramatically different environments. Stops at Lake Fork, Lake Seminole, Santee Cooper Lakes and the Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway will add more opportunities for traditional and technology-driven approaches, while Lake St. Clair will provide a late-season smallmouth test.

Regardless of which events fall on either side of the format, the 2027 Elite Series will once again reward adaptability, decision-making and execution while giving fans two distinct ways to experience — and learn from — the highest level of professional bass fishing.

Be sure to tune in to the live Coin Flip Show on Bassmaster.com, 10 am CT on Oct. 6.

articles.heading: Chinese auto companies race ahead on EV technology, achieving 5-minute ultrafast charging
articles.summary: Major Chinese auto group Geely has unveiled new ultrafast EV charging technology that can recharge a battery from 10% to 70% in just 4.5 minutes
articles.content:
Chinese auto companies race ahead on EV technology, achieving 5-minute ultrafast charging
Major Chinese auto group Geely has unveiled new ultrafast EV charging technology that can recharge a battery from 10% to 70% in just 4.5 minutes
HONG KONG -- Chinese electric vehicles’ ultrafast charging is only getting faster.
On Wednesday, Geely Auto unveiled technology that can charge an electric vehicle battery from 10% to 70% in just 4.5 minutes, a leap analysts called a significant development for the Chinese auto group.
Geely is joining the ranks of BYD, which last year overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker, as well as CATL, the world’s largest EV battery maker, both of which this year rolled out around 5-minute EV ultrafast charging.
By comparison, some of the fastest-charging EVs available in the U.S. currently can take roughly 20 minutes, analysts said.
“China is way, way, way ahead in terms of multiple players engaged in the charging competition,” said Lei Xing, an independent analyst of China's auto industry based in Amherst, Massachusetts.
Chinese automakers are seeking to eliminate the “ultimate barrier” to EV adoption – range anxiety – by narrowing the gap between EV charging and the roughly five-minute refueling experience of gasoline vehicles, explained Stephen Chan, an analyst at S&P Global Ratings.
At a launch event Wednesday, Geely Auto announced its new system that can charge an EV from 10% to 70% in 4.5 minutes, and 10% to 97% in just 8 minutes and 40 seconds.
BYD in March launched a new generation of its “blade” EV battery that it said can charge an EV from 10% to 70% in 5 minutes, and from 10% to 97% in 9 minutes. In April, CATL rolled out technology that can charge an EV from 10% to 80% in 3 minutes and 44 seconds, and from 10% to 98% in 6 minutes and 27 seconds.
Despite the breakthroughs, experts cautioned there are other obstacles.
“The real challenge is whether the battery can accept that level of current quickly and repeatedly without overheating, excessive degradation or internal bottlenecks,” said Chris Liu, a Shanghai-based senior analyst at Omdia, a technology research and advisory group.
With more than 100 domestic passenger car brands, Chinese auto makers face intense competition. Domestic car sales have fallen for months in China as automakers are exporting more cars overseas. A focus on technological advancements like ultrafast charging is a way to set themselves apart and try to improve sales.
But success will depend on factors including the scale of companies' charging network.
For one, the majority of China’s public charging stations still operate below 1 megawatt, while Geely, BYD and CATL’s ultrafast charging technologies rely on higher charging power to reach their full potential, said Chan at S&P. That means network expansions or grid updates will remain as hurdles for large-scale adoption.
Some in the industry are already taking ambitious steps. China's BYD, for instance, is targeting 20,000 superfast charging stations by the end of this year, followed by 30,000 more in 2027 and 40,000 in 2028, bringing the total to 90,000 stations by that time, according to a Deutsche Bank analysis.
Other countries including the U.S. is still behind China when it comes to ultrafast EV charging.
In the U.S., EV fast-charging sessions typically take roughly 20 to 40 minutes to charge from 10% to 80%, according to S&P, although newer models from brands like Hyundai, Kia and Porsche can reduce charging times to approximately 18 to 20 minutes under optimal conditions.
“Overall, while the battery-charging network in the U.S. is growing at a rapid pace, it is still well behind China’s ultrafast charging speeds by orders of magnitude,” said Neal Ganguli, a partner and managing director in the automotive and industrial practice at consultancy AlixPartners.
But Ganguli also believes the U.S. may not be attempting to match China’s “megawatt race” in EV charging at least in the near future, but to pursue a “more moderate” path to upgrades.
