articles.summary: How smart-home technology can calm the morning rush, helping families automate routines, reduce distractions and start the day with confidence.
articles.content:
The hour before the kids leave for school can be a scramble for even the most organized families.
Lunches are being packed. A permission slip is sitting unsigned on the kitchen counter. The dog still needs to go outside. Parents are watching the clock while mentally juggling pickup schedules, after-school activities and their own morning commute.
It's not usually one big problem that creates stress. It's dozens of small decisions competing for attention at the same time.
Did someone lock the back door? Are the lights still on upstairs? Will the house be comfortable when everyone gets home? What if I forget something important?
As families look for ways to simplify busy routines during the school year, many are turning to connected technology to automate everyday tasks and reduce some of the mental load of managing a household.
"Understanding your routine and being able to adapt to it is really important for us at ADT," said James Knox, ADT's Director of Product Management. "Our goal is to recognize when something falls outside a home's normal routine and help homeowners decide whether action is needed."
That philosophy reflects a broader shift in how families use smart-home technology. Instead of simply monitoring what happens at home, connected devices can help households prepare for the day ahead, automate recurring tasks and reduce the number of things parents need to think about before walking out the door.
Here are three ways connected technology can help make hectic mornings a little easier.
Put routine tasks on autopilot
During a busy morning, every task someone doesn't have to remember is one less thing competing for attention.
Connected-home automations can help handle many of the small actions that often become last-minute worries. Families can schedule lights to turn off after everyone leaves, automatically arm their system as the house empties or adjust temperatures before the day begins.
Using the ADT+ app, homeowners can create routines around how their family actually lives, with schedules that differ between weekdays, weekends and school breaks.
Rather than wondering whether the house was secured while rushing from school drop-off to work, parents can have confidence that those tasks happened automatically.
Stay connected without constant check-ins
Even during the morning rush, families are rarely all moving on the same schedule.
One child may leave early for band practice. A teenager might miss the bus and head back home. A grandparent could stop by while everyone is away.
Connected cameras and video doorbells can help families stay informed without requiring texts, calls or constant check-ins.
Through the ADT+ app, homeowners can receive notifications from devices such as doorbell cameras and see who's at the door from virtually anywhere. Two-way audio also allows family members to communicate with visitors or children who arrive home later in the day.
For households that regularly coordinate with trusted family members, caregivers or service providers, Trusted Neighbor† can simplify access by allowing temporary or scheduled entry directly through the ADT+ app.
The result is fewer interruptions and more visibility into what's happening at home throughout the day.
Catch the things busy mornings make easy to miss
The faster a morning moves, the easier it is to overlook something.
A garage door gets left open. A window that's normally closed remains open after everyone leaves. A routine part of the morning simply doesn't happen.
The ADT+ app's Unusual Activity Alerts feature is designed to identify activity that falls outside a home's normal patterns and draw attention to situations that may deserve a second look. Using information from connected devices such as ADT door and window sensors, the feature can help surface issues that might otherwise go unnoticed.
According to Knox, the objective isn't to create more alerts. It's to help homeowners focus on the alerts that matter most.
"The most effective smart-home experiences aren't the ones that create the most notifications," Knox said. "They're the ones that help homeowners quickly understand what matters and decide whether action is needed."
When a busy day becomes something more
Sometimes, however, a situation requires more than a notification. That's where professional monitoring provides an additional layer of support.
ADT's network of company-operated monitoring centers is staffed 24/7/365 by trained professionals who can help when alarm events occur* — whether you’re home or not.
For Knox, that's where technology and people work best together.
"Professional monitoring gives homeowners reassurance that someone is looking out for them,” Knox said. “It provides confidence that support is available when human expertise and response are needed.”
A calmer start to the day
No technology can eliminate the realities of family life. There will still be forgotten lunchboxes, last-minute schedule changes and mornings when everyone is running late.
But when fewer routine tasks require attention, families can spend less time worrying about what they may have forgotten and more time focusing on getting where they need to go.
Sometimes peace of mind doesn't come from adding more information. It comes from having fewer things to think about before the school bus arrives.
ADT products that help support busy families
- ADT Door/Window Sensor: Helps parents stay aware of doors and windows that may have been left open during a rushed morning.
- ADT Smart Light Bulb: Parents can check that lights were turned off for the day or program them to automatically turn on before family members arrive home.
- Google Nest Doorbell (wired, 3rd gen): Allows parents to see who's at the door, receive notifications, and use two-way audio to check in from virtually anywhere.
- Google Nest Learning Thermostat (4th gen): Can automatically adjust temperatures when the house is empty and before it fills up again.
Visit ADT.com to start putting together your ideal professionally installed or ADT Blu DIY security system.
† Trusted Neighbor features require professionally installed ADT system, ADT Complete (includes Nest Aware) pro monitoring plan, Google familiar face detection, ADT Base, and compatible smart lock and camera devices. Familiar face detection is not to be used as definitive identification, and is not available on Nest cameras used in Illinois. Customer is responsible to inform their trusted individuals of any dangerous conditions existing at the premises.
* Professional Monitoring Subscription Required.

Google, Pixel, Nest, Nest Aware, Nest Audio, Nest Cam, Nest Doorbell, Nest Hub, Nest Learning Thermostat, Nest Thermostat and Google Home are trademarks of Google LLC. Google Nest products and services featured are designed to make life easier and to build a helpful home and were not designed specifically for life-sustaining or safety-critical use cases. articles.title: Naperville police officer used Flock technology for stalking, records show
articles.description: Naperville police officer used Flock technology for stalking, records show Chicago Tribune
articles.description_html: Naperville police officer used Flock technology for stalking, records show  Chicago Tribune
articles.article_title: Naperville police officer used Flock technology for stalking, records show
articles.heading: Naperville police officer used Flock technology for stalking, records show
articles.summary: A Naperville police officer used Flock Safety license plate reader technology to track a girlfriend and her ex-fiance, documents show.
articles.content:
A Naperville police officer used Flock Safety license plate reader technology to track a girlfriend and her ex-fiance, according to documents obtained in a Freedom of Information Act request filed by the Naperville Sun.
Oscar Maldonado, who no longer works for the Naperville Police Department, tracked license plates for non-police-related matters hundreds of times between June 18, 2025, and Sept. 15, 2025, records show. When the department received a citizen complaint about the cameras’ misuse, an investigation was conducted.
Maldonado was placed on administrative leave while an internal investigation was done, and ultimately resigned in May prior to the conclusion of the probe, according to a statement from Naperville Police Chief Jason Arres.
Naperville police contacted the Will County sheriff’s office to conduct an independent criminal investigation, which was later turned over to the state’s attorney’s office. A representative for the prosecutor’s office said they could not confirm or deny any investigation being done by their staff.
Automated license plate readers — increasingly synonymous with Flock, though there are other brands on the market — photograph license plates and other identifiers of passing vehicles. Police officers can use the data obtained for investigations.
However, a growing number of officers in the Chicago area and across the country have been accused of searching those databases for personal reasons. Civil liberties activists say they fear law enforcement agencies could use the cameras to work with immigration officials or to surveil law-abiding citizens.
As allegations of misuse mount, police departments and lawmakers are grappling with how to prevent the cameras’ misuse.
“The Naperville Police Department has and will continue to develop strong policies and auditing procedures around these sensitive systems and hold individuals accountable for any misuse,” Arres wrote in the statement. “This is precisely the approach we took in this instance and the standard we are committed to upholding for our community going forward.”
The department updated its internal policy on automated license plate reader usage earlier this month, which now includes a new section on the auditing process. Naperville police also reported both Maldonado’s resignation and internal investigation to the Illinois Law Enforcement and Training Standards Board.
According to the documents obtained in the FOIA request, Maldonado began using Flock to track the woman and her ex-fiance shortly after entering into a relationship with the woman.
In his interrogation with the police department, Maldonado said he did not use the technology for a criminal case involving the woman or her ex-fiance but for personal reasons.
When asked why he used Flock to look up the license plates, Maldonado said it was for the safety of the woman he was seeing, himself and his family.
According to both the internal investigation and his attorney, Patty Kalkanis, there were times when Maldonado felt threatened by the ex-fiance, including multiple incidents in which the ex-fiance allegedly tracked Maldonado.
“It wasn’t our client stalking him and our client being the aggressor. We believe that … Mr. Maldonado was only trying to protect himself,” Kalkanis said.
However, the police investigation casts doubt on Maldonado’s explanation, citing instances in which Maldonado used Flock despite there being no clear threat to his own safety, his family’s or the woman he was seeing.
It also notes that despite the concerning behavior, Maldonado never reported these incidents to law enforcement. He also conceded during the interrogation that the information he obtained would have done little to no good in protecting his family as he wasn’t home.
The police’s internal report found Maldonado violated multiple department regulations, including abusing his authority and breaking the department’s code of ethics.
“(T)here is a preponderance of the evidence that shows Maldonado did commit the crime of official misconduct,” the report said. “Evidence shows that Maldonado performed acts in excess of lawful authority, being the use of FLOCK, with intent to obtain personal advantage.”
But Kalkanis disputes the claim that Maldonado’s actions rise to the level of official misconduct due to a lack of state legislative clarity regarding Flock misuse.
“This is Illinois case law and it is very clear that it is not breaking the law using Flock right now. … There is no law to have been broken. Maybe a violation of an employee manual but I think that’s about as far as it can go,” Kalkanis said.
Other criminal charges, such as stalking, could be possible. Last year, the ex-fiance filed a stalking no contact order against Maldonado, but that case was later dropped and the two agreed to enter into an order to stay away from each other, Kalkanis said.
“Any complaining witness or alleged victim can go to the state’s attorney’s office and say, ‘X, Y and Z happened so charge them’ and the state’s attorney has a job whether to proceed on their word with maybe little to no evidence or not,” she said.
When asked if Maldonado had any regrets about how he used the Flock system, Kalkanis said the only regret he may have is not informing a supervisor sooner about what was going on.
“I think that’s the only regret he has. He does not have a regret using the tools and the resources he has to protect himself and his family,” she said.
Chicago Tribune staff writers Rebecca Johnson and Lila Hempel-Edgers contributed to this report.
cstein@chicagotribune.com

articles.content:
At UN, tech chiefs urge caution in AI development
Leaders of major AI firms told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that the technology calls for heightened vigilance, with Anthropic's CEO pledging to slow down where needed to ensure the safety of new releases.
"This moment calls for extreme care," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in New York at an emergency meeting of the 15-member council.
He warned that as AI systems become more capable and autonomous, they could move faster than institutions or concentrate power into too few hands.
Altman was among industry leaders briefing the council following weeks of global headlines about the risks of uncontrollable artificial intelligence and calls for a slowdown, which have been resisted by US President Donald Trump.
"The industry must not accept too much technological risk just because the benefits are too great and important to slow down," Altman told the United Nations' top body.
He also urged governments to work with each other and the industry on decisions shaping the technology's future.
"In our history, there have been times where countries who compete and don't always like each other very much still come together for shared interests and the collective good in the face of a powerful new technology," he said.
"We believe this must be one of those times," he added.
- Slowing down -
Speaking after Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said his company understands that as AI models become more powerful, "even more stringent standards of safety will be required."
He said Anthropic aims to improve its ability to prevent misuse of the technology.
"We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Amodei said in a video feed.
"If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," Amodei added.
Other speakers included Clement Delangue of Hugging Face, which was the target of a recent cyberattack by autonomous OpenAI software.
This marked the first in a series of incidents that have raised alarm bells over the rapidly evolving technology.
In early September, Jacob Coxon, a researcher who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, decided to leave the industry and accused both companies of "gambling with our lives" in the race to develop AI models capable of self-improvement.
- 'Middle path' -
The executives' remarks come shortly before Trump is due to welcome Chinese leader Xi Jinping, hosting him for a summit where AI will be on the agenda.
On Wednesday, Altman said his company would try to walk a "middle path."
"We don't want to fall into the trap of blind optimism," but he cautioned against falling into "doomerism" too.
Yoshua Bengio, the Canadian computer scientist considered one of the founders of AI, told the Security Council that "more and more people are rightly worried about recent advances."
"We must channel that concern into productive action," he said.

At UN, tech chiefs urge caution in AI development

Leaders of major AI firms told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that the technology calls for heightened vigilance, with Anthropic's CEO pledging to slow down where needed to ensure the safety of new releases.

"This moment calls for extreme care," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in New York at an emergency meeting of the 15-member council.

He warned that as AI systems become more capable and autonomous, they could move faster than institutions or concentrate power into too few hands.

Altman was among industry leaders briefing the council following weeks of global headlines about the risks of uncontrollable artificial intelligence and calls for a slowdown, which have been resisted by US President Donald Trump.

"The industry must not accept too much technological risk just because the benefits are too great and important to slow down," Altman told the United Nations' top body.

He also urged governments to work with each other and the industry on decisions shaping the technology's future.

"In our history, there have been times where countries who compete and don't always like each other very much still come together for shared interests and the collective good in the face of a powerful new technology," he said.

"We believe this must be one of those times," he added.

- Slowing down -

Speaking after Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said his company understands that as AI models become more powerful, "even more stringent standards of safety will be required."

He said Anthropic aims to improve its ability to prevent misuse of the technology.

"We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Amodei said in a video feed.

"If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," Amodei added.

Other speakers included Clement Delangue of Hugging Face, which was the target of a recent cyberattack by autonomous OpenAI software.

This marked the first in a series of incidents that have raised alarm bells over the rapidly evolving technology.

In early September, Jacob Coxon, a researcher who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, decided to leave the industry and accused both companies of "gambling with our lives" in the race to develop AI models capable of self-improvement.

- 'Middle path' -

The executives' remarks come shortly before Trump is due to welcome Chinese leader Xi Jinping, hosting him for a summit where AI will be on the agenda.

On Wednesday, Altman said his company would try to walk a "middle path."

"We don't want to fall into the trap of blind optimism," but he cautioned against falling into "doomerism" too.

Yoshua Bengio, the Canadian computer scientist considered one of the founders of AI, told the Security Council that "more and more people are rightly worried about recent advances."

"We must channel that concern into productive action," he said.

Delangue of Hugging Face noted that while his company was targeted by AI, it also used the technology to fend off the attacks. "The world needs open-source AI more than ever to defend itself."

Altman, Amodei and several other leading AI executives have been calling for global oversight of the technology.

OpenAI has urged the United States to lead a global effort on establishing standards for AI, noting that its industry is at the technical frontier.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Tuesday that Britain would launch an effort to set up global AI standards during its 2027 G20 presidency.

France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot similarly urged joint action within the UN framework and with companies to set rules for a new era.

But diplomatic efforts could clash with the US position.

Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, said rapid advancement is not a reason to pause AI's development or constrain it with new governance structures.

Trump on Tuesday rejected international regulation of AI, calling such proposals a "globalist scheme."

articles.article_title: Prince William County, Va., Taps a New Technology Director
articles.heading: Prince William County, Va., Taps a New Technology Director
articles.summary: Duane Prophet brings more than 25 years of local gov tech experience from adjacent Prince George’s County, Md., to Prince William County, Va., as its incoming director of IT.
articles.content:
Following a national search, the county has appointed Duane Prophet as director of its Department of Information Technology. He will start Monday, taking on a job that covers many parts of the county’s technology operation, including cybersecurity, computer systems, digital services, cloud technology and newer tech.
Prophet has spent much of his career roughly 50 miles away in Prince George’s County, Md., where he rose through the organization during more than 25 years in government technology. He started as an entry-level clerk before moving into technology and leadership positions. Prophet also worked more than 13 years at Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission, an agency serving two counties.
Most recently, Prophet was Prince George’s County’s director of digital government. In 2025, he also served as acting CIO and chaired the county’s AI Task Force. He holds a bachelor’s degree in information systems management from the University of Maryland and has several professional technology certifications.
His move to Prince William County comes after Mancini resigned in February, following nearly nine years as its CIO. He left behind an IT operation that went through major changes during his time at the helm, including upgrades to its computer and communications systems, and improvements in cybersecurity and digital services.
During his tenure, Prince William County also ranked No. 1 among counties with populations from 250,000-499,999, in the Center for Digital Government’s* 2023 Digital Counties Survey.
Prophet will now take over that technology operation and continue its work, connecting with leaders on planning and modernization as the county continues to update its systems.
County Executive Chris Shorter pointed to Prophet’s experience in local government as an important part of his appointment in an announcement Tuesday and said he brings “extensive experience in using technology to strengthen government operations.”
For Prophet, the move is an opportunity to work with the county’s technology team, he said in a statement, on “resilient, innovative and customer-focused solutions” for employees and residents.
*The Center for Digital Government is part of e.Republic, Government Technology's parent company.

articles.title: Caroline Board of Supervisors approve Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center
articles.description: Caroline Board of Supervisors approve Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center Fredericksburg Free Press
articles.description_html: Caroline Board of Supervisors approve Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center  Fredericksburg Free Press
articles.article_title: Caroline Board of Supervisors approve Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center – Fredericksburg Free Press
articles.heading: Caroline Board of Supervisors approve Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center
articles.summary: Caroline Board of Supervisors approve Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center Fredericksburg Free Press
articles.content:
by

The Caroline County Board of Supervisors and community members shared varying viewpoints when it came to a proposed massive industrial park called the Carmel Technology and Enterprise Center.

During a board public hearing on Tuesday, Western Caroline District Supervisor Jeff Black expressed concerns about increased traffic along U.S. Route 1 and the fact that no end-user has been determined for the facility.

Bowling Green District Supervisor Jeff Sili doesn’t believe the road infrastructure can handle the development, while other officials were optimistic about the economic benefits and community projects that developer Luck Stone proposed in exchange for rezoning 916 acres from Rural Preservation to Industrial in the Reedy Church magisterial district.

Bishop Duane Fields Sr., pastor of Oxford Mount Zion Baptist Church, said the board’s decision should be an easy one when considering that Luck Stone is planning to facilitate the construction of a community center for his church, a waterpark at Lowe-Massie Park in the Dawn area, and provide assistance to Jericho Baptist Church, Carmel Baptist Church, and The Carmel School.

“Tonight, I’m asking this board to consider the needs of this district and the future we are creating for the next generation,” Fields said. “Some are asking you to preserve land. I’m asking you to preserve lives. Reedy Church doesn’t need to be managed into stagnation. We need help facilitating our progress.”

In the end, the board voted 4-2 to approve the rezoning as a large flock of Oxford Mount Zion members rejoiced.

Black and Sili cast the dissenting votes. Board Chair Clay Forehand (Madison District), along with Nancy Long (Port Royal District), Floyd Thomas (Mattaponi District), and Reginald Underwood (Reedy Church) voted in favor of the project.

The vote came less than a month after the county’s planning commission voted 3-1 to recommend denial , in large part because no end user has been determined. Charlie Payne, an attorney representing Luck Stone, told the planning commission in July that the vision is for a “typical industrial park” with logistics, distribution, warehousing, manufacturing, and research and development offices. At full capacity in 2031, 5.6 million square feet of building space is projected.

Caroline Director of Public Utilities Joey Schiebel said there is sufficient water for the project, and Underwood asserted that electricity isn’t a concern either.

“They need to shut the hell up, saying there’s not enough water, because that’s not true,” Underwood said. “There is enough electricity. I think utilities are there. So, stop that conversation. Let’s speak about the benefits of this project.”

Those benefits include 1,800 jobs and $15 million in annual projected revenue for the county at full buildout.

Del. Nicole Cole, D-Spotsylvania, attended the public hearing and spoke in favor of the project, citing a potential boost in tax revenue in an area that is “underserved.”

Cole said the construction of the community center and industrial park allows her to entice resources to the county because they’ll have a location in which to operate. Brian Freeman, a Caroline native who specializes in assisting people suffering from drug addiction, said the community center would help prevent childhood traumas that lead to people turning to substance abuse.

Michael Dreiling, the leader of the Virginia Economic Development Partnership Real Estate Solutions team, stressed that recruiting businesses is a lot easier when property is already zoned. Dreiling noted that the VEDP put together real-estate packages for some of the largest projects in Virginia, including L3Harris Technologies in Northern Virginia, AstraZeneca in Albemarle County, and Lego in Chesterfield County. He said large economic development projects like Luck Stone is presenting can be “transformational” for any community.

“What I’ve heard tonight is one of the best cases for the work that we do at the state level that I’ve heard in the last four and a half years that I’ve been in the role that I serve,” Dreiling said. “These opportunities are not going to properties that are not zoned. They have to be fully zoned and proffered. We have not seen a large-scale opportunity go to a single unzoned property in the last four and a half years.”

Reedy Church District resident Kevin Collins, who is planning to compete with Planning Commissioner J.D. Young for Underwood’s board of supervisors’ seat in 2027, said the project is transformational for all the wrong reasons.

“We need to step back and ask a very basic question: ‘Does this project belong here?’” Collins said. “Not whether it can be engineered, not whether roads can eventually be widened, not whether the property can technically be rezoned, but whether transforming more than 1,000 acres of rural land into a massive industrial development is appropriate for this part of the county. I believe it is not. This is not just another business park. The scale of this proposal would fundamentally change this area forever.”

The project area includes several parcels located between Jericho Road and U.S. Route 1 and along Zion Road and Oxford Road.

The supervisors voted 6-0 in August 2024 to approve the Comprehensive Plan amendment to change the land use in that area from Rural Transition to Industrial. Underwood said “nobody twisted our arm” to vote for the amendment.

Still, Black and Sili aren’t sold that the Luck Stone project is good for the area. Black cited a traffic study showing the project will increase daily trips on U.S. Route 1 from 5,500 to 14,778. He also noted that Rappahannock Electric Cooperative is moving its headquarters to the Route 1 area, that Pendleton subdivision is constantly building homes, and that it’s already difficult leaving Lake Caroline to reach the U.S. 1 highway.

“I have major concerns with Route 1 being an absolute nightmare as far as traffic is concerned,” Black said.

However, Underwood and Thomas espoused the benefits of the project, including revised proffers that include a five-mile public walking trail, a $300,000 contribution to a splash pad at Lowe-Massie Park, $100,000 to the Career and Technical Education program at Caroline High School, and the OMZBC community center to provide an outlet for youth, adults, and seniors.

Thomas said former Caroline Superintendent Stanley Jones, a deacon at OMZBC, assured him that church officials would not allow a company to take advantage of them.

“I believe Mr. Jones, and I think the biggest thing is this gives people hope,” Thomas said. “And I think hope is something we don’t have enough of right now. You heard the young lady talk about her son needing tutoring. I believe this community center will provide tutoring.

“There is also going to be a daycare there. Do you know how important it is to be able to drop your kid off somewhere safely and go to work? I know a lot of y’all are doing what I did. You’re driving up to D.C. where the good jobs are. We’re going to make it so the good jobs are here now.”
